en: {...} = [an] unclear syllable.
The first chapter, on Direct Perception (*pratyakṣapariccheda*),
composed by the noble Vinītadeva.
The *Nyāyabinduvistaraṭīkā* (*Śiṣyahitā*):
By the power of whose lineage [he stands] upon the path of pure logic.
They declare that he has attained the supreme siddhi; homage to that sage who spoke thus!

May the Nyāyabinduṭīkā composed by the teacher Dharmottara be triumphant— [the work] of the conqueror of the world, which is the cause for the cessation of the continuous stream of births and misfortunes.
The words of the Sugata, who delights in freedom from passion, bring about the thinning away of the darkness of the mind.
This is a commentary by an unknown author on the *Nyāyabinduṭīkā* composed by Ācārya Dharmottara.
For every distinguished person indeed performs a hymn of praise to their chosen deity at the commencement of a treatise.
Likewise, this noble Dharmottara, demonstrating his own adherence to virtuous conduct,
[expresses] the accumulation of merit through the praise of his chosen deity, and thereby the unimpeded completion of the treatise and its commentary.

Considering that the engagement of listeners preceded by praise generates a superior merit and thus serves the welfare of others, he began the praise of the Blessed Buddha with the words "Victorious," and so forth.
By this verse, worship is offered to the Blessed Buddha alone through hymn of praise, and not to others, because [the qualities] specified arise from him alone.

Since even a hymn of praise can bring about the fulfillment of one's own and others' welfare, [the author] first demonstrates the Blessed One’s fulfillment of his own welfare with the verse beginning "Victorious is she who destroys the calamity of birth" and ending with "Sugata," and then demonstrates the fulfillment of the welfare of others with the verse beginning "Dispelling the darkness of the mind. "Jayanti" means they achieve victory.
The connection is with the word "speech. Whose speech? He says: "of the Sugata."
In this context, the word *su* functions in the senses of "beautiful," "excess," and "non-return," because particles possess multiple meanings.

The term *sugata* means "one who has gone to a beautiful state," like one who possesses excellent conduct; it also means "one who has gone excellently," as in being perfectly complete. Since the accomplishment of all human goals is preceded by right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), that [knowledge] is now explained.
[Now,] the *Nyāyabindu* is analyzed word by word: regarding the term "correctly" (*samyak*).

By the first sentence—"The accomplishment of all human goals is preceded by correct knowledge; therefore, that [knowledge] is here explained"—the connection (*sambandha*), purpose (*prayojana*), and subject matter (*abhidheya*) of this treatise are indicated, as well as the purpose of the purpose itself.

For instance, in the absence of a connection, a purpose, and a subject matter, this treatise— beginning with the words "this treatise is preceded by right knowledge" and so forth— states the subject matter and purpose of this work,
just like a jar.
The Sugata has gone by way of non-return,
like a lamp;
of what specific nature is he?
Thus he says: "Because of the destruction of passion and the rest. Passion (*rāga*) is the first;
those for which passion is the first—namely hatred (*dveṣa*) and so forth—are the afflictions (*kleśa*), beginning with passion.
Their *arāti* is the enemy (*śatru*).
Since all afflictions (*kleśa*) have been completely incinerated by the Blessed One,
for that very reason the Blessed One is the enemy of passion and the other defilements.
For this very reason, he is the conqueror of the world—the realm of living beings within the threefold universe.
By this, his own perfection of purpose, together with its means, is shown.
Of what kind of world is he the conqueror?
Thus he says: "The calamity of birth," and so forth.
*Vyasana* means the production of misfortune.
In the phrase "the calamity (*vyasana*) in birth (*jātau*)," the locative case is used according to Pāṇini Sūtra 2.1.40.
Thus, by means of a grammatical split (*yogavibhāga*), there is a compound;
therein, it amounts to "desire," namely:
"May I become a god."
The desire "May I be a human being.
Alternatively, *vyasana* is that which is variously or in many ways endured or cast upon;
it is a general term for the means of accomplishing [one's aims].

Subsequently, there is a descriptive compound (viśeṣaṇasamāsa) of the word *jāti*: addiction (*vyasana*) is indeed [defined by] birth (*jāti*). Addiction is qualified by birth; therefore, because the word *jāti* functions as the qualifier, it is placed first in the compound.
The "continuity" (*prabandha*) of the calamity of birth is its stream (*pravāha*); its "production" (*prasūti*) is its generation (*prasava*), that is, its arising (*utpatti*).
Its "cause" (*hetu*) is its reason (*kāraṇa*).
"Of him, the conqueror of that world"—
this is the collective meaning therein: because the Blessed One has gone by means of excellence and so forth,
for that very reason he is the enemy of passion and the like.
Since he has utterly consumed the afflictions, he is therefore the conqueror of the world.
Of what kind of words do they say he conquers?
To this he says: "The darkness of the mind," and so forth.
Of the mind—that is, of conceptual cognition (*vikalpavijñāna*). Craving and ignorance are indeed darkness.
By virtue of being "darkness," it does not function as an obstruction like physical gloom or a wall that blocks objects such as pots.
*Tānava* is the state of being thin (*tanu*). The suffix *aṇ* is applied according to Pāṇini Sūtra 5.1.131, *igantācca laghupūrvāt*.
Thus, *tānava* refers to the attenuation of the mind within darkness.

Alternatively, this should be understood as a genitive compound (ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa) meaning "the crushing of speech. The words of the Sugata—consisting of the Sūtra, Abhidharma, and Vinaya—which bring about the thinning away (*tānava*) of the darkness of the mind, that is, which render it subtle for all people through the sequence of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, are victorious.
Furthermore, their victory is characterized by the overcoming of the treatises of the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*).

Since in the teaching of the Blessed One the means is specified as being determined by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and the means characterized by liberation is also taught— and since their scripture lacks such valid cognition regarding both the means and the goal— the words of the Blessed One alone are victorious,
not those of others; this is the praise of the Blessed One.
With the words "by right knowledge" (*samyagjñāna*) and so forth, he refutes the explanation of Vinītadeva;
for the purpose belongs only to the subject matter (*abhidheya*), and it would not follow [the purpose] of those who are approaching [the goal].
Consequently, what is to be explained here?
To dispel this doubt, the subject matter (*abhidheya*) has been stated; to dispel the doubt regarding the absence of a result (*phala*), the purpose (*prayojana*) has been stated;
and to dispel the doubt regarding the absence of a means (*upāya*), the relationship (*sambandha*) has been stated.
Therefore, the connection and other elements were stated for the purpose of increasing the listener's enthusiasm.
In that context, by the phrase "that is explained," both the subject matter and the purpose are stated directly;
however, the connection is established by implication.

And this is the capacity [of the treatise] therein: because the treatise is commenced for the purpose of establishing right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), it is shown by implication that the treatise itself is indeed the means (*upāya*); otherwise, if it were not the means, for what purpose would it be commenced?
Therefore, the connection is established by implication.
In this context, "right knowledge" (samyagjñāna) is the subject matter;
the purpose is the thorough understanding of right knowledge.
Since this treatise is composed for the purpose of explaining that right knowledge through such an understanding, this work serves as the means of establishing that subject matter.
Therefore, the relationship between this treatise and its purpose is characterized by that of the means and the end. And thus, from hearing this treatise,
the nature of right knowledge is understood through its non-delusiveness.

Therefore, the established position is that the context consists of the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) and the thorough comprehension of right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), both of which are to be accomplished by means of an expedient (*upāya*).
Furthermore, this relationship characterized as the goal and the means is precisely one characterized as cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇa*).
And thus, the process is the means of accomplishment and the result is that which is to be accomplished; the process is the cause and the result is the effect.
Therefore, it is established that this treatise is commenced for the purpose of thoroughly understanding right knowledge.
Now, even though this is the case,
if someone were to ask: "What is the purpose in producing right knowledge?"—
then that [production] itself would be purposeless.
This is like an investigation into the teeth of a crow;
let there be no instruction— what is the purpose of this exertion?
Therefore, he says: "The accomplishment of all human goals is preceded by right knowledge.
By this, the purpose of the purpose has been stated.
In this regard, the meaning of the sentence is as follows: since all human goals are twofold, the body of the treatise consists of two parts—word and meaning.
In this context, the purpose of a word is solely the communication of its own denotation, and nothing else;
therefore, that [purpose] is not investigated here.
Nor is it the purpose of the purpose of the treatise, which is the cultivation of right knowledge.
The accomplishment of all human goals (*sarvapuruṣārthasiddhi*) is the purpose of proficiency, which is itself the thorough comprehension of right knowledge (*samyagjñānaparijñāna*).

Since the accomplishment of all human goals is the purpose by which there would be a purpose for a purpose, it follows by implication that this [accomplishment] is stated to be the purpose of the purpose. Thus, [the objection] is refuted.
Now, why is it that the subject matter (*abhidheya*) and the purpose (*prayojana*) of the treatise are stated, but not the body (*śarīra*) and the purpose of the treatise?
To this he says: "For [the purpose] is twofold," and so forth.

Since the body of a treatise consists of two parts—the nature of the treatise itself and its subject matter—it is for this reason that the qualification "the subject matter" (*abhidheya*) is employed.
Now, one might ask: just as the purpose of the subject matter is considered, [is the purpose of the treatise not likewise to be considered?]
Why is this not considered to be the case for sound as well?
To this he says: "In that regard," and so forth;
[the phrase] "for the sake of its comprehension."
For the sake of understanding the subject matter,
"composition" refers to a specific arrangement of words;
by the word "also," the connection between meanings is likewise included.
Since the accomplishment of the goals of human life is necessarily dependent upon right knowledge once liberation has been established,
that [right knowledge] must be explained.
For that exposition arises from this treatise;
therefore, this treatise has been commenced for the purpose of explaining the necessary correct knowledge.
This is the summary of the meaning.
As for the meaning of the individual parts: "preceded by correct cognition" (*samyagjñānapūrvikā*).
Here, "correct cognition" (*samyagjñāna*) is non-discrepant cognition.
That which is non-discrepant with regard to purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) is non-erroneous.
And that alone is right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*);

otherwise, by means of this treatise, there would be a refutation of the Yogācāra system, yet the commencement of this treatise is intended to follow both the Sautrāntika and Yogācāra systems. However, if the subject matter were indeed purposeless, [the treatise would not be begun].
In that case, even the composition of words for the sake of understanding that [subject] would not be undertaken;
just as an investigation into the teeth of a crow should not be undertaken by a discerning person due to the absence of any purpose for them.
Therefore, by demonstrating the necessity of undertaking this treatise, its subject matter and purpose are stated by this [opening verse].
Since the accomplishment of all human goals is preceded by right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), this treatise is commenced for the sake of its attainment; such is the meaning of the sentence here.

Furthermore, in this context, the purpose (*prayojana*) of right knowledge—which is the subject matter (*abhidheya*) of the treatise—is stated to be the cause for the accomplishment of all human goals.
And when this matter is stated, the relationship (*sambandha*), the purpose (*prayojana*), and the subject matter (*abhidheya*) become expressed.

For instance, by saying, "Right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) conducive to human goals is to be elucidated by means of this treatise," right knowledge is the subject matter of this verbal composition, and its elucidation is the purpose.
And this treatise (*prakaraṇa*) is the means for thorough comprehension—this is what is meant.
Therefore, by the power of stating the subject matter and the purpose, the connection and other factors are implicitly stated;
however, this single sentence does not [explicitly] state the connection.
It is capable of directly stating both the subject matter and the purpose; however,
by stating one, it simultaneously demonstrates all three, both directly and by implication.
Regarding the term "examination" (parīkṣā): it is called an examination because one examines by means of it; that is to say, the treatise (śāstra) is meant.
Or, [it is so called] because one examines by means of this.
By the initial statement;
by the words "because" (*yasmāt*) and so forth, he demonstrates the meaning of the whole.
"Herein" means in the initial statement.
But surely, since the subject matter and the purpose are factors for the engagement of discerning people, as are the relationship and so forth, why are those not stated?
To this he says: "In this [work]... and so on.
The meaning is that when this subject matter (*abhidheya*) and its purpose (*prayojana*) have been stated, those other [factors] also become stated by implication.
The "subject matter alone" (*abhidheya eva*) constitutes a part (*bhāga*), a portion (*aṃśa*), of the aggregate consisting of the relationship (*sambandha*) and so forth.
The meaning is that he states its purpose.
He demonstrates this:
the purpose of the subject matter itself is indicated directly as the thing to be expressed.
However, the subject matter (*abhidheya*) and so forth were raised by the opponent as qualifiers of that [purpose],
since he did not perceive them as being primarily expressible.
The proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*) resolved this by means of their implicit presence (*sāmarthya*).
He demonstrates that three distinct meanings cannot be directly shown by a single sentence in the passage beginning with "But this is not... (na tvidam...).

However, the sentence beginning with "One [sentence], however" (*ekaṃ tu*) expresses one primary meaning while simultaneously establishing the triad of the subject matter (*abhidheya*), the derivation (*vyutpatti*), the purpose (*prayojana*), and the connection (*sambandha*) through the section beginning with "Therein, that... (*tatra tat*).
He then shows the meaning of the individual components by means of analysis (*apoddhāra*) in the passage beginning with "In that regard... (*tatra*).
But is it not for the purpose of excluding that?
Therefore, because it encompasses both systems, it should be understood that right cognition (*samyagjñāna*) is precisely non-erroneous knowledge.
That which has right cognition as its precursor is "preceded by right cognition" (*samyagjñānapūrvikā*).
This word "prior" (pūrva) refers to a cause;
because the cause is prior to the effect,
it is therefore called "prior."
The phrase "the instrument of right knowledge" is the ellipsis to be supplied.
Regarding "the accomplishment of all human goals": the goal of the person is "puruṣārtha."
By the word *artha*, "purpose" (*prayojana*) is meant; the remainder of the sense is "the purpose of a person.
And since it is both "all" and "the purpose of a person," it is called "the entire purpose of man" (*sarvapuruṣārtha*).

"All" refers to those things that are near and far, mundane and supramundane, and those objects to be abandoned, adopted, or disregarded. Among these, that which exists in a proximate location is "near," while that which exists in a remote location is "far."
The mundane is included within the midst of saṃsāra;
the supramundane, however, has transcended suffering.
That which is to be abandoned is undesirable.
Characterized by snakes, thorns, poison, colic, and so forth,
that which is desirable is to be accepted; in this context, "that" refers to garlands, sandalwood, clothing, food, and the like.
The word "purpose" (*prayojana*) refers to that which is explained [by the treatise].
Here, the purpose is considered in terms of the speaker’s activity of composing the treatise and the listener’s activity of hearing it.
For instance, all discerning persons act only after seeking the purpose of their engagement.
Therefore, for what purpose was this treatise composed by the Teacher, and for what purpose is it heard by the listeners?
Thus, when such a doubt arises, the purpose is stated to be "instruction" (*vyutpādana*).
This treatise has been composed so that the author, possessing correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), may act as an instructor for those being instructed.
And since the students, desiring instruction for themselves as directed by the teacher, listen to this treatise, the purpose of both the composition and the hearing of the treatise is instruction.
However, there is no word explicitly indicating the relationship [between the base and the suffix];
rather, that [relationship] must be understood through the very force of the context.
It is appropriate to say, "The derivation (*vyutpatti*) is being performed," but why is it expressed with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), as in "it is caused to be derived"? This is the point.
He states its fruit: "And the purpose here," and so forth.
"Here" refers to this treatise (*prakaraṇa*).
The purpose of the activity of composing and listening to the treatise is considered for both the speaker—that is, the author of the scripture—and the listener.
Since both the speaker and the listener possess the two activities of composing and listening to that treatise, why then is the purpose of those two—composing and listening—considered?
To this he says: "For instance," and so forth.
Then, with the words beginning "by the teacher," he shows the purpose of the activity of the two [the author and the listener].

Because, in this sentence—"since by this [treatise] correct knowledge is brought forth"—the instrument (*karaṇa*) for the accomplishment of the act of bringing forth (*vyutpatti*) enters into the necessity of the two activities of hearing;
and that instrument of bringing forth belongs to the author of the treatise alone and to no one else, as indicated by the causative suffix (*ṇic*).

Because correct knowledge (samyagjñāna) impels the students who are being instructed— [impelling them] with the thought, "Be instructed in the correct knowledge that has been explained"— this treatise has begun by making itself the instructor. Therefore, the purpose of the speaker's own activity of composition is instruction.
It does not apply to the vessels and so forth;
for although without them the instruction would not take place, nevertheless they are not the instructors, because they lack the capacity to instigate the disciple.

"By the disciples," and so forth. Because the disciples desire to make for themselves a mastery (vyutpatti) imparted by the teacher as their own, and because they are those who must be trained (pracicya), that treatise is heard by them; thus, the purpose of hearing is mastery.
And these two points have been established by means of the suffix -ṇic;
otherwise, the speaker’s unique activity in the process of instruction would not have been shown, nor would the students’ activity of listening.
Since everything characterized by food, drink, bedding, and seating is entirely dependent upon an instigator,
that which is contrary to the desirable and undesirable is to be disregarded;
for the cause of this great human purpose is right knowledge.

For instance, having ascertained through perception and other means of knowledge that something is a trident, poison, a thorn, and so forth, one avoids it; having ascertained a flower garland and the like, one takes it up; and one remains indifferent toward things distinct from those or others.

Indeed, by this very fact—that this treatise has been commenced by a discerning person for the purpose of generating correct knowledge—it is demonstrated that the relationship between the treatise and its purpose consists in the relation of the means and the end, and not otherwise.

Thus [it is asked]: "But surely, since even the subject matter and so forth previously mentioned are not accepted by discerning persons due to a lack of valid proof (*pramāṇa*) before hearing the treatise, what is the purpose of stating these at the beginning?"
Even when things are stated within a context that has not been heard, they are not definitively ascertained; however,
regarding the subject matter and so forth that have been spoken, even if they lack a formal means of valid cognition, doubt arises, and from that doubt, people proceed to act.
For even a doubt regarding the purpose is a factor for engagement among discerning people,
and even a doubt regarding the lack of purpose is a factor for desisting;
for this very reason, it is appropriate for the author of a treatise to state the relationship and other such elements.
It follows that when there is no injunction (*niyoga*), the students (*śiṣya*) are not prompted to act;
and those who are not prompted to act are independent.

Since independent persons do not hear [instructions] regarding a proficiency (*vyutpatti*) prompted by a teacher because they lack the desire for it, how can the purpose of the activity of hearing be considered? This is established.

But one might object: "Since the words that express [the subject matter] have already been stated by way of extracting the subject matter (*abhidheya*) and the purpose (*prayojana*), why was the word expressing the relationship (*sambandha*) not also mentioned?
To this he says: "The word for demonstrating the relationship, however," and so forth.
This very specific treatise is the means (*upāya*) because it is an easy method; according to the principle that will be explained, *vyutpādana* (the act of explaining) is the goal (*upeya*).
The relationship between the means and the goal is nothing other than the relationship between cause and effect,
and since that is already understood, it has not been explicitly stated by another word.
Thus it has been said:

“Both the treatise and its purpose [are established] by virtue of being the substratum of the connection; therefore, because it is included within the statement of those two, it is not mentioned separately from the purpose.

When the subject matter, the purpose, and so forth have been stated by such a sentence, one who considers that the engagement of authoritative persons (*prāmāṇika*) might otherwise be inconsistent raises an objection with the words beginning with “nanu” (but surely).
He thinks as follows: for one who is authoritative proceeds by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
And prior to hearing the treatise, one does not proceed toward the treatise merely because the purpose and so forth have been stated in the opening sentence.
Because the initial statement lacks authority;
and its lack of authority arises because the word has no connection with its object.
"By these" [refers to the following].
"By means of the subject matter and so forth" means by those stated at the beginning and in the sections; that is to say, by those stated at the outset of the treatise.

Regarding the phrase "In the cases mentioned," and so forth: he thinks as follows— although the opening statement is not an authoritative means (*apramāṇa*) for establishing the purpose [of the treatise], it must nevertheless be presented at the beginning of the work in order to generate doubt regarding the subject matter.

For one who seeks knowledge of reality, having heard such words from the author of the treatise and so forth, entertains doubt regarding it; and because of that doubt, he proceeds to act—this is the intended meaning.
"Therefore" means for this very reason.
Precisely because there is no doubt regarding the meaning in the opening statement,
and since activity proceeds from doubt,
it is for this very reason that the author of the treatise has established the attainment of all human goals; thus, it is the means for accomplishing all human goals.
By the word *siddhi* (accomplishment), the practitioner (*sādhaka*) is meant here.
By this, it is demonstrated that for the accomplishment of all human goals, right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) is certainly the cause.
The word *iti* [is used] because the speech of commentators can be conceived as having other purposes, such as mere playfulness.

However, regarding works composed by human authors, we perceive no purpose for stating a subject matter and so forth that is contrary [to what is actually intended] at the beginning of a treatise, nor do we perceive any motivation [for such a statement].
Therefore, in their case, doubt is appropriate.
However, if it were not stated, listeners might suspect that the subject matter of this treatise is purposeless,
like an examination of a crow’s teeth,
or that it is impossible to carry out.

Or the purpose may be undesirable, such as the instruction on the crest-jewel ornament of the serpent Takṣaka for the sake of curing fever; or the purpose may be something other than what is intended, such as the instruction on the sequence of a mother's marriages;
or there may be a means to that purpose which is even simpler than this treatise.
Or rather, the treatise itself might be suspected of being without a proper means [to its goal].
And among these various suspicions of failure, wise people do not proceed with the composition of a work even when there is a suspicion of failure regarding only one of them.
However, once the subject matter and so forth have been stated, a suspicion of success arises, which is the opposite of a suspicion of failure.
Thus, it is established that discerning persons act in such a manner;

therefore, it is appropriate to state that the connection and other factors are mentioned in order to establish the possibility of the subject matter, which is a necessary condition for the activity of discerning persons. It is logical to say this.
"Not the author of the exposition" means that by this, the statement made by someone— namely, "only the authors of expositions set forth the purpose and so forth"—
is refuted.

By the words "we perceive" (*utpaśyāmaḥ*) and so forth, he shows this: although there is no [direct] means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the meaning is that it is inferred from the composition of this treatise through its extensive structure.

Now, one who seeks the cultivation of correct knowledge might proceed toward that [treatise] even without the Teacher’s statement, being prompted by doubt due to the absence of both subverting and establishing means of valid cognition; so what is the purpose of stating such an introductory sentence?
Thus he says: "In the case of those not mentioned," and so forth.
He thinks as follows: for that which is not to be done at all applies only with respect to one who is not deluded.
For indeed, one who, having seen a treatise such as the *Kākadantaparīkṣā* (The Examination of a Crow's Teeth), perceives it to be devoid of purpose and so forth,
might suspect that this [present work] also lacks purpose and the like; and from such suspicion of futility, he would fail to engage with it.
This is the purpose of stating that [objection].

Once the statement has been made by the author of the treatise, a doubt regarding the meaning arises from that statement in accordance with it; the sense is that one then proceeds [to act] on its basis.

He demonstrates the reasons by which doubt regarding the lack of purpose arises with the words "niṣprayojana" (useless) and so forth. Or rather, the meaning is that, having considered another treatise to be a more easily accessible means than this one, there might be a suspicion that this present treatise lacks essence and is thus not a valid means. Having thus explained the purport of the sentence as a whole, he speaks the words "avisaṃvādaka" (non-contradictory) and so forth in order to show the meaning of its individual parts.

By stating that "non-contradictory knowledge is correct knowledge," the author of the commentary [indicates] that the Mīmāṃsakas postulate knowledge as the apprehension of an object (*arthāvabodhaka*), the Cārvākas postulate it as the mere sight of an object (*arthadarśana*),
and yet some others postulate even erroneous knowledge as being correct.
All that has been refuted,
because these lack the defining characteristic of right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*);
for they are not indeed right knowledges.
Likewise, [these points] have been set aside by [the author] himself in his own commentary (*ṭīkā*).
Therefore, in this sense,
"yat" and "tad" are in a state of constant syntactic connection.
Therefore, since right knowledge (samyagjñāna) must precede the accomplishment of all human goals, it follows that it is precisely for this reason that it is being explained.
Non-contradictory cognition is right knowledge.
In the world, that which causes one to obtain an object previously indicated is called "concordant" (*saṃvādaka*).
Furthermore, regarding the indicated object, it is precisely the state of being a motivator (*pravartakatva*) that constitutes the means of obtaining it, and nothing else.
For instance, a cognition does not cause one to obtain an object by merely producing [a representation of] the object.
Rather, by impelling a person toward an object, it causes that person to attain the object.
Even this quality of being an impeller consists solely in the indication of the objective domain of activity;
for consciousness is not able to impel a person by force.
For this very reason, the apprehension of the object itself is the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Once the object has been apprehended, the person is set in motion, and the object is brought within reach.
And this being the case, the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is completed through the apprehension of the object;
for this very reason, a means of valid cognition has as its object that which has not yet been apprehended.
For by whichever cognition an object is first apprehended, [that cognition alone is the valid means].
By that very [cognition], the person has been set in motion and the object has been attained;
regarding that very object, what further purpose could be served by another cognition?

Therefore, that which has already been apprehended is not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*). In this regard, the object that is known as "seen" is made the objective domain of activity by perception (*pratyakṣa*);
for, in whatever object the operation of perception as direct intuition (*sākṣātkāritva*) is followed by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), [that object is the domain of perception].

The opponent maintains that the validity of the three types of knowledge is established with respect to a single object through their respective distinctions as the indicator (*pradarśaka*), the prompter (*pravartaka*), and the achiever (*prāpaka*);
in order to refute this, [the author] says:
"And when the object has been indicated," and so forth.

When an object has been shown by the first revealing cognition, the second cognition regarding that very same object is what prompts a person to act toward it; the third [cognition] also leads to that very same object.
Therefore, since there is nothing more than the first [cognition] in terms of making it fit for attainment, that alone is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
He supports this very point with the words "For thus," and so forth.
It does not produce or generate an object, because the object has already arisen from its own cause.
By this, the non-difference between that which sets [the person] in motion and that which causes attainment is shown.
In order to demonstrate that even the initiator is non-different from the indicator, he says: "In [the process of] engagement," and so forth.
That very cognition which first arises as an indicator with respect to an object is what makes that object the domain of engagement;
the meaning is that it renders the object fit to be the domain of engagement.
But the second cognition [is not required],
because the object of activity has already been rendered fit for engagement by the first alone.
The word "api" (also/even) refers back to the preceding [statement].

With the words "for this very reason" and so forth, he corroborates his own view with the text of the Master [Ācārya]. From what is this understood? When [the sense organ] merely shows [the object] at first, it does not set it in motion nor does it cause its attainment.
It indeed causes one to engage for a second time as well,

but it does not cause one to attain [the object]. This being the case, would there then be one means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that merely indicates [the object], and another that constitutes the result such as the initiation of action?
But this is not the case; therefore, what was said is correct.

Now, one might object: "Even if the apprehension of the object alone is the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), nevertheless, as long as the subsequent [cognitions]—namely, the motivating cognition (*pravartaka-jñāna*) and the realizing cognition (*prāpaka-jñāna*)—do not occur, the operation of the means of valid cognition regarding that object is not yet complete. To this, he says: "When [the object] is apprehended," and so forth.

He thinks as follows: "Once the object has been apprehended, the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is completed; therefore, with respect to the establishment of their status as valid cognitions, those two [subsequent cognitions] are useless.
Consequently, they are not valid cognitions.
How is the operation of the means of valid cognition completed, and what indeed is it?
Thus he says: "For this very reason.
One's own operation consists in being the producer of the ascertainment of one's own object.
And since that ascertainment has already been accomplished by the first apprehension of the object, it is no longer to be produced; thus [the operation] is completed.
In this context, the word "that" (tat) should be construed as referring to right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), because it is indicated by a neuter gender as denoting its own essential nature;
it does not, however, refer to the immediate accomplishment of all human goals, because that is not the primary subject. // 1 //
Perception is that which reveals; therefore, what is known as being seen is "shown by perception.
Inference, however, determines its object of activity through the observation of a mark (liṅga) and thereby reveals that object.
Thus, perception, while manifesting its object, reveals it as something determinate.
And inference demonstrates an object that is necessarily connected with a mark; therefore, these two demonstrate a necessary object, and by that fact, they are means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
There is no other cognition;
it is the means of attainment (*prāpaka*) because it reveals an object that can be attained,
and it is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) precisely because it is a means of attainment.

An object shown by these two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or by another form of knowledge may be something utterly contrary [to reality], such as water in a mirage; because it is non-existent, it is impossible to attain.
Another [kind of object] is indeterminate with respect to existence and non-existence.
For example, it has the sense of "doubtful.
There is no object in the world that is endowed with both existence and non-existence; therefore, such an object is impossible to attain.
This is because a person's activity proceeds precisely according to the actual state of affairs.
Therefore, for the second [cognition] and subsequent ones, there is no additional operation regarding this very object;
the meaning is that they lack the status of a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇya*) because they apprehend what has already been apprehended.
Thus, the person has been set in motion [by the first cognition].
Because it is capable of inducing activity, it is said to be "induced";
because it is capable of bringing about attainment, it is "brought about.

Having thus established in general that right cognition (*samyagjñāna*) is that which is consistent with reality, he says—demonstrating that perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*) function as right cognitions by performing their respective operations—therein:
By the words "the object which," and so forth,
he demonstrates therein, between those two [means of knowledge], the operation of perception (*pratyakṣa*). "Known as perceived" means determined as perceived.

"It is followed by conceptual construction" means that it is determined by a conceptual construction occurring subsequent to it. What is meant is this: perception is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it produces a determination of the object as it appears and is thus consistent [with reality].
With the words "But inference... and so forth, he shows the object of operation for inference.

The "observation of the mark" (*liṅgadarśana*) is the cognition of the mark; and that consists of both the certain determination of smoke as being non-deviant from fire, and a recollective cognition [of the rule] that it is generally inseparably connected with the probandum.
Just as, having perceived smoke through direct perception, one remembers that "this [smoke] is produced by fire" everywhere;
from that knowledge of the mark (liṅga), one determines and points out the object of activity.
That inference is the knowledge which arises through a specific relationship.
Just as one knows that "the smoke here is born from fire.

What is meant by this is: the operation of perception in generating certainty regarding its own object is non-distinct [from the cognition itself], whereas for inference, the very arising of the cognition in the form of certainty regarding its own object—due to the observation of the logical mark (liṅga)—is the operation of certainty.
Thus, by the words "tathā ca" and so forth, he clarifies the function of these two.

Therefore, by stating that "these alone are the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and no other cognition [is so]," he shows that these two alone are correct cognitions (*samyagjñāna*) and not others such as verbal testimony; because they do not fail to present their determined objects, the operation of correct cognition is thereby demonstrated.
Just as these two are valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), so too is cognition such as doubt (*saṃśaya*) not a valid means of knowledge;
this he demonstrates by the words beginning with "it is possible to attain."

This is what is meant: just as perception and inference lead to the attainment of an object presented by their respective means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), so it is not with doubt and erroneous cognition, because such an [actual] object does not exist for them.

Furthermore, every conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that is not based on a logical mark (*liṅga*) and proceeds without perceiving a restrictive factor must present an object that is entirely indeterminate regarding existence and non-existence.
And that [object] is impossible to attain;

therefore, any other cognition which perceives an object that is unattainable, utterly contrary [to reality], and indeterminate as to existence or non-existence, is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*).
Those who seek purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) search for a cognition that serves as the means for attaining an object capable of such action;
and that which they thus seek is precisely what is investigated in this treatise.
Therefore, correct cognition (*samyagjñāna*) is that which reveals an object capable of purposeful action.
And that which has been demonstrated by it is precisely what is to be attained;
for it has been stated that the means of attainment consists in the realization of the object.
In this regard, any other entity distinct from that which has been demonstrated possesses a different form.
It is [different] in time and different in space;
for an object is distinct [from another] due to its association with contradictory properties.
Furthermore, the distinction of place, time, and form constitutes a connection with contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmasaṃsarga*).

This is because a cognition that apprehends an object as having one form is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding an object that possesses another form; for example, a cognition apprehending a conch as yellow is not valid regarding a white conch.

Likewise, a cognition that apprehends something located in one place is not a valid means of knowledge regarding what is located in another place; for example, a cognition apprehending a gem in the light of a gem situated at the opening of a keyhole is not valid regarding the gem inside the room.

Furthermore, that which apprehends an object associated with a different time is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding an object existing at that other time; for example, a dream-cognition apprehending an object of midday at midnight is not a means of valid cognition regarding the object at the time of midnight. Now, it may be argued: "Let it be that doubt and error are not means of valid cognition because their objects do not exist in that manner; however, why is this cognition, 'There is water in this well,' not another means of valid cognition?"
It is not, first of all, perception, because water is imperceptible there; nor is it inference, due to the absence of a logical mark (liṅga); nor is it of the nature of doubt.

Anticipating the objection, "Is it not also the case that [the cognition] is not erroneous because both components are absent, since there is no object that is contrary [to reality]? he says: "And by all that which is not produced from a sign," and so forth.
He thinks as follows: although a cognition of doubt is not perceived directly,
nevertheless, a cognition such as "there is water in this well"— which consists of a conceptual construction involving doubt— is invalid even without a restrictive indicative mark (liṅga),
because it does not determine a specific object.
Therefore, the meaning is as follows: "There might be water in the well at some time"—this is its nature;
thus, that is merely a cognition of doubt and is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*).
However, it has been established in the *Viniścayaṭīkā* that when one who has acted upon it occasionally obtains water, that [acquisition] results from a different cognition.
Now, one might object: "Even though doubt and the like do not lead to the attainment of the object already indicated, why are they not explained?
To this he says: "And by those seeking purposeful action," and so forth.
The intention is that [such knowledge] is of no use for the accomplishment of human goals (*puruṣārtha*).

Now, one might object: even if valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is correct knowledge because it leads to the attainment of the object indicated, then the cognition of yellow in a white conch shell—[would that not also be valid?]
The cognition of a jewel [arising] from the light of a jewel within the keyhole,
and the dream-cognition at midnight that grasps objects belonging to the time of midday— surely these are restricted by place.
Is it not possible that what is restricted by its form can be attained, yet at the very time it is delimited, it cannot be attained?
It is not said that it must be attained at the same time it is delimited;
for the time of seeing is indeed distinct [from the time of attainment].
Furthermore, although there is another time of attainment,
that which is delimited by time is precisely what must be attained by it;
and due to the determination of non-difference, the unity belonging to the continuum is to be understood.
That [discipline] is described as such because its prior cause is right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*). That which exists prior to an effect is called the "prior cause" (*pūrva-kāraṇa*).
However, if the word "cause" (*kāraṇa*) alone were used, it would be understood as the direct cause for the accomplishment of human goals (*puruṣārtha-siddhi*).
In the word "pūrva," it refers merely to what precedes.
Furthermore, correct cognition (*samyagjñāna*) is of two kinds:
that which manifests as purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), and...
And it is that which prompts activity toward what is incapable of causal efficiency;
between those two, that which is the prompter is what is being examined here,
and that is merely the former.
But it is not the direct cause;
for when right knowledge exists, there is recollection of what was previously seen,
from recollection comes desire, and from desire comes purposeful activity.
And because there is the attainment [of the object] through its occurrence,
it is therefore not a direct cause;
nor does it attain the status of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), because there is the attainment of the mere object as indicated by these [means].
Then, anticipating the objection that [this] is indeed right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), he says: "For it consists in the apprehension of an object," and so forth.

He thinks as follows: because the object shown by these [cognitions]—the yellow form located in the keyhole, which is a gem with a fixed location and a fixed time, namely at midnight—is not actually attained.
Because there is no such thing as a "part" (avayava) or the like that exists apart from space and time,
for this very reason those [cognitions] are indeed not means of valid cognition; they are not correct cognitions.

Although these [examples] are things to be excluded by the inclusion of the term "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*), and thus ought to have been shown precisely in that context where the term "non-erroneous" is introduced, nevertheless, there is no fault here in mentioning them, as this is the context concerning what is to be excluded from "correct cognition" (*samyagjñāna*).
As for the phrase beginning with "But surely... (*nanu ca*):

The opponent thinks as follows: Since that which is restricted by place and form can be apprehended, let it be that there is no means of valid cognition for the apprehension of another form or another place; however, this is not the case for [another] time, because the Blessed One’s moments are momentary and thus not apprehended at a fixed time.
And therefore, just as in the case of a truly blue object, the time of apprehension of the cognition of blue is one thing and the time of its attainment is another,
yet there is validity despite this difference in time;
so too, in the case of a dream-cognition, there will be validity for the attainment of a son at midday, even though the object was shown during the night.

With the words "it is not said," and so forth, the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*) thinks as follows: It is true that there is indeed a difference in the entity due to the difference between moments; however, the definition of validity is not stated with reference to the moment, but rather with reference to the continuum (*santāna*).
Therefore, regarding blue and so forth, that very continuum which is determined by the cognition of blue—
That very [object] is what has been apprehended by that [cognition]; therefore, the cognition of blue is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
It is not so with the cognition of one's son-in-law regarding a son who is presented as distinct by a gross temporal difference.
It is not due to a difference in the time of attainment, because it would be impossible to determine a single continuity [of the object].
By stating that "the unity belonging to the continuity is to be perceived," he demonstrates the relationship of cause and effect between the ascertainment and the subsequent activity.
And how can that causal relationship exist if validity is established with respect to the continuum (*saṃtāna*) and not with respect to the momentary characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*)?
"Right knowledge is that which has [liberation] as its prior cause.
How does the word "prior" (pūrva) function in the sense of "cause"? To this he says: "from the effect," and so forth.
"Why was the term 'cause' (kāraṇa) not used?
To this he says: "The term 'cause,' etc.
Even though the appearance of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is a direct attainment, nevertheless, that [appearance] is not to be examined.
For it is precisely where those who are discerning and seekers are apprehensive that something is investigated;
and when a cognition manifesting purposeful activity is known, the human goal is accomplished.
Therefore, seekers have no apprehension regarding that [result],

and for this reason it need not be examined. Consequently, in order to indicate that right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) is the cause which is worthy of examination— not being the immediate cause— the word "cause" (*kāraṇa*) was set aside and the term "prior" (*pūrva*) was employed.
The "purpose of man" (puruṣārtha) is the object for man;
it is called an "object" (artha) because it is sought after—
that is to say, it is desired.
An object is either to be abandoned or to be adopted;
for an object that is to be abandoned is desired to be abandoned, and one that is to be adopted is desired to be adopted.
Furthermore, there is no category other than that which is to be abandoned (*heya*) and that which is to be accepted (*upādeya*).
For that which is to be disregarded (*upekṣaṇīya*), because it is not to be accepted, becomes a cause for endless abandonment.
With reference to what, then, was the word "prior" (*pūrva*) employed for the sake of grasping something that is obstructed?
Thus he says: "Of two kinds," and so forth.
Now, why is it said that the cognition appearing as causal efficiency (*arthakriyānirbhāsa*) is the immediate cause?
For that is not a cognition of the cause.

Thus, it is rightly said: that cognition which, immediately following the appearance of the means (*sādhana*), produces a cognition appearing as purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), is called the "immediately preceding cause" (*anantarakāraṇa*) of that cognition of the means;
and it is precisely this that is intended here by the term "appearance of purposeful action."

How so? The appearance of causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*)—that is, its reflection—is the arising of a cognition having that form from an immediately preceding cognition; therefore, that cognition of the means is the cognition of the means which has the appearance of that causal efficacy.
In this case as well, the compound should be formed in this manner.

Alternatively, the cognition of purposeful action (*arthakriyājñāna*) alone is the immediate cause; it is the "mediated" [cause] consisting of the cognition appearing as the means (*sādhana*), which functions as the motivator with respect to worldly practice (*vyavahāra*) by bringing about the performance of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted.
If this is so, why is it not examined immediately thereafter?
To this he says: "In that very [cognition]," and so forth.
That is to say, in that very cognition in which a person has doubt regarding the engagement with an object capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsamartha*), [it is that which must be examined].
That very point is now examined:
there is no doubt regarding the cognition of the means [to an end] immediately preceding it, because immediately after that, the cognition of the appearance of pleasure or pain arises.
Since these two are experienced, it is not subject to investigation whether one ought to act based on the cognition of the means.
Alternatively, by this reasoning, that which has the appearance of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is not subject to investigation.
[The word] "artha" is derived from the root *artha* meaning "to request," with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of the object (*karman*). Thus, "that which is requested" and so forth.
It should also be understood as "that which is sought after" (*aryate*).

Because this [root] *ṛ* is an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*), the suffix *sthan* is applied according to the *uṇādi* rules. Vinītadeva’s explanation, beginning with "the object to be abandoned" (*heyo 'rtha*), has been refuted.

For it has been explained in this way: by the word *artha*, "purpose" (*prayojana*) is meant; the purpose of a person is [an action] such as cooking wood, and its *siddhi* is its accomplishment (*niṣpatti*).
And that is incorrect because the accomplishment of an object, such as cooking wood, does not arise from right knowledge; what then?

It arises solely from its own causes, such as fire and so forth. However, in Dharmottara’s commentary, there is no fault, for it states that the accomplishment—which is the practical application—regarding objects to be abandoned or adopted is preceded by right knowledge.
He will demonstrate this very point [later] with the words: "The abandonment of that which is to be abandoned and the practice [of that which is to be adopted].
Now, one might object: "Is there not something else besides the abandonable and the adoptable, namely the indifferent (upekṣaṇīya)?
Why is it not mentioned? Indeed, [it is true].
Its non-establishment consists of abandonment and appropriation;
for establishment is said to be origination, which is dependent upon a cause.
But accomplishment based on knowledge is practice;
and practice consists in the abandoning of that which is to be abandoned and the acquisition of that which is to be acquired.
Thereafter, the accomplishment (*siddhi*) is said to be the performance characterized by the abandonment of what is to be discarded and the acquisition of what is to be adopted;
and all of this is the accomplishment of the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*).
Here, the word "all" (*sarva*) is used in the sense of the totality of substances.
But it does not refer to the entirety of the types [of accomplishment].
Therefore, this is not the meaning: that both types of accomplishment are based solely on right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).
Rather, this is the meaning: whatever accomplishment there may be, all of it in its entirety is based on right knowledge.
For indeed, even by chance (*kākatālīya*), there is no attainment of an object through false cognition (*mithyājñāna*).
To explain: if it causes one to reach the object that was indicated, only then does the attainment of the object occur from that [cognition].
And it is correct knowledge alone that, having shown [an object], causes its attainment;

whereas false knowledge, having shown [an object], does not cause its attainment. And how could that which does not cause attainment be the basis for the accomplishment of the object? Therefore, from whatever there is false knowledge, from that there is no accomplishment of the object;
and from whatever there is accomplishment of the object, that is indeed correct knowledge.
For this very reason, right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) must be explained with effort, since it alone is the basis for the accomplishment of the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*).

Therefore, as much as can be said—that whatever accomplishment of the goals of human life there may be, it is based solely on right knowledge—so much has been stated by the words: "All that is preceded by right knowledge."
The word *iti* has the sense of "therefore" (*tasmāt*), and there is a constant connection between the relative pronoun *yat* and the demonstrative pronoun *tat*.
Thus, the meaning is this: because he says "correctly," and [because he says] "nor is it to be abandoned," and so forth.
He thinks as follows: "It is true that it exists."
However, because it is not to be adopted, it is simply to be rejected; thus, it is not mentioned separately.

Therefore, as for what some have said—that the mention of the rejectable and the adoptable is due to their utility for human goals, whereas the indifferent is not mentioned because it is the opposite of that—[that is refuted].
That has been answered; he explains this very point with the subsequent text beginning with "the word 'all' (*sarvaśabda*)", thereby refuting the interpretation of the commentators (*ṭīkākṛt*).
Vinītadeva and Śāntabhadra, having raised this doubt, have explained it as follows: How was the doubt raised? [They ask:
"But is not the accomplishment of all purposes regarding abandonment and acquisition truly [achieved]?"
It might be suspected that [the attainment of the goal] comes from knowledge alone, or even from false knowledge by mere chance (*kākatālīya*); having raised this doubt, it is refuted:
"True, it exists, but it is explained in this way: this word *sarva* (all) expresses a variety (*prakāra*)."

Therefore, this is the meaning: the accomplishment of all human goals (*puruṣārtha*)—characterized by the accomplishment of the goals of abandonment and acquisition, and characterized by the accomplishment of worldly and transcendental goals—is for the most part based upon right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).
That [objection] is refuted because the word "all" (*sarva*) must be understood here [in its restricted sense].

If [the word] "entirety" (kārtsnya) is accepted, then [the statement] "everything was created by Brahmā" means this: as far as the accomplishment of the entire purpose— characterized by avoidance and acquisition— extends, [so far does his creation].
All [attainments] result from right knowledge alone,
not from false knowledge, because the latter does not lead to the accomplishment of what is desired;
he demonstrates this very point with the following passage.
With the words "Even of two kinds," etc., he shows the interpretation of others;
with the words "But this is the meaning," etc., he presents his own interpretation.

Then, under the guise of a conclusion, by means of the word *iva* used in the phrase "whatever he might say," which expresses restriction, and the word *sarva* used in the sense of "entirety" in the phrase "as much as the meaning [is]," whatever extent of meaning there is, that alone [is intended].
He shows that it exists:
right knowledge is of two kinds.
And that right knowledge is known according to its true nature by means of the refutation of four types of misconceptions.
The four types of misconceptions are: 1) misconception regarding number, and 2) misconception regarding essential nature.
3. Disagreement regarding the object, and 4. disagreement regarding the result.
Among these, disagreement regarding number is as follows: for some, it is one; for others...
As among the followers of Bṛhaspati;
some [recite] three, as among the Sāṅkhyas.
According to the Naiyāyikas there are four [pramāṇas],
and according to the Mīmāṃsakas there are six. Since the accomplishment of all human goals is preceded by knowledge, that correct knowledge (samyagjñāna) is here investigated.
And although right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) is subordinate within the compound, nevertheless, because it is that which is to be explained in this treatise, it is the primary element;
therefore, it alone is connected with the word "that" (*tat*).
"Is explained" means it is demonstrated by way of refuting misconceptions. // 1 //
Furthermore, there are four types of misconception here, concerning number, definition, object, and result.
Among these, in order to refute the misconception regarding number, he says: "it is twofold" (*dvividham*).
That which has two kinds (*vidhau*) or modes (*prakārau*) is "twofold."

And by means of indicating the number, the distinction between individual instances is shown. Now, if it is argued that the accomplishment of the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) is expressed by the *bahuvrīhi* compound, and because of its primacy, it is logical for it to be connected with the word "that" (*tat*), rather than right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*)—[we reply: no.
Thus he says: "Even though," and so forth.
He thinks as follows: for the object of a word is twofold—the verbal [form] and that which is to be communicated.
The objection raised with respect to the word has been answered with respect to the subject to be established,
because it is *samyagjñāna* (right knowledge) alone that is under discussion as that which is to be explained, whereas for the other [type of knowledge], the opposite is established.
Now, what is this "explanation" (*vyutpādana*) of knowledge?
Is it the production of knowledge, or the removal of defects, or else the description of its essential nature?
First of all, production is not being effected by this treatise,
because [the entity] arises from its own causes;
nor is it the removal of defects.
A fault cannot be removed by this argument,
because it is not an agent; nor can it be made known.
Since it is not being understood, this is a fault;
nor is it appropriate to state its essential nature, because the treatise would then be rendered purposeless.
Anticipating this objection, he says: "He explains [it] by means of the removal of misconceptions.
He thinks as follows: "By means of the removal of misconceptions, the true nature of right knowledge is made known through this treatise. (1)
The statement "right knowledge possesses the characteristics that will be described hereafter, and not those of other types" is a definition of its essential nature (*svarūpa*).
He demonstrates that very misconception (*vipratipatti*) in sequence, beginning with the words "of four kinds," meaning "the number and characteristics are of four types," and so forth.
With the words "In that regard," and so forth, he demonstrates the refutation of the [wrong] understanding of the number [of means of valid cognition].
Furthermore, there are many types of misconceptions regarding right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).

For instance, the Mīmāṃsakas consider right knowledge to consist of six types—characterized by perception, inference, verbal testimony, analogy, presumptive testimony, and non-apprehension—as well as word-explanation (*pada-vyākhyā*).
The Naiyāyikas maintain that there are four types of valid cognition, characterized as perception, inference, verbal testimony, and analogy;
however, some Cārvākas hold that there is only one, namely perception. To refute their view, he shows [the truth] by stating: "it is twofold."
Disagreement regarding the essential nature (*svarūpa*) is as follows: for some, perception (*pratyakṣa*) is conceptual (*savikalpaka*); for others, it is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*).
Disagreement regarding the object (*viṣaya*) is as follows: some say that the object of perception is only the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
"The object of inference is exclusively the universal characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa)";
however, others have stated it differently. Regarding the disagreement concerning the result: some accept a distinction between the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) and its result (phala).
Furthermore, some accept non-differentiation;

therefore, by refuting these four types of misconceptions, the nature of right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) is established as being entirely non-delusive. In that regard, for the purpose of refuting misconceptions regarding its number at the very outset, it was stated: "Right knowledge is twofold."
"Dvividham" means "of two kinds," because it consists of two types.
The expression using a numeral is intended to provide a clear demonstration that it is indeed of two kinds;
by this, [theories of] three kinds, one kind, and so forth, are excluded.
Only the twofold nature of enumeration has been established:
namely, that there are exactly two manifestations of right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).
Once the distinction between these manifestations has been demonstrated, it is possible to state the definition of right knowledge as it pertains specifically to each manifestation.

However, as long as the distinction between individual instances (*vyakti*) has not been demonstrated, it is impossible to state a single definition of correct cognition (*samyagjñāna*) that conforms to all its instances.
Therefore, the statement regarding the distinction in number is an integral part of the statement of the definition;
for if the distinction in number—which consists of the distinction between individual instances—is not demonstrated, it is impossible to demonstrate a distinction in the definition.
And precisely because it serves as a limb for the exposition of the characteristics, the enumeration of the distinctions in number is stated first. // 2 //
What, then, is this twofold nature? He says: "perception" (*pratyakṣa*).
It is that which has reached or is directed toward the sense faculty (*akṣa*).
The compound is formed according to the rule: "Words such as *atīta* and *krānta* [form a compound] with a word in the second case when meaning 'gone beyond' (*krānta*) and so forth.

Since in compounds such as *prāpta*, *āpanna*, *alaṅgata*, and *atisamāsa*, the gender of the final member is prohibited, the word *pratyakṣa* is established as being of all genders, following the gender of the referent (*abhidheya*).

Now, one might object: once the definition of correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) has been stated, it is more appropriate to subsequently demonstrate its divisions, namely that "correct knowledge characterized by such-and-such is of two kinds."
"Why was that shown right at the beginning?
To this he says: "And when there is a difference in individuals," and so forth.
He thinks as follows: "This is indeed exactly so."
However, if this distinction in number were not stated here, it would be impossible to correctly state the definition of right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*);
therefore, since another specific definition of perception (*pratyakṣa*) can be stated, the statement of the distinction in number is indeed an auxiliary part of the definition.
[Objection: But surely, from the mention "perception and inference," it is already understood that there are two kinds.
For what purpose is the mention of "two kinds"?
It is said: for the sake of restriction, namely that right knowledge is indeed of two kinds;
by this, the numbers one, three, and four would be excluded.

If it were not stated that there are two [types of valid cognition], there might be the suspicion that while perception and inference are possible, there may also be other means of valid cognition (pramāṇas). // 2 //
By the phrase "that which has gone toward the sense-faculties" (*pratigatamakṣam*), he demonstrates that this is a *gati* compound.
Why is this compound not shown as an *avyayībhāva*, namely *pratyakṣam* (literally, "toward each sense-faculty")?
For if it were an *avyayībhāva* compound, it would be neuter gender;
[the two means of knowledge are] perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*).
What is this twofold nature?
And why is it not fourfold knowledge?
Therefore, it is stated specifically: "perception and inference."
Perception (*pratyakṣa*) is that which is based on the sense-faculties (*akṣa*).
This is a derivative suffix (*nipāta*) indicating that the object of cognition functions as the instrument (*kāraka*) of perception,
just as in the expression "a cow by its going" (*gamanena gauḥ*).
In that case, "going" (*gamana*) is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of "cowness" (*gotva*); therefore, it is understood that a bodily aggregate possessing cowness is the denotation of the word "cow.

Similarly, here too, because the fact that the object of cognition is a causal factor for perception (*pratyakṣakārakatva*) is indicated by its dependence on the sense faculties (*indriyāśritatva*), only the fourfold [division of] perception is accepted as being "perceptual" (*pratyakṣatva*).
*Māna* is that by which one measures; the word "delimiting" (*paricchedaka*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the definition]. The prefix *anu-* indicates immediate succession (*ānantarya*).
Inference (*anumāna*) is that which follows after [perception] (*apścāt*);
the remainder [of the definition] is that it proceeds preceded by the recollection of the connection (*pratibandha*) and the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*).
Furthermore, the etymological basis (*vyutpattinimitta*) of the word is its dependence on the senses (*akṣāśritatva*).
But it is not the basis for the application [of the term].
Rather, by means of this dependence on a sense organ, the direct perception of an object—which is inherent in the same substrate as that [dependence]—is indicated.
That alone is the basis for the application of the word; therefore, whatever cognition directly perceives an object is called "perception" (pratyakṣa).
If, however, being based on a sense faculty were the sole ground for application [of the term], then only sensory cognition would be called "perception" (pratyakṣa),
and not mental cognition and the rest.

Just as the word "cow" (*go*), although derived from the act of going (*gacchati*) in the sense that "that which goes is a cow," takes as its basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) the "cowness" (*gotva*)— which is inherent in the same object and characterized by the act of going—
and just as the word "cow" is established as applying to both a cow that is moving and one that is not moving; so too,
"that by which something is measured is a measure" (*mīyate 'neneti mānam*).

By the word *māna* used in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇasādhana*), the means of valid cognition characterized by similarity (*sārūpyalakṣaṇa*) is denoted. Following the apprehension of the mark (*liṅga*) and the recollection of its relationship [with the probandum], there is inference (*anumāna*). When the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) has been apprehended...
And since inference proceeds once the relationship between the probandum and the probans has been remembered, it is said to occur at a later time;
[this refers] to perception,
and from that, the cognition [arises] through perception.

The expression "the pot is perceptible" (*pratyakṣo ghaṭaḥ*) would not be possible; rather, there would only be the cognitions "this is perceptible" (*idam pratyakṣam*) and "the bowl is perceptible" (*kuṇḍaṃ pratyakṣam*).
However, in the case of a *gati-samāsa*, there occurs agreement with all genders.

But surely, if the etymology is "that which has gone toward the sense organ" (*pratigatam akṣam*), then only sensory cognition (*indriyajñāna*)— which relies upon the sense organs— would be denoted by the term *pratyakṣa*, and not [cognitions] such as those born of inference (*yoni*), because they do not rely upon the sense organs?
Anticipating this objection, he says: "And [the property of] being dependent on the sense-faculty," and so forth.
"Inhering in a single object" means that inherence in a single sensory cognition—that is, the dependence on the sense-faculty and the direct perception of the object—are connected.
By the phrase "characterized by similarity," it is precisely the cognition itself that is meant, as it is characterized by similarity to the object.
Therefore, it is not mere similarity;
otherwise, it would contradict the statement that "cognition regarding the object of inference arises from a dissimilar mark.

Furthermore, if one were to argue against the analysis of *anumāna* as an avyayībhāva compound—meaning "measurement subsequent [to perception]"—then one must instead resort to a *gati*-compound, analyzing it as "measurement that has followed" (*anugataṃ mānam anumānam*).
The word "paścāt" (afterwards) is used as an explanatory gloss;
there is no compound in that sentence.
Furthermore, "pratyakṣam" and "anumānam" are presented with different case endings.

Now, if a difference in objects is understood— just as there is a difference in their grammatical case endings— it follows that there is likewise a difference in their objects; this is the implied meaning.
The word "ca" (and) has the sense of conjunction;
by it, the equal strength of perception and inference is included.

Just as perception, being produced from an object and being non-erroneous, is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), so too is inference a means of valid cognition because it is non-erroneous due to its connection with the object through identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*).
Thus, by this, that which was asserted by some— namely, that among all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) perception (*pratyakṣa*) is the primary one— is refuted;
for non-erroneousness (*abhrāntatva*) is indeed equal in both cases.
For the primacy of direct perception has indeed been established by someone. // 3 //

In order to refute misconceptions regarding its essential nature (*svarūpa*), it is stated therein that "perception (*pratyakṣa*) is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*) and non-erroneous (*abhrānta*).
The word "therein" (*tatra*) has the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*); perception is selected as the first among correct cognitions (*samyagjñāna*) by means of this definition.

By the term "perception" (*pratyakṣam*), the subject to be defined (*lakṣya*) is stated; by the phrase "free from conceptual construction and non-erroneous" (*kalpanāpoḍham abhrāntam*), the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) is stated.
Thus, the meaning expressed is that whatever is free from conceptual construction and non-erroneous, that alone is to be understood as perception.
The word "and" (*ca*) conjoins perception and inference as being of equal authority.

Just as perception is a means of valid cognition because it causes one to attain the object by being inseparably connected with the object as it truly is, so too inference is a means of valid cognition because it causes one to attain the determined object by being inseparably connected with the object. // 3 //
In this context, the word *tatra*, while functioning in the sense of the locative case, is used for the purpose of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*).
Therefore, the meaning of the sentence is as follows: "therein" (*tatra*) is a reference to the aggregate of those two, namely perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*);
"perception" (*pratyakṣa*) is a reference to one part of that aggregate.

Regarding what was stated by Śabarasvāmī and others—that the conjunction (*ca*) indicates that perception and inference possess equal force, and that perception is superior to inference as it is said in the *Mīmāṃsā-bhāṣya*: "When perception is more powerful, how can there be inference?"—that is incorrect; for both possess equal force in their respective functions. He demonstrates this very point with the words beginning, "That which is invariably concomitant with the object," and so forth.
By this, the commentary of Vinītadeva and Śāntabhadra is also refuted.

They have explained it thus: "The mention with different case endings in the phrase *pratyakṣam anumānaṃ ca* indicates a difference in their objects (*viṣaya*) by virtue of the meaning; just as these two are distinguished by different case endings."

Thus, it is also incorrect to say that the object (*viṣaya*) is distinct, because when the case-ending is assigned as singular, the use of the particle *ca* would not demonstrate that [the two] possess equal force (*tulyabalatva*). // 3 //
"By means of the universal (jāti) of perceptibility":
because there are many individual perceptions, it is designated by that universal.
"Having referred to perception" is the indication of the definition.
The statement that "freedom from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍhatva*) and "non-erroneousness" (*abhrāntatva*) are prescribed constitutes the indication of the definition (*lakṣaṇa*).

By demonstrating the relationship between the object to be defined (*lakṣya*) and its definition through this [statement], Vinītadeva’s explanation—which takes the form of a relationship between a name (*saṃjñā*) and the named (*saṃjñin*)—is refuted;
for a name cannot possibly correspond exactly to its referent.

For it is by stating the meaning as it truly is that misconception would be dispelled. Although one could state the meaning as it truly is by means of an etymological definition— that "perception" (*pratyakṣa*) is that which is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*) and non-erroneous (*abhrānta*)—
nevertheless, the actual nature (*svarūpa*) of perception would not have been stated.

Since there is another [definition] as well for the nature of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*): the meaning of the word [is as follows]. Regarding the etymological meaning of the parts: "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*) means that which is excluded from conceptual construction;
the remainder [of the sense] is "separated from conceptual construction. Alternatively, it is "excluded by conceptual construction," hence *kalpanāpoḍha*.
The ellipsis is "devoid of conceptual construction" (kalpanāvivarjitam). It is "non-erroneous," meaning it is not mistaken;
the ellipsis is "non-discrepant with respect to the object that leads to attainment" (prāpakaviṣaye 'visaṃvādakam).
If it is asked why two qualifiers were stated, it is replied: "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*) was stated for the purpose of excluding the erroneous cognition of one suffering from ophthalmia (*timira*);
and "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*) was stated for the purpose of excluding inference (*anumāna*).
Thus, since it is non-erroneous in that regard, "selection" (nirdhāraṇa) is the separation of one part of the genus "perception" from the whole;
having restated perception, [the definition specifies] its being free from conceptual construction.
Non-fatigue is enjoined.

That which is well known among you and us as a direct-perceiving cognition regarding objects should be understood as being endowed with both freedom from conceptual construction and non-erroneousness.

And it should not be thought: "If being free from conceptual construction and non-erroneousness is unestablished, what other nature remains for perceptual cognition that could be restated as the referent of the word 'perception'?
For it is well known to everyone that a cognition which directly manifests objects in accordance with the presence and absence of the sense faculties is the referent of the word 'perception'.
By way of restating that [definition], there is the prescription of being free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*) and non-erroneous (*abhrānta*).
