Since direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) and so forth exist, when the characterized (*lakṣya*) and the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) have been stated, it is stated according to the facts: whatever is direct perception should be understood as being free from conceptual construction and non-erroneous.

For this very reason, the formulation of a definition (*lakṣaṇa*) constitutes the formation of a designation (*saṃjñākaraṇa*), because a definition is not perceived as such [independently]. Having restated the word "sound" (*śabda*), its impermanence is prescribed as the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, since it is understood that impermanence is not itself the designation (*saṃjñā*), there is a distinction between the designation and the definition (*lakṣaṇa*).

As for you, who—having restated these two as they appear in other passages—prescribe perceptibility (*pratyakṣatva*) [for them], by that very act you have, in a roundabout way, explained the relationship between the defined and the definition here in reverse; for at the time of prescribing a definition, the defined object is restated and then the definition is prescribed.
However, the definiendum is not enjoined without first enjoining the definition;
rather, once the relationship between the definiendum and the definition is established, the definiendum is enjoined by means of the enjoining of the definition, as in:
"He who possesses a topknot is a wandering mendicant."
At the time of prescribing the characteristic of the top-knot (*śikhā*), it is the top-knot itself that is enjoined by way of restating the wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*).

Furthermore, the author of the *Viniścaya-ṭīkā* has provided another refutation against this view, namely that it constitutes an "inverted injunction" (*viparīta-vidhāna*); this should be consulted in that very work.

Now, one might object: under the view that this is a rule defining a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa-vidhi*), since direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is not yet established, it cannot be the subject of a restatement (*anuvāda*).

Furthermore, one might ask: "How can the definition [of perception] be made known by restating the characteristic of perception, as in the case of 'the wandering ascetic is recognized by his topknot,' where the characteristic of the topknot is restated and [the qualities of] being free from conceptual construction and so forth are enjoined?
Anticipating this objection, he says: "That which belongs to you," and so on.

He thinks as follows: although perception is not established as such by virtue of being free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*), nevertheless, it is well-known in general as perception by virtue of its direct manifestation of the object (*arthasākṣātkāritva*); therefore, it is said that "perception" is restated (*anūdya*).
Now, one might object: "Since those two [the universal and the particular] are not established, perception itself is indeed unestablished, because perception has them as its intrinsic nature?
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And this should not be thought," and so forth. This is easy to understand.
It is to be accepted regarding the object as the means of attainment (*prāpaka-viṣaya*), but not regarding the object as the focal point (*ālambana-viṣaya*).
If non-erroneousness were admitted regarding the object as the focal point, [it would follow that there is no error].

In this context, there would be a refutation of the Yogācāra system. For the Yogācāras maintain that all cognition possessing an objective support (*ālambana*) is erroneous; "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*) means devoid of conceptualization, that is to say, lacking the intrinsic nature of conceptual construction.
"Non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*) means not being mistaken regarding the nature of a thing that is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākṣama*).
And the nature of a thing capable of causal efficiency consists of color and its limiting conditions (*upādhi*), such as configuration (*sanniveśa*).
That which does not err with respect to this is "non-erroneous."

And these two characteristics are for the purpose of dispelling misconceptions, not for the purpose of excluding inference; for by the very inclusion of the term "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*), inference is already excluded.

In that regard, if the term "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*) were not included, then the perception of a tree as it moves and so forth would [incorrectly] be considered direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because it is free from conceptual construction.

For one might raise the objection that since a mere tree is obtained by one who acts upon it, it is right cognition (*samyagjñāna*) because of its correspondence with reality, and it is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) because it is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*).
To exclude that [objection], the term "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*) is included.
"Devoid of the intrinsic nature of conceptual construction" (kalpanā-svabhāva-rahitam):
this is an expression where the abstract quality (bhāva) is emphasized;
it means "devoid of the very nature of being conceptual construction."

By stating "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*) and "the nature of a thing capable of causal efficiency" (*arthakriyākṣama-vasturūpa*), he demonstrates that the meaning of "non-erroneous" cannot possibly be "non-discrepancy" (*avisaṃvāda*).
He sets forth the subsequent refutation assuming that the word "non-erroneous" is taken in the sense of non-discrepancy.

By the phrase "consisting of color and having spatial arrangement as its limiting condition" (*sanniveśopādhivarṇātmaka*), he shows that there exists nothing else besides color, such as "configuration" (*saṃsthāna*) and so forth, as imagined by others.

By demonstrating the removal of misconceptions through the two terms beginning with "and these two characteristics," Vinītadeva’s commentary—which consists of explaining the exclusion [of non-perception] by means of those two terms—is refuted.

He, however, explained it as follows: "Non-erroneous" (abhrānta) means that which is not inconsistent [with reality]. If this were so, then inference would also fall under the definition of perception; therefore, the inclusion of the term "free from conceptual construction" (kalpanāpoḍha) is for the purpose of excluding that.

If it were explained in this way—that "non-erroneous" means that which is not erroneous with respect to its object—then since all perceptual cognition (*pratyakṣa-jñāna*) is erroneous with respect to its object, nothing at all would possess the status of perception.
And thus it has been said: "All [cognition] is erroneous with respect to its object, except for the cognition of the Tathāgata."
Thus, it is incorrect to say that the Master [Dignāga] included even that [position] here according to the view of the Yogācāras;
for the Master composed the two words for the purpose of dispelling misconceptions, not for the purpose of exclusion (*vyavaccheda*).
For this very reason, Dharmottara, while inferring the intention of the Teacher (Ācārya), explained two words [of the verse].
Now, one might ask: "Why does [the word *anyathā*] not serve the purpose of exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) even in your own position?
To this he says: "And this," and so forth.
He thinks as follows: this term "erroneous" (*bhrānta*) is not taken here in the sense of non-correspondence;

rather, that which does not err with respect to the objective basis (*ālambana*), namely the nature of a thing capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākṣama*), is what is grasped by the term "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*).
[Objection: But would it not follow that the Yogācāra position is not included?
It is said that there is no fault, as the teacher has formulated this definition according to the external system (bāhyana) and in accordance with the Sautrāntika school.

However, according to the Yogācāra school, the term "non-erroneous" (abhrānta) need not be included; for the subject at hand is correct cognition (*samyagjñāna*) which is by nature non-discrepant (*saṃvādaka*), and thus there is nothing else to be excluded.

Therefore, since inference has already been excluded by the inclusion of the term "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*), the inclusion of the term "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*) serves to eliminate a specific disagreement regarding its establishment.
For this very reason, he says: "but not for the purpose of excluding inference.
And in this regard, there is indeed a [certain] opinion.

Consequently, the commencement of this treatise would be for the purpose of refuting that [position]. And the commencement of the treatise is indeed intended for the sake of following both the Sautrāntika and Yogācāra views. Furthermore, the definition of non-discrepancy regarding the object of attainment does not apply here, because it is erroneous; thus, it is not direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Furthermore, because it lacks the quality of being produced from a mark possessing the three characteristics (*trirūpaliṅga*), it is not inference (*anumāna*).
Nor is there any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, it follows that the perception of a tree moving and so forth is false cognition (*mithyājñāna*).
If it is asked, "If it is false cognition, how can there be the attainment of a tree from it?
[the answer is: there is no attainment of a tree from it.
For a tree that moves to various locations is excluded by that [perception],
and a tree restricted to a single location is what is obtained.
Therefore, the place where the moving tree was seen is not the place where it is obtained.
If one were to say that the object which is attained is not seen, then some other object would be attained;
however, it is immediately after cognition that objects such as trees are attained.
Thus, the inclusion of the term "non-erroneous" (abhrānta) is for the purpose of eliminating misconception.
There is a disagreement;

for instance, the Mīmāṃsakas and others say this: "Just as non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*) is valid knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*), so too is the sensory cognition that associates [the object] with genus (*jāti*) and so forth valid knowledge, because it causes one to attain the object as it was presented. And thus they have said:

Furthermore, that cognition by which the object is subsequently determined through its properties such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth is also accepted as being of the nature of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). And thus the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇāḥ*) have said:
If the eternal nature of speech were to depart from consciousness, there would be no manifestation; for manifestation is that which brings about reflective awareness.
There is no cognition in the world that is devoid of the accompaniment of words;
all knowledge appears as if permeated by speech.

Likewise, the view of the Naiyāyikas and others that perception is conceptual (*savikalpaka*) is refuted by the inclusion of the term "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*). Thus, when non-conceptual perception is established by the inclusion of the term "free from conceptual construction," the mention of "non-apprehension" (of conceptual cognition) serves solely to refute misconceptions; for [conceptual cognitions] such as the knowledge of a double moon are already excluded from the category of valid cognition (*samyagjñāna*).

Thus, certain teachers belonging to a particular school (ekadeśīya) maintain that the cognition of yellow in a white conch, the cognition of a tree seen while moving, and the cognition of a fire-brand's circle (alātacakra) are non-erroneous and constitute valid knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), because the object itself is not erroneous, whereas the yellow form and so forth are erroneous.

Since there is such a disagreement, it is refuted by the inclusion of the term "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*); thus it is established that both [terms] serve the purpose of eliminating this disagreement.
This being the case, by the phrase "the inclusion of 'non-erroneous' (*abhrānta*)," etc., he demonstrates that the object of non-error is the subject of dispute.
The intention is that there is no attainment of the tree from that [cognition], because—as has been shown—the moving tree is not reached.
However, [the attainment] occurs precisely from another cognition.
Because a stable tree is apprehended by another direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
5. Conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) is the cognition of an appearance capable of being associated with a verbal expression.
Furthermore, being erroneous is accepted by both parties;
thus, there would be the undesirable consequence that inference, too, would be perception,
for that too is intended to be non-discrepant and indeed non-erroneous.
For this very reason, it was stated that [perception] is "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*) in order to exclude inference.
Therefore, the two qualifiers have the purpose already explained. (4)
In our established doctrine (siddhānta), the [unreal] conceptualization well-known [in other systems] has been rejected.
Conceptual construction (kalpanā) is defined as the cognition of an appearance capable of being associated with verbal expression, for the purpose of teaching worldly conceptualization.

"Verbal expression" (abhilāpa)—so called because one expresses by means of it—refers to the denotable object. Thus, since inference has already been excluded by the inclusion of the term "non-erroneous" (abhrānta), the inclusion of the term "free from conceptual construction" (kalpanāpoḍha) is for the purpose of dispelling misconceptions.
Inference is indeed erroneous because it functions by determining an object that is not present in its own appearance;
perception, however, is not mistaken regarding the form of the apprehended object.
But here, "non-erroneous" should not be understood as merely non-discrepant, because only correct cognition (*samyagjñāna*) is perception, and nothing else.

In that case, since non-contradictoriness is already established by the very fact of being right cognition (*samyagjñāna*), the further inclusion of the term "non-contradicting" would indeed be purposeless.
For the meaning of the sentence would then be: "That cognition called perception which is non-contradicting is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*) and is non-contradicting.
And there is nothing gained by this double inclusion of the term "non-contradicting."
Therefore, in this context, that which is non-erroneous regarding the nature of a thing capable of performing a function upon being apprehended should be understood as non-delusory. // 4 //
But what kind of conceptualization (*kalpanā*) is intended here?
To this he says: "expression" (*abhilāpa*), and so forth.
That by which something is expressed is an "expression."

The expressive word is the signifier (*vācaka*). "Association with expression" (*abhilāpasaṃsarga*) is the meeting of the form of the denotable object (*abhidheya*) with the form of the expression (*abhidhāna*) as objects of apprehension within a single cognition.

Therefore, when the forms of both the denotable and the denotative are present together in a single cognition, then—by means of the phrase "through such erroneous apprehension" and so forth—the inclusion of the term "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*) serves the purpose of refuting misconceptions regarding that [definition].
He demonstrates this;
and the object of misconception has not been shown by the author of the commentary because it is too well known.
As was stated previously: "The meaning of non-contradiction is the meaning of non-delusion."
He demonstrates the fault in grasping that object with the words, "But it is not non-discrepant," and so forth. // 4 //

Furthermore, with the words "What kind of conceptualization, then... and so forth, [the author] asks because he does not know which specific conceptualization is being referred to, given the multiplicity of such conceptualizations.

To explain: according to the Vaibhāṣikas, conceptualization (*kalpanā*) is the sensory consciousness associated with the mental factors of applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*).
And according to the Yogācāra view, with the exception of the non-dual gnosis of the Tathāgata, all cognition that is conceptualized in terms of the grasped and the grasper is conceptualization.
Others, however, state that conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) is mental cognition associated with birth, [age, and so forth].
By the words "expression" (*abhilāpa*) and so on, he shows that this refers to conceptualization associated with verbal expression, and not to those [associations] enumerated in the scriptures;
for if those were included, it would be impossible for sensory cognition to be direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

By the instrumental derivation "that by which something is expressed," this is shown: the expressive [word] is intended here by the term "expression" (abhilāpa), and not the expressed [object], which consists of the nature of sound-universals (śabdasāmānya).
The compound "association with expression" (abhilāpasaṃsarga) means association by means of expression.

Association (*saṃsarga*), however, is a connection (*sambandha*). "Capable of association with verbal expression" means capable of being associated with verbal expression; this refers to the universal of the object (*arthasāmānya*).
For that alone is capable of being expressed because it possesses positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) and is pervaded (*vyāpta*).
However, the specific object (*arthaviśeṣa*) in the form of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is such that the denoter and the denoted exist in a state of mutual connection.
That cognition in which there appears an image of the denoted object's form, which is fit for connection with verbal expression, is described as such.
In this regard, some cognition has an appearance conjoined with verbal expression,
such as the conceptualization of the object "jar" by one who has mastered linguistic conventions, which appears as an object conjoined with the word "jar.

However, some cognition, though not conjoined with verbal expression, has an appearance capable of being conjoined with verbal expression, such as the conceptualization of a child who has not mastered linguistic conventions.

In that context, if it were stated that "conceptualization is that which has an appearance associated with verbal expression," then the conceptualization of one who has not mastered linguistic conventions would not be included.
However, by using the term "capable" (*yogya*), even that is included— namely,
the conceptualization of a newborn infant, even though its appearance is not associated with verbal expression on that very day.
However, there certainly exists that which has an appearance capable of being associated with verbal expression;
and that which is already associated with verbal expression is also capable [of such association].
Therefore, both are included by the term "capable" (yogya).
By this, Vinītadeva’s explanation—that "denotable" (*abhilāpya*) means that which is denoted (*abhilāpa*), namely the universal (*sāmānya*) and so forth—is refuted.
This very [interpretation] must be adopted here; otherwise, by using the term "capable of being grasped" (*grāhya-yogya*), that which is capable of association with words would not have been stated.
If this is so, would it not follow that in Dharmottara’s commentary the non-associative nature of the denoter of genus (*jāti*) and so forth has not been demonstrated?
True, it was not explicitly set forth by him;
however, since he stated that the universal (*sāmānya*) and so on constitute the objective domain during the investigation of the object, it is established by implication—this is the resolution.
The meaning is that there is a conjunction within a single cognition by way of the relationship between the signified and the signifier.
Now, one might object: "Even if there is a merging of two forms within that cognition, nevertheless, there is no actual connection between the word and its object.
To this, he says: "Therefore, when in a single [cognition]," and so forth.
The intention is that even when there is a cognition of the connection between word and object, a merging of their two forms is not possible.

In this context, the passage beginning with "there is a certain cognition" demonstrates the scope of the term "suitable apprehension. It refers to the manifestation of the two forms in relation to one who has mastered the linguistic convention (*saṃketa*).

But surely, for those such as infants or the mute who have not mastered linguistic conventions, there is no association with words in their cognition; thus, the [cognition] lacks even that capacity [for association].
And what is this appearance capable of association?
It is the appearance of words.

In the cognition of the mute and others, however, since there is an absence of linguistic convention (*saṃketa*), even the appearance of words and meanings is impossible; thus, there is no fitness for connection (*sasargayogyatva*) either.
What is this so-called "fitness"?
It is the fitness for establishing a linguistic convention regarding the form of the denotable object.
And in the absence of the mention of a designation, there is neither the appearance of the designated object nor even its fitness;
thus Kumārila said:
For there exists first an indeterminate cognition of mere observation,
similar to the cognition of infants, the mute, and others, which arises from the pure object itself.
It cannot be expressed in words because it is pervaded by them.
That which is a manifestation in cognition capable of being associated with verbal expression is precisely what is meant by "a manifestation capable of being associated with verbal expression.
The phrase "the form of the object" refers to the universal of the object; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
Alternatively: that which is not expressed is "expression" (*abhilāpa*), meaning the object-universal (*arthasāmānya*) that is to be denoted.

The connection with expression is "connection with expression" (*abhilāpasaṃsarga*). That which is capable of such connection with expression is "capable of connection with expression" (*abhilāpasaṃsargayogya*).
It is the generality of the word (*śabdasāmānya*) that,

by virtue of positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*), is capable of denoting the object; however, it cannot be done by the particularity of the word (*śabdaviśeṣa*), because that [particularity] lacks generality.

If it is asked: "In cognition, that appearance which is capable of being associated with a verbal expression is itself the verbal expression; but in the absence of an actual association with a verbal expression, how is its capacity [for such association] established?
[The answer is: Because the appearance is indeterminate.
And its indeterminacy arises from the absence of any cause for the determination of the appearance.
For an object that is to be grasped, in producing consciousness, must produce a determinate appearance;
just as form, in producing visual consciousness, produces a determinate appearance, whereas conceptual consciousness does not arise from an object.
Consequently, because there is no cause for a restriction of manifestation, the manifestation is unrestricted.
But why is it that conceptual construction does not arise from the object?
Because it is independent of the presence of the object.

For even an infant, as long as he does not recognize through recollection that "this is that very same breast" by virtue of its prior familiarity, does not cease crying and apply his mouth to the breast.
Furthermore, a cognition that unifies an object previously seen with one currently seen has a non-present object,
because the previously seen object is no longer present.

It has for its object that which is not present before one, and it is independent of an external referent. Being independent, it possesses an indeterminate manifestation because there is no cause for a fixed manifestation;
and such a [cognition] is capable of being associated with verbal expression.

Then, he presents the opponent's doubt—that the inclusion of the term "capable" (*yogya*) need not be made because it is already excluded by the absence of non-existence—by means of the passage beginning with "in the absence of verbal expression" (*asatyabhilāpe*). He provides the reply with the passage beginning with "with an indeterminate appearance" (*aniyatapratibhāsa*).
He thinks as follows: "What is meant by 'being associated with words' (*śabdasamsargitvam*)?"
Conceptual cognition is indeed of an indeterminate nature.
How is this established?
To this, he says: "indeterminate," and so forth.
For that which arises from an object itself necessarily possesses a determinate appearance;
such is the intention regarding visual consciousness.
[Objection: But will not conceptual cognition also possess a determinate form when it arises from an object?
Thus he says: "conceptual cognition," and so forth.
The intention is that conceptual cognition arises even without the presence of an object.
Therefore, only sensory cognition possesses a determinate appearance.
Conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*), however, has an indeterminate appearance;
thus, he shows that even infants and the mute possess conceptual cognition with a determinate appearance by means of the passage beginning with "Even an infant... [and so forth].
But surely, since an infant lacks proficiency in the articulatory organs such as the palate, there is no utterance of words denoting universals (*sāmānya*) or particulars (*viśeṣa*).
Why, then, is it said, "This is that very same [person]"?
It is true that [the person] does not exist; however, by the expression "this is that very same," the state of conceptual construction (vikalpa) is indicated.
By the expression "this is that very same," it is precisely the fact of having been previously perceived that is expressed.
"Uparataruditaḥ" means "one from whom crying has ceased.

This demonstrates that even an infant possesses conceptual cognition (*vikalpaka-vijñāna*) characterized by the reflection upon preceding and succeeding moments, because it functions toward a restricted object.
Just as one who has grasped a linguistic convention acts through the synthesis of what precedes and what follows;

and that synthesis of the preceding and the following is an indefinite manifestation—the manifestation of the preceding and the following as being capable of connection—and the remainder [of the definition] is "the form of a general word-image" (śabdasāmānyākāra); this is what is meant.

Thus, through this etymological explanation of the term *śleṣa*, it should be understood that for both [types of cognition], there is a conceptualized form (*vikalpākāra*), which is a manifestation capable of being associated with verbal expression.
Sensory perception (*indriyavijñāna*), however, depends upon the object because it grasps only the object present before it;
and because the object is the cause for the restriction of the manifestation, it possesses a restricted manifestation.
Therefore, it is not capable of being associated with verbal expression.

For this very reason, having accepted that the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) itself constitutes the relationship between the signified and the signifier, its non-conceptual nature is asserted.
Even if the particular characteristic itself were both the signified and the signifier, [it would remain non-conceptual].
Nevertheless, cognition whose object is conjoined with verbal expression is conceptual (*savikalpaka*).

And sensory cognition is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*), because its manifestation is restricted by the [actual] object and thus does not possess a manifestation capable of being conjoined with verbal expression.
In that case, auditory cognition grasps the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of sound; [is it not conceptual?]

Furthermore, if some particular characteristic of sound (*śabdasvalakṣaṇa*) were both the signified and the signifier, there would be an appearance capable of being associated with verbal expression, and thus it would be conceptual (*savikalpaka*).

Since [the opponent might argue] that even the cognition of infants or the mute is capable of association because it is superimposed (*āropitatvāt*), the term "capable" (*yogya*) must be included in order to exclude such cases; this is the established position.

By the passage beginning with "sensory cognition" (*indriyavijñāna*), Kumārila has established that sensory cognition—termed "mere observation" (*ālocana*)—is similar to the cognition of infants, the mute, and so forth.
To refute this, [the author] demonstrates their distinction under the guise of a summary, starting with "for this very reason" (*ata eva*).
That sensory cognition which arises by the power of an object and possesses a determinate appearance (*niyatapratibhāsa*) is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*).

For this very reason, even while accepting that there is a relationship of denoted and denoter (*vācya-vācaka*) between a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and its word or object, the non-conceptual nature of sensory cognition (*indriyajñāna*) is established.
However, it is settled that conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*), even though the particular characteristic appears as both the denoted and the denoter, is indeed conceptual.
By the phrase "even though" (*yadyapi*), he demonstrates the acceptance of the relationship of denoted and denoter between the two particular characteristics.

According to the reasoning that, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), the relationship of signifier and signified belongs only to two universals (*sāmānya*) and not to specific objects or words, one must necessarily admit a signifier-signified relationship between two particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). Why? Because [the relationship] is being rejected precisely during the investigation of the object of the two universals; thus, the statement here regarding their non-conceptual nature (*nirvikalpatva*) would be futile.
For even that [conceptual cognition] has as its object only the non-conceptual, by way of considering whether something is an object or a non-object.
Therefore, Vinītadeva’s demonstration of the non-conceptual nature of sensory consciousness— by accepting a signifier-signified relationship between two universals—
is refuted through this line of reasoning.

With the passage beginning "In that case, auditory consciousness... and so forth, the opponent demonstrates the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of the position that the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is the relationship between the signifier and the signified.
Furthermore, the non-conceptual nature of sensory consciousness must be established;
one cannot accept a relationship of signifier and signified between two universals (*sāmānya*) and then claim that the particular characteristic of sound is the signified.
When the word "pot" or the word "sound" expresses a sound by means of a sound,
then there is a certain expressed particular characteristic of sound (*śabdasvalakṣaṇa*) and a certain expressing particular characteristic of sound.
Direct perception is cognition that is devoid of that [conceptualization] and is not produced by the delusions caused by darkness, rapid motion, traveling in a boat, ship, or the like.
"Recognition" (pratīti) means the act of cognizing; "by the intellect" (buddhyā) is the ellipsis. // 5 //
"Devoid of that" means devoid of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*);
the remainder of the sense is "devoid of the turbidity of conceptual construction.
By this statement, it is meant that the cognition which is devoid of the generic form (*sāmānyākāra*) of word and object—that very cognition [is the intended one].
This is what is meant by saying that it alone is the means of direct perception (*pratyakṣapramāṇa*).
Regarding the phrase "not produced by the delusions caused by cataracts, rapid rotation, traveling in a boat, or physical agitation":
here, "cataract" (*timira*) refers to an affliction of the eye.
"Whirling firebrand" refers to a circle of fire produced by a whirling torch and the like;
"traveling by boat" refers to traveling by means of a ship.
There is no fault in this concise formulation.

Even if there were a relationship of denoted and denoter between the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and the word, the particular characteristic perceived as having been seen at the time of the convention would have to be grasped as both the denoted and the denoter.
However, the state of being an object of perception existing at the time of the convention does not exist for the entity now.
For instance, the perception that existed at the time of the convention has ceased today.

In the same way, the object does not possess that status as an object [of the word] at the present time. Therefore, auditory cognition—which perceives the relationship between the signifier and the signified (*vācyavācakabhāva*)—does not perceive the fact that [the object] was seen at a previous time.

By this very logic, even the cognition of a yogi, despite its manifestation of all words and objects, is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) because it does not grasp the fact that [the object] was seen at the time of the linguistic convention (*saṃketa*). // 5 //

"By that": by that conceptualization (*kalpanā*), which is of the nature of conceptualization, [the object] is devoid [of it]; thus, the connection with what follows is: "that non-erroneous cognition which is empty [of conceptualization] is perception.

Since being free from conceptualization (*kalpanāpoḍhatva*) and being non-erroneous (*abhrāntatva*) are mutually dependent, when both are heard as pure [qualities], there is the appearance of both words in the verbal cognition; therefore, the intention is that auditory sensory cognition would be conceptual (*savikalpaka*) because its appearance is not restricted [to a single aspect].
"Even though," and so forth.

He thinks as follows: even if there is a relationship of signifier and signified (*vācya-vācaka*) between two specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), nevertheless, they do not appear as signifier and signified within auditory consciousness.
Rather, there is the manifestation of two pure [entities] alone,
because auditory consciousness arises by the power of the proximity of sounds; and yet, between two sounds that are merely proximate, there exists no relationship of signifier and signified.
As long as the recollection of the word existing at the time of the convention does not occur, how could there be either the state of being denoted or the state of being a denoter?
To the objection that this very word shall become the denoter through recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), he says: "And not at the time of the convention," and so forth.
The distinction between those two, the former and the latter, arises from the difference in their objects.
And what is the object of the convention for a word? It is that which has been made an object by the cognition existing at the time of the convention.
That which was previously made an object by cognition does not exist now, because when the previous cognition has perished, the state of being an object of that previous cognition is absent.

Therefore, not perceiving the state of being an object from the previous time, it arises as purely non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) through the power of the auditory organ with respect to the present object.

Even if both sound and its object are apprehended simultaneously at one time by the cognition of a yogi and by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), he shows that they must nevertheless be apprehended by the former because it pertains to a present object, with the verse beginning "The cognition of a yogi" and so forth. //5//
One might object: "Is not even conceptual cognition empty of a further conceptualization?
And if so, does it not follow that it too becomes non-conceptual?
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In that way, by means of conceptualization, i.e., by its very nature as conceptualization," and so forth.
Thus, there is a disturbance of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) due to the provocation of wind, bile, and phlegm.
"Timira, rapid spinning, traveling by boat, and agitation"—these are the first of those [conditions], hence they are called "timira, rapid spinning, traveling by boat, agitation, and so forth.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of conditions such as loss of vision and yellow vision is intended.
That in which delusion is placed is "that wherein delusion is placed" (*āhitavibhrama*);
that which is not so is "not having delusion placed in it" (*anāhitavibhrama*).
[The compound] *timirāśubhramaṇanauyānasaṃkṣobhānāhitavibhrama* means "that in which delusion has not been produced by cataracts, rapid spinning, or the agitation of traveling by boat."
And likewise, due to the disease of cataracts (timira), one sees two moons;
due to the movement of a boat, trees on the bank appear to be moving;
and due to the provocation of wind, bile, and so forth, objects appear as if they are blazing and the like.

In order to show that the definition of perception does not apply to each [term] individually, it is demonstrated that when those two definitions— being devoid of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) and being non-erroneous (*abhrānta*)— are mutually dependent, they together constitute the object of perception;
"timira" refers to a disorder of the eyes.
This cause of delusion resides in the sense faculties;
it is the rapid whirling of a firebrand and the like.
For when a firebrand or similar object is whirled slowly, the illusion of a wheel does not arise.
For that purpose, the wandering is qualified by the term "swift.
And this is the cause of error residing in the object.
"Nauyāna" means traveling by boat.
For one standing on a moving boat, the illusion of moving trees and so forth arises; thus, the mention of "yoga" [connection] is made.
And this is a cause of error residing in an external basis.
Alternatively, it refers to the disturbance of wind, bile, and phlegm.
For when the wind and other [humors] become disturbed, an illusion of a blazing pillar arises;
this is the cause of delusion pertaining to the internal.

And by all causes of delusion—whether they pertain to the external objects of the senses or to the internal basis—the sense organ is characterized as the substratum (dharmin) by conceptual cognition; here, "conceptuality" is the property (dharma) being defined.

Just as "horned" implies the state of having horns, so too, that cognition which is devoid of the nature of conceptual construction (*kalpanātva*) is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*). And there is no fault in this, for a conceptual cognition is not itself devoid of the nature of conceptual construction. Thus, between the two characteristics—being free from conceptual construction and being non-erroneous—there is a relationship of mutual qualifier and qualified.

In order to show that these two do not possess distinct characteristics independently, the word "perception" (*pratyakṣa*) is taken at the end and connected to both; by the phrase "that perception," it is linked with what follows,
showing that this cause of error resides in the sense organ,
because the sense organ has been affected by cataracts (*timira*).
"Rapid rotation" is the exclusion of the qualification "rotating slowly.
"Located in the object" [is the exclusion of its being located in the self].
Because objects such as a whirling firebrand serve as the cause for the appearance of a circle;
"the movement of a boat" is a question concerning the whole.

By the words "on a moving boat" (*gaccatyāṃ nāvī*) and so forth, he demonstrates the purpose [of the example] with the phrase "situated upon an external support" (*bāhyāśrayasthitam*). The "external" refers to the boat; that itself is the support. For one situated there, an error is said to occur by way of that support.
The agitation of the wind and other elements is their falling into a state of disorder, which is the cause of internal delusion.

Now, is it not the case that the cause of delusion is said to reside only within the sense faculties, such that the sense faculty undergoes modification through other factors residing in the sense faculties?
To this, he says: "By all [of them]," and so forth.
[The error] is caused by darkness directly, as in the case of a fire-brand wheel (*alātacakra*), and indirectly [in other cases].
This has also been explained in detail in the *Viniścayaṭīkā*.
Having formed a *dvandva* compound with the word "agitation" (*saṃkṣobha*), [it is then used] as a *bahuvrīhi*—
That is fourfold.
Regarding the statement "knowledge is direct perception," knowledge is not explicitly mentioned in the Sūtra. If it is asked how this is obtained:
Conceptual construction is bound exclusively to cognition,
and even error is seen to be a property of cognition;
therefore, [perception] is simply cognition that is free from conceptual construction and non-erroneous.

Just as when one says, "Let the cow without its calf be brought," it is not some horse that is brought, but rather the cow itself, because only that [cow] is seen to have a connection with the calf; so too here,
since a connection with cognition alone is observed for both error and conceptual construction,
and not with anything else, cognition itself is accepted as being perception.
Regarding the statement that "it is fourfold":
that which was called direct perception (pratyakṣa) consists of: 1) that produced by the sense faculties, and 2) mental [perception].
Self-awareness and the cognition of yogis—thus the object of knowledge is to be understood as fourfold.
This distinction must be established in this very way; for if the sense organ were unmodified, a sensory illusion would be impossible.
Those [defects] beginning with agitation (saṃkṣobha) and ending with those [just mentioned] are what is meant by the expression "and so forth" (ādi).

By the inclusion of "and so forth," defects residing in the sense organs (*indriya-stha*) such as cataracts (*kāca*) and jaundice (*kāmalā*) are included, as well as those residing in the objects (*viṣaya-stha*) such as rapid movement toward or away from [the object].
For when a fire-brand is whirled rapidly, there arises the illusion of a staff possessing the color of fire;
here, external bases such as riding an elephant and so forth,
as well as internal bases such as severe blows to the vital organs and so forth, are understood to be the causes of delusion.
That knowledge in which there is no appearance not produced by those [senses] is such that it is perception. // 6 //
Having thus explained the definition, [the author] shows that some have imagined the sense-faculty itself to be the seer, [and others] that it is mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*).

Regarding the term *viniścaya*, [the commentators] form a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) with the word *saṃkṣobha* and a possessive compound (*bahuvrīhisamāsa*) with the word *ādi*; what is the intention of the author of the *Ṣaṣṭhīkā* [in this regard]?
This is merely a difference in etymological derivation, not a difference in meaning.

When the word *saṃkṣobha* is understood as a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*), it includes wind, bile, and so forth, because they serve as indicators (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the causes of delusion residing in that substratum; thus, there is no difference in meaning.
Now, for what purpose is there the inclusion of "rapid spinning," "grasping," and so forth; let it simply be stated as "timira and so forth" (timirādi),
since by the inclusion of "and so forth" (ādi), all [such cases] will be subsumed?

It is said: if the mention of rapid rotation and so forth were absent, one might suspect that by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), only defects residing in the sense organs—such as cataracts or jaundice—are intended.
Therefore, rapid rotation and the rest are included.
When these are included, [the full range of causes is established].

If the inclusion of the word "etc. (ādi) were not made, then there would be only the apprehension of their specific forms, and not the indication of their modes; therefore, the word "etc. is included.

Therefore, it is established that when both [qualifiers] are employed, the entirety of both [the absence of error and the presence of clarity], such as the removal of visual impairment (*timira*), is obtained.

Although the term "cognition" (*jñāna*) is not explicitly mentioned in the Sūtra, there is no fault; for even though that [erroneous perception] is a cognition, it is excluded because it possesses the nature of error, and thus only valid cognition (*jñāna*) is understood as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
In Vinītadeva’s commentary, however, there is an explanation of the meaning of the sūtra on direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), stating: "Direct perception is cognition.
Therefore, it is established that non-conceptual cognition is direct perception and is non-erroneous. // 6 //
The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that it is the sense faculty itself which is conceptualized as the seer;
they assert that "the eye sees forms," and they have pointed out the fault in the position that mental perception (mānasa-pratyakṣa) exists.
"Monks, form is seen by two [consciousnesses]: by visual consciousness and by the mental consciousness drawn forth by it.
Thus, the mind is established for me.
8. Produced by the sense-faculties (*indriyajanya*). This is taught for the purpose of refuting [the opposing view]:
some maintain that the sense-faculty alone is intended to be the agent of seeing.
To refute that [view], it is stated first:
perception is indeed knowledge produced by the sense faculties,
but not the sense faculty itself.
Some have raised objections regarding mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*), and the second [section] is for the purpose of refuting those objections.
Some do not accept the self-cognition (*ātmasaṃvedana*) of the mind and its mental factors (*citta-caitta*); the third [section] is for the purpose of refuting that view.
Some do not accept the perception of yogins;
in order to refute that [position], the fourth type of perception was stated. // 7 //

Regarding the phrase "produced by the sense-faculties" (*indriyajanya*): only the five faculties, beginning with the eye, are accepted as being [the senses] in their capacity as *indriyas*. The mind (*manas*), however, is not [included here as a sense-faculty], because mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*) is mentioned separately.
Therefore, perception produced by the sense organs is simply the cognition that relies upon the sense organs, such as the eye and so forth. // 8 //
Furthermore, a fault has been pointed out regarding the definition,
and neither self-cognition nor the cognition of a yogi is accepted.
In order to refute their misconceptions, he states—showing the different types of perception—that "it is fourfold. (7)

Regarding "sensory cognition" (*indriyajñāna*): sensory cognition is the cognition of the sense faculty. That cognition which is dependent upon the sense faculties is perception (*pratyakṣa*). // 8 //
The Master Dignāga has demonstrated that cognition is perception (*pratyakṣa*).
This was refuted by others, such as Kumārila and his followers, who did not understand its defining characteristic.

[They argue: "If that mental cognition (*manojñāna*) operates upon the object of sensory cognition, then it is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it apprehends what has already been apprehended; however, if it operates upon a different object..."
If direct perception were to occur regarding an object that is obstructed, would that mental consciousness (manovijñāna) depend upon the sense faculty or not?
If it were dependent upon the sense faculty, it would simply be sensory consciousness (indriyavijñāna).

Alternatively, if [perception] were independent [of the senses], then even the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that lacks a sense faculty would be perception; thus, the objection was raised regarding the non-existence of the blind, the deaf, and so forth.
Furthermore, self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is not accepted [as perception].
By the Mīmāṃsakas, it is held that this [self-awareness] is a perceptual cognition to be understood through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).
The Naiyāyikas and others, however, maintain that cognition is apprehended by another cognition,

and not established through self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*), because it is contradictory for something to act upon itself; furthermore, they do not accept the existence of the knowledge of a yogi— this is the connection [of the argument].
The Mīmāṃsakas and others say this: "Yogins do not exist at present, because there is a lack of valid means of knowledge [to establish them]; how much less, then, can their cognition exist? // 7 //
Regarding the phrase "dependent on the faculties":
this refers to the four faculties beginning with the eye, and not to the mental faculty (*manaindriya*).
Because that [eye] is being established as being [known] through the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*).

By stating that "perception is cognition dependent on the sense faculties," the author of the *Vārttika* has effectively declared that the eye is not the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since it is the cognition itself— by virtue of its conformity with presence and absence—
that possesses the capacity for the perception of form and so forth.
It is not [the case] for the eye.
As for what was said: "If consciousness sees, why does it not see even that which is obstructed?"
As for the claim that "there can be no denoter of that which is formless," that is incorrect;
because that cognition is produced by an object situated in a suitable location, and not by one that is obstructed, since such [obstructed] cognition is never observed. // 8 //

That mental consciousness is produced by sensory cognition acting as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), which functions as a cooperative cause for the object immediately following its own object.

"Mental consciousness is that which is produced by sensory cognition as its immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), acting in cooperation with the object immediately following its own object.
In this context, "its own object" (*svaviṣaya*) means its own objective support (*ālambana*). This is the remainder of the sense.

"Immediately following its own object" (*svaviṣayānantara*) means that which occurs immediately after its own object. That which arises in the second moment and is of a similar nature is expressed by the word "immediately following.

It is called "having as its object that which is immediately following its own object" (*svaviṣayānantaraviṣaya*) because it has as its object that which is both immediately following its own object and an object.
That sensory cognition which has as its cooperative cause a sensory cognition whose object is immediately subsequent to its own object—

that very [cognition] produced by the sensory cognition acting as an immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) is mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*), because it relies solely upon the mind.
Regarding this mental perception, a certain objection has been raised by others.
To refute that [position], he states the definition of mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*), beginning with "its own object" (*svaviṣaya*) and so forth.

"Its own" (*sva*) means belonging to itself; "object" (*viṣaya*) refers to the object of sensory cognition (*indriyajñāna*). "Immediate" (*anantara*) means that there is no interval (*antara*) between it [the sensory cognition] and this [mental perception]. Thus, it is "immediate."
Furthermore, "immediacy" (*anantaram*) and "distinction" (*viśeṣaḥ*) are stated [as qualifiers].
Consequently, when an interval is excluded, a moment of the same kind as the object of the sensory cognition—namely, the second moment or the subsequent moment—is understood.
This being the case, the subsequent moment following the moment that was the object of the sensory cognition is grasped as being included within the same continuum.
That sensory cognition which has such an auxiliary is described as "having that [auxiliary].
And the auxiliary is of two kinds: that which assists mutually, and that which produces a single effect.
Furthermore, since it is impossible to impart any excellence (*atiśaya*) to a momentary entity, a cooperative cause (*sahakārī*) is understood by virtue of performing a single function together.
For it is through both the object and the sense-faculty that a single mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is produced;
therefore, these two possess mutual cooperation.
The explanation of the term *sva* (own) is "belonging to oneself" (*ātmīya*). It refers to the momentary object belonging to the sensory consciousness (*indriyavijñāna*).
The explanation of the phrase "immediately following that" (*tasyānantaram*) is "it does not wait," and so forth.
The explanation of the word *antara* is "interposition" (*vyavadhāna*), and so forth.

A moment of the same kind that is the object of sensory consciousness (*indriyavijñāna*)—a homogeneous moment that is not separated [from it]—is called the "homogeneous moment. That is the object, which is a moment to be appropriated (*upādeyakṣaṇa*).
By the mention of "the grasping of the object," intermediate light is excluded.
The grammatical connection is: "that which has such a [light] as its auxiliary cause.
But how can a momentary object be an auxiliary cause?
Is it because there is no relationship of benefactor and beneficiary in a single moment?
To this he says: "And by the two kinds," and so forth.
He thinks as follows: here, [the cause] is not a cooperative cause (*sahakārin*) by virtue of being a benefactor.
Rather, it is because they perform a single function;
he demonstrates this very point with the words beginning "viṣaya" (object), etc.,
by the phrase "by such [a means]," and so forth.
By means of sensory cognition, which has as its cooperative cause an object immediately following its own object;
that is, by means of that which serves as the objective condition (*ālambanapratyaya*).
This refers to when the cognition of a yogi takes as its object the various kinds of cognitions belonging to others.
Yogic cognition is produced by that which has become its object;
and this [object] is "equal" because even the immediately preceding moment is a cognition.
The term *smantara* also takes the form with a *ṣatva* suffix due to its inclusion in the list beginning with *śakan* (Pāṇini 8.3.106).

Therefore, the statement "and that" (*sa ceti*) here—referring to an object immediately following its own object—should be understood as intended to avoid two faults: the fault of apprehending what has already been apprehended (*gṛhītagrahaṇa*), and likewise the fault of apprehending an object of a different class (*asamānajātīya*).

For instance, mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*) is held to have as its object that which arises in the second moment immediately following the object of sensory consciousness (*indriyajñāna*). Therefore, how could there be the apprehension of what has already been apprehended?
Even by such a sensory consciousness, acting as an objective support (*ālambana*), the cognition of a yogin is produced.
To refute that [view], the term "immediately preceding condition" (*samanantarapratyaya*) was employed;
it is "equal" (*sama*) by virtue of being cognition, and "immediate" (*anantara*) by virtue of being uninterrupted.
And that [mental consciousness] is a condition (pratyaya) because it is a cause; thus, it is "produced by the immediately preceding condition" (samanantarapratyaya).

By this, it is stated that mental consciousness is direct perception (pratyakṣa) when there exists a relationship of producer and produced between sensory cognition and mental consciousness, both of which are included within a single continuum.

Consequently, the objection that the cognition of a yogin— which exists within the mental continuum of another— is invalid has been refuted. Furthermore, when the object of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is distinct from the object of sensory perception,
the defect of invalidity imputed on the grounds of apprehending what has already been apprehended (*gṛhītagrahaṇa*) is likewise refuted.
"Immediately preceding" means "because it is a cause";
this is an explanation of the meaning of the term *pratyaya*.

By the passage beginning with "produced by that," he explains this: that which is produced by sensory consciousness—which has its own object as a cooperative cause and serves as the substantial cause (upādāna)—is precisely what constitutes mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
The meaning is not that it is produced by [the object] serving as its objective support (*ālambana*).
By the passage beginning with "and when," the objection raised by the opponent—having taken one object for both [sensory and mental consciousness]—is refuted.

The object of sensory consciousness in the preceding moment is the object of mental consciousness in the second moment; thus, mental consciousness apprehends what has not yet been apprehended. As for the objection raised by Citta and others—that if mental consciousness were dependent upon the sense faculties, there would be no object of mental consciousness other than the object of sensory consciousness—[this is refuted as follows]:
In that case, there would be the absence of blindness, deafness, and so forth;
as for the argument that there might be perception of an obstructed blue object or the like,
that has already been refuted.

Since the object of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is the second moment of the object of sensory consciousness (*indriyavijñāna*), which serves as its appropriated cause (*upādeya*), therefore, an object separated by an interval is not its [mental consciousness’s] object; thus, there is no super-sensory cognition for those such as the blind or the deaf. Furthermore, the immediately preceding object of the [sensory] consciousness exists as a cooperative condition (*sahakāripratyaya*).
By this, it is refuted that mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) does not arise for them.

However, if it is stated that [mental consciousness arises] with the immediately preceding object of its own domain as a cooperative cause, then mental consciousness directed toward sound would not be possible;
for no subsequent moment of the "appropriated" (*upādeya*) arises from a sound that is the object of auditory consciousness.
Because sound is perishable,
and because one sound does not arise from another sound, mental perception must necessarily be admitted as having sound as its object;
otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the statement that "the five external [objects] are cognizable."

By the phrase "the object immediately following its own object," that which is capable of being the object immediately following the object of auditory consciousness is intended, not merely the momentary factor to be grasped (*upādeya*). Therefore, when another sound arises in the location of the object of that [auditory] consciousness, at that time mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*) is produced by having as its cooperative cause that object immediately following its own object; thus there is no fault.

Furthermore, the word "immediately following" (*anantara*) refers to that which belongs to the same class (*samānajātīya*); therefore, there is no undesirable consequence of [mental perception] apprehending an object of a different class.

Why is this so? Because it is stated that [mental consciousness] is produced by the sensory consciousness acting as its immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), when a moment that has become the object and the material cause for a sensory consciousness is apprehended, then—since another object not apprehended by the sensory cognition is grasped—the consequence of the defect that the blind and the deaf would not exist is refuted.
Furthermore, this mental consciousness is accepted as being perceptual (*pratyakṣa*) when the visual faculty has ceased its operation.
However, whatever cognition of form occurs when the eye is unimpaired is entirely dependent upon the eye; otherwise, the dependence of any consciousness whatsoever upon the eye would be untenable.
And this is what is known as mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*) established in our own tenets, yet there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that proves its existence.
If it were of such a nature, there would be no fault whatsoever; thus, its definition has been stated in order to express this. // 9 //

With the words "And this," etc., he shows the object of the arising of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Regarding the phrase "when the eye has ceased": when the eye, having perceived its object, has ceased, the visual consciousness that had arisen with respect to that perceived object does not, in the second moment, arise again with respect to an object immediately following its own object.

Because the sense faculties have no activity therein, it is established that direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) arises through that sensory consciousness, assisted by an object immediately following its own [sensory] object.

Now, one might object: "If it arises in a single moment, no purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) is achieved therein; therefore, since it is of no use for human goals (*puruṣārtha*), how can it attain the status of valid cognition (*prāmāṇya*)?"
It is said: for people like us, the attainment of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) does not occur through mental perception;
rather, it occurs for yogis who are free from passion and the like.
And they, having realized the object presented in that moment within the mind, attain purposeful action such as the teaching of the Dharma; thus, there is no fault.
Now, one might ask: "If the eye possesses activity, why is the arising of mental cognition (mānasa) not obstructed?
To this, he says: "Possessing activity," and so forth.
Knowledge based on all the sense-faculties is indeed visual consciousness (cakṣurvijñāna).
The intention is that there is no arising of mental consciousness [at the first moment].
But surely, when the eye is active, sensory consciousness occurs in the first moment, and mental consciousness occurs in the second moment?
Even though there is no simultaneous arising of two things of the same kind, he says "otherwise," and so forth.
He thinks as follows: why is it that when the eye is functioning, sensory consciousness does not arise [simultaneously]?
In the second moment, when the appropriate causal conditions are present, it possesses an identical form; therefore, why should these two not be designated as sensory cognition (*indriya-vijñāna*)?
Now, if mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*) were distinct from sensory cognition and established as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) such as direct perception, [then it would indeed be so].
If one asks, "In that case, how could its characteristic even exist as established by valid cognition?
he says: "And this," and so forth;
[meaning] "of such a kind."
It is similar to sensory consciousness.

This very argument— "because of the arising of conceptual construction"— which was put forward as a proof for the existence of mental perception by masters such as Jñānagarbha and others, who were demonstrating that this [mental perception] is established by scripture according to Dharmottara,
has been refuted precisely by the determination [of the nature of conceptualization] through its own internal logic.
Thus it has been explained by you: when the eye is active, sensory cognition and mental cognition arise; however, self-awareness of all minds and mental factors cannot be established. (3)
The fault of the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) has been refuted.

In the case of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) of those who are blind or deaf, there is no sensory consciousness (*indriyavijñāna*) acting as its immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
Therefore, as for what some have said—that the direct perception of external objects is admitted by means of the mental consciousness—[that is rejected].
Thus, it should be understood that the statement regarding the consequence of the non-existence of blind men, those born blind, and so forth, has been refuted. // 9 //
"All mental states and mental factors are self-cognizing. "All those [which are] mind and mental factors" is the term *sarvacittacaittāḥ*.
He says "all mind," and so forth, in order to explain self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*).

The mind (*citta*) grasps the mere object, while mental factors (*caitta*), such as pleasure and so forth, grasp specific states [of that object]. All these minds and mental factors are said to be "all minds" because there is no simultaneous arising of two [identical] things; for there is no [simultaneous arising] of two [minds] based on the same sense faculty.
There is no simultaneous arising of two [cognitions] from different sense-faculties, according to the statement that "the six [cognitions] do not arise simultaneously.
Consequently, there is a simultaneous arising of two [cognitions] from the same sense-faculty.

Nor can it be said that the mental [perception] does not exist there simply because it is not apprehended as distinct [from the sensory perception], for there arises a conceptualization of blue belonging to the same class [of objects].
Moreover, if that [initial perception] were not mental,
the subsequent conceptualization of blue would not occur at all.
For conceptual construction arises from a homogeneous mental self,
not from a heterogeneous sensory cognition;
just as when Devadatta perceives blue, Yajñadatta does not have a determination of blue.
Likewise, the continuum of sensory consciousnesses is distinct [from the mental continuum] because they are different; however,

there is no difference in the continuum between the mental consciousness (*mānasa*) and mental conceptualization (*manovikalpa*), because both are non-sensory and both are designated as "mind" (*manas*).

To this it is replied: as for what was stated—that [the cognition] arises from a conceptualization of a similar class—that proof for its existence is inconclusive (anaikāntika), because production is observed even from a dissimilar class through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka). Furthermore, there is no arising of mental cognition while the eye is active.
Furthermore, the simultaneous arising of two non-conceptual cognitions of blue is not observed,
because such a thing is not perceived.

Therefore, since conceptual cognition arises from a sensory cognition that is of a different class and not from another conceptual cognition, this is the reason for establishing the existence of mental cognition (*mānasa*).
Furthermore, conceptual and non-conceptual cognitions do not exist in separate continua like Devadatta and Yajñadatta,
such that production from a non-conceptual cognition in a different continuum would be impossible; for those two belong to a single continuum.
Furthermore, the arising of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) must necessarily be admitted,
since the author of the *Vārttika* has stated: "That [conceptualization] occurs through the power of consciousness regarding those very things already seen."
"Because it performs its own function through recollection," and so forth.
By the term "savicca," only sensory consciousness (*indriya-vijñāna*) is meant, not mental consciousness (*mānasa*).
Consequently, how could a conceptual cognition (*vikalpa-vijñāna*) arising from its power be a recollection?
Because they are of a different nature (*vijātīyatva*).

Furthermore, mental cognition (*mānasa-saṃvit*) is not said to exist there [in that context] because sensory consciousness (*indriya-vijñāna*) is treated according to conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), since its validity (*prāmāṇya*) is what is being investigated. Moreover, how could sensory consciousness possess validity?
If it performs its own function?
But its own function consists in nothing other than generating a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) regarding its own object;
and since a conceptual construction can arise even from that which is of a different class, this [objection] is trivial. // 9 //

Now, one might object: since it would have been sufficient to say "mind and mental factors" (*cittacaittāḥ*), the inclusion of the term "all" (*sarva*) is pointless, as there is nothing to be excluded.
[We reply: By saying "all," even erroneous cognitions (*bhrāntijñāna*) are included;
and the manifestation of their own nature is what constitutes self-awareness (*ātmasaṃvedana*).
For all minds and mental factors, because they have the nature of being manifest, are revealers of their own form; just as a lamp, because it has the nature of illumination,
illuminates itself and does not require another lamp for the illumination of its own form, so too are the mental factors.
The term "all" is employed to dispel the doubt that pleasure and so forth alone are self-cognized because they are clearly experienced, whereas other states of mind are not;
for there is no state of mind whatsoever [that is not self-cognized].
In that case, the self-awareness of the self would not be direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
For in whatever form the self is experienced, that form constitutes the direct perception of self-awareness.
And here, when an external object such as a visible form is being perceived, one experiences an internal aspect such as pleasure and so forth at the same time.

Nor can it be said that the apprehended form, such as blue and so forth, is experienced as having the nature of pleasure (*sāta*); for it is certain that blue and so forth are experienced as having the nature of pleasure.
For if it were certain that this blue and so forth is experienced as having the nature of pleasure, then it would possess the nature of pleasure and so on.
That form in which the direct-perceiving activity (*sākṣātkāritva*) of perception is followed by conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is perception.
Thus he says: "Pleasure and so forth alone," and so on.
The intended meaning is that not only well-known mental states such as pleasure, which are self-cognized (*svasaṃvedana*), are grasped, but others as well are self-cognized.
He demonstrates this very point with the words beginning "it does not exist" (nāsti).
The intended meaning is that he asserts the non-existence of the pure state of mind which is unperceived.
By speaking thus, the author of the commentary (*ṭīkākṛt*) has shown his intention that there is indeed an absence of pure mind during the state of the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
In that state, no mental state whatsoever is experienced;
for has it not been stated that there is no self-awareness (*ātmasaṃvedana*) of minds and mental factors (*cittacaitta*), because of the contradiction in [the same thing] acting upon itself?
Thus he says: "By which," and so forth.
Because one experiences the nature of the self by means of this nature of consciousness, that is called direct perception as self-cognition (*ātmasaṃvedana*).

He thinks as follows: just as a lamp, by its very nature of illumination, reveals its own form and does not require another lamp for its own manifestation, so too the mind and other such entities, by their nature of consciousness (*saṃvid*), reveal their own form and do not require another cognition for their self-awareness.
Nor is there a contradiction in something acting upon itself.
Since there is an absence of real agency,
even here the relationship of object and agent exists through conceptual construction by way of being the illuminated and the illuminator.
In that case as well, the very arising of the form of blue constitutes the illumination of the cognition, just as for a lamp, it is simply its prior existence [that constitutes its illumination].
The nature of manifestation is a conceptual operation;
however, for consciousness, its very arising in the form of awareness is its self-luminosity.
Therefore, since consciousness is experienced through direct perception in its form as awareness, how can you deny it by claiming that consciousness is imperceptible?
Thus far, for the sake of the Mīmāṃsakas and others, consciousness has been pointed out as being established by the perception of self-awareness (saṃvedana).
But as for the Sāṃkhya who maintains that pleasure and so forth are external forms, he says in response to him: "And here..."
(4) And there is the yogic cognition produced from the ultimate limit of the intensification of the cultivation of an object that was previously heard.
Likewise, mental states and mental factors also do not depend on another cognition for the awareness of their own nature;
therefore, being established by themselves, they are themselves the means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*). // 10 //
Yogic cognition is that which arises from the ultimate limit of the intensification of the cultivation of the real object (*bhūtārtha*). Here,
"real object" (*bhūtārtha*) means an object (*artha*) that is "real" (*bhūta*), i.e., non-erroneous (*aviparīta*),
such as the four noble truths.
Its cultivation is the cultivation of the real object.
Regarding this "cultivation," the nature of pleasure is not perceived in the blue [object].
Therefore, at the time of experiencing the blue, that which is experienced as pleasure is indeed something other than the unpleasant blue object.
And that [object] is indeed cognition itself;
therefore, there is the experience of cognition.
And that Devadatta, who is of the nature of cognition, is a direct perception of the self, free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpaka*).
And it is non-erroneous;
therefore, it is direct perception (pratyakṣa). // 10 //
Desiring to explain yogic direct perception (*yogipratyakṣa*), he says: "A real object," and so forth.
A "real" (*bhūta*) object is one that truly exists;
it is "truly existent" (*sadbhūta*) because it has been perceived by a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For example: the four noble truths. Cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is the repeated mental application of that which is real.
The culmination of cultivation is the commencement of the clarity of the cognition in which the object being cultivated appears.

The limit of excellence (*prakarṣa*) is when the state of appearing clearly (*sphuṭābhatva*) becomes slightly incomplete. For as long as the clarity is not fully perfected, there is a progression toward that excellence.
This refers to the passage beginning with "when form and so forth are being perceived," and so on.

He thinks as follows: the experience of pleasure and so forth, which is distinct from the blue form and is perceived through direct perception, cannot be said to be non-different in nature from the external object or to be insentient.
He demonstrates this point with the words beginning "na ca gṛhyamāṇākāra" (nor is the apprehended form...
and so on, [concluding with] "the operation of direct manifestation."
The function belongs to direct perception;
the conceptual construction follows upon it.
Furthermore, the nature of blue as being pleasurable is not apprehended [by perception].
The meaning is that the blue and so forth are subsequently followed by a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) in the form of pleasure (*sāta*).

Therefore, the blue and so forth do not have pleasure as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), as this is not established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). By thus refuting the Sāṅkhya, [the author] has demonstrated that direct perception—which consists of the forms of pleasure and so forth—is distinct from the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*).
Consequently, what was stated by some is correct: "A grasper distinct from the grasped is not experienced through direct perception."
Therefore, it has been stated that nothing whatsoever is denied [by this].

Consequently, all these minds and mental factors are directly perceived through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*). He applies their definitions, beginning with the words "And that... and so forth.
That perception is of the nature of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) and is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*), because there is an absence of association with words and so forth therein.
Why? Because there is an absence of linguistic convention (*saṃketa*) with respect to the word.
And that cognition is non-erroneous (*abhrānta*), because it is not inverted regarding its own nature (*svarūpa*).
And because there is no subverting evidence. // 10 //
"Of that which has the appearance of the object being cultivated" means of that which apprehends momentariness and so forth;
"the beginning of the onset of clarity" means from the commencement of this excellence.

Because there is no further excellence beyond that point for cognition, and because it is momentary, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) which grasps [the object] as momentary and so forth is cultivated until it is slightly incomplete; this final moment is called the "culmination of excellence" (*prakarṣaparyanta*). He demonstrates that very point with the word "practice" (*abhyāsa*).
Its excellence is the excellence of the cultivation of the true object;
[it consists of] the applications of mindfulness, the stages of heat, the summits, and the patiences.
Its limit is the limit of the excellence of the cultivation of the true object.
The limit, however, is the highest stage (*agradharmā*).
That which is born from that is "born from the culmination of the excellence of the cultivation of the true object.
Yoga is meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Those who possess this are yogins;
their knowledge is "yogic knowledge.
For thus, through the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), there arises an unerring light that reveals, according to reality, the past, future, and present.
Just as when dream-cognitions become complete with respect to past and future events through the power of the gods and so forth,
there is no further progression;
therefore, the state preceding the state of completion is called the limit of the excellence of vivid manifestation.
Therefore, the cognition that arises from that ultimate limit—which, for the yogin, grasps the clearer aspect of the object being cultivated as if it were present—is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
In this context, the stage of the commencement of its appearance as clear is the state of the intensification of cultivation (*bhāvanāprakarṣa*).
When one sees the object being cultivated as if separated by mica, that is the state of the culmination of intensification (*prakarṣaparyantāvasthā*).
The perception of an object being meditated upon as clearly as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one's hand is the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the yogin;
for that indeed possesses a vivid appearance,
as indicated by the passage beginning with "when there is vivid appearance" and so forth.
