Thus, here, by means of the concluding verse beginning with "the commencement of clarity" (*sphuṭābhatvārambha*), he shows the three states of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) of the yogi: the first is the state of the excellence of cultivation (*bhāvanāprakarṣa*);
the second is the state at the limit of excellence (*prakarṣaparyanta*);
and the third is the yogi’s perception of the object being cultivated as clearly as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand.

Thus, by the passage beginning with "clearly appearing" (*sphuṭābham*), [the author] shows that even the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) of the yogin is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) precisely because of its clarity, just like sensory consciousness. According to the principle that "for one bound to non-conceptuality, a clear object appears," although the word and its referent are grasped simultaneously by the mental consciousness at the culmination of the excellence of cultivation, nevertheless, because the intrinsic natures (*svarūpa*) of both are being grasped due to their presence, [it remains non-conceptual].
The consciousness that grasps that [object] is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*).
But is it not the case that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), when being cultivated, appears as conjoined with the signified and the signifier?
Just so, when the mental consciousness is cultivated to the ultimate limit of excellence, it becomes clearly manifest, appearing without the manifestation of signified and signifier.

Regarding what was asserted by the opponent—that because it appears clearly at that time, this [cognition] is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*), and thus the reason [adduced] is inconclusive—the author begins to refute that with the words "For conceptual cognition... and so forth.
He thinks as follows: even though mental cognition (*manovijñāna*) manifests as a fusion of the signified and the signifier, [it is not non-conceptual].
Nevertheless, in the state of vivid manifestation, that unreal form consisting of the signified and the signifier disappears; its own nature, however, is the form of consciousness.
Therefore, that very knowledge, which is the nature of consciousness, becomes clearly manifest.
Nor can it be said that [the cognition] has the form of the signifier and the signified, because those two are superimposed forms;
for if there were grasping of a superimposed form, there would simply be no clarity [of the cognition], and thus the reason— "because of appearing clearly"— is not inconclusive.
But when conceptual consciousness apprehends an object capable of being associated with a word, it apprehends that object as having been perceived at the time of the linguistic convention;
since that [object] is not present [at the time of cognition], non-erroneous cognitions arise with respect to various objects.
In the same way, through the power of yoga, there arises for those who meditate a luminous form of knowledge that illuminates objects—whether past or future, distant or separated, and even subtle.
Therefore, it is accepted as being a means of valid cognition (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*).

Here is the formal argument (*prayoga*): The knowledge of the lords of yogis whose minds are one-pointed is a valid means of cognition regarding past and future entities, because it is the cause for the non-erroneous presentation of the entire range of knowable past and future things.
Just as in the case of one possessed by a particular spirit or graha,
that which is not authoritative is not a cause for the non-erroneous presentation of a class of objects— whether past, present, or future— that is beyond the scope of measurement,
such as the cognition of a madman.

Even for that which does not bring about attainment, there would have to be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that is incapable and even harmful, for the sake of presenting non-erroneously a multitude of objects—past and future—that are immeasurable.
Indeed, the non-erroneous presentation of an immeasurable entity is not possible through mere deception.
Its explanation is as follows: just as, when possessed by a particular planetary spirit, there is the instruction regarding a collection of past and future things.
Likewise, among yogis as well, instruction regarding past and future things is found to be unerring.
For example, the unerring instruction of Caraka and other masters that the *harītakī* and so forth are capable of warding off future diseases is observed.

Or, for instance, in the teaching of the Blessed Śākyamuni, the non-erroneous attainment of signs concerning future places is observed, such as the arrival of Mātṛceṭa, Kālakṣaya, King Aśoka, and others in regions like Āśāvana and Kaśmīra.
And it is precisely because of its vivid manifestation (*sphuṭābhatva*) that [this cognition] is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*).

For a conceptualizing consciousness (*vikalpavijñāna*), in grasping an object as having been seen at the time of the linguistic convention (*saṃketa*), would grasp it as being fit for association with words. And "having been seen at the time of the convention" means being the object of a cognition produced at the time of the convention.
Just as a previously arisen cognition that has perished is non-existent at present,
so too a previously perished cognition does not exist at present as a real entity; thus,
[the subsequent cognition], apprehending that entity in its non-existent form, [is erroneous].
Because it grasps an object that is not present [before the senses], conceptual cognition has an unclear appearance;
therefore, because it has a clear appearance, non-conceptual cognition is free from conceptual construction.
Furthermore, because it grasps an object purified by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is reliable.
Therefore, this is direct perception,
like other forms of direct perception;
"yoga" means meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
He who possesses that [yoga] is a yogin;
his knowledge is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
The word "iti" indicates the conclusion.
This alone is perception. // 11 //
Because there is no linguistic convention for that [object];
and that previously perceived object was the domain of a prior cognition;
and that prior cognition does not exist now, at the time of grasping the object capable of being associated with a word.
Because cognition is momentary, the former object of consciousness no longer exists at present;

since the cognizing consciousness is absent, the object—the referent existing at the time of the linguistic convention—is also absent. Thus, the conceptual cognition that grasps by superimposing that object which was present at the time of the convention is indistinct.
Thus it is said: "It exists.
Since clarity is excluded from that [non-conceptual state], the pervasion—that one abides in the non-conceptual—is established.

Therefore, because of its clarity, the non-conceptual cognition of the yogin is non-erroneous; and because it apprehends a pure object, it is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) since it is consistent with reality.
"Only this much" means that from sensory perception up to the knowledge of yogins, there is not only sensory direct perception;
nor is there anything more, because nothing further is perceived. // 11 //
Its object is the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa).
In order to dispel misconceptions regarding its object, he says: "Its object is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

Regarding that which was stated as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) called perception (*pratyakṣa*), it should be understood that its object is exclusively the particular characteristic, and not the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), because a universal is not a real entity (*avastu*).
And because the nature of the thing is apprehended through direct perception. // 12 //

Thus, having established the different varieties of perception—which is characterized by being free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*) and non-erroneous (*abhrānta*)—the author, desiring to refute misconceptions regarding its object, says: "Of that," and so forth.
The object of that fourfold perception should be understood as the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Its own (*svam*)—that is, its unique (*asādhāraṇa*)—characteristic or reality is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
For an object possesses both an uncommon essence and a universal essence.
Of these, that which is uncommon is the apprehended object (*grāhya*) of perception.
For the object of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is twofold: the apprehended object, which is the form according to which [the cognition] arises; and...
And that which one determines is what is to be attained;
for indeed, the object of apprehension is one thing, while the object of determination is another.

For in the case of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), only a single moment is the object of apprehension (*grāhya*); however, what is determined (*adhyavaseya*) is the continuum (*santāna*) itself by means of the ascertainment produced through the power of that perception. And it is precisely this continuum that is to be attained (*prāpaṇīya*) by perception.
Because it is impossible to reach [the object] in a single moment;
likewise, inference also grasps what is not the object, since it functions by determining its own internal representation—which is not the actual object—to be the object.
This refers to the distinction in modes [of apprehension].
The meaning is: having established that perception is non-conceptual and non-erroneous with respect to the universal (*sāmānya*),
and that its specific varieties include sensory cognition (*indriyajñāna*) and so forth.
Regarding the "misconception concerning the object":
here, some Mīmāṃsakas have postulated that both the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*) are objects of perception (*pratyakṣa*),
whereas for inference (*anumāna*), only the universal is the object, not the particular.
According to the Sāṃkhya, the object of both [perception and inference] is intended to be the particular (*viśeṣa*), because of the absence of a universal (*sāmānya*).

According to the Vedāntin, however, the object of both is the universal alone, because everything is one due to its being non-different from the Self; thus, there is a disagreement regarding the object of perception and the other means of knowledge, namely that for the former it is the particular, while for the latter it is the universal.
"Specific characteristic" (svalakṣaṇa):
by this, he indicates the intended object.
"Reality" (tattva): [by this, he indicates the intended nature].
It is that which performs a purposeful action (*arthakriyākārin*).
By this, the word "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) is explained:
that by means of which a purposeful action such as burning and so forth is characterized (*lakṣyate*) is a characteristic.
This demonstrates that the unique (*asādhāraṇa*) essence alone is the true nature (*rūpa*) of a thing;
whereas the common (*sādhāraṇa*) essence is a superimposed form (*āropita-rūpa*), because preceding and succeeding moments are determined to be non-different in name.
Therefore, a thing has two forms: the unique and—
And [it concerns] the universal.
In that regard, he shows that the unique reality (*asādhāraṇatattva*) is the object grasped by perception with the words beginning "that which is unique," and so forth.
Now, what is meant by the term "object grasped" (*grāhyaviṣaya*)?
To what extent is there another object for perception? He says that there is: "of two kinds," and so forth; [it is that] which one determines.
That object which exists as a continuum is determined by a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that arises subsequent to it.
But how can a continuum be the object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*),
given that it is the object of conceptual construction?
It is said: [it is] by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*).

Because it is made an object by conceptualization (*vikalpa*) through the operation of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as that which is to be determined (*adhyavaseya*), it is called an "object of direct perception" by way of metaphorical designation; thus there is no fault.
He clarifies this very twofold nature with the words beginning "for another... and so forth.
That object, through whose presence or absence there is a difference in the manifestation of cognition, is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
If it is asked what the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is to be understood as, he says in that regard: "of which" (*yasya*).
"Proximity" (*sannidhāna*) means staying in a suitable location.
Non-proximity (*asannidhāna*) is staying in an unsuitable place and being entirely absent everywhere;
proximity (*sannidhāna*) and non-proximity together constitute "proximity and non-proximity."
For by those two, a distinction is made in cognition between clarity and lack of clarity:

when [the object] is present, a cognition with a clear manifestation arises; when it is absent, however, that superimposed object, being grasped, is determined as if it were a specific particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), because of which [it appears so].
Therefore, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) has been established as the object of engagement for inference;
however, the [external] thing itself is the apprehended object (*grāhya*).

Thus, in this context, by demonstrating the apprehended object of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is stated that the particular characteristic is the object of perception (*pratyakṣa*). // 12 //

But what is this object of cognition that is to be understood as the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)? To this he says: "Of which object," and so forth. The word *artha* is a synonym for *viṣaya* (object).
The proximity (*sannidhāna*) of that object of knowledge is its abiding in a nearby location,
while its non-proximity (*asannidhāna*) is its abiding in a distant location.
Therefore, due to proximity and non-proximity, there is a distinction between the appearance of cognition and its objective aspect, characterized by clarity and lack of clarity.
Likewise, with the words "inference" and so forth, he demonstrates through this incidental discussion that inference also possesses a twofold object:
"it is determined as a specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)."
The meaning is that [the object] is determined as being capable of performing causal functions such as burning.

By the words "tadanena" and so forth, he demonstrates that in the investigation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), this [cognition] has the perceived object as its domain, not the object to be attained.
Because there is disagreement among all [schools] regarding the very object that is to be apprehended. // 12 //
"But what is that object? and so forth.

He thinks thus: when it is stated that "the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is the object of perception," one might ask whether the universal (*sāmānya*) is also its object, in which case it would follow that the universal is also a particular characteristic. This is the question.
By stating that "non-proximity" means "abiding at a distance," Vinītadeva’s explanation has been refuted.
For this very reason, it has been explained that the non-existence and non-presence of an object in every respect [is what is meant by "absence"].
This is inconsistent, because when an object is absent there, there is indeed cognition;
and consequently, the distinction between the appearances of cognitions would not be possible.
With the words "For that which... and so forth, he demonstrates this:

the distinction between clear and unclear appearances arises solely from the presence or absence of that which is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsamartha*), and not of the universal (*sāmānya*).
"The universal (*sāmānya*) is not the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), because that which has a superimposed form is always indistinct from both far and near.
[The opponent objects: "But surely it is only the universal that, when apprehended at a distance, appears indistinctly, and not the particular characteristic?
To this he says: "All indeed," and so forth.
The question is: "Because the universal (sāmānya) does not exist.
Therefore, it is those very particular characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) that appear clearly or unclearly, not the universal.
Now, if the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) were to possess two forms— a clear appearance and an unclear appearance—
due to being distant or near, then for one standing nearby, there would have to be two appearances; yet there is no such rule that it must be unclear when distant and clear when near.

It is said: for a blue object cannot be both clearly manifest and not clearly manifest; rather, that which is blue and capable of performing the intended causal function is alone ultimately real (*paramārthasat*).
Furthermore, an indistinct cognition arises;
that object which causes a distinction in the manifestation within that cognition is precisely the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa). // 13 //
Granted that the ultimate reality (*paramārthasat*) is the object of perception;
if it is asked why the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is its object, he says in response: "That very [reality] itself."
It is "ultimate reality" (paramārtha) because it is both supreme (parama) and an object (artha).
"Supreme" means uncreated; the remainder [of the definition] is that it is devoid of superimposition (āropa).
That which exists as the ultimate reality is "ultimately existent" (*paramārthasat*).
For only the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is ultimately existent;
therefore, the aforementioned fault does not apply. // 14 //
That which, being present, produces a clear appearance in cognition when it is the object of that cognition,
but produces an unclear appearance when not present— provided it remains in a suitable location—
is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
For indeed, all things are seen indistinctly from a distance, but clearly when near; these very things are the particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). // 13 //

But why is it that only the object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), whereas fire, which is also the object of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), is determined as having a perceptible nature?
To this he says: "That alone is ultimately real" (*tadeva paramārthasat*).
The ultimate object (*paramārtha*) is the uncontrived, non-superimposed nature; that which exists by virtue of this is "ultimately existent" (*paramārthasat*).
That very object which, through its presence or absence, produces a clear or unclear appearance is alone ultimately existent.
And since that is the object of direct perception, therefore it alone is the particular (svalakṣaṇa). // 14 //
There are two blue atoms;
moreover, the distinct and indistinct forms are produced by adventitious conditions (*upādhi*).
When one perceives blue from a distance, because the atoms of light are overwhelmed by the atoms of dust, the cognition arises as an indistinct appearance.

However, because of the great number of light-atoms (*āloka-paramāṇu*) nearby, those [light-atoms] are not overwhelmed by the dust-atoms (*rajas-paramāṇu*); thus, a cognition with a clear manifestation arises.
Through the clarity of the cognition, the object takes on clear or unclear forms, but this is not so in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*).
But for the universal, because it is accessed through cognition, there are no distinct and non-distinct forms;
therefore, it is not a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). // 13 //
Now, it has been stated that its object is the particular (svalakṣaṇa); in that case, if the particular is the object of perception alone and not of anything else, [how can this be so?]
In that case, inference and the like would have the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as their object;
however, this is not so, because the object of perception is something else.
Now, if the particular characteristic is the object of perception and nothing else, [then...]

Thinking that, in that case, it would follow that inference has the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object because it is not excluded [from being so], he asks with the words "But why... and so forth.
[The answer is: The object of inference—that is, of conceptual construction—is not real.
How does it become a specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)?
To this he says: "For instance" (*tathā hi*), and so forth.
Even though the object of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is not a real entity (*vastu*), [it is nevertheless a specific characteristic].

Nevertheless, the intended meaning is that it is precisely that which is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), because it is determined as having the nature of causal efficiency such as burning and so forth;
that alone is what is ultimately real (*paramārthasat*).
He thinks thus: for a non-entity does not become an entity through the force of superimposition, because an entity is characterized by the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).
16. The other is the general characteristic.
If it is asked why the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) alone is ultimately real (*paramārthasat*), he says "artha" and so forth. Here, *artha* means purpose (*prayojana*).
Action is accomplishment.
The action of an object is "objective action" (*arthakriyā*);
the remainder of the sense is that it is the accomplishment of a purpose.
In that context, "capacity" means the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*).

That thing whose characteristic or intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is the capacity for causal efficiency is "that which has the capacity for causal efficiency as its characteristic" (*arthakriyāsāmarthya-lakṣaṇa*).
The state of being such is "having the capacity for causal efficiency as its characteristic" (*arthakriyāsāmarthya-lakṣaṇatva*).

Therefore, because [reality] is characterized by the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*), that which is capable of causal efficiency is alone the real entity (*vastu*). Thus, it is demonstrated that causal efficiency belongs only to the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). Consequently, only the particular characteristic is ultimately existent (*paramārthasat*). // 15 //
Why, then, is that alone ultimately real? To this he says: "artha," and so forth.
It is called *artha* because it is sought (*arthita*); that is, it is both to be abandoned (*heya*) and to be adopted (*upādeya*).
For that which is to be abandoned is intended to be abandoned,
and that which is to be accepted is intended to be accepted; this refers to the purpose or objective.
Action is accomplishment;
capacity is the power for that [accomplishment];
that very thing is the characteristic—the essential form—of the entity.
That is characterized by the capacity for causal efficiency;
"from that" means from its existence as such.
The word *vastu* (entity) is a synonym for the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
This is the meaning: because that which is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is called ultimately real (*paramārthasat*),
and because an object that differentiates the appearance in cognition through its presence or absence is what possesses causal efficiency,
therefore that alone is ultimately real.
For it is precisely from the object of direct perception that purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) is obtained,
not from the object of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
Therefore, although the object of conceptual construction is determined as if it were the perceived [object], [it is not so].

Nevertheless, it is not merely the visible [object], because from that [visible object alone] there is an absence of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), whereas such action exists from the visible [particular].
Therefore, that alone is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
It is not an object of conceptual construction. // 15 //
"Other than this," and so forth.

That which is other than this particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa)—that is, another particular characteristic—is not [non-existent], because otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that everything, such as a rabbit's horn, would be a real entity (vastu).
A real entity is that which possesses its own nature in a non-figurative sense (anupacarita-svarūpa).
Therefore, that alone is the definition of a property-possessor (dharmin). // 14 //

But is it not the case that even an object which is the domain of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is indeed ultimately real? For this alone constitutes ultimate reality: namely, appearing within cognition.
And the universal (*sāmānya*) also appears within cognition.
Thinking that even this [conventional reality] is ultimately real (*paramārthasat*), he asks: "Why, then, is only that ultimately real?
With the words beginning with "it is sought" (*arthyate*), he explains the meaning of the phrase "having the characteristic of the capacity for causal efficiency" (*arthakriyāsāmarthyalakṣaṇatva*).
With the words beginning with "this is the meaning," he shows the intended purport (*tātparya*) of the individual words within the compound.
He thinks as follows: since that which is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is ultimately real (*paramārthasat*), the universal (*sāmānya*) is not ultimately real,
because it is useless for causal efficiency such as burning and so forth.
Nor can reality be established by the force of appearance, because even that which has a non-existent form appears through the power of ignorance (*avidyā*).

Furthermore, the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) does not consist in being a producer of cognition, since that cognition arises from the force of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) even without a universal (*sāmānya*), appearing as if it were a universal. // 15 //
With the words "from this" (*etasmāt*) and so forth, he shows the object of inference (*anumāna*).
With the words "for thus" (*tathā hi*) and so forth, [he shows] the object of perception (*pratyakṣa*);
that is the object of inference.
"Another is the universal characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa)":
that object of cognition (prameya) which is other than the nature of the specifically characterized (svalakṣaṇa) as previously described is precisely the universal characteristic;
it is that in whose presence knowledge remains uniform in its form. // 16 //
Thus, it is the object of inference.
The general characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) is the object of inference alone, because it is pervaded by the presence of positive and negative concomitance (anvayavyatireka).
Fearing that there might be an excess of words even when this is not the occasion for them, the general definition (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) was stated.

For instance, at this point—being the occasion for stating the specific definition (svalakṣaṇa)—it is easy to understand the definition of its opposite through an introductory transition; thus, the general definition was stated.
That which becomes the object of knowledge is the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
Being determined by conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*), it does not differentiate between the mere appearance in cognition based on proximity or non-proximity.
For instance, the fire being superimposed exists by virtue of that superimposition; and due to that superimposition, it is both distant and near.
Because of the proximity or non-proximity of that superimposed [fire], there is no difference in the manifestation within cognition in terms of its clarity.
Or, it is because it is not clearly manifest (*asphuṭatva*).
Therefore, it is said to be other than that particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
A "general characteristic" (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) is a characteristic by way of generality (*sāmānyena*).
The meaning is that it is a common form (*sādhāraṇa-rūpa*). For the form being superimposed is common to all fires; therefore, it is a general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). // 16 //
And in order to demonstrate that which is to be apprehended by inference, he says: "That [is] of inference," and so forth.
That is the object of inference, having the nature of the apprehended (*grāhya*).
By the use of the pronoun, there is the inclusion of the logical mark (*liṅga*), just as in the case of a denoted referent.

One who wishes to explain that the object of inference is the universal characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) would have to introduce this section explaining the nature of the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa).
Therefore, for the sake of brevity, the object of inference has been stated right here in the chapter on direct perception (pratyakṣa). // 17 //
He demonstrates the dissimilarity of the universal (sāmānya), which is the object of conceptual construction (vikalpa). But how can the universal be the object of conceptual construction?
To this he says: "being superimposed" (samāropyamāṇa).
The underlying intention is that because the universal form is perceived as common to all fires. // 16 //
Thus, it is said that the object of inference has the nature of being graspable (*grāhyarūpa*).
The term *grāhyarūpa* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has a graspable form.
Here too, the object is established in relation to what is graspable.
This is not due to a dependence on what is to be attained, because there is no disagreement regarding that point.
[Objection: Since the word "sāmānyam" (universal) was introduced in the neuter gender, how can there be a reference to it by the pronoun "saḥ" (he/that), which is in the masculine gender?
To this, he says: "sarvanāmnaḥ" and so forth.

But why did the author of the Vārttika refute the misconceptions regarding the object of inference (*anumāna*) in the section on direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and not in the section on inference itself?
To this he says: "The general characteristic," and so forth.
He thinks thus:
"And that very same perceptual cognition is the fruit of the means of valid cognition."
Thus, the presentation is made in these few words: "Therefore, it is the object of inference.
Otherwise, for the purpose of demonstrating the object of inference, the utterance of this entire statement would be necessary. // 17 //
To refute misconceptions regarding the result (*phala*), he says: "And that very [cognition]...

The connection here is as follows: if the validity of perception is accepted, then there must be a result of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇaphala*) characterized by the examination of the objects of cognition (*prameya*), such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth.
Just as when a tree is cut with an axe, the visible result is its being split into two pieces.
To this he says: "That very perceptual cognition is the fruit of the means of valid cognition.
That very perceptual cognition is the fruit of the means of valid cognition; there is no fruit distinct from the perception, that is, from the perceptual cognition itself. // 18 //

Having refuted the misconception regarding the object, he says "tadeva" (that very same) in order to refute the misconception regarding the result: "That very perception which was just mentioned is itself the result of the means of valid cognition. (18)
If the object of inference were to be established in the section on inference (*anumānapariccheda*), then the text there should have been composed as follows:
"What is this object of inference?
It is that which is other than the object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)."
What is this object of perception itself,
which is distinct from that [object of inference]?
If one were to say "it is the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa)" once again, there would be redundancy.
Therefore, for the sake of brevity, it has been explained right here. // 17 //
He says this in order to refute misconceptions regarding the result (*phala*).
How is there a misconception regarding the result of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?
For instance, a means of valid cognition cannot exist as a cause without the activity of valid cognition (*pramiti*).
Just as there can be no axe without its cutting edge, so too,

from that very reason of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the result— characterized by the engagement with the object— must be distinct [from the cause], because it is contradictory for something to act upon itself.
For the axe is not the cutting edge itself.

Therefore, the Mīmāṃsaka maintains that the sense faculty (*indriya*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), as well as the contact between the sense faculty and its object (*indriyārthasannikarṣa*),
the contact between the mind and the sense faculty (*manaindriyasannikarṣa*),
and the contact with the self (*ātmasannikarṣa*).

"And all types of proximity. As it has been said: "Or rather, the sense organ may be the means of valid cognition, or its contact with the object, or the connection of the mind with the sense organs, or [the connection] of the self with all of these."
Thus, the comprehension of the object is the fruit,
and its status as a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) arises from its operation therein.
Therefore, knowledge is the fruit, and its status as a means of valid cognition arises from its operation therein.
When they have no activity, then the fruit is not produced.
It has also been stated that each preceding [factor] is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and each succeeding one is the result (*phala*);
even in that case, the arising of the cognition is the means of valid cognition.
The fruit consists of activity and so forth.
Likewise, the Naiyāyikas and others also maintain that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its fruit (*phala*) are of this very same nature;
however, this is the additional point: [the fruit] consists in the form of the cognition of the object as qualified (*viśeṣaṇa*).
In response to the doubt, "Why is it that perception alone has the nature of a result? he says: "Because its nature is the cognition of the object.
Here, *pratīti* means ascertainment (*niścaya*).
Form (*rūpa*) is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

That which exists for direct perception is precisely that which has the form of the cognition of the object; the state of being that is "having the form of the cognition of the object" (*arthapratītirūpatva*).
Therefore, because it consists in the cognition of the object, how is it the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*)? To this he says: "the cognition of the object," and so forth.

The apprehension (*pratīti*) of an object is its comprehension (*avagama*); that which has this very [apprehension] as its form is "that which has the apprehension of the object as its form" (*arthapratītirūpa*);
[the ablative case ending indicates] because of the state of being that.
This is what is meant: valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that which brings about attainment.

And this power of bringing about attainment does not arise from mere inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) with the object; for even though a sprout is inseparably connected to its seed and so forth, it does not bring about attainment [of the seed].

Therefore, although this cognition arises from the object to be attained, there must necessarily be some activity of bringing about attainment on the part of this cognition, by the performance of which the object is said to have been attained.
And that very thing is the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), namely, that knowledge which becomes a bringer [of attainment] through its implementation.
And it was stated previously: "The function of that which brings about attainment is precisely the pointing out of the object of activity.
Knowledge is the means of valid cognition.
The cognition of the qualified object is the result.
As Kumārila has stated:
"The two cognitions of the qualifier and the qualified function as the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) and its result (phala)."
Even then, the previously mentioned refutation of the difference in meaning remains in force. Thus [it is said].
That itself is the lack of disagreement;
he says "that itself" in order to refute that [objection]. // 18 //
But how is it that the form of the cognition of the object is the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and not the consciousness that impels one toward the object and so forth?
To this he says: "Of the object," and so on.

He thinks as follows: that very result which, once accomplished, immediately gives rise to the designation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as an instrument—that alone is the result, and nothing else.

When consciousness has arisen through its capacity to delimit an object, and it produces the ascertainment of its own object, the operation of the means of knowledge (*jñāna*) is completed. Therefore, the delimitation of the object itself is the result.
It is not [the means] such as the initiator (*pravartaka*) and so forth.
He demonstrates this very point with the words "This has been said," and so on.

To show the distinctness of the result, which consists of the cognition of the object delimited by the mirror-like means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he shows once again the nature of the instrumental cognition (*pramāṇajñāna*), even though it was previously shown, with the words "The cognition that brings about attainment," and so on.

He thinks as follows: since we accept that consciousness which brings about attainment (*prāpaka*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), therefore that power of attainment is nothing other than the determination of the object (*arthaparicitti*), and not such things as its arising from the object.
He demonstrates this very point with the words beginning "the capacity for attainment" (prāpaṇaśakti).
Why is it that the very state of being inseparable from the object does not constitute the capacity for attainment?
To this he says: "from the seed," and so forth.
The intention is this: since the sprout arises from the seed and so forth as an appearance of an object,
yet the seed and so forth do not reach [the place where the sprout appears], for even a seed situated inside a granary or a pit can produce a sprout.
Therefore, by the words beginning with "tasmāt," it is stated that since cognition arises from the apprehension of the object— that is, from its attainment—
its similarity to the object (*arthasārūpya*) is its means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
21. Because the establishment of the perception of the reflection occurs through the power of that [object].

Thus, when the conventional usage of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and objects of cognition (*prameya*) is superimposed [upon reality], the result (*phala*), characterized by the ascertainment of the object, comes into being.
Knowledge has the nature of ascertaining the object;
it is perception itself that is intended as the nature of the result.
Therefore, it is stated that since perception has the nature of ascertaining the object, it should be understood that perception itself must have the nature of the result. // 19 //
If direct perception itself is the nature of the result, then what is to be understood as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?
In response to this doubt, he says: "The object," and so forth.

"Conformity" (sārūpya) means similarity. "Of this" refers to perception. The remainder [of the sentence] is that the perception which possesses the form of the object is itself the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). // 20 //

Anticipating the objection, "How can mere conformity with the object (*arthasārūpya*) itself be the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)," he says: "Because the cognition of the object is established by virtue of that [conformity].
And that very [cognition] is perception (*pratyakṣa*), which consists in the cognition of the object and has the nature of manifesting the object.
Therefore, that very [cognition] is the fruit of the means of valid cognition. // 19 //
If, then, cognition is the fruit of the means of valid cognition because it consists of the act of cognizing, what then is the fruit of the means of valid cognition?
To this he says: "The object," and so forth.
The similarity or resemblance that this cognition has with its object is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For in this world, from whichever object a cognition arises, it becomes similar to that object; just as a cognition arising from blue is similar to blue.
And that similarity is the resemblance.
It is designated as "aspect" (ākāra) and also as "appearance" (ābhāsa). // 20 //
But surely, similarity is not distinct from cognition;
and that being so, that very cognition is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
and that alone is the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇavyāpāra*).
If, in this way, the capacity to cause attainment is the fruit,
then the fruit is not of the nature of the cognition of the object,
because it is that which causes attainment.
He says that [the cognition] is distinct from the relinquishing of the object, stating: "And it has been said previously," and so forth.

That very cognition which is the means of attainment (*prāpaka*) is itself the motivator (*pravartaka*), and it is also that which reveals the object; this was described previously during the investigation into the nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Consequently, it is established that only that which presents the object is the means of attainment (*prāpaka*), and its power to bring about attainment is nothing other than the cognition of the object itself, since the operation of the instrument of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is completed by that much. Thus, the fruit of the instrument of knowledge is precisely the form of the cognition of the object, and nothing else. // 19 //

Thinking that if the fruit of cognition consists in the form of valid knowledge (*pramiti*), then the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) must be distinct from the cognition itself, he asks with the words "If, then," etc., [stating]:
"Its similarity to the object is its means of knowledge."
The explanation of this is: "that which is the similarity with the object," and so forth.
He thinks as follows: the similarity of consciousness with the object is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), not the sense faculty and so forth.

He demonstrates that what arises from an object becomes similar to that object, and thus it is precisely this "sārūpya" (conformity) that is called "sādṛśya" (similarity), by means of the passage beginning with "iha yasmāt": *iha yasmāt...* [etc. // 20 //
"Now, as for the passage beginning with 'nanu ca' and so forth:
the opponent thinks thus—'The sense faculties and so on have been stated by us to be the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa);
why then is it that very [faculty] which, through the power of the representation of the object, brings about ascertainment?'"
Therefore, that very similarity [of form] is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For it is by this alone that the determination is established: "This is the cognition of blue, not of yellow.
And that which is the cause in this regard is precisely what is intended as the means of valid cognition.
However, the sense faculty lacks the capacity to establish this distinction;
for since that sense faculty is a common cause for all cognition, how could it be capable of establishing the determination of each individual [cognition]?
And if that very [faculty] were the fruit of valid cognition, [it would be untenable].

Furthermore, it is not tenable for a single entity to be both the object to be proven (*sādhya*) and the means of proof (*sādhana*); so how can similarity (*sārūpya*) be the instrument of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)?
To this he says: "By virtue of that" (*tadvaśāt*).
"Tad" means similarity; by virtue of that— that is, through the power of that similarity—
there is the cognition, that is, the comprehension, of the object.
Its establishment [is as follows]:
because of that establishment,
the perceptual consciousness, which has the nature of the cognition of an object, is established by virtue of its similarity [to that object].
The meaning is that it becomes cognized.
For since consciousness appears as blue, the cognition of the blue is thereby determined.
Indeed, from those [causes] such as the eye and so forth, consciousness arises.
It cannot be established that the cognition of that [object] is the awareness of blue on account of its dependence upon it;
rather, being experienced as resembling blue, it is established as the awareness of blue.
Furthermore, in this case, the relationship between the probandum and the probans is not based on the relationship of produced and producer.
By which there would be a contradiction in a single entity;
rather, it is by way of the relationship between the established and the establisher.
Therefore, even for a Buddhist, this is not accepted for a single entity.
Regarding the claim that "the correspondence with the object (arthasārūpya) is the means of valid cognition" (pramāṇa):

if some form of correspondence with the object is accepted as the means of valid cognition, then because the means of valid cognition and its fruit (pramāṇaphala) would be identical, the objection raised—that one and the same thing cannot simultaneously be both the object (karman) and the instrument (karaṇa)—remains in force.
This is addressed by the passage beginning with "by virtue of that" (tadvaśāt), and so forth.

He thinks as follows: among the causal factors (*kāraka*), that which is the most effective means (*sādhakatama*) is the instrument (*karaṇa*), and that is the very similarity of form (*sārūpya*) with the object, because it is through its power that the cognition of the object is established;
it is not the sense organ and so forth.
"Because in the absence of a resemblance to the object, there is no cognition of the object.
He demonstrates this very point with the words beginning "the cognition of the object is its apprehension," and with the words beginning "for [cognition] appearing as blue," and so forth.
It shows that the blue form is the cause for establishing the cognition of blue as the apprehension of blue;
because when the cognition’s blue form is apprehended, the perception of blue is understood.
Therefore, the form of the object is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since it possesses the nature of an instrument (*karaṇadharman*).

But surely, consciousness arises from the eye and other [senses] and indeed cognizes a specific object; so how can the objective form (*arthākāra*) be said to be the most excellent contributing factor?
To this he says: "For from which... and so forth.
This explains that even for the eye and other [senses], there exists the status of being a causal condition (*nimitta*) for the arising of consciousness.
However, because they serve as the cause for the arising of omniscience (*sarvajñāna*), they do not serve as the cause for the determination of a specific object.
Rather, because the form of the object (*arthākāra*) is unique, it serves as the cause for the determination of a specific object; therefore, that alone is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
As for what was urged by the opponent—that since the means of valid cognition and its fruit are identical, there would be neither a goal nor a means—[that objection does not apply].
He refutes that with the passage beginning "And here, [there is] no contradiction between the produced and the producer," and so forth.

This contradiction of one thing [with itself] would exist if this relation of producer and produced were the relation of means and result (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*) between the means of valid cognition and its fruit; what then is it?
It is the relation of the determiner and the determined (*vyavasthāpyavyavasthāpakabhāva*).
Why? Because the context concerns knowledge (*jñāna*).

Since a distinguished object is made known by the cognizer when a distinguished knowledge has arisen, the [external] object would be the producer of the very knowledge of blue, which is beyond the senses.
Furthermore, the cognition of yellow and so forth would not be capable of being restricted to that very [object] at that time.
Moreover, even proximity (*sannidhāna*) is not a cause for restriction because it is common to all [objects], just like the sense faculty (*indriya*).
A certain form (*rūpa*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Nothing contradicts the result of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*).
For similarity (*sārūpya*) is the cause for establishing that cognition,
and what is to be established is the awareness of blue.
If it is asked, "How can there be a relationship of the established and the establisher (*vyavasthāpya-vyavasthāpaka-bhāva*) for a single cognition?", it is said in reply:
because that cognition, having experienced something resembling blue, is established as the apprehender of blue by means of a determinative cognition (*niścaya-pratyaya*);
therefore, the experienced similarity of form (*sārūpya*) is the cause of its establishment.
And that cognition, being established as the awareness of blue by means of a determinative cognition (*niścayapratyaya*), is what is determined.

Therefore, similarity (*sārūpya*)—by way of the exclusion of dissimilarity—is the cause for establishing the cognition; and its nature as the awareness of blue is determined by the exclusion of the awareness of non-blue.
Furthermore, the conceptualizing cognition (*vikalpapratyaya*) that establishes [the object] should be understood as arising through the power of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
For it is not the case that non-conceptual perception itself can establish its own nature as having the form of the cognition of blue;
even if a consciousness has the form of the cognition of blue, if it is not established by a determining cognition (*niścayapratyaya*), it is as good as non-existent.
Therefore, consciousness, which is definitively established as having the nature of the cognition of blue, exists by virtue of its identity as the cognition of blue.

Consequently, it is only when perception performs a determinative judgment (*adhyavasāya*) that it becomes a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). However, if the determinative judgment is not performed, consciousness remains unestablished as having the nature of the cognition of blue.
And thus, the result of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-phala*) is the object, but the object is not produced [by the cognition].
For instance, when a cognition arises in the form of blue, it establishes a specific knowledge, namely:
"the cognition of blue has been experienced"; it does not produce the cognition itself.

By the phrase "something" (*kiñcit*) and so forth, [the author] demonstrates that a single cognition itself possesses the relationship of the determined (*vyavasthāpya*) and the determiner (*vyavasthāpaka*) through its own parts and the whole.

Anticipating the objection— "But how can there be a relationship of the determined and the determiner as parts and whole within that very same non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*) which has arisen with a specific form at one and the same time?"— he asks, beginning with the words "the determined and the determiner," etc.
Regarding the term "similar":

he thinks as follows— it is not consciousness alone that establishes itself as non-conceptual, but rather it is established by a determinative cognition (niścayapratyaya) that arises subsequent to direct perception (pratyakṣa).

In this context, the object-aspect (arthākāra) is the cause for the establishment [of cognition] by virtue of being the awareness of the object through its exclusion from what is dissimilar; the established [cognition] arises through that production, while feeling (vedana) is that which is established, and the determining cognition (niścayapratyaya) is the establisher.
He demonstrates this very point with the words beginning "Therefore" (tasmāt).

Now, the cognition of blue that has arisen is established by the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedanapratyakṣa*). If the determination of what constitutes a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is obtained through the power of ascertainment (*niścaya*), then it is reasonable to say that "it is determined by the cognition of ascertainment.
However, does a valid means of knowledge not indeed exist even without the cognition of ascertainment?

Thus he says: "Not established by means of a definitive cognition," and so forth. However, similarity (sārūpya) serves as the cause for the establishment of individual definitive cognitions because it is unique [to each].
For instance, that which is the blue aspect (*nīlākāra*) of a cognition of blue does not exist in a cognition of yellow and so forth; thus, there would be an establishment [of distinction].
Since this very cognition arises from the fact of having a blue aspect—that "this is blue"—there is no mental state [arising] that "it is yellow."
Therefore, the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is simply the conformity [of the cognition] with the object. // 21 //
Thus ends the first chapter, on direct perception, in the *Nyāyabindu-vistara-ṭīkā* entitled *Śiṣyahitā*.
The form of the apprehension is unestablished;
therefore, because it lacks the status of being the most effective means (*sādhakatama*), cognition itself would not be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

However, when cognition—whose nature is the awareness of blue—is established through the force of similarity by means of the resulting determination (*adhyavasāya*), it becomes established as a means of valid cognition, because it is the cause for establishing that similarity.
If it is argued that, in this case, perception would be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) only when accompanied by conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), and not by itself—
this is not so; for an object is determined as being "visible" by a conceptual determination that has arisen through the power of perception.

It is not by way of conceptual construction (*utprekṣitatva*). Furthermore, "seeing" is the function of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), termed the direct realization of the object; whereas conceptual construction is the function of discursive thought (*vikalpa*).

For instance, when conceptualizing an object that is beyond the senses, we say, "we imagine it, but we do not see it"; thus, through experience, they determine that the operation of conceptualization consists of imagination (*utprekṣā*).

Therefore, setting aside its own [conceptual] operation, it displays the operation of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*): namely, in a case where the determination (*adhyavasāya*) is preceded by direct perception of the object.
In that regard, perception alone is the sole means of valid cognition. // 21 //
The first chapter, on direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), in the *Nyāyabinduṭīkā* composed by Ācārya Dharmottara, is completed.

It demonstrates this: as long as perception does not produce a determination regarding its own object and itself, it does not become a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because its own function has not been accomplished.
Therefore, it is only while performing the act of ascertainment (*adhyavasāya*) that it is a means of valid cognition; thus, it depends upon determination.
Now, one might object: "If perception accompanied by conceptual construction cannot be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) without certainty,

then perception alone would be the valid means of knowledge, and not [perception] together with that [conceptualization]," thinking thus, he raises an objection with the words "yadi evam" and so forth.
This is not so...
[End of] the second chapter on inference for oneself. Inference is of two kinds.
2. One's own welfare and the welfare of others.
In that context, inference for oneself is the cognition regarding the object of inference which arises from a mark possessing the three characteristics.

Right knowledge has been stated to be of two kinds, distinguished as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*). Among these, direct perception has already been explained in detail. Now, in order to authorize the exposition of inference, he says: "Inference is twofold."
Two types of inference are to be understood:

inference for oneself and inference for others, which consist respectively of cognition and verbal expression. Since there is no single general definition applicable to both, why was a definition not stated previously?
And by means of classification, the specific characteristic can be easily stated;
therefore, classification was explained first. // 1 //
Regarding the phrase "for one's own sake":
by distinguishing between "for one's own sake" and "for the sake of others," only this twofold division is demonstrated.
Here, "sake" (artha) means "incentive" (prayojana).
The remainder [of the definition] is "one's own purpose" and "the purpose of another.

That by which there is comprehension for oneself is to be understood as "for one's own sake" (svārtha), and that by which there is comprehension for another is to be understood as "for the sake of another" (parārtha). // 2 //
Having thus explained direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and desiring to explain inference (*anumāna*), he says: "Inference..."
Inference is twofold, of two kinds. Now, when the definition of inference is to be stated, why is this division of types mentioned out of the blue?
It is said: inference for the sake of others (parārthānumāna) consists of speech.
Inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*), however, consists of cognition;
because there is an absolute difference between the two, they do not share a single definition.
Therefore, in order to state their respective specific definitions, the distinction between their modes is explained.
For the distinction of types is the distinction of individuals;
and when the distinction of individuals has been stated, it is possible to state a definition that is restricted to each individual, but not otherwise.
Therefore, the statement of the distinction of types is indeed an integral part of the presentation of the definition.
Having recognized that it is impossible to provide a definition without first stating the different types [of the object], the classification of types is stated beforehand. // 1 //
What, then, is this twofold nature? He says: "for one's own sake" (*svārtham*).
This is "for one's own sake" (*svartha*) because it is for oneself (*svasmai*).

That by which one practices for oneself is for one's own benefit (svārtha); this [teaching] for the sake of another is the ultimate benefit (paramārtha); that by which one instructs another is for the benefit of others (parārtha). // 2 //

Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*): between those two, namely inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*) and inference for others (*parārthānumāna*), what is the nature of the knowledge that constitutes inference for oneself?
To this he says: "from that which has three forms" (*trirūpāt*).
That which possesses three forms—whose characteristics will be stated below—is "that which has three forms."
A *liṅga* is that by which an object is indicated (*liṅgyate*) or understood (*gamyate*).
Therefore, from this three-featured *liṅga*,
the determination of the result of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-phala*) occurs here just as it does in the case of perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Furthermore, the three characteristics of the logical mark (liṅga) are: its existence only in the object of inference (anumeya), its existence only in the similar instances (sapakṣa),
and its certain non-existence in the dissimilar instances (asapakṣa).

Regarding the term "therein" (*tatra*): that which possesses three forms is "three-formed" (*trirūpa*). That by which an object is indicated is a "mark" (*liṅga*). That which is inferred is the "object of inference" (*anumeya*).

The cognition that arises regarding the object of inference (anumeya) from a reason (hetu) possessing the three characteristics is precisely what constitutes inference for the sake of another (parārthānumāna).
The term "object of inference" (anumeya) is stated in order to exclude the possibility that the cognition arising from a fallacious mark (liṅgābhāsa) might also be considered inference.
Furthermore, the mention of "cognition" (jñāna) is intended to exclude the view that the mark itself is, in reality, the inference. // 3 //
If the cognition of the object to be inferred itself is intended as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then what would be called the result (*phala*)?
In response to this doubt, he says: "The means of valid cognition... and so forth.
Just as in the case of perception, that which is produced by it alone is stated to be the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*),
so too here, inference itself would be the fruit of the means of valid cognition, because its nature consists in the ascertainment of the object.
Just as the conformity of perception to the object is the means of valid cognition, [so too is it for inference].

Likewise, for inference as well, the correspondence with the object is alone the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), because it is by virtue of that [correspondence] that the ascertainment of the object is established. // 4 //
It has been stated, "from a logical mark possessing three characteristics. To the inquiry, "And what are those three characteristics? he says: "The tri-modal nature" (trairūpyam).
"That which has arisen as knowledge"—
this is a qualification by way of its cause.
Since that [knowledge] also arises from a three-featured logical mark (liṅga) and has a three-featured logical mark as its object, he specifies it as "the inferable" (anumeya).
And this is a qualification by way of its object:
that cognition which arises from a mark possessing the three characteristics and has the inferable as its objective support is inference for oneself. // 3 //
Having refuted misconceptions regarding the definition, he speaks—"pramāṇasya," etc.—in order to refute misconceptions regarding the result (*phala*).

Whatever the determination of the result of this means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) may be, that should be understood here in inference just as it is in perception (*pratyakṣa*), like perception itself.
For just as perception, when experienced as having the same form as the blue object, is established as having the nature of the cognition of blue;
Therefore, the conformity with the blue object (*nīlasārūpya*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as the cause of establishment,
while the nature of the cognition of the blue (*nīlabodharūpa*), which is being established, is the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*).
Similarly, inference, arising in the form of the blue, is established as having the nature of the cognition of the blue.

Therefore, its similarity to the blue object is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), while its nature as a conceptualization of the blue is the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*);
for it is by virtue of this similarity that its form as the cognition of the blue is established, and not otherwise.

Thus, here the disagreements regarding number, definition, and result have been addressed; however, in the section on direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), the disagreement concerning its object (*gocara*) was refuted. Furthermore, in the context of establishing the definition [of inference], the three-fold mark (*trirūpa-liṅga*) was introduced.

The state of having three forms is "trairūpya. First, "existence in the inferable object" (anumeye sattvam eva) means that existence precisely in the definition of the inferable object as set forth below is the first form.
In that context, by stating "existence therein" (*tatra sattvam*), [the fallacy] such as "because of being visible" (*cākṣuṣatvāt*) is excluded.
By the additional statement "only" (*eva*), [fallacies] such as partial non-establishment (*deśāsiddhi*) regarding one side are excluded.
[The phrase] "existence only in the similar class" (*sapakṣe eva sattvam*) [is thus established].
In this context, "form" refers specifically to a second entity that is of the same class (*samajātīya*).
By stating "an entity" (*sattva*) here, the uncommon inconclusive (*asādhāraṇānaikāntika*) reason is excluded.
By the addition of the word "specifically" (*eva*), the common inconclusive (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*) reason is excluded.
By stating both [conditions], the contradictory [reason] is excluded.
"And non-existence in the dissimilar class" means that the third characteristic is non-existence in anything whatsoever that is not of the same kind.

By stating "non-existence here," the common inconclusive reason (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*) is excluded. By the additional mention of "only" (*eva*), there is an avoidance of [the fallacy] where [the reason] does not occur in one part of the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*). He says "the three-fold nature" (*trairūpyam*) and so forth in order to explain this.
The "threefold nature" (*trairūpya*) of the logical mark (*liṅga*) refers to its three characteristics; the ellipsis is that "this is what is being stated.
But what, then, is that threefold nature?
Thus he says: "the inferable" (anumeya).
The inferable is that which will have its definition stated later; in that [inferable], the mere existence of the logical mark (liṅga) is ascertained—this is one form [of the evidence].
Although the term "ascertained" (*niścita*) is not explicitly used here,

it must nevertheless be understood as applying to both types of forms under discussion because a logical mark (*liṅga*) is not the cause of the cognition of an imperceptible object by virtue of its mere suitability.
Just as a seed [is the cause] of a sprout;
for fire is not apprehended from smoke that is itself unperceived.
Nor does the manifestation of an imperceptible object depend upon a cognition whose own object is [that very imperceptible thing].

For example, a lamp [is not the cause of the cognition] of a jar and so forth, because even though it is perceived, there is no cognition [of the object] since the relationship [between them] is not ascertained.

Therefore, the function of the logical mark (*liṅga*) in communicating a remote object consists precisely in its being ascertained as being invariably concomitant (*nāntarīyakatayā*) with that remote object.
There is nothing else [required].

Therefore, the ascertainment of the positive concomitance (anvaya), negative concomitance (vyatireka), and the property-of-the-subject (pakṣadharmatva) must necessarily be performed, as it constitutes the very operation of the logical mark (liṅga); thus, the term "ascertained" (niścita) must be required for all the characteristics [of a valid reason].
Among these, by the mention of "existence" (sattva), the unestablished (asiddha) reasons such as "being visible to the eye" (cākṣuṣatva) are excluded.

By the word "only" (eva), the fallacy of being unestablished in part of the subject (*pakṣaikadeśāsiddha*) is excluded. For example, when trees are made the subject with the argument "trees are conscious because they sleep," sleep characterized by the closing of leaves is not established in every part of the subject, namely the trees.
For not all trees possess the property of closing their leaves at night, but only some; thus,
by means of the reason stated after the mention of "sentient beings," the uncommon (asādhāraṇa) logical mark is excluded.
For if one were to state "existence in the probandum alone," then audibility itself would be the reason.
By the inclusion of the term "ascertained" (niścita), all cases of the unestablished where the reason is doubtful (sandigdhāsiddha) are excluded.

The similar instance (*sapakṣa*) has its definition to be stated later; the second characteristic is that the [reason] is ascertained to exist only in that. Here too, by the inclusion of the term "existence," the contradictory [reason] is excluded.
For that [reason] does not exist in the similar class (sapakṣa).
By the word "only" (eva), the common inconclusive [reason] is excluded;
for that [reason] does not reside in the similar class alone.
However, in this case, the subject (dharmin) whose specific property is sought to be known is inferable from both [the similar and the dissimilar instances].
Since it is stated that "it must be ascertained beforehand," it should be understood that this ascertainment applies only to these three [characteristics].

Furthermore, those three forms must themselves be grasped as having been ascertained by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) according to their respective natures; otherwise, it would be impossible to bring about understanding regarding the object of inference (*anumeya*). // 5 //
And who is the object of inference?
To this doubt, he says: "the object of inference" (*anumeya*).

Here too, by the inclusion of the term "existence" (*sattva*) and by the statement of the prior restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), it is stated that even that which exists only partially in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), such as the property of arising after effort (*prayatnāntarīyaka*), can serve as a logical reason (*hetu*).

If, however, the restrictive particle *eva* were placed after [the word *sapakṣe*], the meaning would be: "That which exists only in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) is the logical reason (*hetu*). In that case, "being produced immediately after effort" (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*) would not be a valid reason.
By the use of the word "ascertained" (*niścita*), the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) reason whose positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is doubtful is excluded;
for example: "Someone is omniscient, because he is a speaker."

For the property of being a speaker is doubtful in the similar instance (sapakṣa), namely, the omniscient one. The dissimilar instance (asapakṣa) has its definition to be stated; the certainty of its non-existence therein is the third characteristic.
In this context, by the inclusion of the term "non-existent" (asat), the contradictory [reason] is excluded;
for the contradictory exists in the dissimilar class (vipakṣa).
By the particle "only" (eva), the common [reason] that occurs in a portion of the dissimilar class is excluded.

For when "being produced by effort" is the property to be proven (*sādhya*), "impermanence" exists in one part of the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), such as lightning, but does not exist in others, such as space; therefore,
it is necessarily excluded from this [latter case].

For if the restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*) were placed before the word "non-existent" (*asattva*), the meaning would be this: "That which exists only in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) is the logical reason (*hetu*).

In that case, since the property of "being produced immediately after an effort" (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*) does not exist in all similar instances (*sapakṣa*), it would consequently not be a valid reason.
Therefore, it was not formulated previously.
By the inclusion of the term "ascertained" (niścita), the inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika*) whose exclusion from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) is doubtful is excluded.
Now, one might object: when it is stated that [the reason] must exist only in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), [does this not already imply certainty?]
It is already understood that [the reason] must be absent in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*);
for what purpose, then, was the inclusion of both [positive and negative concomitance] made?

It is said: the inclusion of both was made to demonstrate that either positive concomitance (*anvaya*) or negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) must be employed as something necessarily restricted (*niyamavat*), and not otherwise.

For if both [conditions] were applied without restriction, the meaning would be this: "a reason is that which exists in the similar class (sapakṣa) and does not exist in the dissimilar class (vipakṣa).
And if that were the case, [the argument] "he is dark-skinned because he is his son" [would be valid].
The statement "like the son who is being seen" would serve as a reason for his being that son;

therefore, one must employ only positive and negative concomitances (anvaya and vyatireka) that possess necessity, so that the necessary connection of the probans with the probandum may be understood.

Since both [positive and negative] formulations must necessarily be employed when one follows a rule, only one of the two should be used, not both; thus, for the sake of instruction that either the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) or the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) alone should be employed, both are presented. In the context of explaining the three forms [of the reason], the subject of inference (*anumeya*), the similar class (*sapakṣa*), and the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*) have been mentioned;
their definitions must now be stated.
In that regard, what is the object of inference (*anumeya*)?
He says: "The object of inference here," and so forth.

Here, when the definition of the reason (*hetu*) is to be ascertained, the locus (*dharmin*) is the object of inference; but elsewhere, at the time of the comprehension of the probandum (*sādhya*), the aggregate (*samudāya*) is the object of inference.
At the time of ascertaining the pervasion (vyāpti),
a similar instance (sapakṣa) is an object that is similar by virtue of the general property to be proven (sādhyadharma).
8. That which is not a similar instance (sapakṣa) is a non-similar instance (asapakṣa).
9. Furthermore, there is that which is other than it, that which is contradictory to it, and its non-existence.
"Herein" means in the definition of the reason (*hetu*).
"Desired to be known" means wished to be understood.
"A particularity" (*viśeṣa*) means...
Dharma is that which possesses a distinct characteristic.

That in which a particular quality is sought to be known is "that whose particularity is sought to be known" (jijñāsitaviśeṣa). That in which various attributes exist is a "possessor of attributes" (dharmī).
Therefore, the meaning is that the subject (*dharmin*) for which some particular property (*viśeṣa*) is intended to be inferred is the "object of inference" (*anumeya*).

And it has been stated that this [subject] is to be understood precisely at the occasion of defining the logical reason (*hetu*). Elsewhere, however, it is said that the subject qualified by its property (*dharmaviśiṣṭadharmin*) is the object of inference. // 6 //

What, then, is the similar instance (*sapakṣa*)? In response to this doubt, he says: "That which has the same measure as the probandum," and so forth. One who possesses the same measure (*māna*) is "similar" (*samāna*).
It is to be delimited by the same cognition; "similar" is the understood remainder. And that object which is similar is the *sapakṣa* (similar instance).
If it is asked, "In what manner is there a commonality? it is stated in this regard: "by way of a commonality of the property to be proven" (*sādhyadharmasāmānyena*).
That which is both the "to-be-proven" (*sādhya*) and a "property" (*dharma*) is the "property to be proven" (*sādhyadharma*).
Its generality is the generality of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*). For the property to be proven has particular instances,
due to its restriction to each respective object.

And because there would be a contradiction due to that [reason] being identical [to the probandum], it was stated [in the definition] "by way of the generality of the property to be proven" (sādhyadharma-sāmānyena).
What, then, is the non-concordant instance (asapakṣa)?
In response to this doubt, he says: "that which is not a concordant instance" (na sapakṣaḥ).
And whatever is not a similar instance (sapakṣa) is entirely a dissimilar instance (asapakṣa). // 8 //

"Other than that" refers to a reason that is contradictory to the similar class (*sapakṣa*). For example, when "hot touch" is the property to be proven (*sādhya*), [the reason] "a substance that is neither hot nor cold."
However, the property (dharma) is what is to be inferred; it is mentioned here in order to demonstrate this.
That subject (dharmin) whose specific property is sought—that is, desired to be known—is as previously described. // 6 //
What is the similar class (*sapakṣa*)? To this he says: "The property to be proved," and so forth.
A similar object is the similar class (*sapakṣa*).
That object which is similar—that is, identical—to the subject (pakṣa) is called the "similar instance" (sapakṣa) by way of metaphorical designation (upacāra). It is qualified by the word "similar":
a similar subject is a "similar instance" (sapakṣa).
And that [suffix] is a substitute for the word *samāna*.
One might ask: what is that commonality between the subject (*pakṣa*) and the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), by virtue of which the similar instance is "similar" (*samāna*) to the subject?
Thus he says: "by means of the generality of the property to be proven" (*sādhyadharmasāmānyena*).

It is "to be proven" (*sādhya*) because it is not yet established, and it is a "property" (*dharma*) because it is dependent upon another; therefore, it is the "property to be proven" (*sādhyadharma*).
Furthermore, a particular (*viśeṣa*) is not what is to be proven.
Moreover, [the property] is a generality (*sāmānya*).
Therefore, it is stated here that the generality is the probandum (*sādhya*).

And since this is both a property to be proven and a generality, it is called "the property to be proven as a generality"; the meaning is that the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) is that which is similar to the subject (*pakṣa*) by virtue of possessing that generality as its property to be proven. // 7 //

What is the non-similar instance (asapakṣa)? He says: that which is not a similar instance (sapakṣa) is the non-similar instance. That which does not exist as a similar instance is the non-similar instance. // 8 //
And what is that which does not constitute a similar instance (*sapakṣa*)?
To this he says: "from that" (*tataḥ*).
That is, other than that similar instance; by that [means].
And the three triads are indeed the three marks.
11. Non-apprehension, essential nature, and effect.
12. Among these, non-apprehension is as follows: there is no jar in a particular location, because that which meets the conditions for apprehension is not apprehended.
"Contrary to that" means contrary to the similar instances (*sapakṣa*).
For example, when "hot touch" alone is the property to be proven (*sādhya*), [citing] "a cold substance" [as a reason].
"Non-existence of that" means the absence of a similar instance (sapakṣa).
For example, for a Sautrāntika, when impermanence is to be proven, the very absence of impermanence is the non-similar instance (asapakṣa).
In that system, since even space and so forth are accepted as eternal,
it should be understood that there is no such thing as a "similar instance" (sapakṣa) or a "dissimilar instance" (asapakṣa) regarding the threefold object [of existence].
Non-existence, however, is by its very nature not a similar instance.
And that which is contradictory to another [property] is not, even indirectly, a similar instance (sapakṣa). // 9 //
In response to the doubt, "How many kinds of reasons are there that are endowed with the principle of cause and effect as previously described?", he says: "They possess three characteristics.
The three characteristics as previously described are possible only in these three [types of reasons].
The word "only" (eva) has the sense of restriction, meaning "not more than.
