Each of the three types of evidence (liṅga) should be understood as having exactly three forms;
it must never have only one form or two forms. // 10 //
And what are the three marks?
In response to this doubt, he says: "non-apprehension.
Here, the three marks are indicated by their own names. // 11 //
In that context, "non-apprehension" refers to the essential nature of non-apprehension;
as for the word "as follows":
The word *upapradarśana* means "pointing out.
In a specific location, the statement "there is no jar" refers to the nearby place.
The connection, however, is as follows: in that specific location...
And it is contradictory;
furthermore, there is an absence of such a similar instance (sapakṣa). It is not possible, at least, to ascertain either its being other than the sapakṣa or its being contradictory to it.
As long as the absence of the nature of the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) has not been cognized,

then— by virtue of the capacity of the cognition of difference and contradiction— the two [reasons] that consist in the absence of the similar instance are cognized as being different and contradictory.
Therefore, the absence is directly cognized as having the form of the absence of the similar instance.
By implication, the other two [types of reasons] are understood to be of the nature of non-existence because they are contradictory;
therefore, all three are *asapakṣa* (non-homologous). // 9 //
By the three-fold nature already mentioned, there are exactly three types of logical marks (*liṅga*).
The word "and" (*ca*) serves to include other points yet to be stated. The three-fold nature was inquired about first.
And the logical marks (liṅga) possess three characteristics according to the opponent.

In that regard, the threefold nature has been stated; now the [marks] possessing those three characteristics are being described—the logical marks possessing three characteristics are indeed three, and indeed three.
The meaning is that there are three types for each of the three categories of gods, forms, and gender-marks. // 10 //
What, then, are they? He says: "Non-apprehension," and so forth.
Non-apprehension of the object to be negated, which is the probandum, possesses the three characteristics.
And the nature of the subject to be proven (the sādhya) is threefold: [the essential property] and the effect. // 11 //
In order to provide an illustration of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), he says "tatra" and so forth;
and "yathā" and so forth.
The word "yathā" is used for the purpose of demonstration.
The meaning is that just as this non-apprehension [is a cause of knowledge], so too is another; it is not only this one.
"Place" (*pradeśa*) means a particular location (*ekadeśa*). It is accepted [as such].
13. Attainment of the conditions for perception consists of the completeness of the other causal factors for perception and a specific nature.
In the phrase "in some place there is no jar," the locus (*dharmin*) is indicated by the words "in some place";
the term "specific location" serves as its qualification. The meaning is that there is no jar in the place intended by the proponent.
If "the place" were stated [as the subject], then because everything would constitute the locus of the thesis (*pakṣa*), the establishment of the absence of a jar would not even be possible;
moreover, that [place] would not even be perceptible.
This is why it is said: "of that which has reached the conditions for perception."
By this, the qualification of the reason is stated.
"Apprehension" (upalabdhi) refers to cognition;
it is called a "characteristic" (lakṣaṇa) because it is that by which something is characterized.
The word "object" (*viṣaya*) is to be supplied as the remainder.

"Characterized by apprehension" (*upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa*) means the definition of apprehension; that which has reached this [definition] is "that which has attained the characteristics of apprehension" (*upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpta*).
The phrase "the object of a capable perception" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
"Because of non-perception" means because of not seeing it.

The meaning is this: because of the non-perception of a visible object such as a jar in a particular location and so forth; the remainder of the sense is "because of the perception of a location empty of a jar. // 12 //
To the doubt, "What indeed is this 'attainment of the conditions for perception'? he says: "Perception," and so forth.
Thus, this distinction is directly perceived by the cognizer.
And not every location is of such a kind;
thus he says "in some place.
The locus (*dharmin*) is "only in some specific location" as perceived by the cognizer.
"It is not a jar" is the thesis to be proven. Perception is cognition;
its defining characteristic is the causal complex that produces it.
For by that [perception], apprehension is characterized;
the object reached by that [apprehension] is [said to be] "attained" because it is included within the causal complex by virtue of being its producer.
The meaning is that an object which has attained the characteristics of apprehension is "visible."
"Because of its non-apprehension"—this is the reason.
Now, how could that which does not exist in a certain place be perceptible there?
It is called "perceptible" even though it is non-existent, due to the superimposition of perceptibility.
And that which is thus conceived— namely, "if this [object] were not present, it would be visible"—
is a visible object that, though non-existent there, is superimposed.
And what is it that is thus conceived?
For one for whom all the causes for seeing their own object of apprehension are complete. And when are those [causes] understood to be complete?
When there is the perception of another thing within the same cognition.
Two objects that are graspable by a single sensory cognition, directed toward the visual faculty and so forth, and mutually dependent, are said to be conjoined within a single cognition.
For when both exist, there is no rule that the apprehension of one occurs [while the other does not], because their capacity is indistinguishable for both.

Therefore, when one object among those associated with a single cognition is being perceived, if the other were present with its entire causal complex for perception complete, it would necessarily be perceived; thus, the potentiality of being perceived is superposed upon it.
The non-perception of that [potential object] is "non-perception of the perceptible" (*dṛśyānupalambha*).

Therefore, that very spot devoid of the jar, and the cognition having that as its object, are called "non-perception of the perceptible" because they are the cause for determining the non-perception of the perceptible.
For as long as the object associated with the same cognitive act is not determined, [the non-perception remains uncertain].
And that cognition is not, for its part, the ascertainment of the non-perception of the perceptible;
therefore, both the object and the cognition thereof are called "non-perception."
The mere cessation of perception is itself non-informative because it is not ascertained [by itself].

Therefore, the place devoid of the visible jar and the cognition thereof must be understood as being described by the very force of the statement as having the nature of the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalambha*). // 12 //
What, then, is "attainment of the conditions for perception"?
To this he says: "Perception," and so forth.
That specific nature which, even when other conditions for perception are present, becomes directly perceived—that specific nature is what is meant.
15. Essential nature (*svabhāva*) is a reason (*hetu*) when the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) exists by virtue of its own mere existence.
"Apprehension" means cognition;
its other conditions are the "other conditions for apprehension."
In that context, the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) is the jar itself;
the others, such as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and so forth,
constitute the completeness of those [conditions], which is the completeness of the other conditions for perception.
By the word *sākalya* (completeness), inclusion is expressed.
"Intrinsic nature and particularity" is the compound *svabhāvaviśeṣa*.
These two are expressed by the term *upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpti* (attainment of the conditions for perception). // 13 //
If it is asked, "What indeed is this specific nature? he says, in response to that expectation: "When [the causes] exist," etc.
That nature which, while existing, is not remote—due to the three modes of remoteness—in the presence of the eye and other [causes], and is capable of being seen; [that is the specific nature].
That very same distinction between the two states is expressed here.
Therefore, even when the eye and other [senses] are present, because a pot capable of being perceived is not apprehended, the meaning "there is no pot here" is what is stated. // 14 //
In order to explain the definition of the reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*), he says: "essential nature" (*svabhāva*).

"Attainment of the characteristic" (*lakṣaṇaprāpti*) means the state of having attained the characteristic of perceptibility; for a jar, this is the completeness of all other conditions for its perception.
For cognition, even the jar is a producer,
as are other factors such as the eye;
apart from the visible jar, other causes are the various conditions (*pratyaya*).
Their "sālya" is accumulation (*sannidhi*).

"Specificity" (*viśeṣa*) means that the very nature (*svabhāva*) itself is distinguished from others; that is to say, it is "distinguished" (*viśiṣṭa*). Thus, this twofold [condition]—the specific nature and the completeness of other conditions—is to be understood as the fulfillment of the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptatva*) in the case of a jar or similar objects. // 13 //
What kind of specific nature is it?
To this he says: "That which is the nature," and so forth;
"when [the conditions] exist," and so forth.

Among those other conditions for perception apart from the visible object such as a jar, that specific nature which, being present, becomes directly perceived is the "specific nature" (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*).
This is the meaning here: this definition of the conditions for perception is relative to a single perceiver.
And that being so, for a single observer who has set out to see, an entity that is being shown possesses both [the general nature and the specific nature].

However, those things which are not perceived are remote in terms of place, time, or nature, and lack specific characteristics; yet they possess the completeness of conditions. For those very conditions by which the seer sees are present, and it is because they are present that he has set out to see.

However, for one who has not set out to see, even those objects situated in a suitable location cannot be seen because they lack other causal conditions (*pratyaya*), though they possess their own specific intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-viśeṣa*).
But distant hairs or darkness lack both [conditions].
Thus, for someone who is seeing, there is no such thing as a lack of other causal conditions.
But it would be devoid of its specific intrinsic nature (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*).
However, that which is situated in a suitable location can be seen by one who does not see [it], provided it lacks other conditions (*pratyayāntara*); others, however, lack both. // 14 //
Having cited non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), he says "svabhāva" and so forth in order to cite essential nature (*svabhāva*). Essential nature is, for example:
"This is a tree, because it is a *śiṃśapā*."
17. An example of an effect is: "There is fire here, because of smoke."
18. Herein, two [reasons] establish a positive entity, while one is a reason for negation.
"Sattāmātram" means the mere existence of the means of proof. That which has the nature of existing in mere existence is "sattāmātrabhāvī."
In that case, when the property to be proven (sādhyadharma) exists as a mere presence, the essential nature as a reason (svabhāvahetu) is to be understood. // 15 //
As in the case of "it is a tree":
here, the tree is connected with being a *śiṃśapā* alone;
therefore, it is established by that. // 16 //
The effect-reason (kāryahetu) is illustrated as follows:
because smoke arises necessarily from fire, it is understood that "wherever there is smoke, there is fire. // 17 //
Now, in response to the doubt as to why the logical mark (*liṅga*) is established as being of three kinds, he says: "In this case, there are two.
This is because the object to be inferred (*anumeya*) is of two kinds, consisting of both existence and non-existence.
Therefore, the reason (hetu) is also of only two kinds: that which establishes existence (bhāvasādhana) and that which establishes non-existence (abhāvasādhana).
The object of inference (*anumeya*), being of the nature of an existent (*bhāva-rūpa*), is also twofold: 1) distinct (*bhinna*) and 2) non-distinct (*abhinna*).
This is to be connected with the word "reason" (*hetu*).
What kind of reason is the nature (*svabhāva*) of the probandum? To this he says: its own existence (*sattā*), that alone, which is merely its own existence (*svasattāmātra*).
That which has the nature of coming into being when that [cause] exists:
whatever exists in dependence upon the existence of its own cause,
and does not depend on any cause other than the existence of that cause, is a probandum (*sādhya*) that arises from its own mere existence.
The reason (hetu) that exists in that which is to be proven (sādhya) is the very nature (svabhāva) of that sādhya, and nothing else. // 15 //
The example is as follows:
"this" refers to the subject (*dharmin*); "tree" is the property to be proven (*sādhya*).
"Because it is a *śiṃśapā*" is the reason (*hetu*).
The meaning of this is: "This is fit for the conventional designation 'tree,' because it is fit for the conventional designation 'śiṃśapā.'"

In that case, when a dull-witted person who is unfamiliar with the linguistic convention for "śiṃśapā" is shown a tall *śiṃśapā* tree in a region where such trees abound and told, "This is a tree," he— due to his dullness— concludes that even the height of the *śiṃśapā* is a cause for the application of the term "tree. Thus, that deluded person is led to apply the convention "tree" based solely on the property of being a *śiṃśapā*.
In this case, permanence and other such qualities are not further grounds for the conventional usage of the term "tree"; rather, the sole ground is the state of being a *śiṃśapā*.
This means that the possession of branches and so forth belonging to a *śiṃśapā* is the ground. // 16 //
He says "the effect" and so forth in order to illustrate the effect (*kārya*): "fire" is the property to be proven (*sādhya*);
"here" is the locus (*dharmin*).

"From smoke" is the reason (*hetu*). Since the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is well-known in the world as being based on perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*), the definition of the effect (*kārya*) has not been stated here in the same manner as that of the essential nature (*svabhāva*). // 17 //
But surely, since it possesses three forms, it is logical that there is only one *liṅga*; here, the distinction is based on the difference in its modes.
This being the case, since a single *svabhāvahetu* has infinite modes, is it not improper to speak of a triad?
Thus he says: "In this regard, there are two [types of reasons].

(19) For when there is an essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*), one object can lead to the cognition of another object; (20) because for that which is not so connected, there is no certainty of non-deviation from it.

Because the object of inference (*anumeya*) that exists as a positive entity (*bhāva-rūpa*) is of two kinds, the proof of existence (*bhāva-sādhana*) is also twofold. To explain: 1) when there is a difference in the essential nature (*svarūpa-bheda*) between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the reason (*hetu*), [the reason] cannot establish an undifferentiated probandum;
2) and when there is no difference in the essential nature between the probandum and the reason, it cannot establish a differentiated probandum.
In that regard, when there is non-difference between the probandum and the probans, it is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*);
when there is difference between the probandum and the property of similarity, it is a reason based on effect (*kāryahetu*);
and non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), however, is a reason based on absence (*abhāvahetu*).
By this it is shown that since two [reasons] establish existence and one establishes negation,
therefore the logical mark (liṅga) is of three kinds— two being those that establish existence.
And thus, one reason for negation has been shown. // 18 //
Now, if it is asked why there are only two [types of] proofs for an entity (*vastu*), he says in response: "essential nature" (*svabhāva*).
An essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*) is a connection by way of essential nature—that is, by way of its own-form (*svarūpa*).

The remainder [of the sentence] is: "Only when that [reason] exists is there the communication of the meaning characterized as the probandum by means of the meaning characterized as the logical mark. // 19 //

If it is asked: "Why is it that only when there is an essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*) does one object (*artha*) make another object known? To this he replies: "Because of the non-cognition of that," and so forth.

Here, "here" means among these three types of reasons (*hetu*); two of the reasons are "provers of a real entity" (*vastusādhana*), meaning they are the means of proving and making known an affirmation (*vidhi*).
One [type of reason] is the indicator of a negation. "Negation" should be understood as referring both to non-existence (*abhāva*) and to the conventional usage of non-existence (*abhāvavyavahāra*).
Thus, the meaning is this: the reason is a constituent part of the probandum (*sādhyāṅga*), because it serves the purpose of establishing the probandum.
The probandum is the primary element.

Therefore, the distinction between the reason, which is an instrument for the probandum, and the primary probandum arises from their difference as primary and instrumental, not from a difference in their intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, that which is to be proven is either an affirmation or a negation;
and since affirmation and negation do not coexist by way of mutual exclusion, their respective logical reasons are distinct.
Even among positive presences (*vidhi*), some causes are distinct and some are non-distinct;
because the two— distinction and non-distinction— exist by way of excluding one another, their causes are distinct.
Therefore, because the objects to be proven (sādhya) are mutually contradictory, the reasons (hetu) are distinct; it is not, however, due to their own inherent nature. // 18 //
Now, raising the doubt as to why these three alone possess the status of causes, while others do not, [the author] explains how it is precisely these three that are the causes:
To demonstrate both that other [factors] lack the status of being a cause, he says: "essential connection" (*svabhāvapratibandha*).
An essential connection is a connection by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
The compound "kṛtāḥ sādhane" means "established in the proof.
"Being connected by nature" (svabhāvapratibaddhatva) means having a nature that is connected.

When either the cause or the essential nature is the probandum (sādhya), the connection by way of essential nature is indistinguishable for both the effect and the essential nature; thus, both are included by means of this single compound.
The word *hi* has the sense of "because.

Because, when there is an essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*), the meaning of the probans (*sādhana*) would cause the probandum (*sādhya*) to be understood, therefore the three possess the capacity to indicate [the object].
Other [words] lack the capacity to convey meaning. // 19 //

But why is it that the relationship of the signifier and the signified exists only when there is an essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*), and not otherwise? And that connection belongs to the logical mark (*liṅga*) with respect to the object to be proven (*sādhya*).
Since that which is not dependent [on another] does not possess an infallible determination of its object with respect to that [other],
therefore, it should be understood that the relationship of the signifier and the signified exists only when there is a necessary connection (pratibandha).
"Not otherwise. // 20 //
And as for that [inherence], what is its object of obstruction, and in what form does the obstruction occur?
To demonstrate this, he says: "And that... and so forth.

Since, from the perspective of ultimate reality, a logical mark (liṅga) in some cases has the very nature of the probandum (sādhya), it is therefore necessarily connected with that [probandum]. // 21 //
Thus he says: "of that which is not bound to that. Here, "that" refers to the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). That which is not bound by that intrinsic nature is "not bound to that."
For that which is intrinsically connected to something else, there is no necessity of non-deviation from it if it were not so connected;
for there can be no non-deviation from an object to which one is not connected. Non-deviation from that [object] is what constitutes its non-deviation.
Its "restriction" is the restriction of its non-deviation from that [object],
and because of the absence of that [restriction],
the meaning is this: for indeed, that which is not intrinsically connected to something else cannot [be restricted to it].

Since that [probans] does not necessarily fail to deviate from an object that is not subject to obstruction, there is no rule of non-deviation—that is, no rule of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*)—between those two.
And it is from the rule of non-deviation that the relationship of the signified and the signifier arises.
For a logical mark (*liṅga*) is not accepted as the cause for the cognition of an imperceptible object by way of mere capacity, like a lamp.
Rather, it is ascertained by way of its non-deviation.

Therefore, when there is an essential connection (svabhāvapratibandha), there is the ascertainment of the state of being inseparable; from that, the relationship of the signified and the signifier arises.
Therefore, it is established that only when there is an essential connection (svabhāvapratibandha) can one object cause another object to be understood, and not otherwise. // 20 //
But surely, an obstruction applies to that which is dependent upon another with respect to that which is not so dependent;
therefore, in this case, between the probandum and the probans, what is obstructed by what?
To this he says: "And that... (sa ca).

And that essential connection (svabhāvapratibandha) belongs to the logical mark (liṅga) with respect to the object to be proven (sādhya). The logical mark is connected because it is dependent [on the object],
whereas the object to be proven is the locus of the connection because it is not dependent [on anything else].

But the meaning is that it is not "obstructed" (*pratibaddha*). In this context, the meaning is as follows: even though there is a specific identity (*tādātmya*), that which is obstructed is the indicator (*gamaka*), and that which is the object of the obstruction is the indicated (*gamya*).
Whatever is the fixed intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of a given phenomenon is bound to that [nature],
just as the property called "arising immediately after effort" is bound to impermanence.
However, that which possesses both this and another intrinsic nature is the object of the connection.
But it is not restricted [in its occurrence],
as is the case with the property called impermanence with respect to the property called being produced immediately after effort;
for the relationship between the signifier and the signified depends upon ascertainment.
Furthermore, the very fact of being produced immediately after an effort is ascertained to be the nature of impermanence;
therefore, that alone is invariably concomitant with impermanence.
Consequently, the relationship between the signifier and the signified exists only within a restricted domain.
"Not otherwise. // 21 //
22. Because of identity with the object to be proven, and because of arising from the object to be proven.
23. Because that which does not have that as its intrinsic nature and does not arise from it lacks an essential nature that is necessarily connected to it.
"Because of its identity with the object to be proven (sādhyārtha)":
since the mark (liṅga) arises in some cases from the very object to be proven, it is therefore necessarily connected (pratibaddha) with that object. // 22 //

Now, if it is asked: "How is it said that the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) of the logical mark (*liṅga*) arises from its identity with the object to be proven (*sādhyārtha*) and from its production from the object to be proven?
To this he replies: "of that which does not have that as its nature" (*atatsvabhāvasya*).
And that which does not have the object to be proven as its sole nature—

Furthermore, if [the reason] does not arise from the object to be proven (*sādhyārtha*), how could its necessary connection (*pratibandha*) with that [object] be stated? And that which is unconnected cannot be a logical mark (*liṅga*),
because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Therefore, the necessary connection (pratibandha) must be stated as arising only from identity (tādātmya) or causality (tadutpatti), and not otherwise. // 23 //
"Let it be so for now;
but what follows from that? If this is asked, he says: "And those two. Why, then, is there an essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*) of the logical mark (*liṅga*)?
Thus he says: "In reality," and so forth.
That which has as its essence (ātman) the object to be proven (sādhya)—that is, its own nature (svabhāva)—is "of that nature" (tadātman);
the state of being that is "identity" (tādātmya).
For that reason;
since the means of proof (*sādhana*) has the same nature as the probandum (*sādhya*),
therefore there is an essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*) in that case— this is the meaning.

If the means of proof (*sādhana*) were of the same nature as the probandum (*sādhya*), then, because there would be no distinction between the probandum and the means of proof, the reason (*hetu*) would be merely a part of the meaning of the thesis (*pratijñā*).
To this, he says: "In reality" (*vastutaḥ*).
In terms of their nature as ultimate reality, there is no difference between the two;
however, the distinction between the probandum and the probans depends upon that superimposed form which is the object of conceptual construction.
For the relationship between the signifier and the signified depends entirely upon ascertainment;
therefore, it is logical that their distinction depends solely on the form as it is established by ascertainment,
whereas in reality there is no difference.
The essential connection of the logical mark (liṅga) with the object to be proven (sādhya) arises not only from identity (tādātmya), but also from origination from that (tadutpatti). // 22 //
Why is the essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*) of the logical mark (*liṅga*) based on these two types of evidence and not on any other?
To this he says: "Of that which does not have that as its nature," and so forth.
That which is the nature of this [object] is its "essential nature" (*tatsvabhāva*).
That which is not of its own nature is "not of that nature.
Therefore, its arising from that is "arising from that" (*tad-utpatti*); it is not an arising from something other than that.

That which does not have a certain intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) nor arise from a certain [cause]—namely, that which lacks that intrinsic nature and lacks that origination—is, in this context, unconnected to that which lacks its intrinsic nature and that which lacks its origination. That which has such an unconnected intrinsic nature is called "one whose intrinsic nature is unconnected" (*apratibaddhasvabhāva*);
the state of being such is "the condition of having an unconnected intrinsic nature" (*apratibaddhasvabhāvatva*).
Therefore, because it lacks an essential nature that is restricted [to another],
if something were to possess an essential nature restricted to that which has a different nature or that which does not produce [the effect],
then there might be an essential-nature restriction even from another cause.
For the nature of being dependent is indeed what constitutes an essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*). And there is nothing else whatsoever that has a dependent nature.
Therefore, the essential connection exists only through identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*). // 23 //
Granted that the essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*) exists only through identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*),

and since these two— identity and causality— belong only to essential nature (*svabhāva*) and effect (*kārya*), it is by means of these two alone that the existence of a real entity (*vastu*) is established.
The establishment of a negation also proceeds from non-apprehension exactly as previously described.
26. Because that [non-existence] is impossible when a thing exists.

Identity is the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) for the essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*); origination from that is the necessary connection for the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*). For this very reason, it has been stated that the establishment of a real entity occurs through these two alone.

Since identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*) belong only to essential nature (*svabhāva*) and effect (*kārya*), therefore, the establishment of a real entity (*vastu*) is possible only through these two, and not by any other means that lacks a necessary connection (*apratibaddha*).
And thus, it is established that the proof of a real entity occurs through these two alone. // 24 //
It was stated that there is one reason for negation; what indeed is it? To this he says:
"The non-apprehension of that which has reached the conditions for apprehension," as was previously mentioned.
Therefore, these two alone are the reasons for negation. // 25 //
If it is asked, "How so?
he says: "When the entity exists.
For indeed, as long as the entity is present, that [destruction] is not possible. // 26 //
If it is asked why it is that only the aforementioned non-apprehension (anupalabdhi) establishes the conventional usage of the absence of a thing,
he says: "Otherwise."
But how is it that they alone possess the capacity to convey [the meaning]?
To this he says: "And those... The word "iti" is used in the sense of "therefore."

Since identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*) are established only with respect to the essential nature (*svabhāva*) and the effect (*kārya*), and since the relationship between the signified and the signifier (*gamyagamakabhāva*) is based upon those two, it follows that the proof of the existence of a real entity (*vastu*) is accomplished solely through these two: the effect and the essential nature. // 24 //
Now, why is the establishment of negation not also accepted as resulting from the non-perception of the unobservable?
To this he says: "The establishment of the conventional usage of negation," and so forth.

Since the establishment of the conventional usage of negation occurs precisely through that aforementioned non-perception of the observable, for that reason it is not stated [to arise] from anything else. // 25 //
Then, why does it exist? To this he says: "When [it] exists," and so forth.
When that object to be negated exists, [the negation occurs].
Since the non-perception of the perceptible is not possible, it follows that from its impossibility, the negation [of the object] is established. // 26 //
Now, why is it precisely from that [point]? He says: "And otherwise" (*anyathā ca*).
The meaning of the word "otherwise" is: because that non-perception of the unobservable is possible when the object exists.
Therefore, the proof of negation does not arise from any other [type of] non-apprehension. Why is this so? Because that [non-apprehension] is possible even when an entity exists.
To explain this, he says: "In the case of those things that have reached the conditions for non-apprehension," and so forth.

In this case, because of the completeness of other causal conditions and due to a specific nature, there is no certainty regarding non-existence based on the cessation of one's own perception with respect to objects that are remote in terms of place, time, or nature, and which have not reached the conditions for perception. Otherwise, such a certainty would be impossible.

The cessation of the cognizer’s direct perception—both past and present—of one whose mental impressions and memory are unconfused, is the means for establishing the conventional usage of non-existence.
If the aforementioned qualification is not accepted,

then regarding those objects that are remote in terms of place, time, or nature, and which are thus obstructed and have not reached the conditions for perception (*upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpta*), it is impossible to determine their non-existence based on the absence of the perceiver's direct perception (*pratyakṣa-nivṛtti*).
And as for the word "ca" (and):
it should be understood in the sense of "because.
"Place, time, and intrinsic nature"—that is, "place-time-intrinsic-nature"; the meaning is "in those things remote from these."

In this context, those things separated by an immeasurable distance are "spatially remote"; those separated by many eons are "temporally remote"; and those entities that transcend the senses are to be understood as "essentially remote."
Therefore, in this context, by the phrase "not meeting the conditions for perception" (*anupalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*), the absence of the totality of the causal conditions for perception is stated.
By the phrase "remote in terms of place, time, and intrinsic nature" (*deśakālasvabhāvaviprakṛṣṭa*), non-existence is demonstrated through a specific characteristic of intrinsic nature.
Consequently, it is established that only the aforementioned non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) is the means of proving negation.
Thus, it is said that even when there is no perception at a particular time, the aforementioned non-perception alone serves as the means for establishing a negation. // 27 //
Now, in order to indicate the accomplishment [of the practice] at the specific time mentioned, he says "amūḍha" and so forth.
"Smṛtisaṃskāraḥ" means the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) that produces memory;
the remainder of the sense is "the seed of memory."
An object that has reached the condition of being perceived is defined as one characterized by non-delusion and the attainment of memory.
In the absence of either of these two [conditions], an object is said to have reached the condition of non-perception.
Therefore, in this context, those things described as "having reached the condition of non-perception" are said to possess a deficiency of other causal conditions.
Regarding the phrase "those remote by way of place, time, and intrinsic nature," it is stated that they are devoid of specific intrinsic natures (*svabhāva-viśeṣa*).
The analysis of the compound is: "remote (*viprakṛṣṭa*) by means of place, time, and intrinsic nature.
Because there is no certainty of non-existence with respect to those things, their non-existence is asserted even though the entity may actually exist.
Why is there an absence of certainty? To this he says: because of the cessation of that perception which belongs to the cognizer himself regarding those [objects], there is an absence of certainty.

For, in the case of things that have reached the conditions for non-perception (*anupalabdhi-lakṣaṇaprāpta*), since there is no cessation of one's own perception, there is no certainty of their non-existence.
Therefore, even when an entity exists, there is the possibility of non-apprehension characterized by the cessation of one's own direct perception;
from that, the establishment of negation occurs precisely as previously described. // 27 //
Now, at what time is this non-perception of the perceptible a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), what is its essential nature (*svabhāva*),
and what is its function (*vyāpāra*)?
Thus he says: "not deluded," and so forth.
The object, such as a jar, is perceived by the cognizer;
its absence is non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*).
This means that its nature is the absence of that [object].
For this very reason, non-existence is not the probandum of the non-perception of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*),
because it is already established.

Furthermore, even though [the object] such as a jar is not being perceived, it is so described because it possesses a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) associated with the same single cognition as that jar.
This refers to the cessation of the perceiver’s direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of both past and present [objects].

That which was perceived as an empty location and so forth during the past and present times—that jar or similar object which is of the same nature and fitness as that location is precisely what is designated by the terms "past" and "present."
Otherwise, how could there be pastness or presentness in the absence of a jar and so forth in a particular location? Furthermore, there is the cognizer, such as Devadatta;
since the jar and so forth are to be determined by his perception, the jar and so forth are perceptible.

In this case as well, a jar or similar object is said to be "perceptible" because its form possesses the same fitness as the location and other factors that are not themselves determined by perception.
However, in ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), since the jar and so forth do not exist there, how could there be perceptibility?

Thus, according to the manner described, the cessation of a perceived object—whether past or present—is characterized as a distinct entity (*aparavastu*) because it is based on non-existence (*abhāva*).
The remainder [of the sentence] is that [the cognition] has as its nature a particular location devoid of a jar and so forth.
Furthermore, the conventional usage of non-existence (*abhāvavyavahāra*) consists of the cognition in the form "there is no jar here," as well as the verbal expression thereof.
And there is the activity characterized by moving to a place such as a spot free from doubt.

Conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) is characterized by the activity of cognition and its verbal designation. When the ground appears, it is said to be "perceptible" (*pratyakṣa*) because it is known with its entire causal complex complete and is conceived as being visible.
For this very reason, the object appearing in conjunction with that cognition, as well as that cognition itself, is called the "cessation of perception" (*pratyakṣanivṛtti*).

For, from that object which is being perceived and from the cognition thereof—which is conceived as being perceptual because it possesses the complete causal complex for perception—the cessation [of the object] is determined.
Therefore, the absence of the pot is said to be the very non-existence of the object and its cognition as perception;
however, in this context, "absence" does not consist of mere cessation.
Because the cessation of the visible object is not certain from mere cessation [of cognition].
But is it not the case that the cessation of the visible object is ascertained through the non-perception of the visible?
This is indeed true: when only a single object of cognition is perceived, if a jar were present, it would necessarily be perceived; thus, its perceptibility is postulated.
Consequently, the non-perception of the perceptible is ascertained.
And by the very power of the ascertainment of the non-perception of the perceptible, the absence of the perceptible is ascertained.
For if the object were present there, its non-perception would not occur;
therefore, from the ascertainment of the non-perception of the perceptible, the absence of the perceptible is established by implication.
"One has not been perceived" means that it should be treated as such by means of the non-perception of the perceptible.

Therefore, it should be understood that "the absence of perception" refers to another object—namely, something perceptible that is associated with the same cognition—as well as that cognition itself, because they serve as the cause for determining the cessation [of the object]. Thus it is said to be the "cessation of perception."
Just as the perceptibility of a jar is superimposed— even though it is non-existent— upon a perception that is associated with the same single cognition,

so too should it be understood that the respective forms of the jar are superimposed— even though they are non-existent— upon that which is past but possesses unobstructed memory-impressions, and upon that which is present, both being associated with the same single cognition.
And by this, the non-perception of the perceptible has been stated as having the nature of the absence of the jar through direct perception, and that is established;
therefore, the absence of the jar is not something to be proven.
Moreover, it has been stated that this is the "linguistic convention of non-existence" (*abhāvavyavahāra*).
That by which something is established is called the "means of establishing the linguistic convention of non-existence" (*abhāvavyavahārasādhanī*).
Thus, it is precisely non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) regarding objects that are past, present, or yet to arise that is the means of establishing the linguistic convention of non-existence.
However, it has been stated that this is not the case for a future object;
for indeed, the locus (dharmin) such as a location and so forth belonging to a future time is not perceived by direct perception,
and thus even non-apprehension— characterized by the apprehension of an empty location— is not established.
However, in the case of past time, the locus (dharmin) is perceived and the place devoid of the jar is remembered;
because both of these are causes, it is said that the latent impression for memory is unimpaired.
Therefore, through the recollection of the place devoid of the jar and so forth from days long past, the establishment of the linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) of non-existence occurs.
Furthermore, the substratum (*dharmin*) of the present time—such as a jar or an empty space—is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Therefore, the application of the conventional usage of "non-existence" (*abhāvavyavahāra*) toward that [substratum] is easily obtained.
By stating "one whose memory-impressions are not confused," the charge of the reason being unestablished (*hetvasiddhi*) has been refuted.
Otherwise, if one does not remember an empty location and so forth, non-apprehension itself would not be established.
By the words "past" and "present," a specific time is indicated.

That [object], such as a jar, in which there exists an unimpaired—that is, unlost—latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by perception and consisting in the generation of memory, is described as such.
The connection is that [it refers to] "that which has passed" as being directly perceived by the cognizer;
and the connection is that it refers to "the present" as being directly perceived by the cognizer.
However, the inclusion of the phrase "whose mental traces of memory are unconfused" is not a qualification of the present.

Because, when one has seen a place devoid of a jar in the past, there is confusion regarding the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of memory when the visible jar is not perceived, yet there is no confusion regarding the visible jar itself;
whereas in the present, upon seeing a place devoid of a jar, there is no confusion regarding the latent impression of memory.
For this very reason, there is neither confusion regarding the absence of the jar nor confusion regarding the jar itself when it is not perceived.
Therefore, the inclusion of the phrase "having unimpaired memory-impressions" (*amūḍhasmṛtisaṃskāra*) is not a qualifier for the present object of negation.
This is because there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the memory-impressions of a present object.
For this very reason, it says "and of the present."
The word "and" (ca) is employed so that it may be understood as a conjunction of a present [non-perception] devoid of a qualifier with a past [non-perception] possessing a qualifier.
This is the meaning: a past non-perception clearly remembered is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), as is a present one.
Therefore, it is possible to know: "There was no jar here because it was not perceived," and "It does not exist because it is not being perceived."

However, it is not possible to know that "a jar will not exist here because it is not perceived," because there is doubt regarding the existence of a future non-perception; thus, the specific time [condition] for non-perception has been explained.
He demonstrates its function: the linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) regarding absence is a cognition of the form "it does not exist."
The verbal [expression] is of this very form,
and the physical conventional usage regarding non-existence is activity characterized by going and coming without hesitation;
for when the absence of a jar is known, one proceeds to go and come without hesitation.

Thus, for all three types of this conventional usage regarding non-existence (*abhāvavyavahāra*), the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*) is the means of operation, the proof, and the instigator.
And although the cognition "the jar does not exist" arises from non-perception alone,
this very [cognition] is the ascertainment of non-existence.
Nevertheless, because only the bare location is apprehended by perception, the ascertainment of absence follows the operation of perception itself in the form "there is no jar here.
Therefore, the ascertainment of absence, which conforms to the perceptual operation of grasping the bare location, is produced by perception;
for that [ascertainment] arises precisely from that [perceptual] determination of absence.
And that [compassion] is of eleven types according to the distinctions of its application.
Having stated that [the absence of cognition] is perceptible to the cognizer, the perceptibility of all cognizers has been refuted;

for the reason stated as being perceptible to all cognizers would indeed be unestablished (*asiddha*). Furthermore, the exclusion of the perceptibility of all cognizers is unestablished for the opponent (*prativādī*). // 28 //
If one asks why it is precisely this non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) just mentioned that establishes the conventional usage of absence (*abhāvavyavahāra*), he says:
"Of that" (*tasyāḥ*).

It is by the very cessation of that object-entity—whether past, present, or arisen—which was previously perceived by one whose seeds of memory are unimpaired, that the ascertainment of absence is possible.
But it does not [arise] through another cognition whose object is yet to be. // 29 //
Thus, by the aforementioned reason, both the nature of non-apprehension and its specific temporal conditions have been stated.
To demonstrate the different applications (*prayoga*) of that [non-apprehension], he says: "And that...
*Prayoga* refers to the verbal expression of a three-characterized proof (*trilakṣaṇasādhana*).
Due to those distinctions, non-apprehension (anupalabdhi) becomes elevenfold. // 30 //

Furthermore, by the very capacity to determine the non-perception of what is perceptible, non-existence is determined through perception itself according to the principle previously stated. However, because it is possible for even unperceived things to exist,
one is unable to employ the conventional usage of "non-existence" due to the suspicion that they might exist.
Therefore, non-perception brings about the conventional usage of "non-existence"— that is, because a perceptible object is not perceived,
it follows that "it does not exist. Thus,
the non-perception of a perceptible object initiates the cognition of non-existence.

"One does not do what has not been done"—this certainty of non-existence, although set in motion by non-perception (*anupalambha*), is said to be "effected" by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and "initiated" by non-perception; thus, non-perception is that which initiates the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) of non-existence.
But why is it that non-perception is a means of cognition (*gamika*) regarding both the past and the present?
Thus he says: because there is no certainty regarding the non-existence [of an object] based on its non-perception during the aforementioned time.
For non-perception in the future is itself of a doubtful nature;
since that [non-perception] is unestablished, there is no certainty regarding non-existence.
But rather, [it belongs] to that which is past and present. // 29 //
In order to demonstrate the different varieties of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) in the present context, he says: "And that," and so forth.
"And that" refers to this non-apprehension; it has eleven modes, meaning its modes are eleven, hence it is "of eleven modes.
From what [source] does this difference in modes arise?
Because of the difference in application (*prayoga*).
Application (*prayoga*) means employment (*prayukti*); it is said to be the denotative function (*abhidhā-vyāpāra*) of a word.
For a word directly expresses either another positive entity in some cases, or another negation in others;

however, in all instances, the non-perception of the perceptible is understood even when not explicitly conveyed by the word. Thus, there is a distinction between the types of non-apprehension based on the difference in the operation of the expressive word.
But it is not due to a difference in essential nature, as has been explained at length. // 30 //

31. Non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*), as for example: "There is no smoke here," which is the non-perception of that which has reached the conditions for perception (*upalabdhi-lakṣaṇaprāpta*). (1) 32. Non-perception of the effect (*kāryānupalabdhi*), as for example: "The causes of smoke, whose capacity is unimpeded, do not exist here, because of the absence of smoke. (2)
In order to explain the distinction between its types, he says: "non-perception of intrinsic nature" (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*).
This means the non-perception of intrinsic nature, that is, the essential character of a thing.
In order to demonstrate an example, he says: "as follows" (*yathā*).
The word "example" (dṛṣṭānta) is used here;
it should be understood in this same way throughout all instances.
Regarding the word "here" (atra):
By this, the property of the subject (dharmin) is stated;
by "not smoke," the property to be proven (sādhyadharma) is stated.
The remainder [of the definition] is: "the non-perception of smoke, which has a nature capable [of being perceived], even though other conditions for perception are present. // 31 //
"Non-perception of the effect" (*kāryānupalabdhi*) is a compound analyzed as "non-perception of the effect" (*kāryasya anupalabdhi*).
He states an example: "Just as there are no causes of smoke here whose capacities are unimpeded.
Regarding those whose capacities are unimpeded, he says "by way of a distinction of types," beginning with "essential nature" (*svabhāva*) and so forth.
This refers to how there is a non-perception of the essential nature of that which is to be negated.
In this context, "the subject" (dharmin) is [the mountain];
"there is no smoke" is the thesis (sādhya);
and "because of the non-perception of that which has reached the conditions for perception" is the reason (hetu).
And this reason is to be explained as before. // 31 //
The non-perception of that which is the effect of the object to be negated is illustrated by the words "the effect," and so forth;
as for example: [text follows].
"Here" refers to the subject (*dharmin*).
"Those whose capacity is unimpeded" means those whose capacity for producing smoke is unhindered (*anupahata*).
"They do not exist" is the proposition to be proven (*sādhya*).
"Because of the absence of smoke" is the reason (*hetu*).

Since causes do not necessarily possess their effects, what is to be proven (*sādhya*) by the non-perception of the effect is the absence of those [causes] whose capacities are unimpeded, and not that of others.
Furthermore, only those things that exist in the final moment possess unimpeded causal capacities,
because for others, the possibility of obstruction exists. And the non-perception of the effect is employed only in cases where the cause is perceptible.
When the object of perception is to be established, it is precisely the non-perception of the perceptible that serves as the means of cognition.
In this regard, a person standing on the roof of a white house, although not seeing the courtyard itself, sees the area extending to the walls on all four sides.
He perceives the space within the vicinity of the walls—known as "light"—as being devoid of smoke.
In that case, because of the certainty of the absence of smoke,
it must be understood that there is an absence of fire whose capacity is unimpeded, since smoke produced by fire located in a particular place would necessarily exist in that same place.
And smoke produced by fire within that area of the house's courtyard would belong to that same location; therefore, the absence of fire in that location must be understood.

Thus, that area of the house's courtyard—enclosed by walls—together with the space of the sky devoid of smoke, which is itself enclosed by the limits of the walls and consists of light, constitutes the subject (*dharmin*).

Therefore, the locus (*dharmin*)—which consists of a collection of both perceived and unperceived spatial parts of space—is established by the force of the cognition of the absence of fire; it is not merely that which is currently perceived.
In this context, however, the demonstrative "here" (*atra*) is a perceptual reference with respect to the perceived portion.

33. Non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*): for example, "There is no *śiṃśapā* tree here, because there is no tree. (3) 34. Perception of what is incompatible with the essential nature (*svabhāvaviruddhopalabdhi*): for example, "There is no sensation of cold here, because of fire. (4)
The causes of smoke, such as firewood and so forth, are what have been described by that term.
Here, by the word "here" (atra), the subject (dharmin) is stated;
by the phrase "the unimpeded causal capacities for smoke do not exist," the property to be proven (sādhyadharma) is stated.
"Because of the absence of smoke": the ellipsis is "because smoke is absent here, therefore [the fire is absent]."
If the causes of smoke were present here with their capacities unimpeded, then smoke would certainly be produced as well. // 32 //
Regarding "non-perception of the pervader" (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*): it pervades, thus it is the "pervader"; the meaning is the non-perception of that.
"Just as [there is no] *śiṃśapā* here because it is a tree"—
by this, the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is stated.
For a tree is the pervader (*vyāpaka*) of the *śiṃśapā*.
Upon its cessation, that [property] also becomes ceased;
"herein" refers to the substratum (dharmin) mentioned by this [term].
"Because of the absence of trees"— by this, the reason (hetu) is stated; "there is no śiṃśapā."
By this, the property to be proven (sādhyadharma) has been stated. // 33 //
Regarding "perception of what is contradictory to the essential nature" (*svabhāvaviruddhopalabdhi*):
that which is contradictory by way of its essential nature is "contradictory to the essential nature" (*svabhāvaviruddha*); the meaning is the perception of such a thing.
He states an example: "Just as there is no cold touch here, because of fire. By the word "here," the locus (*dharmin*) is indicated.
It is not only in this case that the collection of the visible and the invisible constitutes the locus.
Moreover, it is also otherwise:
when the momentariness of sound is to be proven, one particular sound is perceptible, while another is imperceptible.
The same applies here as well.

Just as in this case the subject (*dharmin*)—which serves as the locus for the comprehension of the probandum (*sādhya*) and consists of both visible and invisible parts—has been shown, so too should it be understood for oneself in all subsequent applications. // 32 //
The non-perception of that which pervades the property to be negated—the pervader—is cited [as an example], beginning with "the pervader," etc.
As for "for example":
here, "here" refers to the locus (*dharmin*).
"It is not a *śiṃśapā*":
the absence of a *śiṃśapā* is the probandum (*sādhya*).
"Because of the absence of the tree," which is its pervader (*vyāpaka*), is the reason (*hetu*).
This non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is also employed in the absence of the pervaded (*vyāpya*), such as the state of being a *śiṃśapā* tree, which is perceptible.
However, when the pervaded meets the conditions for apprehension (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*), it is the non-apprehension of the perceptible that serves as the means of cognition.
In that case, when there are two adjacent regions that are elevated, [the following applies].
Of those two, one is endowed with a dense thicket of trees, while the other is composed of a single rock and lacks any tree thickets;
even one who observes the trees situated there, though seeing them, does not discern the distinction between *śiṃśapā* and other species.
Its being a tree is perceptible, whereas its being a *śiṃśapā* is imperceptible.
For he determines the absence of a tree on that single stone slab— which is devoid of trees— on account of its visibility, since there is no apprehension of what is visible.
The absence of *śiṃśapā*-ness, however, follows from the absence of the pervader, which is "tree-ness. In such a case, this [inference] is employed as a proof for non-existence. // 33 //
The perception of that which is incompatible with the nature of the object to be negated is illustrated by the passage beginning with "svabhāva" (intrinsic nature) and so forth.
The word "yathā" (as for example) indicates the subject (*dharmin*) in this context.
The negation of cold touch, namely "there is no cold touch," is the probandum (*sādhya*).
(35) Perception of the contradictory (*viruddhakāryopalabdhi*): for example, "There is no cold touch here, because of smoke.

(36) Perception of what is pervaded by the contradictory (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhi*): for example, "Even for an entity that has come into being, there is no necessity of permanence, because destruction depends upon other causes."
By the phrase "of fire," the reason (*hetu*) is stated;
by the phrase "not a cold touch," the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is stated.
For instance—because there is a contradiction between fire and a cold touch, the presence of that [fire] excludes the cold touch. // 34 //
"Perception of a contradictory effect" (viruddhakāryopalabdhi) means that the effect of a contradictory [thing] is a "contradictory effect," and it is the perception of that; such is the meaning.
For example: "There is no sensation of cold here because of smoke.
By this, that [non-apprehension] is expressed.
Here, "here" refers to the locus (*dharmin*).
"Because of smoke" is the reason (*hetu*).
"Not a cold touch" is the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*).
Fire is that which is opposed to a cold touch.
Smoke is its effect;
therefore, wherever there is smoke, there is also fire, and where there is fire, how could there be the sensation of cold? // 35 //
"Perception of that which is pervaded by the contradictory":
"pervaded by the contradictory" means pervaded by something contradictory;
the meaning is the perception of that.
He states an illustration: "Just as there is no certainty of existence for even an entity that has come into being, [namely] its destruction.
The phrase "certainly existing" (dhruvabhāvī) means "having the property of necessarily coming into being"; this is the implied sense.
[The phrase] "even for an entity that has come into being" refers to the following.
The phrase "of a thing that has arisen" refers to fire; this is the reason.

And this non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is to be employed where the sensation of cold is invisible, because the application of the non-apprehension of the visible occurs only when the object is visible.
Therefore, where fire is visible due to a particular color, while its cold touch— though present— is invisible because of distance, there the formal argument (prayoga) is as follows: // 34 //
The perception of that which is the effect of what is contradictory to the object to be negated is the means of cognition;
for example,
"here" refers to the locus (dharmin).
The probandum (*sādhya*) is the absence of cold touch, expressed as "there is no cold touch";
"because of smoke" (*dhūmāt*) is the reason (*hetu*); [the example is:
where cold touch would be visible if it were present.
In that case, the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*) is the means of cognition;
where fire is perceptible,
the perception of its contradictory (*viruddhopalabdhi*) is the means of cognition.
However, when both [the object to be negated and its counter-correlate] are beyond direct perception (*parokṣa*), the perception of a contradictory effect (*viruddhakāryopalabdhi*) is employed.
In that case, when one sees a specific mass of smoke emerging from a room— serving as an indicator of a fire capable of eliminating the cold present throughout the entire room—
one then infers the cessation of the sensation of cold from the fire inferred from that specific smoke.

In this case, the entire interior space of the room, together with the visible portion of the doorway, is the subject (dharmin); it should be understood as being "like the previous [example]" because of the pursuit of the realization of the probandum (sādhya). // 35 //
An instance [of the reason] should be cited as the perception of another property that is pervaded by what is contradictory to the negation. For example:
"dhruvabhāva" means that which necessarily exists.
"No" is the negation of the state of being necessarily existent; this is the probandum (sādhya).
"Destruction" is the subject (dharmin).
"Of an existence that has already come to be" is the qualification of the subject.

The meaning of the word "api" (even/also) is that even for that which has come into being— that is, for what is born— the perishable nature is not necessarily inevitable, much less so for that which has not been born.
"Another cause" (*hetvantaram*) refers to a cause other than the productive cause, such as a hammer or similar instrument.
That [non-apprehension] depends upon that;
for example, non-apprehension of what is incompatible with the effect: "There are no causes of cold here whose capacity is unimpeded, because of fire."
"O Śeṣa! By the phrase 'the destruction of even an existent entity,' the subject (dharmin) is stated;
by the phrase 'not necessarily occurring,' the property to be proven (sādhyadharma) is stated.
Thus, the final meaning established is that the destruction of an entity that has arisen is not eternal."
If it is asked, "How is this so?
he says: "Because of the dependence upon another cause.
For in this way, the dependence upon another cause is admitted.
Those things which depend upon other causes are not necessarily present,
just as the redness of a kārsāsa cloth [depends on dyeing].
Here too, the state of being necessarily produced is contradictory to the state of not being necessarily produced.
Therefore, dependence on other causes is pervaded by it;
consequently, wherever there is dependence on other causes, there is the state of not being necessarily produced.
Where there is the state of being non-inherently existent, how could there be the state of being inherently existent? // 36 //
Regarding the term "perception of what is incompatible with the effect" (*kāryaviruddhopalabdhi*): that which is incompatible with the effect is "incompatible with the effect";
the remainder of the definition is "the perception thereof."
It is perishable;
"because of dependence" is the reason.
Dependence upon another cause is pervaded by the state of not being necessarily produced.
For example, the dependence of a dye on other causes for its coloring of a cloth is pervaded by the state of not being necessarily produced;
and the state of not being necessarily produced is the opposite of the state of being necessarily produced.
Furthermore, destruction, which is by nature perishable, is held to depend upon other causes.
Therefore, because one observes the requirement of another reason that is pervaded by the opposite [of the probandum], there is a negation of "inevitable occurrence" (*dhruvabhāvitva*).
Here, "inevitable occurrence" means permanence (*nityatva*), while "non-inevitable occurrence" means impermanence (*anityatva*).
Furthermore, because permanence and impermanence exist by way of mutual exclusion, there is a contradiction in a single locus.
This being the case, when one of two mutually exclusive things is perceived, the identity of the second with that locus must be negated.
And such a negation of identity is possible only for that which is accepted as being perceptible.
Since this is so, the negation of identity is thus formulated: if this which is being perceived were eternal, it would be perceived as having an eternal nature;
yet it is not perceived as having an eternal nature.
Therefore, it is not eternal.
And thus, by accepting that the negation of eternality has a perceptible nature, the negation is established.
Even if the negation of a non-perceptible entity, such as a *piśāca*, being identical in nature to a perceptible object like a jar is made, [the same logic applies].
This must be established by accepting that it has the nature of being visible:
if this pot, while being seen, were of the nature of a piśāca, then the piśāca would be seen;
yet it is not seen.

Therefore, [the statement] "it is not a *piśāca*" is a negation of the identity— whether of a real or unreal thing— with a perceptible object such as a jar, preceded by the admission that [the *piśāca*] possesses the nature of being perceptible. This being the case,
just as the negation of a jar’s existence is based solely on the non-perception of the perceptible after having admitted its perceptibility, so too is it here.
Similarly, when two things that are mutually exclusive are observed elsewhere, the negation [of one] occurs solely through the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalambha*).
Thus, this type of formal argument (*prayoga*) is included within the non-perception of essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*). // 36 //
An example of the perception of that which is contradictory to the effect of the object to be negated is as follows:
(38) the perception of that which is contradictory to the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*), for instance: "There is no sensation of frost here, because of fire."
39. Non-perception of the cause is, for example: "There is no smoke here because of the absence of fire."
He states an example: "Just as here, when fire is present, the causes of cold do not possess unobstructed efficacy.
Here, "here" refers to the subject (*dharmin*); "of fire" expresses the reason (*hetu*).
"There are no causes of cold whose capacity is unimpeded"—
this states the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*).
In this context, the effect of the causes of cold is coldness.
Cold is incompatible with fire;
where there is fire, how can there be the entry of cold?
And where there is the sensation of cold, how could the causes of cold, whose capacities are unimpeded, ever exist there?
If such things were to exist, then there would necessarily also be a cold tactile sensation. // 37 //
"Perception of that which is contradictory to the pervader" (vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi) means:
that which is contradictory to the pervader is "contradictory to the pervader" (vyāpakaviruddha);
the perception of that is its meaning.
He states an example: "Just as there is no touch of frost here because of fire.
Here, the word "here" (atra) denotes the locus (*dharmin*).
"Of fire"—
by this the reason is stated;
"but not the touch of frost."
By this, the property to be proven (sādhyadharma) is stated:
"contact with frost" means contact with snow;
its pervader (vyāpaka) is "cold contact."
Fire is the opposite of that [cold];
therefore, where there is fire, how could there be the sensation of cold? And where there is the sensation of cold, there can by no means be the sensation of frost either. (38)
"Non-perception of the cause" (kāraṇānupalabdhi): the analysis [of the compound] is "the non-perception of a cause.
Here, "here" refers to the subject (dharmin).
The thesis to be proven is that those causes of cold which possess an unobstructed capacity for producing cold do not exist;
"because of fire" is the reason.
Where the causes of cold are invisible and the sensation of cold touch is also invisible, this reason should be employed there.
If, however, the cold touch or its causes were perceptible, then either the non-perception of their effect or the non-perception of the perceptible itself would be the indicator [of their absence].
Therefore, this too is a means of proving non-existence.

Therefore, in a location where the cause of cold exists even though it is invisible due to distance, and fire is visible from afar because of its brilliant color, this formal argument (prayoga) is applied. // 37 //
The perception of that which is contradictory to what pervades the object of negation should be illustrated as follows:
"here" refers to the subject (*dharmin*);
"there is no touch of frost" is the thesis (*sādhya*).
"Fire" is the reason (*hetu*). Wherever there is the pervaded (*vyāpya*), namely hot touch, and the pervader (*vyāpaka*), namely cold touch, is not perceived, there this reason applies.

Because the non-apprehension of both the essential nature (*svabhāva*) and the pervader (*vyāpaka*) must be employed when these two are perceptible; and this being the case, it serves to establish non-existence. Furthermore, for an observer situated at a distance, the touch of frost is a specific instance of cold touch.
Coldness alone is imperceptible,
whereas fire, due to its specific color-form (*rūpa*), is perceptible even when situated at a distance;
therefore, the absence of coldness is established through fire.
Consequently, there arises the ascertainment of the absence of the touch of coldness specific to snow;
since that specific coldness is pervaded by coldness in general, this [inference] is employed with respect to a qualified object. // 38 //

An example of the non-perception of the cause of that which is to be negated is as follows: "In this case," [there is] the perception of something incompatible with the cause, such as: "He does not possess particular qualities such as horripilation, because there is a particular fire nearby."
He states an example: "Just as there is no smoke here because of the absence of fire.
By the word "here," the locus (*dharmin*) is indicated;
and by the phrase "because of the absence of fire," the faultless reason (*hetu*) is proclaimed.
"Not smoke"—
by this, the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is stated;
and here, "smoke is the effect of fire."
Where there is an absence of fire, there can be no smoke whatsoever.

"Perception of what is contradictory to the cause" (kāraṇaviruddhopalabdhi) means that which is contradictory to the cause is "contradictory to the cause" (kāraṇaviruddha); the meaning is the perception of that.
He states an illustration: "Just as there are no specific qualities such as horripilation in this [person].
By the word *asya* ("in this"), the subject (*dharmin*) is expressed.
"There is no specific [state] such as horripilation"
— by this, the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is stated.
"Horripilation," however, refers to the bristling of the body hairs.
Those for which that [fear] is the first are "those beginning with horripilation" (*romaharṣādayaḥ*).
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the clenching of teeth, trembling of the body, and so forth are included.
And since those very things—horripilation and the rest—are the specific manifestations (*viśeṣa*), they are called "the specific manifestations beginning with horripilation" (*romaharṣādiviśeṣāḥ*).

Horripilation and the like also arise from fear, joy, and so forth; therefore, the term "specific" (*viśeṣa*) was stated for the purpose of excluding those [other causes]. And here, one should understand that only those horripilations belonging to one afflicted by cold wind are intended.
"Because it is a particular fire that is present.
In this context, "particular fire" means a specific kind of fire; "present" means being in proximity.
One who has a specific fire nearby is "one for whom a specific fire is proximate" (*sannihitadahanaviśeṣa*);
the state of being such is its "nature" (*tattva*).
Therefore, because it is a specific fire proximate to a fire,
the thesis to be proven is that such a specific fire possesses the property of coldness, and not smoke.
"Because of the absence of fire" is the reason (*hetu*). This application [of the reason] occurs in a case where an effect, although present, is invisible.
However, when the effect is perceptible, it is the non-perception of the perceptible that establishes its absence;

therefore, this too is a means of proving non-existence. For instance, when a lake is filled with still, clear water and the mist arising from it is sparse due to the winter season, and the twilight darkness is present, although smoke exists there, it is not perceived; thus, it is negated by the non-perception of its cause.
If, however, that fire were floating upon the water while burning,
it would be perceived solely by its specific form;
but if it were not burning, it would be situated within the fuel.

In that case as well, since perception is based on the locus of the fire, the fire must be visible either in its own form or in the form of its substratum; therefore, this [inference] is employed therein. // 39 //

An example of the perception of that which is contradictory to the cause of the object to be negated is as follows: "As for this," refers to the subject (dharmin). "The bristling of the hair" means its emergence.

Those things beginning with it—such as the teeth-vina and so forth—which are produced by cold, are distinguished from others produced by fear, faith, and the like; thus, there are specific instances such as the bristling of the hair.
That these do not exist is what is to be proven.
Fire itself is distinguished from other fires by its capacity to remove cold; thus, there is a specific instance of fire.
Something may be fire yet not capable of removing cold,
such as a lamp;
the inclusion of the qualification [“hot”] is for the purpose of excluding such cases.
That which has a specific fire present in it is so described; the state of being that is the reason [for the inference].

Where the cold touch exists but is invisible, there is the perception of an effect contrary to the cause of horripilation, as for example: "This region does not contain a person possessed of specific qualities such as horripilation, because of smoke."
It has been stated that a specific property (viśeṣa) is mentioned for the sake of establishing such [a subject] which is capable of refuting [the contrary].
For instance, in this case, the cause of the specific effect such as horripilation is the sensation of cold; fire is the opposite of that.
The heat of fire wards off cold;
if cold were absent, there could not possibly be specific effects such as the bristling of hair. (40)
"The perception of an effect that is incompatible with the cause" means:
that which is opposed to a cause is "incompatible with the cause" (*kāraṇaviruddha*); the effect of that is the "effect incompatible with the cause" (*kāraṇaviruddhakārya*).
The perception of that [is as follows]:
it is the perception of the effect of something incompatible with the cause.
He states an example: "This place does not contain a person characterized by specific signs such as horripilation, because there is smoke."
By the phrase "this place," the subject (*dharmin*) is stated;
by "because of smoke," the reason (*hetu*) is stated;
and by "possessing a person characterized by specific signs such as horripilation," the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is stated.
"One endowed with specific qualities such as horripilation" means one who possesses specific qualities such as horripilation.
That person who is endowed with specific qualities such as horripilation is "the person endowed with specific qualities such as horripilation";
the region in which that person exists is "the region possessing a person endowed with specific qualities such as horripilation."
In this case, the cause of specific effects such as horripilation is the sensation of cold;
fire is its opposite;
and smoke is the effect of fire.

Furthermore, specific states such as joy and so forth are invisible. In this regard, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: if the specific states such as horripilation were visible, then the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*) should be employed;
if the sensation of cold were visible, then the non-perception of the cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*) should be employed.
Therefore, this is a proof for existence:
for one sees fire from a distance due to its specific form (*rūpa-viśeṣa*),
whereas cold touch is invisible, as are the specific qualities such as the bristling of body hair.
One establishes their non-existence through the perception of something incompatible with their cause; such is its application in that case. // 40 //
The perception of that which is the effect of what is contradictory to the cause of that which is to be negated should be illustrated— namely,
"this place" as the subject (*dharmin*), and "conjunction" (*yoga*) as the property (*dharma*).
The term "endowed with specific qualities such as horripilation" means possessing specific qualities like horripilation;
a person related to that is a "person endowed with specific qualities such as horripilation.
The thesis (*sādhya*) is that [the subject] does not possess such a person.
"Because of smoke" is the logical reason (*hetu*).
When the specific qualities such as horripilation are perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), there is the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*).
When the cause, namely the sensation of cold touch, is perceived through direct perception, there is the non-perception of the cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*).
If [the three factors] are perceptible, the "perception of what is incompatible with the cause" (*kāraṇaviruddhopalabdhi*) should be employed;
if all three are imperceptible, this [present] formulation is to be used.
Therefore, this is a means of proving non-existence (*abhāva*).
In that case, although the specific qualities of the fire— such as its heat, cold touch, and the bristling of the hair— are imperceptible to the cognizer standing at a distance,
