smoke is perceptible; wherever that [smoke] exists, this [inference] is a means of valid cognition.
Smoke, however, is that which is to be understood here as the indicator of fire capable of removing the cold situated in that location;

for even if fire in general is inferred from smoke in general, there is no removal of the sensation of cold. Furthermore, all these ten applications of non-perception, beginning with the non-perception of the effect, are included within the non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*).
43. This is because, although there is a difference in formulation due to affirmation and negation of other meanings through traditional succession, [the underlying principle remains the same].
Therefore, where there is smoke, there is fire;
where there is fire, there is no sensation of cold;
and where there is no sensation of cold, how could its effects—such as specific symptoms like horripilation—possibly exist? // 41 //
Previously, non-perception of that which has reached the conditions for perception was stated as one reason for negation;

now, if it is asked how negation occurs through the non-perception of the effect (*kāryānupalabdhi*) and so forth, or through the perception of what is incompatible with the essential nature (*svabhāvaviruddhopalabdhi*) and so forth, he says in response:
"These" (*ime*), referring to those just mentioned without interval.

"All" (sarve) means the entirety, not limited by the number ten; and all applications of non-apprehension (anupalabdhi-prayoga) are included within the non-apprehension of intrinsic nature (svabhāvānupalabdhi). // 42 //
The application of the non-perception of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*) is one thing, while the non-perception of the effect (*kāryānupalabdhi*) and so forth are another.
For instance, in the case of the non-perception of the effect and the like, there is the negation of other things (*arthāntarapratiṣedha*).
And in cases such as the perception of what is incompatible with the intrinsic nature (*svabhāvaviruddhopalabdhi*), there is the affirmation of another thing (*arthāntaravidhi*).
If it is asked, "How then is [the negation] included therein?
he says: "In another thing," and so forth.
It should be understood that because the cessation of specific states such as joy can be discerned, "mere smoke" is not the logical reason (*hetu*). // 41 //
If only one reason for negation has been stated, how can there be reasons for the absence of even a single part?
To this he says: "All these," and so forth.
These are the applications of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*).
These have been explained as they were introduced here.
In that regard, to how many of them does the inclusion apply?

He says: "The non-perception of the effect, and so forth. [An objection is raised: Is there not the consequence that three or four types—beginning with the non-perception of the effect—are being mentioned? He replies: "Ten. Since there is then the consequence of mentioning all ten as mere examples, he says: "All."
This is what is meant: even those not actually employed [in the examples] are similar to the examples that have been employed;
thus, "all" indeed [is intended].
If the term "all" were used without the mention of "ten," one might conclude that the entirety of the examples actually employed was being referred to.

However, since the totality [of the examples] is understood through the mention of "ten," the mention of "all" arises as something redundant for the purpose of understanding a totality similar to those already cited.

They enter into the inclusion within the non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*) by way of identity; the meaning is that they have the non-perception of the essential nature as their own nature. // 42 //
But surely, since non-perception of effect and the others differ from the application of the non-perception of essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*), how do they fall within its scope?
To this he says: "by way of a succession" (*pāramparyeṇa*).
"Even though there is a difference in application" means that they are included even when there is a difference in the application, which is the operation of the word.
How is there a difference in application?
Thus he says: "The affirmation of another object.

In the applications of non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), such as the perception of what is incompatible with the nature [of the object to be negated], there is the affirmation—that is, the perception—of an object other than the object to be negated. In the applications such as the non-perception of the effect (*kāryānupalabdhi*), there is negation.

Because one observes its application through the affirmation of another meaning (*arthāntaravidhi*) and the negation of another meaning (*arthāntarapratiṣedha*), a cognition of exclusion (*vyavacchedapratīti*) arises in this very way even for oneself; thus, its formulation is indicated even in inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*).

Even though there is indeed a difference in usage between the affirmation of something other than the subject and its negation, nevertheless, their inclusion within that [negation] is intended only by way of a mediated succession (paramparayā), and not in reality.

For instance, in some cases, through the non-perception of the effect (*kāryānupalabdhi*), when the absence of the cause of smoke—whose capacity is unimpeded—is established, there arises the cognition of its absence.

In every place where there is an absence of smoke, there is the non-perception of that very cause which has not met the conditions for perceptibility; thus, it is included within the non-perception of essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*). The distinction [between these types] arises from the difference in the investigator's mode of reflection: for some, the cognition of the absence of the cause occurs by way of the absence of the effect.
However, for some [non-perceptions], their inclusion is to be understood as occurring through the door of essential nature (*svabhāva*),
and likewise through the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) and the non-perception of the cause (*kāraṇa*) by way of a succession.
Furthermore, in the case of the perception of what is contradictory to the essential nature (*svabhāvaviruddhopalabdhi*), there is the cognition of the absence of cold by means of fire.

Where there is fire, there is the non-perception of cold touch that has reached the conditions for perceptibility; thus, it is included within the non-perception of essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*).

In the case of the perception of what is pervaded by the contradictory (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhi*), with respect to other causes, even though light is the essential nature of all colors, it is likewise [included] as the non-perception of essential nature.
Similarly, in the case of the perception of the effect of what is contradictory to the cause (*kāraṇaviruddhakāryopalabdhi*), fire is established by means of smoke.
And when cold has ceased there, the non-existence of its opposite—a person characterized by specific signs such as horripilation—is established.

Since that [non-existence] consists in the non-perception of a person who, if present, would have met the conditions for perceptibility (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*), it is included within the very category of "non-perception of essential nature" (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*). // 43 //

As for those who say that the non-perception of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*) is included [within the other types of non-apprehension] through metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), on account of the absence of difference due to the pervasion of both cause and effect and their non-difference—
according to them, its inclusion occurs by way of such metaphorical designation;

however, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthatas*), even if a part of the thesis (*pratijñaikadeśa*) were to function as the reason (*hetu*), the indirect meaning (*paramparārtha*) would still not be tenable.

Furthermore, in cases such as the perception of what is contradictory to the intrinsic nature (*svabhāvaviruddhopalabdhi*), the negation is expressed by means of a heterogeneous means of valid cognition (*vijātīyapramāṇa*). How could this possibly be the same as [the other types]? It is not possible within the formulation of inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*).
If one asks, "Why then are there eleven specific varieties of the application of non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) therein? [the answer follows].
Therefore, he says: "Because of the observation of usage," and so forth.
And usages do differ;
for if, in other usages, there were the affirmation or negation of a different meaning, [the word would not be established].
How, then, are they included? To this he says: "indirectly" (pāramparyeṇa);
that is to say, by way of a sequence (praṇālikayā).
This is what is meant: these formal arguments do not directly express the non-apprehension of the perceptible;
rather, they express the affirmation or negation of another entity that is invariably concomitant with the non-apprehension of the perceptible.
Therefore, these are included within the non-apprehension of essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*) by way of a mediate process.
"Not directly. // 43 //
If this distinction arises from a difference in formulation, then it must be stated in the case of inference for others;
for a difference in formulation is indeed a difference in verbal expression.
Anticipating the objection, "And is not verbal testimony (śabda) inference for the sake of others (parārthānumāna)?", he says: "By the observation of formal arguments," and so forth.
The "observation" (darśana) refers to the perception (upalambha) of formal arguments (prayoga) as they are recited in the treatises (śāstra).
Its practice is its repeated recurrence; from that cause,
[it arises] even by itself.
"Also for the self of the practitioner";
"thus" means by the sequence just mentioned; "the cognition of exclusion occurs"—here the word *iti* has the sense of "therefore."

And in all these cases of non-apprehension which establish the negation of existence, it should be understood that the apprehension and non-apprehension of those things— such as the perception of intrinsic natures that are contradictory and so forth, or the non-perception of causes and so forth— must pertain only to those things that have reached the conditions for perceptibility (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*).
The "observation of applications" is their comprehension;
the repeated recurrence of that is "practice.
Therefore, when through an excellence of practice regarding these applications, a person's own comprehension of exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) occurs, [that is the result].
At that time, the cognition occurs precisely through the form of a formal application (*prayoga*).

For this very reason, even in inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*), there is a specific mention of the application of non-perception (*anupalabdhi*). The remainder [of the definition] is that the cognition of exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) is the communication of a negation (*pratiṣedha*).
Alternatively, the cognition of exclusion is the comprehension of the specific [property]; this is the remainder [of the sentence]. // 44 //

The distinction of the non-perception of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*) has been stated. If it is asked, "Since that [non-perception] exists in the case of the non-perception of the effect (*kāryānupalabdhi*) and so forth, how can there be non-deviation (*avyabhicāritva*)? he says in response: "In the absence... (*abhāva...*).
All those various kinds of non-apprehensions that have been stated as establishing the conventional usage of non-existence are to be understood as being included within that very [category].
This is because, if there were apprehension of a cause or the like—

The meaning of this is as follows: since one understands for oneself in this very way through this means by means of the practice of application (*prayoga*), therefore, this variety of application, which is also useful for one's own understanding, is described in the context of inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*). However, that which is employed solely for the sake of another’s understanding—
Therefore, it must be stated only in the context of inference for others (*parārthānumāna*). // 44 //

But surely, in the case of the non-perception of the effect and so forth, there is a negation of causes and the like that are themselves imperceptible, because if one were negating what is perceptible, it would follow that one must employ the formal argument of the non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*). This being the case, their negation is not by means of the non-perception of the perceptible;
so how can these arguments be included within the non-perception of the perceptible?
Thus he says, "And everywhere," and so forth. Non-existence and the linguistic convention regarding it are the two "non-existence conventions.
In the case of the non-perception of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*), the linguistic convention of non-existence is the probandum (*sādhya*).
There is an absence [of the probans] in the remaining cases; that is,
when the two are not perceived as being established,
and in all other instances as well.
The word "ca" (and) has the sense of the word "hi" (for/because).
For, in every case of non-apprehension, the negation that is stated applies only to those things which have reached the conditions for apprehension—that is, to those which are perceptible.
Therefore, [all other types of non-apprehension] are included within the non-apprehension of the perceptible.
Why is this so only for those things that are visible?
To this he says: "By their own nature," and so forth.
Here too, the word "and" (ca) has the sense of a reason.

Since negation has been stated through the perception of those things whose beginning is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) that is contradictory [to the probandum], and through the non-perception of those things whose beginning is the cause (*kāraṇa*), the meaning is that negation applies only to perceptible objects.

Even if negation has been stated through the perception of what is contradictory to intrinsic nature (*svabhāvaviruddhopalabdhi*) and so forth, as well as through the non-perception of causes (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*) and so forth, how is it that negation applies only to those things that are perceptible (*dṛśya*)?
To this he says: "Perception," and so forth.
Here too, the word "ca" (and) has the sense of a reason (*hetu*).

For, since those things which are contradictory, which stand in the relation of pervader and pervaded, and which stand in the relation of cause and effect are known, their perception necessarily occurs.
And non-apprehension is preceded by apprehension; otherwise, contradiction would not be established for others, because the causal relationship and its absence would remain unproven.
If there were non-perception of that which has reached the conditions for perceptibility, then the negation of an effect and so forth would be possible; it is not possible otherwise. // 45 //

Even [reasons] such as those contradictory to the intrinsic nature (*svabhāvaviruddha*) are capable of negating the opposite only if they themselves meet the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*), and not otherwise.
If one asks why this is so:
Regarding this, he says: "of others.
Contradiction, the relation of cause and effect, and non-existence—these are "contradiction, causal relation, and non-existence"; it has been stated that there is no establishment of these.
Thus, for those things that have not reached the conditions of perceptibility, their contradiction is unestablished,
the absence of contradiction is also unestablished,
and the relation of cause and effect is unestablished.
It is thus demonstrated that even the absence of the relationship between cause and effect is unestablished;
this is what should be understood—that is, known.
Furthermore, both perception and non-perception exist for these two.
These [objects] are indeed perceptible.

Therefore, when the negation of contradictory factors and so forth—possessing perception and non-perception—is effected through the perception of what is incompatible with their intrinsic nature (*svabhāvaviruddhopalabdhi*) and through the non-perception of causes and so forth (*kāraṇādy-anupalabdhi*), this negation is made only regarding those things that are perceptible.
When many objections have been raised, the word "and" (*ca*) serves the purpose of a reason (*hetvartha*) for the sake of summing up the refutations.
The meaning of the word "ca" (and) is that because these respective solutions exist, those various objections are untenable. // 45 //
Why, then, should the perception and non-perception of the things to be negated—such as the contradictory and so forth—be understood?
To this he says: "Of others.

Those which are other than those possessing perception and non-perception are precisely those that are unperceived; their contradiction, their relation of cause and effect, their non-existence together with something else, and the absence of the pervaded when the pervader is absent [are to be understood].

Since the contradictory relationship, the causal relationship, and non-existence are not established for anything other than that [perceptible realm], it follows that only those things characterized by perception and non-perception— namely, the contradictory and so forth— are to be negated. Furthermore, since both types must be perceptible, negation applies only to perceptible objects.

This is the meaning: contradiction (*virodha*), the relation of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), and the absence of the pervaded (*vyāpyābhāva*) when there is an absence of the pervader (*vyāpakābhāva*)—all these result from the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*) alone.
Contradiction is known through the cognition of the absence of one thing when another is present.
And the relation of cause and effect is established through the cognition of the absence of that which is considered the effect when that which is considered the cause is absent.

When the absence of that which is considered the pervader (*vyāpaka*) is ascertained, the absence of that which is considered the pervaded (*vyāpya*) is also ascertained; thus, the relationship of pervader and pervaded is established.
In this regard, non-existence (*abhāva*) should be understood as the basis for the cognition of the relationship between the pervaded and the pervader.
For when the absence of a tree is apprehended here, and the absence of being a *śiṃśapā* tree is cognized, the relationship of pervader and pervaded is thereby cognized.
And the cognition of non-existence occurs everywhere solely through the non-perception of what is perceptible;
therefore, [one establishes] contradiction and the relation of cause and effect.

And for one who recalls the relationship of pervader and pervaded (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*), the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*)— which is the basis for the cognition of the absence of the objects of the relationship of pervader and pervaded and the relationship of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*)— must be recalled as constituting contradiction (*virodha*). When there is no recollection of the non-perception of the perceptible, however, non-perception regarding remote objects (*viprakṛṣṭaviṣaya*), characterized by the cessation of perception and inference, becomes a cause of doubt regarding such contradictions and so forth.

For instance: when those things which possess the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*) are observed as having a necessary concomitance, it is possible to demonstrate their contradiction with something else that disappears in their presence;
and that which is present is likewise contradictory [to what is absent].
However, it is determined that when that [absent thing] is perceived, there is no contradiction.

Thus, when something that has reached the conditions for perception is not previously seen to exist among those things that have reached the conditions for perception, yet is perceived [at a later time],
and it is not perceived in its absence,
then it is produced from that; by this, the causal relationship between those two is determined.
When something is perceived even in the absence of another, the absence of a causal relationship between those two is determined.

Thus, it is stated that even in this way, the establishment of the conventional usage of "non-existence" is based upon the non-perception of that which has met the conditions for perceptibility. // 46 //
If it is objected that establishment [of an object] occurs sometimes even by means other than those two, it is said: "remote," and so forth.
A remote object, which is of the nature of the cessation of both perception and inference, is the cause of doubt.
It is not the cause for the conventional usage of intrinsic nature. // 47 //
[And] there would be recollection [of it].
This being the case, the cognition of the absence of anything other [than the perceived object] would not arise from the affirmation and negation of contradictions and so forth.

Furthermore, since the non-perception of the perceptible—which must necessarily be recollected at the time when the contradiction and so forth are apprehended—it is from that very [non-perception] that the cognition of absence occurs.
In that regard, although the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*) does not exist at present, it did exist at the time when the contradiction and so forth were apprehended;
that very non-perception of the perceptible which is now being remembered is the basis for the cognition of non-existence.
Therefore, at present, the applications of the non-perception of the effect and so forth do not differ from the application of the non-perception of the perceptible.
Since the non-perception of the perceptible is implied by the affirmation of the contradictory and by the negation of the cause and so forth,
the comprehension of absence results solely from the non-perception of the perceptible as it existed at another time and has become an object of memory.

And these applications are included within the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*). Therefore, it should be understood that by all of this, the inclusion of the ten types of non-perception applications within the non-perception of the perceptible has been demonstrated through a traditional sequence. // 46 //
The non-perception of the perceptible has been explained as [the means of cognition] regarding absence,
and as the instrument of proof for establishing the conventional usage of absence; but what is the nature of the non-perception of the imperceptible?
What is its function?
To this he says: "viprakṛṣṭa... and so forth.
That whose object is remote—remote by way of the three types of remoteness, namely spatial, temporal, and essential—is a "cause of doubt" because its object is remote.
"What is its nature?

To this he says: "That which has the cessation of perception and inference as its characteristic" (*pratyakṣānumānanivṛttilakṣaṇā*) means that whose nature is defined by the absence of both direct cognition and inference;
that is to say, it does not have the nature of either knowledge or an object of knowledge. // 47 //
48. Because the non-existence of an object is established even when the means of valid cognition have ceased to function.
Why is that so?
He says: "By the non-operation of the means of valid cognition," and so forth.
Non-apprehension of remote objects is characterized by the cessation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Even the cessation of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) does not establish the non-existence of an object;
for while a means of valid cognition is the effect of an object, the cessation of the means of valid cognition does not prove the cessation of the mere cause [the object]. // 48 //
Thus ends the second chapter of the *Śiṣyahitā*, the detailed commentary on the *Nyāyabindu*.

But is it not the case that the existence of objects of cognition (*prameya*) is established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and therefore, due to the absence of valid cognition, the apprehension of the absence of objects of cognition is logical?
To this he says: "Even when the means of valid cognition have ceased," and so forth.
A cause, when it is absent, would cause the absence of its effect, and a pervader, when it is absent, would cause the absence of its pervaded;
however, a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is neither the cause nor the pervader of the object of cognition (*prameya*).
Therefore, even when the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) are absent, the absence of the object (artha), which is the object of cognition (prameya), is not established.
Consequently, non-perception of the imperceptible (adṛśyānupalabdhi) is an unestablished cause for doubt;
it is not a cause for certainty.
Furthermore, it is logical that the existence of the object of cognition (prameya) is established by the existence of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa);
for the means of valid cognition is the effect of the object of cognition.
And there can be no effect in the absence of its cause.
However, causes do not necessarily possess their effects.

Therefore, the existence of the object of cognition (prameya) is established by means of the instrument of cognition (pramāṇa), but the non-existence of the object of cognition is not established by the absence of the instrument of cognition. // 48 //
The second chapter, titled "Inference for Oneself," in the *Vyāyabindu-ṭīkā* composed by Ācārya Dharmottara.
The third chapter: On Inference for Others (Parārthānumāna).
1. Inference for others consists in the communication of a logical mark (liṅga) possessing the three characteristics.
2. Because the effect is metaphorically attributed to the cause.
In the course of defining right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), inference (*anumāna*) was accepted as being twofold, distinguished by its own purpose (*svārtha*) and the purpose of others (*parārtha*).
Among these, inference for one's own sake has been defined in detail.
Now, for the purpose of stating inference for the sake of others, he introduces it with the words "possessing the three characteristics" (*trirūpa*), and so forth.
That by which something is expressed is "ākhyāna," meaning "statement.
That which possesses three forms (rūpa) is "trirūpa."
"Trirūpaliṅga" means that which is both three-fold in form and a logical mark (liṅga); the meaning is "the statement of that. // 1 //
Since it has been stated that inference is right knowledge, one might ask: "How can speech be inference?
To this, he says: "Because it is the cause."

Having explained inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*), [the author], desiring to explain inference for others (*parārthānumāna*), says: "The statement of the three-fold mark" (*trirūpaliṅgākhyāna*).
That which possesses three forms—namely, those designated as positive concomitance (*anvaya*), negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), and presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*)—is "three-fold."
And that which is the "explanation" (ākhyāna) is the "explanation" of that three-featured mark (liṅga).
It is called an "explanation" because by means of it [the mark] is explained—that is, it is made manifest.
What, then, is that? It is speech (vacana).
For by means of speech, the three-featured logical mark (liṅga) is expressed; this [speech] is for the sake of another, hence it is "for the sake of another" (parārtha). // 1 //
Now, an objection is raised: "Has it not already been stated that inference consists of right cognition (*samyagjñāna*);
for what purpose, then, is inference now being described as consisting of speech (*vacana*)?
To this he replies: "Because of the metaphorical application (*upacāra*) of the effect to the cause."
From the statement of the three-featured logical mark (trirūpaliṅga), the recollection of the three-featured logical mark arises; and from that recollection, inference [occurs].
Therefore, the statement of the three-featured logical mark is the cause of inference by way of a causal chain.
In that case, a metaphorical attribution (upacāra), that is, a superimposition (samāropa), is made of the effect, namely inference, upon the cause, which is the statement.
Because of that superimposition, the cause—the statement—is expressed by the word "inference.
Thus, the statement is inferential in a figurative sense (aupacārikam).
The meaning is that it is not the primary [meaning].
Not everything that can be expressed by the word "inference" through metaphorical usage need be explained;
rather, since one who desires to explain inference must explain its essential nature, the cause [of that nature] is what must be explained.
The sign (nimitta) is the three-fold mark (liṅga);
and that becomes the basis for inference either when it is cognized by oneself or when it is established by another.
Therefore, both the nature of the logical mark (*liṅga*) and the word that expresses it must be explained.
Among these, its nature has been explained in the context of inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*).
And the expressive word is of two kinds,
according to the difference in its application.
It consists of both that which possesses similarity and that which possesses dissimilarity.
For speech is the cause and inference is the effect; thus, because inference is superimposed upon that speech, that very speech is designated as "inference.
The implication is that it is called "inference" because it is the cause of inference. // 2 //
"It is of two kinds":
here, "it" refers to inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*).
It is the communication of the three-featured logical mark (*trirūpaliṅga*). (3)
If it is asked how it is twofold, he says: "Because of the difference in application.
Application (*prayoga*), however, is presentation by means of words.
Through its division, it is of two kinds. // 4 //
What is that which is to be abandoned by means of its specific mode?
He says: "Like that which possesses common properties" (*sādharmyavat*).
That which has a common property (*samāna dharma*) is "possessing common properties" (*sadharmā*).
The state of having the same properties is *sādharmya*;
that which possesses this is *sādharmyavat*.
That which has dissimilar properties is *vidharmā*.
The state of having different properties is *vaidharmya* (heterogeneity);
that which possesses this is *vaidharmyavat*.
The remainder [of the definition] is "possessing positive concomitance (*anvayavat*) and possessing negative concomitance (*vyatirekavat*). // 5 //
This is what must be explained here.
Therefore, the ultimate point is that the Teacher, demonstrating that the expressive word must necessarily be stated, spoke by means of the term "inference" (anumāna). // 2 //
Desiring to show the different types of inference for others (parārthānumāna), he says: "That is of two kinds.
"That" refers to inference for others.
That which has two kinds, that is, two modes (prakāra), is "of two kinds" (dvividha). // 3 //
From what does the twofold nature arise?
He says: from the distinction of the application (*prayoga*), which is the operation of the word (*śabda*).
Application (*prayukti*) is the same as application (*prayoga*).
The expression of meaning.
Inference is of two kinds, due to the distinction between the operation of a word in expressing its meaning and [the operation of an inferential mark]. //4//
To demonstrate that very twofold nature based on the function of naming, he says: "possessing similarity" (*sādharmyavat*) and "possessing dissimilarity" (*vaidharmyavat*).
That which has a common property (*samāna dharma*) is *sadharmā*; the state of being such is *sādharmya*.
A property that is dissimilar to it is *vidharma*; the state of being such a *vidharma* is *vaidharmya*.
The similarity between the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*) and the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*), produced by the reason (*hetu*), is called *sādharmya*.
And dissimilarity (*asādṛśya*), produced by a cause, is called heterogeneity (*vaidharmya*).
In that context, a syllogistic statement whose intended subject matter is similarity is "possessing similarity" (*sādharmyavat*);
for example: "Whatever is produced is impermanent."
In the case of "as is a jar,
so is sound produced," the similarity between the example and the subject of the thesis (sādhyadharmin) based on the property of being produced is what is to be expressed;
however, that for which dissimilarity is to be expressed is "possessing dissimilarity" (vaidharmyavat).
For example: "That which is eternal is seen to be unproduced, as is the case with space;

sound, however, is produced. Here, the dissimilarity between the property of the subject (*sādhya*) and the property of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharma*)—namely, being produced versus being unproduced—between sound and space, is what is to be stated. // 5 //
In terms of their meaning, there is no difference whatsoever between these two.
Except for a difference in application.

8. Therein, the formulation based on similarity (*sādharmyavat-prayoga*) is as follows: whatever, being capable of being perceived (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*), is not perceived, is established as not being an object of dualistic linguistic usage (*advayavyavahāraviṣaya*), just like some other observed thing such as a rabbit's horn.
And a jar, though meeting the conditions for perception, is not perceived in a certain particular location—this is the formulation of non-perception (*anupalabdhi-prayoga*).
If the formulation based on similarity possesses positive concomitance (anvaya) and the formulation based on dissimilarity possesses negative concomitance (vyatireka),
then there would be a difference even in terms of their meaning.
If it is asked, "Why is it said that there are two types due to a difference in application?
he says in response: "Of these two...
Even that which possesses similarity (sādharmya) depends upon the three characteristics (trirūpa).

Even that which possesses dissimilarity (vaidharmya) depends upon the three characteristics; therefore, because the three characteristics are present in all cases, there is not even a trace of difference in meaning. //6//
"Except for a difference in application";
here there is only a difference in application, but not in every respect.

For instance: in the first case, although positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is stated in terms of the actual fact, negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is understood by implication; and in the second case, although negative concomitance is stated in terms of the actual fact, positive concomitance is known through the sense of the matter. // 7 //
In that regard, the one possessing similarity (*sādharmyavat*) is presented first.
That which, having reached the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*), is not perceived—that is the denotable object (*abhidheya*) of these two applications (*prayoga*).
If their denotable objects are distinct, how then is the three-featured logical mark (*trirūpa-liṅga*) revealed as non-distinct?
Thus he says: "Not [different] in terms of their meaning.
"Meaning" (artha) refers to the purpose (prayojana). That purpose is the object which, having been indicated, is employed in an inference.
Therefore, there is no difference whatsoever between these two in terms of their purpose;
for it is the three-featured logical mark (*liṅga*) that must be made manifest,
and both of these are employed with reference to that.

By both [types of proof], the three-featured logical mark (*liṅga*) is indeed made manifest; therefore, the purpose to be manifested by these two is non-different. And thus, there is no distinction whatsoever between them. // 6 //
"In that case, would there not also be no distinction between the objects denoted?
To this he says: "Except for a difference in usage.
"Usage" (prayoga) means expression (abhidhāna).
The meaning is that there is no distinction other than the distinction of denotative power (*vācakatva*); that is, a distinction created by purpose does not exist.
This is what is being said: the denoted object (*abhidheya*) is one thing, while the manifest object (*prakāśya*)—the purpose—is another.
In that regard, expressiveness (*vācakatva*) is differentiated with respect to the objects to be expressed (*abhidheya*), whereas the object to be illuminated (*prakāśya*) is undifferentiated.
For when positive concomitance (*anvaya*) has been stated, the understanding of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) follows by means of the principle to be explained hereafter.

And where there is exclusion (vyatireka), there is the comprehension of positive concomitance (anvaya). Therefore, the three-featured logical mark (liṅga) reveals that which is non-different [from the object]. Nor is there a difference in the denotable meaning (abhidheya-bheda) therein.
In that regard, even an object understood through implication (sāmarthyagamya) may differ;

for although there is a difference in the expressed meaning (*abhidheya*) between these two sentences—"The fat Devadatta does not eat by day" and "The fat Devadatta eats at night"—the implied meaning is one and the same.
Likewise here, despite the difference in the expressed meanings, the thing being implied is one and the same. // 7 //

9. Likewise, the formulation of the essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*) is as follows: "Whatever exists is all impermanent, just like a pot and so forth. This is the formulation of the pure essential reason.
"The object of conventional usage is established"—
here, the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of non-perception is stated,
as for example, when something like a rabbit's horn is observed [to be non-existent].
The object of the conventional usage of "non-existent" has been observed.
An example of this—such as a hare's horn—is established as being observed;
the word "examined" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
By the statement "no illustration is found," the property of the subject (pakṣadharma) is expressed. // 8 //

Regarding the application of the essential nature as a reason (*svabhāvahetu*): the application characterized by similarity (*sādharmya*) for the second type of reason is shown by the words "that which... and so forth.

Of those two types of inference—those characterized by similarity and dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*)—he first provides an example of that characterized by similarity, stating "that which... and so on, concerning non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*).
"That which is perceptible is not apprehended"— by this, the non-apprehension of the perceptible is restated;
that [non-apprehension] is established as the objective basis for the conventional usage of "non-existent."
The meaning is that it should be conventionally designated as "non-existent. By this, the prescription for its fitness for conventional designation as non-existent is established.
Consequently, the non-perception of the perceptible is stated to be invariably concomitant with fitness for the conventional designation of non-existence.

The meaning is that what is perceived is unapprehended [in its ultimate nature] and is therefore merely fit for conventional discourse (*vyavahāra*). Furthermore, stating the necessity of the probans (*sādhana*) with respect to the object to be proven (*sādhya*) is the statement of pervasion (*vyāpti*).
As it has been said: "Pervasion is either the necessary presence of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) there, or the presence of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) only there."
The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is the object of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes pervasion (*vyāpti*). To demonstrate precisely that, he says: "as another" (*yathānya*).
The meaning is that the example is something other than the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*).
"Seen" means ascertained by a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For a rabbit's horn has not been made an object of the visual faculty.
Rather, it is understood through the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—namely, the non-perception of the perceptible—that something is fit for the conventional usage of "non-existent.
That which has the rabbit's horn and so forth as its first instance is what is described as the object of such non-existent usage.
For in the case of the rabbit's horn and the like, the conventional usage of "non-existent" is established by valid cognition, being based solely on the non-perception of the perceptible.
From that very same means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the pervasion (*vyāpti*) being expressed by this statement must be understood.
Having now stated the pervasion, he says "and it is not perceived" in order to demonstrate the property-of-the-subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) of the non-perception of the perceptible.
"The place" (*pradeśaḥ*) refers to a single region of the earth.
That very thing is distinguished from another, thus it is a "distinction" (viśeṣa); this is one [meaning]. "In a specific location" (pradeśaviśeṣa) means in a single location.
Regarding the phrase "in some place":
even a single location that is perceptible to the cognizer is the locus for the conventional usage of absence; it is precisely that which is perceptible to the cognizer, and nothing else.
"Having attained the conditions for perception" means being visible.
And just as even a non-existent jar can be superposed as having attained the conditions for perception, so it has been explained. // 8 //
In order to show the formal application (prayoga) based on similarity for the reason of essential nature (svabhāvahetu), he says: "in the same way.
The meaning is that just as there is [an application] for non-perception (anupalabdhi), so too is there an application based on similarity for the reason of essential nature.
Having restated existence by means of the term "that which exists," it is predicated that all of that is impermanent; thus, the impermanence of what is permanent [in its nature] is enjoined.

And the inclusion of the word "all" is for the sake of restriction: namely, that whatever possesses origination is impermanent. This is an application of the essential nature (*svabhāva*) through a distinction of a property that constitutes that essential nature.
"That which is produced is impermanent" is [stated] by way of a distinction in limiting conditions (*upādhi*).
Whatever exists is entirely impermanent,
just like a jar and so forth;
"whatever" refers to every suitable entity that exists.
All that is entirely impermanent;
by this, the positive concomitance (anvaya) alone has been stated,
as it is the application of a pure essential reason (svabhāvahetu).
The remaining point is that this is the formulation of the essential reason (svabhāvahetu) without qualification. // 9 //
The statement "whatever is characterized by heat is impermanent" is the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of the second type of essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*).
This is an application of an essential reason by way of a distinction within a property that constitutes its very nature (*svabhāva*);
for the application of an essential reason is made by making a distinction within a property that is itself the essence [of the subject].
For instance: the arising (*utpatti*) of a thing is its acquisition of its own nature (*ātma-lābha*).
That which possesses arising is called "possessing-arising" (*utpattimat*); thus it is expressed by way of distinction. // 10 //
"That which is produced is impermanent"—
by this, the positive concomitance (anvaya) of the third [type of] essential reason (svabhāvahetu) is stated.
"By means of a distinction in limiting conditions" (upādhibheda).

In this context, *upādhi* means a qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*). The remainder of the sense is that this is an application of an essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*) in which the qualification is not explicitly manifested. // 11 //
Everything is impermanent;
there is nothing that is not impermanent.
Whatever exists is necessarily impermanent.
Because there is no existence in anything other than impermanence—that is, in permanence—existence is thus shown to be invariably concomitant with the probandum, impermanence.
And this being so, the statement demonstrating the pervasion is as follows:
"just as in the case of a jar and so forth."
This is the statement of the object of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that establishes pervasion (vyāpti).
"Of the pure" means:
the application of an essential nature (svabhāva) without any qualification. // 9 //
To demonstrate [the reason] with its qualification, he says: "that which has origination" (*yadutpattimat*).
That which possesses origination—that is, the acquisition of its own nature—is "that which has origination.
Having restated the state of having origination, the injunction of impermanence is made by saying "that is impermanent" (*tadanityam*).
And this being the case, having an origin is declared to be necessarily concomitant with impermanence;
for a phenomenon that has come into being has that [origin] as its very nature, and it is by way of its distinction from that [nature] [that permanence would be asserted].
The formal argument (prayoga) takes this distinction as its reason:
for a thing is called "arisen" by relying on its exclusion from those things that have not arisen.
When that very same exclusion is intended to be expressed without reference to any further exclusion, [it is termed "existence"].
Then it is indicated as if distinct—namely, "the arising of an entity.
And thus, a thing qualified by arising is stated to be "possessing arising" (*utpattimat*) as if it were distinct [from itself].

Therefore, it should be understood that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is employed as being qualified by a property (*dharma*) that constitutes its own nature, even though a distinction is conceptually constructed. // 10 //
Regarding the phrase "that which is produced":
having restated the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*), impermanence (*anityatva*) is predicated; thus, it is stated that being produced is invariably concomitant with impermanence.
Therefore, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of being produced by impermanence is demonstrated.
The connection is that there is an application of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) through a distinction of limiting conditions (*upādhi*).
A limiting condition is a qualifier; the meaning is that the intrinsic nature, as qualified by a distinct limiting condition—that is, by a differentiating attribute—is applied.
For an entity whose own nature is not yet accomplished is called "produced" (kṛtaka) when it depends upon the operation of another.

In the same way, properties such as being immediately subsequent to effort (prayatnāntarīyakatva) and being differentiated by the difference of conditions (pratyayabhedabheditva) are also to be understood.

If it is asked, "In what sense are their specific qualities unmanifested? he says in response: "For an entity is 'produced' (kṛtaka) when, in the accomplishment of its own nature, it depends upon the operation of another.
The analysis of the compound is: that by which the operation of another is depended upon.
And that entity which depends upon the operation of causes for the production of its own nature—
as has been stated regarding the "produced" (kṛtaka)— therefore, this is another reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*), characterized by the qualification "unmanifested. // 12 //

"Thus" means: these too, depending on the distinction of limiting conditions (*upādhi*), should be regarded as nothing but essential reasons (*svabhāvahetu*). For instance, that which is established when there is effort—that is, the operation of a cause—is "arising subsequent to effort. Therefore, the [inference] "impermanent, because of arising subsequent to effort" is likewise an essential reason whose qualification is unmanifested.

The difference of conditions is "pratyayabheda. That which has the nature of being differentiated by the difference of conditions is "pratyayabhedabhedin"; the state of being that is "pratyayabhedabheditva."
The remainder [of the definition] is "possessing a form conformable to the diversity of its causes.
For instance, from a small lump of clay, a small jar is produced; but from a large one, a large one is produced.
In this context, skilled [exponents] sometimes express the mere object itself,
sometimes as qualified by a non-distinct qualifier, and sometimes by a distinct one.
"Devadatta" is [the name of] a pure [individual];

"lambakarṇaḥ" (long-eared) is [an individual] characterized by two unseparated ears; "citraguḥ" (possessor of brindled cows) is [an individual] characterized by brindled cows that are distinct [from himself].
Similarly, "pure" [is the subject];
"having the property of arising" is a non-distinct qualification, while "being produced" is a distinct qualification. // 11 //
But one might object: "In the word *citragu* (‘one who has brindled cows’), there exist the words *citra* and *go*, which denote a distinct qualifier;
however, in the word *kṛtaka* (‘produced’), there is the employment of a term that expresses nothing but the thing itself, without a qualifier.
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Because [the qualifier] is required (*apekṣita*)."
The operation of other causes is required for the production of an intrinsic nature; that which requires such operation by others is described as such.
The word "hi" is used in the sense of "because";
because that which requires the operation of others is called "produced" (*kṛtaka*).
Therefore, an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) qualified by a distinct qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is expressed;
even if a distinct word for the qualifier is not employed, nevertheless, a distinct word for the qualifier is already included within the word "made" (*kṛta*) itself.
Therefore, this term *kṛtaka* is a type of name (*saṃjñā*), because the suffix *-kan* is prescribed here in the sense of a name;
and in such cases, a qualifier is included within the term itself.
In that case, a qualifying word is not employed;
however, sometimes a qualifier is understood by implication, as when "done" is said, the phrase "by causes" is understood.
And in that case, the word "cause" (hetu) is sometimes employed and sometimes not. // 12 //

And the word "of itself" (*sva-śabda*) is employed [in the compound] just as the word "difference of conditions" (*pratyaya-bheda*) is [employed] within the phrase "differentiated by the difference of conditions" (*pratyaya-bheda-bhedin*),
and just as the word "produced" (*kṛta*) expresses a nature consisting of distinct qualifiers;
likewise, [the term] "having the differentiation by the difference of conditions as its first" (*pratyaya-bheda-bheditva-ādi*) refers to those [qualities] for which that is the initial [member].
14. "Sound is either existent or produced"—this is the demonstration of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*).

All these properties of the probans (sādhanadharma) are to be understood as being invariably concomitant with the property to be proven (sādhyadharma) solely through the mere presence of the probandum, as established by their respective means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
When the activity of a potter is present, [the jar] becomes beautiful; when the activity of an unskilled potter is present, it becomes ugly.

Therefore, because it varies according to the difference in conditions, it is impermanent. This too is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*), though its specific qualification is not explicitly stated. // 13 //
Previously, only the positive concomitance (anvaya) of the three types of essential natures (svabhāvahetu) was stated;
now, for that reason, the properties of the subject (pakṣadharma) are being set forth:
"Sound exists," and "Sound is produced."
"Sound is produced" is stated for the purpose of showing the different forms of formal application (prayoga). // 14 //

Regarding the definition of the essential nature (*svabhāva*) as a reason (*hetu*) previously stated— that "the essential nature is the reason when the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is necessarily concomitant with that [nature] alone"—
he states "all these are properties of the means of proof" for the purpose of its formal application (*prayoga*).
This refers to those three types of essential-nature reasons whose properties of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) were explained previously.
"By their respective measures" means by those measures which belong to each [reason] as its own;

these are also to be seen as applications of the essential nature (*svabhāva*) reason that express an essential nature qualified by different attributes, such as "being immediately subsequent to an effort" (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*).
*Pratyaya* means causes;
*bheda* means distinction.
That which has the nature of being distinguished by that distinction of causes is "the word distinguished by its causes" (*pratyayabheda-śabda*).
The state of that [sound] is its being differentiated by the difference of conditions (*pratyayabhedabheditva*).
From that— namely, from its being differentiated by the difference of conditions— the produced nature (*kṛtatva*) of sound is established,
as well as its being immediately subsequent to effort (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*) and its impermanence (*anityatva*).

In that context, the word *pratyayabheda* (difference in conditions) is employed in the term *pratyayabhedabhedi* (that which differs according to the difference in conditions) as a designation for a distinct qualifier;
and in the term *prayatnānantarīyaka* (following immediately upon effort), the word *prayatna* (effort) is used.
Thus, the threefold application of the essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*) has been demonstrated: first, the pure (*śuddha*).
[Reasons] with non-distinct qualifiers and [reasons] with distinct qualifiers.
This has been stated for this purpose: so that no one may fall into confusion even when a svabhāva-hetu is employed, due to the difference in the mode of expression. // 13 //

Now, should these reasons based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*) be employed when the essential nature whose relation is established is the probandum, or rather when the relation is not established? In order to demonstrate this, he says: "All these... and so forth.
They are called "means of proof" (sādhana) because they are indicative, and they are called "properties" (dharma) because they depend upon another;
thus, the "proving properties" (sādhanadharma) are simply the mere proving properties themselves.
By the word *mātra* (mere), the exclusion of anything additional or required is intended.
Its *anubandha*—that is, its following along or concomitance—is its *anvaya*.
That whose concomitance with the mere object of the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) is established is described as such (*siddhasādhanakarmamātrānubandha*).
By what is it established? He says:
because that very [nature] has that as its intrinsic nature (svabhāva).

It should be understood that [the concomitance] exists only when the property to be proven (sādhyadharma) is invariably connected with the mere property that serves as the means of proof (sādhanadharmamātra).
The very nature of the property serving as the means of proof is "the mere property serving as the means of proof" (sādhanadharmamātra).
The connection with that mere property serving as the means of proof is "invariable connection with the mere property serving as the means of proof" (sādhanadharmamātrānubandha).
*Anubandhaḥ* means *sambandhaḥ* (connection);
the word *anvayaḥ* is to be understood as the remainder [of the compound].
It refers to that which has a connection with the probandum-property (*sādhya-dharma*) solely through the presence of the probans-property (*sādhana-dharma*).

Only when it has been established that the property of the probans follows upon the mere presence of the property to be proven (sādhyadharma) in each respective case, are those properties of the subject (pakṣadharma) to be stated as reasons (hetu). // 15 //
If it is asked, "Why is there an invariable concomitance of the property to be proven with the mere presence of the proving property?
[the author] says in response: "Of that very [property]," and so forth.
For instance, in ultimate reality, that which is produced has nothing other than an impermanent nature.
But it is not the case that "the produced is one thing and the impermanent is another.
If you ask why?
Whatever is produced by causes and conditions has a nature that is inherently subject to destruction. // 16 //

"By their respective means of valid cognition" (yathāsvaṃ pramāṇaiḥ) means that a given property to be proven (sādhyadharma) is established by whatever means of valid cognition belongs to it; that is, by that very means of valid cognition.

And because there are many varieties of essential-reason (svabhāvahetu), the means of valid cognition for establishing the relationship [between the reason and the probandum] are also many; thus, the plural form "by means of valid cognitions" (pramāṇaiḥ) is employed.
Because it is that which is to be understood, it is the "probandum" (sādhya); and because it is dependent upon another, it is a "property" (dharma).
Thus, the ultimate point is this: the reason (hetu) is not an indicator by virtue of its inherent capacity (*yogyatā*), like a lamp.
Moreover, it is determined by way of invariable concomitance (*nāntarīyakatā*).
For the function of a reason (*hetu*) in establishing the probandum (*sādhya*) consists solely in the determination that it is invariably concomitant with the probandum,
and nothing else whatsoever.

First, the necessary connection of the reason with the probandum must be ascertained by a subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*). Then, at the time of inference, the proof must be remembered in its general form as being invariably concomitant with the probandum—namely, that "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) has the nature of impermanence. Having thus remembered it in its general form, one then applies it to the specific case: "This 'being produced' which exists in sound also has the very same nature of impermanence."
In this context, the recollection of the general [property] is the cognition of the mark (liṅga).

However, the recollection of the specific [property], namely the state of being produced (kṛtakatva) residing in the sound which has impermanence as its intrinsic nature (svabhāva), is inferential cognition (anumāna-jñāna). Thus, the very cognition of the state of being invariably concomitant (avinābhāvitva) is what is called "the capacity to establish an object that is beyond the senses."

Therefore, it has been stated that essential nature reasons (svabhāvahetu) should be employed only when the property to be proven (sādhyadharma) is necessarily connected to its corresponding subtle element (tanmātra), and not otherwise. // 15 //

If the relationship must be ascertained in this way between the probandum and the means of proof, why is it that only the concomitance of the probandum with the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is sought to be ascertained?
To this he says: "Of that very [property]" (*tasyaiva*).
[This refers to] that which is invariably concomitant with the mere property to be proven;
because it has that as its nature—
that is, because it has the nature of the property serving as the proof.

For that property which is to be proven (sādhyadharma) and which is invariably concomitant with the mere presence of the proving property (sādhanadharma) is alone the essential nature (svabhāva) of that proving property, and nothing else. // 16 //
17 And because intrinsic nature is not a cause.
In reality, there is identity between those two.
19. Because that which is not yet produced lacks the nature of being that [already produced thing] when it comes into existence.
Regarding the phrase "of the intrinsic nature" (*svabhāvasya*): here, the very intrinsic nature of the probandum (*sādhya*) is stated as the reason (*hetu*).
How could it not be invariably concomitant with the probandum? For it is precisely the intrinsic nature that is the necessary concomitance with that [probandum] alone. // 17 //
And why is that so?
To this he says: "In the establishment of that" (*tanniṣpattau*).

If, upon the proof of the probans-property (*sādhanadharma*) such as being produced (*kṛtakatva*), the property to be proven (*sādhya*) such as impermanence (*anityatva*) were not established, [then the probans would be inconclusive].
In that case, being produced and impermanence would not, from the perspective of ultimate reality, possess a single intrinsic nature. // 19 //
Let it be that such is indeed the intrinsic nature (svabhāva);
however, why is there an employment of a reason (hetu) when the intrinsic nature itself is what is to be proven (sādhya)?
For [it is argued] that the intrinsic nature is the reason.
In this context, it is intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) alone that has been introduced as the reason;
therefore, only that which is the intrinsic nature of the probans (*sādhana*) should be made the probandum (*sādhya*).
And intrinsic nature is that which is invariably concomitant with the mere property of the probans, and nothing else. (17)
If the property to be proven were the very nature of the probans, then the reason would be a part of the meaning of the proposition itself; to this he says: "in reality."
In reality, from the perspective of ultimate truth, there is identity between the probandum and the probans;
however, the distinction between probandum and probans is merely superimposed.
For the relationship of probandum and probans exists only in a form established by conceptual determination (*niścaya*).

Furthermore, a form established through ascertainment is differentiated by means of a superimposed distinction consisting of mutual exclusion; thus, the means of proof (sādhana) is one thing and the object to be proven (sādhya) is another.
For from a distance, an object possessing branches and so forth is ascertained as a "tree," but not as a "śiṃśapā."
And yet, it is that very same tree, that very same *śiṃśapā*.
Therefore, even though a thing is non-different, the ascertainment presents it as differentiated by way of the distinction between exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*).
Therefore, with respect to that which has attained the form of certainty, the means of proof is one thing and the probandum is another;
hence, the reason is not a part of the meaning of the proposition itself.
And this identity is real. // 18 //

But why is it that only the essential nature (*svabhāva*) which is invariably concomitant with the property of the probans (*sādhanadharma*) is the property to be proven (*sādhya*), and not any other? To this he says: "In its production" (*tanniṣpattau*). For whatever is invariably concomitant with something else is itself unproduced [as a distinct entity] when that thing is produced.
It is illogical for that which is unestablished at the time of its own establishment to possess the nature of a means of proof;
for establishment and non-establishment are, by their very nature,
existence and non-existence, and existence and non-existence abide through mutual exclusion.
And if there were identity between that which is previously established and that which is unestablished,
then existence and non-existence would belong to one and the same object simultaneously.
Furthermore, the identity of existence and non-existence, which are contradictory, is not tenable;
for the absence of oneness consists precisely in the association with contradictory properties.
Moreover, that which arises later has a cause distinct from that which was previously established.
And [the reason is fallacious] because of the possibility of deviation, which is preceded by a difference in the cause.
21. The application of the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*): Wherever there is smoke, there is fire, as in the kitchen and so forth;
and here there is smoke.
22. Here too, only when the causal relationship is already established may the effect-reason (kāryahetu) be stated when the cause is to be proven.

If impermanence were produced at a later time by another cause such as a staff, despite the fact that [the object] was already produced and not yet perfected, then there would be a logical deviation (*vyabhicāra*),
because the staff and so forth are also produced in dependence upon their own respective conditions.
Therefore, it necessarily follows that there is no possibility of the destruction of anything whatsoever that has not already arisen. // 20 //
Regarding the "application of the effect-reason" (*kāryahetu*):
the application of the effect-reason within an inference based on similarity (*sādharmya*) is demonstrated as follows:
"Wherever there is smoke, there is fire."
"Where there is smoke, there is fire everywhere"— this is the positive concomitance (*anvaya*). "As in the kitchen and so forth" indicates the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) by this [phrase].
And there is smoke here;
since smoke is seen in the intended location, the property of the subject (pakṣadharma) has been shown. // 21 //
Even in the case of the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*), first the causal relationship must be established, and subsequently the effect-reason must be stated for the purpose of proving the cause.
For it is thus: a logical mark (*liṅga*) must be known as already ascertained in its own nature, and not as something unascertained. // 22 //
There is a difference in their effects;

consequently, there is a difference consisting in the association with contradictory properties between that which is produced and that which is unproduced, and the cause of this difference is the difference in their causes. How, then, could there be identity? Therefore, the essential nature (svabhāva) that is to be proven is necessarily concomitant only with the property that serves as the means of proof (sādhana), and nothing else. // 19 //
Let it be that the nature of what is posterior does not exist in what is prior;
but why should it not be the probandum (*sādhya*)?
To this he says: "Because of deviation," and so forth.
Because there is the possibility of deviation—that is, the abandonment—of what is produced later by that which was produced earlier, the later-produced is not to be proven by the earlier-produced.
Therefore, the essential nature (svabhāva) is that which is invariably concomitant with the mere property to be proven (sādhanadharma); and that alone is the probandum (sādhya).

And thus it is established that, in the case of an essential nature (*svabhāva*), reasons based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*) should be employed only when the property to be proven is necessarily connected to the mere presence of the reason. // 20 //
Regarding the formulation of the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*):

it should be understood from the context that it possesses similarity (*sādharmyavat*). In the statement "where there is smoke," having referred to smoke (*anūdya*), the injunction (*vidhi*) is "there is fire."
And in this way, the purpose of the restriction (niyama) is to be understood as before.
Thus, by this, the pervasion (vyāpti) based on the existence of cause and effect has been shown.
To show the object of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that establishes this pervasion, he says: "as in the kitchen and so forth."
For in a kitchen or similar location, the inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*), which consists of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), is ascertained through perception and non-perception.
And since it exists here [in the subject], there is the application of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmopasaṃhāra*) to the locus of the probandum (*sādhyadharmin*). // 21 //

"Even here" means: not only in the case of the essential nature as a reason (svabhāvahetu), but here too, in the case of the effect as a reason (kāryahetu). "Is indeed established" means: [it is already proven].

Once the relationship of cause and effect has been ascertained, the determination of that causal relation must necessarily be made; for it has been stated that a reason does not indicate [its object] by virtue of its mere capacity, but rather because of its invariable concomitance (*nāntarīyakatva*). // 22 //
23. The formulation based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*): Whatever exists and meets the conditions for perception is necessarily perceived, just as specific qualities such as blue and so forth.
However, in this case, there is no perception of the jar, even though it exists and meets the conditions for perception. This is the formulation of non-perception (*anupalabdhi*).
In the absence of impermanence,
there is no existence, nor possession of origination, nor being produced; yet sound exists, possesses origination, or is produced— this is the formulation of an essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*).
"Vaidharmya," etc.:
those inferences characterized by dissimilarity (vaidharmyavat) must also be stated.
Whatever exists and meets the conditions for perception is necessarily perceived.
If there were any existent thing that met the conditions for perception, it would necessarily be perceived.
By this, the negative concomitance (vyatireka) has been stated; "just as in the case of specific qualities such as blue" is the example based on dissimilarity (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta).
And yet, there is no such perception here of a jar that has met the conditions for perceptibility.
By "perception" is meant that a jar of the same kind as the specific blue object or other things which are perceived when they meet the conditions for perceptibility—
such a jar does not exist here.
By the word "here," the intended location is expressed.
"The application of non-perception" refers to this [formulation] which possesses the negative concomitance (*vaidharmya*) of non-perception. // 23 //
In the absence of impermanence, there is neither existence nor the state of having an origin;
by this, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of the three types of essential reasons (*svabhāvahetu*) is taught.
And sound is existent and has an origin.
"Or is it produced?"—these are stated as properties of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) in the formulation of the essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*).
And these are the formulations of the essential reason that possess negative concomitance (*vaidharmya*). // 24 //

The formulation of the positive concomitance (*sādharmya*) for the [three types of reason]—essential nature (*svabhāva*), effect (*kārya*), and non-perception (*anupalambha*)—has been shown; now, in order to show the negative concomitance (*vaidharmya*), he says: "of that which possesses negative concomitance" (*vaidharmyavataḥ*).
"That which exists and meets the conditions for perception" (*yat sad upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptam*).
That "the existent is visible" is a restatement of its existence;
that "it is perceived" is the prescription for perception.
By this, it is stated that the existence of the visible is pervaded by being an object of vision.
The absence of a sentient being is non-existence,
and the absence of perception is perception.
Thus, by way of restating the absence of the probandum, the absence of the probans is established.
And thus, because the cessation of the probandum is necessarily concomitant with the cessation of the probans, it is stated that the former is pervaded by the latter;
for if the property to be proven did not exist in the subject,
the logical reason would likewise not exist.
Because the absence of the probandum is pervaded by the absence of the reason,

and yet the reason is present, there follows the absence of the absence of the means of proof— the pervader— which results in the absence of the absence of the probandum— the pervaded; thus, the realization of the probandum occurs.

Therefore, in the application of the method of difference (vaidharmya-prayoga), it is the rule that one must demonstrate everywhere that the absence of the probandum is necessarily concomitant with the absence of the probans. // 23 //
He states the formulation of the dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya-prayoga*) for the essential reason (*svabhāva-hetu*): "If impermanence were non-existent...
Here, the absence of the probandum (*sādhya*), which is impermanence, is stated to be necessarily concomitant with the absence of the reason.
Thus, by means of the absence of the reason, there is the absence of the probandum.
Where there is no fire, smoke certainly does not exist;
yet here there is smoke—this is the formulation of the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*).
For even in an argument formulated by way of similarity, the dissimilarity is understood by implication.
27. Because, in its absence, there would be no positive concomitance (anvaya) of the reason with the probandum.
"When fire is absent, smoke certainly does not exist"—
by this, the negative concomitance (vyatireka) is stated;
and here, by the word "exists" (asti), the property of the subject (pakṣadharma) is stated.
"An application of the effect-reason (kāryahetu)" means that an application characterized by dissimilarity (vaidharmya) to the effect-reason has been demonstrated. // 25 //

If it is asked: "In an inference based on similarity (sādharmya-anumāna), the three features—the presence of the reason in the subject (pakṣadharmatva), the positive concomitance (anvaya), and the negative concomitance (vyatireka)—are not explicitly manifested; how then can inference for the sake of others (parārthānumāna) be defined as the statement of a three-featured logical mark (trirūpaliṅga)?"
Regarding this, he says: "by way of similarity" (*sādharmyeṇa*).

Since, by means of implication (*sāmarthya*), there is an understanding of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) even in a formal argument that possesses similarity (*sādharmyavat-prayoga*), therefore the aforementioned undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) does not occur. // 26 //
And what kind of capacity is this?
He says: "If it were non-existent.
That is, if there were no negative concomitance (vyatireka).
In that case, the positive concomitance (anvaya) of the reason with the probandum would likewise remain unestablished. // 27 //

It has been stated that [the reason] is pervaded in all three types of essential reasons (*svabhāvahetu*): "Sound is existent," "sound is produced," or "sound is created. This constitutes the statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) for all three as well.

And here, the absence of the pervader, which is the absence of the means of proof (sādhana), has been stated; therefore, the absence of the probandum (sādhya), being the pervaded, is also excluded—thus there is the comprehension of the probandum. // 24 //
He states the formulation of the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) with a dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya*): "In the absence of fire," and so forth.
Here too, the absence of fire is stated to be pervaded by the absence of smoke;
yet, there is smoke here.

The presence of the pervader, which is the absence of smoke, has been stated; from that, there follows the comprehension of the probandum, namely the absence of the pervaded, which is the absence of fire. // 25 //

But surely, in the case of the positive concomitance (*sādharmya*), the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not stated, and in the case of the negative concomitance (*vaidharmya*), the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is not; so how can this be called the statement of the three-fold mark (*trirūpaliṅga*)?
Thus he says: "by way of similarity" (*sādharmyeṇa*).

This means that when an argument is formulated using a subject matter characterized by similarity, there occurs—by implication and through the force of logic—the understanding of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), which is the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
The word "hi" (indeed) is used because [this is so].

Therefore, this is the statement of the three-featured logical mark (*trirūpaliṅga*). Even if the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not explicitly stated along with the positive concomitance (*anvaya*), nevertheless, that which expresses the positive concomitance is understood by implication alone. // 26 //

How so? Because, in the absence of that exclusion (*vyatireka*) determined by the intellect, there would be an absence of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of the reason with the probandum as determined by the intellect.

One who determines the means of proof (*sādhana*) as necessarily restricted to the probandum (*sādhya*) through the statement of positive concomitance must not suspect the presence of the means of proof where the probandum is absent;
otherwise, the restriction of the means of proof to the probandum would not be cognized at all.
The comprehension of the absence of the probans when the probandum is absent is the comprehension of negative concomitance (vyatireka).

Therefore, because of the capacity of the statement of the probans—which is necessarily restricted to the probandum—to imply it, the negative concomitance is established within the positive statement (anvaya-vākya). // 27 //
28. Likewise, there is also the understanding of positive concomitance through dissimilarity.
29. Because, in the absence of that probandum, the absence of the reason would remain unestablished.
30. For when there is no essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*), the necessary cessation of one thing upon the cessation of another does not occur.
And that [invariable concomitance] is of two kinds: characterized by identity with everything, and characterized by origination from it; so it has been stated.
Even in the formulation of a dissimilar instance (*vaidharmyavat-prayoga*), the understanding of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) occurs by implication. // 28 //
Now, if it is asked what kind of similarity (*sādharmya*) that is, he says: "If [the reason] does not exist" (*asati*).
If there were no positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of the reason with the probandum, then how could there be an absence of the reason even in the absence of the probandum? // 29 //
If it is asked, "Why is it that in the absence of positive concomitance (anvaya), negative concomitance (vyatireka) is unestablished?
he says in response: "For not," and so forth.

If there were no essential connection (svabhāvapratibandha)—that is, if there were no connection by way of intrinsic nature—then even upon the cessation of one thing, the cessation of the other would not necessarily follow.
Just as, for example, in some cases the absence of cows does not follow from the absence of horses. // 30 //
And that [obstruction] of everything is of two kinds:
whatever obstruction is found to be possible for any object whatsoever, all of it is included within these two types;
namely, that characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) and that characterized by origination from that (*tadutpatti*), as has been stated.

"So be it. Just as in the case of the statement of positive concomitance (anvaya), so too in the application by way of dissimilarity (vaidharmya), there is an understanding of the positive concomitance even though it is not explicitly stated, simply by the force of the meaning. // 28 //

How so? Because if that positive concomitance (*anvaya*) were not apprehended by the intellect, the absence of the reason (*hetvabhāva*) would remain unestablished in the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*), since there would be no determination [of their relationship].
