One who determines from the statement of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) that the absence of the probandum is necessarily restricted to the absence of the reason must not suspect the presence of the absence of the probandum when the reason is possible;
otherwise, the restriction of the absence of the probandum to the absence of the reason would not be cognized.
And when there is the state of having a reason (*hetumattva*), the understanding of the presence of the probandum (*sādhyasattva*) is the understanding of positive concomitance (*anvaya*).

Therefore, because of the capacity of the statement of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) to express the absence of the probandum as being necessarily concomitant with the absence of the means of proof (*sādhanābhāva*), the understanding of positive concomitance occurs therein. // 29 //

Even if there is indeed an absence of the probans where there is an absence of the probandum in space and so forth, why does the presence of the probandum necessarily follow from the presence of the probans?
To this he says: "Not indeed."

The essential connection is that wherein, in the absence of one [factor], the necessary cessation of the other—the probandum—is logically established as a rule; that is, the cessation is invariably concomitant. // 30 //
And that essential connection (svabhāvapratibandha) is of two kinds for everything that is connected:

that which has identity (tādātmya) as its defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa) or cause (nimitta) is so described; that which has origination from that (tadutpatti) as its defining characteristic or cause is so described.

Whatever is dependent upon something else, that object which serves as its basis of dependence must be either its essential nature (*svabhāva*) or its cause (*kāraṇa*), because it is impossible for it to be established through anything other than these two.

Therefore, it has been stated that it is of two kinds; and this was explained in the intervening passage [beginning with] "And that [is the basis] of the logical mark (*liṅga*) with respect to the object to be proven (*sādhya*). (31)
Therefore, when stating a negation (*nivṛtti*), the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) must be demonstrated;
for the statement of a negation consists precisely in the demonstration of the implied connection.

And that demonstration of the connection is itself the statement of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*); thus, by means of a single sentence, whether through the method of agreement (*anvayamukha*) or the method of difference (*vyatirekamukha*), [the relationship is established].

Alternatively, by employing one [of the two statements], the demonstration of the presence or absence of the logical mark (liṅga) in the similar instances (sapakṣa) and dissimilar instances (asapakṣa) is accomplished; thus, the employment of both sentences is not strictly necessary.

"Identity" (tādātmya) means that its self is that [other], i.e., it has that as its self; the state of having that as its self is identity; that which has identity as its defining characteristic is "identity-characterized."
Therefore, "arising from that" means arising from that;
the analysis of the compound is: "that which has 'arising from that' as its characteristic is 'characterized by arising from that'.
And this has already been stated previously. // 31 //
Because when there is a necessary connection (*pratibandha*), the cessation of one thing results in the cessation of the other;

in the absence of such a connection, the cessation of some one thing by that cause is not said to entail the cessation of another. By this, the necessary connection between the object to be excluded (*nivartya*) and the excluding factor (*nivartaka*) has been stated.
By the very mention of cessation, the connection is implied;
if that were indeed the case, what would follow from it?
If this is asked, he says: "The very demonstration of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is itself the positive concomitance (*anvaya*).

Therefore, even by a single statement—whether formulated by way of positive concomitance or by way of negative concomitance—the existence or non-existence of the logical mark (*liṅga*) in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar instance (*asapakṣa*) is made known. This is so even when [the statement] is formulated by way of positive concomitance.
The word *hi* is used in the sense of "because.

Because the relationship between that which is to be excluded (*nivartya*) and that which excludes (*nivartaka*) exists only when there is an essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*), therefore, one who states that the probans (*sādhana*) is excluded when the probandum (*sādhya*) is excluded must demonstrate the connection between the two— the excluded and the excluding.
For if the means of proof were necessarily connected to the probandum, then it would necessarily cease upon the cessation of the probandum; and therefore,
that connection must be demonstrated.

Therefore, the statement regarding the cessation of the probans when there is a cessation of the probandum implies the demonstration of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*). And that implied demonstration of the necessary connection is itself the statement of positive concomitance (*anvaya*).
If the necessary connection must necessarily be demonstrated, [then it must be stated].
In that case, the positive concomitance (anvaya) need not be stated separately;
for the positive concomitance is nothing other than the very demonstration of the necessary connection (pratibandha) by means of valid cognition within the example.
Therefore, the necessary connection between that which is to be excluded and that which excludes it must be known; in this way, the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) itself becomes known.
The word *iti* indicates the reason.

Since the understanding of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) occurs even through positive concomitance (*anvaya*), and the understanding of positive concomitance occurs even through negative concomitance,
therefore, by means of a single [statement], both the presence in the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and the absence in the dissimilar class (*asapakṣa*) are made manifest.
A statement whose "face" (*mukha*)— meaning its means (*upāya*)— is positive concomitance because it expresses that [concomitance] is called a "positive-concomitance-faced" (*anvayamukha*) statement.
Thus, that which has "exclusion" (*vyatireka*) as its primary feature [is the negative inference].
For this reason— that is,
because by means of even a single statement, both [the positive and negative aspects] are understood— [it is so called].

Therefore, in a single argumentative statement, the employment of both the positive concomitance (anvaya) and the negative concomitance (vyatireka) must necessarily be made; they should not be omitted.

33. Even in the case of non-apprehension, when it is stated that "whatever exists and meets the conditions for apprehension is necessarily apprehended," there is a positive concomitance (anvaya) because one understands that such a thing, being unapprehended, is non-existent.
In both of these applications, the statement of the thesis (pakṣa) is not necessarily required.
If the formal application (prayoga) is made by way of negative concomitance (vyatireka), it is likewise appropriate;

nevertheless, since the very statement of the presence and absence [of the reason] in the similar and dissimilar instances in the manner described constitutes the demonstration of its existence and non-existence, the logical mark (liṅga) is applied to each case by both means, and thus the employment of two separate sentences is not strictly necessary.
Therefore, in a single application, it is not necessary to employ both a statement possessing similarity and a statement possessing dissimilarity. // 32 //

Thus, the mutual implication between the positive concomitance (anvaya) and negative concomitance (vyatireka) of the effect-reason (kāryahetu) and the essential-nature reason (svabhāvahetu) has been stated. For the purpose of indicating the third type of reason, he says: "also in the case of non-apprehension" (anupalabdhāv api). The ellipsis to be supplied is: "of that which is not established by means of the effect-reason or the essential-nature reason."
When it is stated as a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) that "if something were to meet the conditions for perception, it would necessarily be perceived," then,
by the force of the non-perception of that which meets the conditions for perception, the cognition arises that "it does not exist."
Therefore, the establishment of the positive concomitance (anvaya) is indeed implied. Thus, the implication of the positive concomitance has been stated.
As for the implication of the negative concomitance (vyatireka) in the case of non-apprehension (anupalabdhi), it should be understood by oneself. // 33 //

If it is argued that in both types of inference— those based on similarity (*sādharmya*) and those based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*)— there is no mention of the subject (*pakṣa*), and thus one should simply assume the absence of any mention of the subject, he replies: "In both cases as well."
As for the rule that a position must necessarily be stated, that does not exist. // 34 //
For the employment of words has as its purpose the comprehension of meaning.
If the meaning is already understood, what is the use of employing words?
One should employ either only a positive statement (anvaya-vākya) or a negative statement (vyatireka-vākya). // 32 //

Even in the case of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), there is an understanding of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) through the stated negative concomitance (*vyatireka*): "whatever is existent and meets the conditions for apprehension. This expresses the cessation of the probandum—the fitness for the conventional usage of "non-existent"—in the form of the existence of the perceptible.
"That it is indeed perceived" expresses non-perception as having the nature of perception by way of its cessation. By this,
it is shown that the cessation of the probandum is pervaded by the cessation of the probans.
Furthermore, if the negation of the probandum (sādhya) were to occur even when the probans (sādhana) is present, it would not be pervaded by the absence of the probans;
therefore, one who seeks to establish pervasion must understand that the presence of the probans is pervaded by the presence of the probandum.
For this very reason, he says: "such [an object] being unperceived."
This is the [correct] view; for since there is a cognition that [the object] is non-existent, the establishment of positive concomitance (anvaya) follows from present experience. // 33 //

Since the proof (sādhana) must be understood as being necessarily connected to the property to be proven (sādhyadharma) through either identity (tādātmya) or causality (tadutpatti) in both types of formal argument (prayoga),
therefore the thesis (pakṣa) need not be explicitly stated at all.

For once the proof is recognized as being invariably concomitant with the probandum, the cognition of the probandum arises simply from seeing that proof in the subject of the inference (sādhyadharmin).
Therefore, there is no indication whatsoever of a probandum. // 34 //

35. Because even in an application based on similarity (sādharmya), that which meets the conditions for perception is not perceived, and is therefore the object of the conventional usage of non-existence;
and since here too a jar meeting the conditions for perception is not perceived, it follows by the very force of this [argument] that "there is no jar here."

Likewise, even in the formulation of the argument based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmyavat*), when it is stated: "Whatever is the object of the conventional usage of existence and meets the conditions for perception is necessarily perceived;
yet no such jar is perceived here," it follows by the very force of the implication that "this is not an object of the conventional usage of existence."

"Whatever meets the conditions for perception yet is not perceived, all that is the object of the conventional designation 'non-existent'"; thus, a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) must be established by including all possible categories of entities. Furthermore, since the thesis (*sādhya*) is established by the force of these two—the statement of the positive concomitance through the inclusion of all categories and the statement that the reason is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*)—what is the purpose of stating the thesis (*pakṣanirdeśa*)? [The answer is:

The statement of the thesis is not required because the proposition is understood through the force of both the statement of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) through the inclusion of all categories and the statement that the reason is a property of the subject.
Otherwise, that which is not understood would have to be explicitly pointed out.
When the meaning of the proposition is understood through implication, then who would be so obstinate as to persist in hearing the verbal statement of the proposition even when it is obstructed?
And thus, when the determination of the object of investigation occurs through implication, [the explicit statement is redundant].

Furthermore, since the meaning of the thesis (*pratijñā*) is understood through the power of the indication of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and the pervasion (*vyāpti*), what is the use of stating the subject there?
This should be understood from the statement of the *Viniścaya*.
[The author] demonstrates this very point in the application of non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) by saying "because" (*yasmāt*), which serves as an elaboration (*prapañca*).
Even in an application based on similarity (*sādharmyavat*), the conclusion "there is no jar in this place" follows by implication alone.
What, then, is that implication?

He says: the restatement of non-perception—that "that which has reached the conditions for perceptibility is not perceived"—is the basis for the conventional usage of non-existence (*asadvayavahāra*).
This is the formulation [of the reason] as the fitness for the conventional usage of non-existence.
This being the case, the non-perception of the perceptible has been shown to be pervaded by the fitness for the conventional usage of non-existence;
and by the words "it is not perceived," etc., the presence of the logical mark (*liṅga*) in the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*) is demonstrated.
And if the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) were not present there in that subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*), the proving property (*sādhanadharma*) would also not be present;
for it follows by implication that the proving property is necessarily restricted to the property to be proven. (35)

Just as it is in the formulation based on similarity (*sādharmyavat-prayoga*), so too in the formulation based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmyavat-prayoga*), there occurs [the statement]: "A jar is not here an object of the conventional usage of 'existent'.
To demonstrate this capacity, he says: "That which is an object of the conventional usage of 'existent'"—meaning, that which is currently existing.
Regarding the phrase "having reached the conditions for perception" (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*): this means "visible. This is the negation of the probandum (*sādhyanivṛtti*).
[The implication is: "that [object] is indeed perceived."
Regarding the phrase "the cessation of the probandum":
by this, it is shown that the cessation of the probandum is pervaded by the cessation of the probans.
"Not so" means...
Just as another visible object is perceived, so too is there no such [object] here in this place;
the visible object is a jar,
and it is perceived.
By this, it is shown that the absence of the pervader— which is the absence of the probandum— is non-existent in the subject of the probandum.
Furthermore, if the property to be proven were not present in the subject of the probandum,
what kind of "thesis" (pakṣa) could then be specified?
A thesis is that which is intended by the proponent himself in its very own form, is not contradicted, and is capable of being stated.
"By its own nature" means "intended as that which is to be proven."
"By its very nature alone" means it is intended solely as that which is to be established (the probandum), and not also as a means of establishment (the probans).
There is no fault whatsoever in stating the thesis for the purpose of designation;
for this very reason, it was stated that there is no restriction.
However, if one were instead intent upon the absolute prohibition of stating the thesis in every respect, [then the following would apply].
In that case, it follows that this statement would necessarily not have been taught; such is what has been stated. // 36 //

If it is said that the "indication of the thesis" (pakṣanirdeśa) consists in the statement of the definitive word, and that where there is an elaborate expression (prapañcābhidhāna) there is an indication, then one might ask: what kind of characteristics must it possess to be designated as the thesis?
He asked: "Of what kind? [The answer is:

That object which is intended by the proponent (*vādin*) as the subject of debate and is stated solely in the form of the probandum (*sādhya*), and which is not refuted by perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth—such an object is to be designated as the "thesis" (*pakṣa*).
Such is the summarized meaning. // 38 //

As for the meaning of the individual words: "in its own form" (*svarūpeṇa*) means that it is not tenable [for the subject] to exist in any other form apart from the form of the probandum (*sādhya*). Therefore, what has been stated as being in its own form must be understood precisely as the probandum. // 39 //

By this statement, it is established that only that which is to be designated in the form of the mere probandum (sādhya) is to be called the "subject" (pakṣa), and not that which is to be designated in any other form. // 40 //
The property [to be proved] would also not exist;
yet the property that serves as the means of proof does exist—this is the force [of the argument].
Therefore, by implication, there is no statement of a thesis (pakṣanirdeśa) here, because it is already understood that "there is no jar here."

Thus, since comprehension also arises through the force of the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) and the essential-nature reason (*svabhāvahetu*), there is no need for the formal statement of the thesis (*pakṣanirdeśa*). // 36 //
Furthermore, what is the meaning of "proposition" (*pakṣa*)?
It is that which is to be indicated or expressed by this word. // 37 //
"By the very nature of water" means as that which is to be proven;
"by himself" means by the proponent.
Regarding the term "intended" (*iṣṭa*): it does not mean merely "stated," but rather "also intended.
An object of this nature, which is not sublated by perception and the other means of valid cognition, is called the *pakṣa* (the thesis).
Now, if the thesis were not to be stated, how could a definition of that which is not to be stated be given?
Its definition was not stated because it is a constituent part of the proof-statement (*sādhanavākya*).
Moreover, some maintain that what is impossible is possible, and what is possible is impossible;
others hold such views.
The definition of the thesis (pakṣa) was stated for the purpose of refuting misconceptions regarding what is to be proven and what is not to be proven. // 38 //
The explanation of the phrase "desired by its own nature" (*svarūpeṇeṣṭa*) is: "by its own nature" (*svarūpeṇa*). Regarding "desired as the probandum" (*sādhyatveneṣṭa*):
since the subject (*pakṣa*) possesses the state of being the probandum, there is no other form [for it].
Therefore, the essential nature [of the object] is that which is to be accomplished. // 39 //
He speaks "svarūpeṇaiva" (by its very nature) in order to explain the word *eva*.
Now, is it not the case that the word *eva* alone [is sufficient],
as when "visibility" (*cākṣuṣatva*) is the reason for proving the impermanence of sound?

Since it is unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to the word, it is something to be proven (*sādhya*); however, it is not intended here solely as that which is to be proven, because it is also designated as a means of proof (*sādhana*).
"By the proponent himself."
43. He who at that time stated the proof.
If one asks, "What kind of statement is the indication of that which is qualified by a nature other than the probandum?", he says: "For example.
When it is stated, "Whatever is sound, that is impermanent," then that visibility (cākṣuṣatva) is unestablished (asiddha) in sound, and thus it becomes the probandum (sādhya).

Therefore, in the absence of the specification "by its very nature" (*svarūpeṇaiva*), there would be the undesirable consequence that even the specification of "being visible" (*cākṣuṣatva*) would be the subject (*pakṣa*).
If it is asked: "If the form of the probandum (*sādhyarūpa*) indeed exists in that [specification], why is it not the subject?", he says: "In this case" (*atra*).
Even though it possesses the nature of the probandum (sādhya) in its state as being visible (cākṣuṣatva),
nevertheless, because it is specified as a reason (hetu), it does not consist solely of the nature of the probandum;
it also possesses the nature of the means of proof (sādhana).

Therefore, even though it is the probandum (*sādhya*), because its existence consists of a means of proof distinct [from the subject], the status of being the thesis (*pakṣatva*) for that which is stated in excess is refuted. // 41 //

When stating a proof (sādhana), that very object which is intended by [the proponent] himself is the thesis (pakṣa); it is implied that what is intended by the author of a treatise (śāstrakāra) is not [the thesis]. // 42 //
It should be reflected upon: for what purpose has it been reflected upon here together with the word "svarūpa" (own-form)?
It is said in reply: the particle *eva* is an indicator (*dyotaka*).
It illuminates the specific quality of the meaning expressed by another word; thus, it is indicated together with another word that denotes the substantive.
"Nor as a means" means that whatever is indicated as a means is intended as a means.
And because it is unestablished, it is also intended as something to be proven;
the word "eva" is used precisely for the purpose of excluding that. // 40 //
He illustrates this with the words "for example" (*yathā*).

When the impermanence of sound is the probandum (*sādhya*), the property of being visible (*cākṣuṣatva*) is a reason that is unestablished (*asiddha*) in respect to sound; by the phrase "it is the probandum," he expresses the intendedness [of that reason] as something yet to be proven. "That" refers to the property of being visible.
The word "here" (*iha*) refers to the term [in the definition].
By saying "intended precisely as the probandum" (*sādhyatvenaiveṣṭam*),
he states that there is no restriction regarding the intention [to prove it] as the probandum.
"Because it is designated as a means.
Since it is designated as a means,
for that reason it is also intended as a means.
Not as being solely that which is to be proven. // 41 //
Having introduced the word *svayam* as that which is to be explained by the term "itself" (*svayam*), he states its meaning:
"Itself" (*svayam*). The indeclinable (*nipāta*) *svayam* occurs in the sense of both the genitive ending *ātmanaḥ* and the instrumental ending *ātmanā*.
Thus, in this context, the word *svayam* functions in the sense of the word *svātman* (one's own self).
Furthermore, the word "ātman" (self) is a relative term,
and the "proponent" (vādī) is the one most closely associated with it;
therefore, it is the proponent whose self is connected with the meaning of the third case [instrumental].
That very [term] is indicated by the proponent as being joined with the sense of the third case;
however, "svayaṃ" (himself) is not a synonym for "vādinā" (by the proponent). // 42 //
Who, then, is this proponent? To this he says: "he who, at that time"—that is, at the time of the debate—states the proof (*sādhana*). Not one...

By this, although one may be established in a certain treatise and state a proof, even though the author of that treatise accepts many properties in that subject (*dharmin*), it is thereby stated that only that property which the proponent himself intends to prove at that time is the *sādhya* (the thing to be proven), and no other.

45. Regarding the term "desired" (iṣṭa): when a proof is presented in dispute concerning a certain object, that object becomes the probandum (sādhya) for one who desires its establishment, even if it is not explicitly stated by words.
The term "that" refers to the very subject (pakṣa) which is to be pointed out by the proponent. // 43 //
Someone may be established in a certain treatise and have indeed reached a firm conviction regarding its position;
let such a conviction exist,
yet even so, if [that conviction] is extracted from the treatise and made into a means of valid cognition— this is the implied sense.

In whatever treatise the proponent states a proof, even if many properties are accepted by the author of that treatise regarding the subject which is the object of investigation, nevertheless, only that property which the proponent himself desires to establish is the *sādhya* (the probandum). This is because the property desired by the author of the treatise is not accepted by the proponent as being the "thesis" (*pakṣa*) to be demonstrated; therefore, it is only that property which the proponent wishes to refine—which serves as an aid by way of accepting the treatise—that constitutes the *sādhya*.
By this statement, it is expressed that "only that [which is established by valid cognition] is the probandum (sādhya), but not that which is merely accepted by the author of the treatise. // 44 //
Even though a proponent may exist, this is a qualification of the proponent himself with respect to that which is expressed by the word [proponent].
For it has been stated: "that which is desired by the proponent is the probandum."
And what is expressed by this?
At that time, during the debate, whatever property (*dharma*) is intended to be proven by that proponent himself— that alone is the *sādhya* (the thing to be proven).
It is meant that it is not any other property;
the point is that the purpose of this statement is to exclude the possibility of proving a property undesirable to the proponent. // 43 //

Now, what being present is there the possibility of [the property] being provable by another means of knowledge, such that its exclusion must be stated? To this he says: "And that [is stated] by the author of the treatise."

Furthermore, regarding the treatise accepted by that proponent: when the author of that treatise has accepted many properties in that subject (*sādhyadharmin*), there is the possibility of proving other properties [than the one intended].
For instance, there is a misconception that "whatever property is established by a treatise accepted by someone, all such properties must be proven by them"; this [definition] excludes that.
Even when many properties are admitted, only that which is desired by the proponent is the probandum, and no other.
Now, one might object: "The logical mark (liṅga) functions by the force of the thing itself, independent of treatises;
therefore, since it is not dependent [on them], the debate should not be conducted by adhering to a treatise."

True; however, even if one states a proof because one is established in some treatise or has accepted some treatise out of mere self-importance (*āhopuruṣikā*), this [definition] was stated in order to make it known that only that which is intended by him is the probandum (*sādhya*). // 44 //

Having introduced the term "iṣṭa" (accepted), he explains it: "iṣṭa" means that in which a meaning is accepted by oneself; for a dispute has that [meaning] as its locus because it is contradictory [to it].
For example: "The eyes and so forth exist for the sake of another because they are composite, like beds, seats, and so on.
Here, even though it is not explicitly stated that they exist "for the sake of a self," the fact of existing for the sake of a self is what is to be proven (*sādhya*).
Therefore, it is shown that it is not merely what is stated [in the reason] that constitutes the *sādhya*.
The intended meaning of the word "intended" (*iṣṭa*) is explained as follows:

when a dispute has arisen concerning a certain object, that very object which is presented as the thing to be proven (*sādhya*) by one who wishes to establish it— that object is what is meant by "intended."
Even if that object which is the domain of discursive thought is not expressed by words, it nevertheless remains the very thing to be established. // 45 //

If it is asked why that is so, he says: "Because it is the locus of that. Precisely for that reason, since the dispute [concerns it], how could this very dispute not be the thing to be proven (sādhya)? // 46 //

And as for that which is a matter of dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*), even if not explicitly stated by words, it is intended to be the very thing to be proven (*sādhya*). If one asks how so, he says: "Just as...

The discussion (*vāda*) has commenced: the discourse negating the self (*ātmapratiṣedhavāda*), namely "the self does not exist," is opposed to the discourse asserting the existence of the self (*ātmasattāvāda*).
Because of the contradiction between affirmation and negation,

that object which has been presented as a proof by means of that very dispute is called "the probandum" (sādhya) by the proponent who desires the establishment— that is, the ascertainment— of his own position; this is expressed by the word "intended" (iṣṭa).
The phrase "that which was stated as 'that'" at the end must be referred back here to complete the sentence.

Although in the inference for others (*parārthānumāna*) it is logical that only what has been stated is the probandum (*sādhya*), nevertheless, even that which has not been explicitly stated by words is the probandum.
Because that [meaning] is expressed by implication. // 45 //
Whence is this [known]? He says: "tad" (that).
That object is the *adhikaraṇa*—the locus or substratum—of which; that is "tad-adhikaraṇa," namely the dispute (*vivāda*).
The state of being that is "tattva"; from that [it follows].
This is what is meant: since a proof has been presented by the proponent who wishes to refute a dispute, therefore that very subject which is the locus of the dispute is the probandum (*sādhya*).
For if that which was presented as a proof in order to remove a contradictory position were not the probandum, [then the proof would be useless].
What now could possibly be established as something determined by its very nature? // 46 //
Even if not explicitly stated, that which is intended as the probandum (*sādhya*) in an inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*) is desired;
he illustrates this with the words "for the sake of others.
Those things of which the eyes and so forth are the first—namely, the ears and so forth—are "those beginning with the eyes"; this is the subject (*dharmin*).
The thesis (*sādhya*) is that these [constituents] exist for the sake of another, which is their "being-for-another" (*pārārthya*);
the reason (*hetu*) is "because they are composite" (*saṅghātatvāt*);
and the demonstration of the domain of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is by means of the example of the parts of a bed, a seat, and so forth.
Bedding and seating belong first to someone; thus, that which consists of bedding, seating, and so forth is a composite form that serves as an accessory for a person's enjoyment.

Similarly, in this proof, although the fact that the eyes and other faculties serve the purpose of a self has not been explicitly stated, the fact that they serve the purpose of a self remains the thesis to be proven, even though unstated.

Regarding the term "not set aside" (*anirākṛta*): even when the other characteristics are present, that object which, though intended to be proven, is set aside by perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), common knowledge (*pratīti*), or one's own words (*svavacana*)—that is not a thesis (*pakṣa*).
This is stated for the purpose of demonstrating this point.
49. Among these, that which is refuted by perception (*pratyakṣa-nirākṛta*) is, for example: "Sound is inaudible."

Just as bedding, seats, and so forth are seen to be for the sake of another because they are composite in nature, so too the eyes and other [senses] are also for the sake of another precisely because they are composite in nature; such is the meaning of the formal argument (prayoga). // 47 //
In this syllogism, although it is not explicitly stated that the eyes and so forth exist for the sake of a self,
nevertheless, their being for the sake of a self is precisely what is being proved.
Otherwise, if only their being for the sake of another were proved, it would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).
Because it is presented as the probandum through a disagreement regarding the self (or the purpose of the self),
therefore that alone constitutes the probandum.
Since that which is thus questioned is made an object of desire, it is desired precisely as something to be proven (*sādhya*);
therefore, that which is merely stated [as a fact] does not become a *sādhya*.
If one asks, "How so?"
Because even that which is made an object by way of being desired is indeed the probandum (sādhya). // 48 //
For it has been stated by the Sāṅkhya: "The self exists.
Contrary to that, the Buddhist has stated: "The self does not exist.

Therefore, the Sāṅkhya, taking the Buddhist position—which contradicts his own doctrine—as the reason (*hetu*), has presented a formal argument (*sādhana*) for the purpose of refuting the contradictory doctrine and establishing his own doctrine.
Therefore, even though it is not explicitly stated, the fact that [the body] exists for the sake of the self (*ātman*) is what must be proven, because the dispute concerns that very point.
For in the case of beds, seats, and other such items that serve as instruments for human enjoyment, their being for the sake of the self is not commonly recognized.
Since the state of being an aggregate is established merely by the fact of being for the sake of another,
it is therefore stated that "the eye and so forth are for the sake of another."
Here, by the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*), consciousness (*vijñāna*) is also intended to be established as being for the sake of another.

Since that which is other than consciousness must be the self (*ātman*), it is understood that by the power of the argument—that consciousness accomplishes the purpose of another—the fact that the eyes and so forth exist for the sake of the self is established; it is with this in mind that the term "for the sake of another" (*parārtha*) was employed.
By this statement that "the probandum is what is intended," it is not merely what has been explicitly stated;

rather, because it is the subject of dispute for the opponent, the probandum is that which the proponent intends to prove—whether it has been explicitly stated or not, provided it is understood from the context. This is what is meant. // 47 //
"Not refuted" is to be explained;
"this" refers to that [which follows].

The definition of the thesis (*pakṣa*) that was just mentioned—namely, "that which is intended as the probandum" (*sādhyatveneṣṭaḥ*), and so forth—even when a subject possesses this definition, there are cases where the object is not a thesis; for the purpose of demonstrating and explaining this, the term "unrefuted" (*anirākṛta*) has been included.
What kind of object is not a thesis, even if it is intended to be proven?

Thus he says: "That object which is intended to be proven, if it is contradicted by perception, inference, consensus, or one's own statement—and if its opposite is thereby established—that is not a [valid] thesis. // 48 //

Regarding the word *tatra*: among those four [types of objects] refuted by perception and so forth, what is the one refuted by perception (*pratyakṣanirākṛta*)? As for the word *yathā*: its meaning is that just as this [example] is refuted, so too should the others be understood.
(50) An example of that which is refuted by inference (*anumānanirākṛta*) is: "Sound is eternal."
51. An example of that which is refuted by common consensus (*pratītinirākṛta*) is: "The hare-marked one (*śaśin*) is not the moon (*acandra*)."

Even if a subject possesses the characteristics as previously described, if that subject is refuted at the stage of proof by perception, inference, what is commonly recognized, or one's own words, then that subject does not constitute a valid thesis (pakṣa); it is for the purpose of demonstrating this that the term "unrefuted" (anirākṛta) was stated. // 48 //
In this context, "hearing" (*śravaṇa*) means listening; the remainder [of the sense] is that it is the cognition of the ear,
or rather, the perception of what is audible.
That which is to be grasped by hearing is "audible" (śrāvaṇa). That which is not audible is "non-audible" (aśrāvaṇa);
the remainder [of the definition] is that it is not perceived by auditory consciousness (karṇavijñāna).
And likewise, in this case, sound is the subject (dharmin);
"being inaudible" is the property to be proven (sādhyadharma).
However, the thesis (pratijñā) that "sound is inaudible" is refuted by direct perception (pratyakṣa).
For instance, the fact that auditory consciousness makes sound manifest is understood by all living beings for themselves;
therefore, since the quality of being audible (*śrāvaṇatva*) in sound is apprehended through one's own cognition, its non-audibility (*aśrāvaṇatva*) is refuted. // 49 //
In this case, the permanence of the jar, which has been asserted, is refuted by the inference based on its being a product and so forth;
for it is observed that what is produced is impermanent,
and the jar, too, is a product.
Therefore, how can there be permanence? // 50 //

If someone were to make the proposition that "the hare-marked one (śaśin) is not denotable by the word 'candra' (moon)," it would be refuted by common consensus (*prasiddhi*) that "that very hare-marked one is indeed denotable by the word 'candra'.
Furthermore, it is also refuted by the fact that every word has everything as its denotable object (*vācya*).
Because the relationship between word and meaning is indicated by convention, just as even a jar possesses the fitness to be designated by the word "moon. (51)
That which is grasped by hearing is "audible" (*śrāvaṇa*); that which is not audible is "inaudible" (*aśrāvaṇa*).
The meaning of the thesis is that it is not graspable by the sense of hearing.
The claim that sound is not apprehended by the ear is sublated by the fact that it is apprehended by the ear, as established through direct perception. // 49 //
An example of what is refuted by inference (*anumānanirākṛta*) is as follows: "Sound is eternal.
The eternity of sound, which is the thesis (*pratijñāta*), is refuted by impermanence, which is established through inference. // 50 //
"Because it is refuted by common consensus, it is not denotable by the word 'candra' (moon)";
this is the thesis that "it is the hare-marked one" (*śaśin*),
and this [thesis] is refuted by common consensus.
A "cognized object" (pratīto 'rthaḥ) is said to be the object of conceptualizing consciousness (vikalpavijñāna).
"Cognition" (pratītiḥ) is the state of being cognized (pratītatva), which is intended here as the state of being the object of conceptualizing consciousness.
By means of that conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*), which has the nature of a mental apprehension, the fact that the moon is denotable by the word "candra" is indeed established. For instance:
whatever is graspable by conceptual consciousness is capable of being associated with the form of a word;
and whatever is capable of being associated with the form of a word can be expressed by a conventional term.

Therefore, by virtue of being established as the object of conceptual cognition in the form of a mental apprehension, the status of being denotable by the word "moon" serves as a sublater of non-moonhood;
and this apprehension is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

Since being denotable by a conventional term is necessarily concomitant with being merely an object of conceptual construction, it should be understood that the denotability by the word "moon"—established through a reason of essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*)—is the sublater of non-denotability. // 51 //
52. An example of what is refuted by one's own words: "Inference is not a means of valid cognition."
When someone asserts that inference is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), this is contradicted by their own words.
For if inference were not indeed a valid means of knowledge, this very statement could not even be uttered.
For even a statement is indeed included within inference;
and if inference were not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), from what source could a statement possibly be a valid means of knowledge?
If that statement were not a valid means of knowledge, [how could it establish its object?]
Why is it said [that way]? Because it is contradicted by one's own words. // 52 //
One's own statement is the word that expresses the meaning of one's own proposition; if the meaning of the proposition is refuted by that [statement], it is not to be proven.
For example: "Inference is not a valid means of knowledge."
In this context, the purpose of the proposition is the negation of the validity of inference;
however, that [negation] is sublated by the very sentence containing its own expression, namely, "inference is not a valid means of knowledge.
For when this sentence is employed, it indicates that the speaker intends the verbal cognition produced by it to have a real object.
For instance, if the speaker were to show that "the comprehension of meaning which arises in you from my statement is false in its object," he would not utter the statement at all;
for if the meaning of the speech is to be known by the other as false, the speaking is purposeless.
For even one who says, "I speak everything falsely," utters that very sentence while demonstrating its own truthfulness;
if this sentence were not demonstrated to have a truthful meaning, [it could not be uttered].
In this way, other statements that have the self as their subject are shown to have unreal objects;
however, if this very [statement] has an unreal object, then other [statements] would not be shown to have unreal objects.
Consequently, since there would be no fruit for utterance whatsoever, one should not utter it.
Therefore, a speaker utters a sentence only by demonstrating that the cognition which has as its object the meaning of the sentence arising from the sentence possesses a real object.
This being the case, by showing that the word is invariably concomitant with an external thing, the cognition born of the word must be shown to possess a real object.

Therefore, by demonstrating that the cognition produced from a word—which has an external object as its causal basis—possesses a real object, verbal cognition (*śābda*) is shown to be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) arising from the mark of an effect (*kāryaliṅga*).

Consequently, for one who asserts that inference is not a valid means of knowledge, it follows that he is asserting that the object apprehended by verbal cognition is unreal. For it is precisely this unreality of the object that constitutes invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*), and nothing else.
Furthermore, by the power of the utterance of the word, its own term—which is invariably concomitant—is shown;

and thus, the existent object is shown. Consequently, the existence inferred from that word, which is the effect of a conceptualized indicator, when asserted as a proposition, precludes non-existence.
Thus, the meaning here is this: non-existence, being sublated by existence as inferred from one's own words, is said to be "sublated by one's own words.
Others, however, say: the cognition arising from a word—which is the effect of an intention—has that intention as its object;
and the employment of a word occurs for one who desires a real object.
"Therefore, the non-authoritativeness he has asserted is contradicted.
This is incorrect; for in this case, the cognition [of the object] functions as a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*), while his own statement functions as an effect (*kārya*).
Thus, these four fallacious positions are refuted.
54. Thus, regarding that which is established,
and also regarding that which is not yet established but is intended as a means of proof,
and at that time is undesired by the proponent himself to be proven—

It has been stated that the thesis (*pakṣa*) is that which is intended by the proponent in its very own form, is not contradicted, and is the opposite of what has already been stated or refuted. By this, the definition of the thesis has been shown.

In this context, it has been stated that [the fallacy of] contradiction with scripture (āgamaviruddha) is included within contradiction with one's own words (svavacanaviruddha), and thus all four types of fallacious theses (pakṣābhāsa) have been enumerated.

Furthermore, it has been explained that because scripture lacks a basis when an inference functions by the force of real entities (vastubalapravṛtta), there can be no contradiction [between such an inference and scripture]. Thus it is said.
In the manner already described. // 53 //
In this context, the term "contrary" (viparīta) should be applied to each [of the following]:
the contrary of that which is established, the contrary of that which is unestablished, and the contrary of that which is intended as a means of proof (sādhana).

Thus, it is stated that the meaning is as follows: the opposite of what the proponent himself intends to prove, the opposite of what has been merely stated, and the opposite of what has been merely refuted, should be regarded as the thesis (pakṣa).
And thus, this is a statement defining the subject (*pakṣa*) by way of its opposite:
the status of being a reason (*hetutva*) is intended as conceptual (*kalpita*),
not real (*vāstava*).
Furthermore, the capacity to be expressed by words is indeed real for the word; therefore, that is not what is grasped here.
For example, just as inference cognizes the non-deviation of smoke from fire, [so too does it cognize the object].
Likewise, one will not accept that sound is non-deviant with respect to intention;
yet, sound is employed for the purpose of conveying external objects.
In that case, the employment of sound is preceded by the admission that sound is invariably concomitant with intention.
Moreover, a word is not uttered for the purpose of communicating one's own intention, but rather for the purpose of conveying an external entity;
therefore, the application of a word is preceded by the admission of its inseparable connection with an external object.
Therefore, that which was explained previously is indeed faultless. // 52 //

And this being the case, by the inclusion of the term "unrefuted," the four positions just mentioned—which appear as if they were valid positions—are excluded as fallacious positions (*pakṣābhāsa*). // 53 //

Now, in order to show what kind of meaning for the thesis (*pakṣa*) is obtained through the exclusion of those things which are excluded by the words defining the characteristics of the thesis, he briefly demonstrates that exclusion with the word "thus" (*evam*): that is,
by the sequence just mentioned.
The probandum (sādhya) is to be understood by way of the opposite—that is, by reason of being the reverse—of the established (siddha).
The meaning is that the object which is the reverse of the established object is the probandum;
and the reverse of the established is the unestablished (asiddha).
Because that which is unestablished (asiddha) is what is to be proven (sādhya). Furthermore, not everything unestablished is [the probandum],
but rather it is that which is unestablished even though it was stated as a means of proof (sādhana), by way of its contrariety.

The probandum (*sādhya*) is that which is not desired to be established by the proponent himself, even if it is unestablished; likewise, it is that which is unestablished merely because it has been stated in such a manner; and likewise, it is that which is unestablished even though it has been refuted—each of these being understood through their respective contraries.
It has been stated that inference for the sake of others (parārthānumāna) is the communication of a logical mark (liṅga) possessing three characteristics (trirūpa).
In this regard, if even one of these three characteristics is not stated, it is a fallacious proof (sādhanābhāsa).
Even when [the reason] has been stated, if it is unestablished (asiddha) or doubtful (sandeha) for both the proponent and the opponent, [it remains a fallacy].
"In that very form" means "as that which is to be proven (sādhya)"; this is the ellipsis. "Intended by the proponent" [is the meaning].
The [position] desired by the author of the treatise has been refuted.
The word "desired" is used merely to indicate that it was indeed stated;
the phrase "not refuted" means it is not to be abandoned—this is the remainder [of the sense].
Regarding the term "pakṣa" (the subject):
the word "sādhya" (the probandum) is to be understood as the ellipsis.
Thus, the definition of the subject is shown to be presented without deficiency.
Thus, the definition of the thesis (pakṣa), free from defects, has been explained. In this way, inference characterized by its true nature has been fully expounded. // 54 //

He says "it has been stated" for the purpose of permitting the designation of fallacious inference (*anumānābhāsa*). Having stated [the definition], the connection of the fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) is now being explained.
At that time, it constitutes the deficiency (*nyūna*) which is a fault of the proof (*sādhana*). // 55 //

Even if only one of the three forms [of the reason] is improper—such that it is unestablished (*asiddha*), contradictory (*viruddha*), or doubtful (*sandigdha*) for either the proponent or the opponent—that too would be a fallacy of proof (*sādhanābhāsa*). Thus, the application of fallacies of proof has been demonstrated. // 56 //

And that object which is devoid of the five points of disqualification, which is not established [by other means], which is not a proof for the proponent, which is intended by the proponent himself to be proven—whether explicitly stated or unstated—and which is not refuted by valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), is the "probandum" (*sādhya*).
This very thing, when intended by the proponent in its own form and unrefuted, is expressed by these words; this is the meaning. And that which is the probandum is called the "thesis" (*pakṣa*).

The word *iti* has the sense of "thus. Thus, the definition of the thesis (*pakṣa-lakṣaṇa*) is "faultless" (*anavadya*). That which has no fault (*avadya*) = defect (*doṣa*) is "faultless" (*anavadya*).
It has been shown; it has been explained. // 54 //

Having completed the exposition of the three-fold mark (*trirūpaliṅga*) and having stated the definition of the thesis (*pakṣa*) as it arose in the context, the author, desiring to speak of the fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*), prepares the introduction to them with the words beginning "the three-fold," etc.
This is what is meant: by one who wishes to state the three-fold mark, that [mark] must be clearly stated.

And thus it is clearly stated: if that [is described] and its counterpart is also described, then, when what is to be abandoned is known, that which is to be adopted— being distinct from it— becomes well understood.
It was stated previously that "inference for the sake of others (parārthānumāna) is the communication of a logical mark possessing the three characteristics.
Regarding the word "therein" (tatra): it means when that exists;
that is to say, when there is the communication of a logical mark possessing the three characteristics, which constitutes inference for the sake of others.
If not even one of the three characteristics is stated,
or— by the force of the word "even"— if two are not stated,
it is a semblance of a proof (*sādhanābhāsa*), that is, something resembling a proof.
The meaning is that it is not a proof (*sādhana*).
The deficiency of the three characteristics (*rūpa*) is indeed a fault of the proof (*sādhanadoṣa*). // 55 //
It is not only when unstated, but even when stated, [the fallacy occurs] in the case of non-establishment or doubt.
Of whom? He says: for the opponent (*prativādin*) who is to be convinced and for the proponent (*vādin*) who is the persuader, there is a pseudo-reason (*hetvābhāsa*). // 56 //
57. When the essential nature of one [of the two] or its relation to the subject (dharmin) is unestablished or doubtful, it is the fallacious reason (hetvābhāsa) called "unestablished" (asiddha).
For example, when "sound is impermanent" is the thesis to be proven, "visibility" is unestablished for both [the proponent and the opponent].
Regarding the thesis that "trees possess volition," death resulting from the removal of all bark is unestablished for the opponent;
for they accept that death is characterized by the cessation of consciousness, the sense faculties, and life-force,
and because these are impossible in trees.
He says "of one" for the purpose of specifying:
"connection with the subject" (dharmisambandha) means connection with the locus of properties; that is to say, the property of the subject (pakṣadharma).
When that [reason] is unestablished or when there is doubt regarding it, the fallacy of the reason known as "unestablished" (asiddha) occurs. // 57 //
He says "just as" in order to provide an illustration.
For the visibility of sound is indeed unaccepted by both the proponent and the opponent. (58)

If the Digambaras state that trees possess consciousness because they die when their entire bark is stripped away, and this is then employed as a formal argument (*prayoga*) by the Buddhists, then the death of trees upon the stripping of their entire bark is unestablished (*asiddha*) for the Buddhists.
If one asks why it is unestablished:
He says: "Consciousness," and so forth.
Now, when one single characteristic (*rūpa*) is unestablished or doubtful, what kind of fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) is it called? To this he says: "Of one single characteristic."
The connection with the subject (*dharmin*) is "connection with the subject.
When the presence of the reason (*hetu*) in the subject is either unestablished or doubtful, it is the fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) designated as "unestablished" (*asiddha*).
And precisely because it is unestablished, it is a cause for the non-comprehension of the subject.
It is not a reason for that which is to be proven, nor for the contradictory, nor for the doubtful.

Rather, it is a cause for non-comprehension; for no one comprehends anything from this [statement]. And this meaning is to be understood precisely from the application of the technical term "unestablished" (asiddha). // 57 //

He states an example, beginning with "yathā" (for instance): "Sound is impermanent. Here, when sound qualified by impermanence is the probandum (*sādhya*), the property of being visible—that is, being graspable by the eye—is unestablished (*asiddha*) for both the proponent and the opponent regarding sound. // 58 //
Regarding the statement "trees possess consciousness":
when it is to be proven that trees have consciousness,
the argument presented by the Digambaras— that death occurs when the entire bark is stripped away— is unestablished (*asiddha*) for the Buddhist opponent.
Why is it unestablished?
To this he says: "consciousness," and so forth.
"Consciousness," "the sense faculty," and "life-force" form a *dvandva* compound; therein, consciousness is that which is produced by the eye and the other [senses].

The sense-faculty (*indriya*) is that form (*rūpa*) situated within the eyeball and so forth, which is inferred from the arising of consciousnesses such as visual consciousness and is included among the effects.
In common worldly usage, "life-force" (*āyus*) refers to the vital breaths (*prāṇa*).
Furthermore, it is not appropriate to assert here that [the existence of the sense-faculties] is established by scriptural authority (*āgama*).
Therefore, in this context, "life" has the nature of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Their "cessation" is their cessation or disappearance.
That which has this as its characteristic or reality is described as such; for it is by means of this [treatise] that death, being of such a nature, is asserted by the Buddhist.

When "pleasure and so forth are insentient" is the proposition to be proven (*sādhya*), the reason—whether it be "possessing origination" or "impermanence"—is unestablished (*asiddha*) for the Sāṅkhya himself, who is the proponent (*vādī*).
The analysis of the compound is: consciousness (*vijñāna*), the sense faculties (*indriya*), and life-force (*āyus*).
The cessation of these is the "cessation of consciousness, faculties, and life-force.
Death is that which has this as its characteristic; thus, death is characterized by the cessation of consciousness, faculties, and life-force.
For the Buddhists, however, such a form of death is accepted, but not mere withering;
for such a death is not possible in the case of trees. (59)

When it is stated by the Sāṅkhyas that pleasure and so forth are insentient because they possess origination and are impermanent, and this is then established by the Buddhists, at that time the origination or impermanence of pleasure and so forth is unproven for the Sāṅkhyas themselves; for nothing whatsoever originates for them.
Or rather, nothing at all perishes. // 60 //
If this is indeed the case, how then is it unestablished?
To this he says: because that which consists of the cessation of consciousness and so forth is impossible in trees.
Cessation is preceded by existence;
therefore, how could one who desires the cessation of consciousness not desire consciousness itself?
Therefore, since consciousness is not admitted [to exist], cessation is also not admitted in trees.
But surely withering is also called death, and that is established in trees?
True; that death which is pervaded solely by the existence of consciousness is the cause here.
And the cessation of consciousness is pervaded by its [consciousness's] existence, not mere desiccation.
Therefore, that death which is the cause is unestablished in trees;
however, that which is established as consisting of withering is not the cause.
But the Digambara, without distinguishing between death that is pervaded by or coextensive with the probandum and mere death, has stated "mere death" as the reason.
Death, which serves as the reason for this proponent, is not known [to him];
because it is unknown, the form of withering is established, since death in the form of withering is observed in trees. However, for the opponent, it is known.
Therefore, it is unestablished.
However, when it is known even by the proponent, then it would be unestablished for the proponent as well; such is the logical principle. // 59 //
"Pleasure and so forth are insentient":
those things of which pleasure is the first—namely, pain and the rest—are "pleasure and so forth.
When their lack of sentience is to be proven, [the reason] is "possessing the quality of being produced" (utpattimattva).
Alternatively, impermanence is presented as the logical mark:
those things which possess origination or are impermanent are not sentient,
just like form and so forth.
And thus: pleasure and the like are insentient because they possess origination or because they are impermanent;
consciousness, however, is the very nature of the *puruṣa*.
In this case, "possessing origination" and "impermanence" function as reasons alternatively, not simultaneously.
Furthermore, neither of these two is established for the Sāṃkhya proponent;
for the presentation of a reason is for the sake of another. Therefore, that which is established for the other must be stated as the reason.
Furthermore, the arising of what was previously non-existent for another, and the destruction of what exists without any continuity— this is established as impermanence;
such [impermanence] is unestablished for the Sāṃkhya.
Here too, there is non-establishment [of the reason] if there is doubt regarding its impermanence, its production, or whether it itself is based upon that [subject].

For example, when a collection of elements (*bhūtasamghāta*) that is being doubted as being vapor or the like is presented for the purpose of proving fire, it is an "unestablished due to doubt" (*sandigdhāsiddha*).
For example: "There is a peacock in this bower, because of its cry."
When there is doubt regarding the reason itself, or its locus, then it constitutes the fallacy of the unestablished (asiddha). // 61 //
In this regard, there is an illustration: "just as" (yathā).
That which has vapor and so forth as its beginning is "vapor-and-the-rest" (vāṣpādi);
the state of those is "the state of vapor-and-the-rest" (vāṣpādibhāva).
The phrase "the nature of vapor and so forth" is the ellipsis [to be supplied].
A collection of elements is a *bhūtasanghāta*.
If it is argued that this is being established as the reason for proving the existence of fire?
"Is this vapor, or dust, or mist?"—being thus doubted as to its nature as vapor and so forth, it constitutes the fallacy of an unestablished reason (*asiddha-hetvābhāsa*). // 62 //
He says "as follows" (yathā) for the purpose of indicating the doubt regarding its basis.
The continuous flow of the peacock's cry is called *kekāyita*.
A *nikuñja* is a particular mountain cleft. If someone were to say, "There is a peacock here in this *nikuñja*," [the listener would understand].
If it is inferred from the sound of a peacock's cry, then the presence of the peacock's voice in that desired bower remains indeed doubtful. // 63 //
Because of the disputant's lack of knowledge regarding the proof of existence, [the reason] is unestablished for the disputant.
However, if the disputant were to know the validity of both impermanence and having an origin, then it would be established for the disputant as well.
Therefore, because it is not known through a means of valid cognition, this is unestablished for the proponent. (60)
To demonstrate the "doubtful-unestablished" (sandigdhāsiddha), he says: "In the same way.
"By itself" means that when the reason itself is in doubt, it is unestablished;
or else, [unestablished] because its locus is so.

The "resort" (āśrayaṇa) is the resorting to that reason. It is called a "resort" because the reason is resorted to in it; thus, the subject of the thesis (sādhyadharmin), which is distinct from the reason and serves as its basis, is being described.
For in that case, a present reason is relied upon as that which makes [the object] known; when there is doubt regarding that reliance, [the reason] is doubtful. // 61 //
He says "as follows" (yathā) in order to cite an example of that which is being doubted by oneself:
"vāṣpādi" means that of which steam (vāṣpa) and so forth are the beginning;
thus, it is a collection of elements (bhūtasaṅghāta) being doubted as having the nature of steam and so forth (vāṣpāditva).
The "aggregate" (saṃghāta) refers to a collection of elements such as earth and so forth.
In the context of proving fire, that which is being employed for the purpose of proving fire is unestablished (asiddha).
What is meant by this is: when even smoke is itself doubtful—being suspected of being mere vapor and the like—[it cannot serve as a valid reason].
In that case, it is unestablished (*asiddha*),
because its nature as a signifier is not certain.
That which is ascertained as being smoke is a signifier because it is produced by fire.
When, however, it is doubtful, then it is not a prover; this is the fallacy known as "unestablished" (asiddha). // 62 //
He provides an example of that which is unestablished due to its locus (*āśrayāsiddha*) with the words "as follows" (*yathā*).
Here, "in this bower" (*iha nikuñje*) is the subject (*dharmin*). A bower (*nikuñja*) is a portion of ground concealed by a mountain slope that extends outwards horizontally.
"Peacock" is the probandum (*sādhya*);
"because of its *kekāyita*" is the reason (*hetu*);
*kekāyita* is the cry of a peacock. //63//
64. When there is confusion regarding the location of its appearance.

65. [The reason] is unestablished even when the property of the subject is established—just as, for example, when "the self is omnipresent" is the thesis, [the reason] "having qualities perceived everywhere" [is unestablished].
If it is asked, "In what way is it doubtful? he says: "At that time.
The location where the sound of the peacock first appears is indeed doubtful;
for there is precisely a doubt as to from which part of the bower that sound of the peacock is emerging. 64.
"Omnipresent" means pervading everything;
"all-pervasive" is the understood term.
The analysis of the compound is: he whose qualities are perceived everywhere.
Its state is the quality of being perceived everywhere.
Someone attempts to prove the omnipresence of the self by means of this quality of being perceived everywhere;
in that case, the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished with respect to its locus (*āśrayāsiddha*).
For instance, that whose property is said to be "being perceived as a quality in all [persons]" does not exist at all—that is the self (*ātman*).
This, however, is the opponent's argument:
it is well known that pleasure and so forth are qualities of the self.
And those [qualities] of Devadatta are perceived in every location;
because of the absence of action, coming and going do not exist in the self,
since its qualities are perceived everywhere.
Therefore, it is certain that the self (ātman) is present everywhere. // 65 //
How is this [reason] unestablished in respect of its substratum (*āśrayāsiddha*)?
To this he says: "the arrival of that.
The arrival (*āpāta*) is the coming (*āgamana*) of that *kekāyita* (the cry of a peacock).
That place from which the *kekāyita* (the cry of the peacock) comes is called its "location. When there is confusion or delusion regarding that location, this [inference] lacks a basis for reliance.

For instance, when there are many dense groves in close proximity, if one is confused as to which specific grove the *kekāyita* has come from—thinking, "Has the *kekāyita* come from this grove?"—then the inference fails.
Or perhaps from something else?
In that case, this [reason] is unestablished with respect to its locus (āśrayāsiddha). // 64 //
He illustrates the lack of proof even regarding the subject (*dharmī*) with the words "for example" (*yathā*). "Omnipresent" (*sarvagata*) means gone to or situated in everything;
that is to say, pervasive (*vyāpin*).
When the all-pervasiveness of the self is to be proven, the logical mark (*liṅga*) is the fact that its qualities are perceived everywhere.
This refers to the state or nature (*tattva*) of that self whose qualities—such as pleasure, pain, desire, attachment, and aversion—are perceived in every location.
Qualities do not exist apart from the possessor of qualities (*guṇin*).
Because qualities are inherent in that which possesses qualities,
and the self is inactive;
therefore, if it were not all-pervading, [it could not be connected with all qualities].

How could suffering and the like, perceived in the southern region (Dakṣiṇāpatha), be perceived in the central region (Madhyadeśa)? Therefore, the self must be omnipresent. But here, for the Buddhist, the very existence of a self is not established; how much less, then, can its quality of being perceived everywhere be established? Since that [self] is unestablished, this is a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*). Previously, by means of the doubt regarding the substratum (*āśraya*), a doubt regarding the subject (*dharmin*) was stated.
But now, there is this distinction between the two: [the former] is unestablished, while [the latter] is stated as belonging to the subject (*dharmī*).
Thus, when one of the characteristics—namely, the connection with the subject—is unestablished, it is the fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) known as "unestablished" (*asiddha*). // 65 //
Likewise, when the presence of a single instance of the property (*rūpa*) in the dissimilar class (*asapakṣa*) is unestablished, it is an inconclusive pseudo-reason (*anaikāntika hetvābhāsa*).

For example, when a property such as impermanence is to be proven of sound, a property such as "knowability" exists either throughout or in some part of both the similar instances (sapakṣa) and the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa).
When the negative concomitance (vyatireka) is not established, the fallacious reason (hetvābhāsa) known as "inconclusive" (anaikāntika) should be cited. // 66 //
He says "just as" (yathā) for the purpose of providing an illustration.

That property which has "eternality" as its first [member] is "eternality and so forth" (*nityatvādika*). Likewise, that which has "knowability" (*prameyatva*) as its first is "knowability and so forth" (*prameyatvādika*).
When "sound is non-eternal because it is knowable" is the probandum (*sādhya*), knowability exists everywhere in both the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*).

In the case of the proof "Sound is not produced by effort because it is impermanent," impermanence exists in one part of the similar instances (sapakṣa) and in all of the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa).
[Conversely,] sound is produced by effort.
Because of impermanence;

likewise, when another single property called "absence from the dissimilar class" (asapakṣe 'sattva) is unestablished, the reason is a fallacious reason (hetvābhāsa) that is inconclusive (anaikāntika).
*Eka-anta* means a single end, that is, certainty; that which has this as its purpose is *aikāntika*. That which is not *aikāntika* is *anaikāntika*.
Because there is no certainty regarding either the probandum or its opposite, but rather its reverse— namely, doubt—
it is stated that a reason which causes doubt concerning both the probandum and its contrary is "inconclusive" (anaikāntika). // 66 //
He illustrates this with the words "as for example" (*yathā*) and so forth.
"Impermanence and the rest" (*anityatvādika*) refers to those properties beginning with impermanence.
By the word "and the rest" (*ādi*), non-subsequent-to-effort (*aprayatnānantarīyakatva*), subsequent-to-effort (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*), and permanence (*nityatva*) are included.

That which has "knowability" (*prameyatva*) as its first [member] is "knowability and so forth" (*prameyatvādika*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), "non-eternality" (*anityatva*) and "further non-eternality" (*punaranityatva*) are included.
And incorporeality is also apprehended.
When a property such as impermanence is to be proven of the subject (dharmin) that is sound, a property such as knowability is inconclusive (anaikāntika).
For in all four cases, its absence from the counter-example (vipakṣa) is unestablished.

For instance: "Sound is impermanent, because it is an object of cognition, like a pot and like space. Here, being an object of cognition exists both in the similar instances (sapakṣa) and in the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa).
"Sound is not produced immediately after an effort;

[it is] impermanent, like lightning and space, and like a jar. Here, the property of impermanence exists in one part of the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), such as lightning and so forth, but not in [all] parts such as space and so forth; it pervades the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), because it exists everywhere in that which is produced immediately after an effort.

"Sound is produced immediately after effort because it is impermanent, like a pot, and like lightning and space"— in this [inference], impermanence resides in only a portion of the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*);
it exists in lightning and so forth, [but not in space].
It does not exist in space and so forth; it pervades the similar class (sapakṣa), because it exists in every case that is produced through effort.
"Sound is eternal, because it is incorporeal."
Like space and an atom, and like action and a jar— thus, incorporeality (amūrtatva) resides in one part of both;
it exists in one part of both [space and action], namely in space and in action, whereas in the case of the atom, however—
68. Likewise, even when there is doubt regarding this very nature [of the subject], the reason is indeed inconclusive (anaikāntika).

69. For example, when it is to be proven that a certain intended person is not omniscient or possesses passion and so forth, the property of being a speaker and the like has a doubtful exclusion from the dissimilar instances (sandigdhavipakṣavyāvṛttika).
In the case of the probandum "impermanence," [the reason] exists in the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and in one part of the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*) everywhere.
In the case of the probandum "sound is eternal, because it is intangible,"...
The absence of contact exists in one part of both the similar instances (sapakṣa) and the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa).
By this, the fourfold common inconclusive (sādhāraṇānaikāntika) reason has been described. // 67 //
Even when its non-existence in the counter-example is itself doubtful, it remains inconclusive. // 68 //
He states "just as" (*yathā*) for the purpose of providing an illustration:

suppose someone intends to say that a certain person is not omniscient because he is a speaker, or that he possesses passion and so forth because he is a speaker; when this is being asserted, the property of being a speaker (*vaktṛtva*) and so on is indeed inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
If one asks, "What is the name of such an inconclusive [reason]?"—
He says: "Doubtful," and so forth.

That for which the exclusion from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) is doubtful is "one whose exclusion from the dissimilar instance is doubtful. The remainder of the phrase is "doubtful negative concomitance" (*sandigdhavyatireka*).
The absence of a speaker who is omniscient does not establish a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), even though such a person is not observed. // 69 //
It does not exist in some parts of the similar class (sapakṣa), such as a jar, nor in some parts of the dissimilar class (vipakṣa),
because jars, atoms, and so forth possess corporeality (mūrtatva);
for the Vaiśeṣikas maintain that atoms are eternal.
Consequently, [the reason] is included within the similar class (sapakṣa).
Since the non-existence of this fourfold property of the subject (pakṣadharma) in the dissimilar class (vipakṣa) is unestablished, there is therefore inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatā). // 67 //

Just as this form [of the reason] is inconclusive due to its non-establishment (*asiddha*), so too is it inconclusive when there is doubt regarding the absence of that very same form in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*). // 68 //
He illustrates this with the words "as follows" (*yathā*):
"not omniscient" (*asarvajña*).
Here, "non-omniscience" is the property to be proven (*sādhya*).
"Someone intended to be spoken of" means the person intended by the speaker;
this person is the subject (dharmin).
That which has passion (*rāga*) and so forth—such as hatred (*dveṣa*) and the like—is "passion and so forth" (*rāgādi*);
one who possesses that is "one possessing passion and so forth" (*rāgādimān*). This is the second probandum (*sādhya*).
The inclusion of the word "or" (*vā*) is for the purpose of indicating that "possessing passion and so forth" is a separate probandum.
Therefore, when "non-omniscience" or "possessing passion and so forth" is the property to be proven (*sādhya*) in the context at hand, the property consisting of "being a speaker"—
that is, the capacity for speech— and that which begins with it, such as the opening and closing of the eyes, is an "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*) reason.
This is said because its exclusion from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) is doubtful.
When non-omniscience is the property to be proven (sādhya), omniscience is the counter-example (vipakṣa).
In that case, it is doubtful whether speech and so forth exist or do not exist;
therefore, it is not known whether the speaker is omniscient.
Or is he not omniscient?
Thus, the property of being a speaker is inconclusive. // 69 //
Because non-perception of the form "an omniscient speaker is not found" has as its object something invisible by nature, it serves as a cause for doubt;
therefore, the exclusion of the opposite of non-omniscience—namely, the exclusion of being a speaker and so forth—is itself doubtful.

Furthermore, since there is no contradiction between being a speaker and being omniscient, even if one does not observe that "whoever is omniscient is not a speaker," the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not established due to doubt.
If it is asked, "How is this inconclusive?
he says in response: "In this way," even when there is observation of an omniscient speaker.

This non-apprehension has for its object a self that is imperceptible; because its object is an imperceptible self, it is itself a cause of doubt. It does not establish a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).

Since non-apprehension of an imperceptible object is a cause of doubt alone, the exclusion of the reason characterized by "speakership" from the omniscient being—by way of the negation of non-omniscience—is itself doubtful. (70)

If it is argued: "Let non-apprehension not establish the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) because its object is an invisible nature; rather, let its establishment come through the apprehension of a contradiction with essential nature (*svabhāvavirodhopalabdhi*)."
To this he replies: "Regarding the state of being a speaker" (*vaktṛtva*).
There is no contradiction between the state of being a speaker and omniscience.

Therefore, even if an omniscient speaker is not observed, because there is no contradiction between the state of being a speaker and omniscience, it is not established that the state of being a speaker is excluded from omniscience, since doubt remains.
But surely, an omniscient speaker is not perceived;

how then can the statement regarding an omniscient being be doubtful? Precisely because a non-perception of this kind—such as the claim that "an omniscient speaker is not perceived"—is a cause for doubt.
Why is this so? He says: "The state of having an imperceptible self as its object is *adṛśyātmaviṣayatvam*.
By that [state], there is the quality of being a cause for doubt.
For non-apprehension whose object is imperceptible is a cause for doubt, not a cause for certainty."
Therefore, the exclusion of "being a speaker" and so forth from the omniscient one—which is the opposite of the non-omniscient—is doubtful. (70)
We do not say that the quality of being a speaker is non-existent in an omniscient being merely because it is not perceived;
rather, it is because there is a contradiction between being a speaker and being omniscient.
This is not so.
The connection [of the argument] is as follows: there is no contradiction between omniscience and being a speaker;
