and because of this absence of contradiction, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not established.
He demonstrates the negative concomitance that possesses pervasion (*vyāpti*) with the words: "He who is omniscient..."

Having restated omniscience as being of the nature of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*), the absence of the means of proof (*sādhana*), namely "being a speaker" (*vaktṛtva*), is enjoined by the statement "he is not a speaker.
Thus, because the absence of the probandum is necessarily concomitant with the absence of the means of proof, it is stated to be pervaded (*vyāpta*) by the absence of the means of proof.
Such a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) characterized by pervasion would be established if there were a contradiction between "being a speaker" and "omniscience."
And there is no contradiction;
therefore, it is not established. Why? He says: "Because of doubt."
Since there is contradiction, there is doubt; from doubt follows the non-establishment of the negative concomitance (vyatireka). // 71 //
For contradiction among categories is indeed twofold.
The understanding of contradiction arises because that which exists with its causes complete does not exist when another thing is present.
If it is asked, "How is there an absence of contradiction between those two? he says in response: "It is twofold.
Whatever contradiction is perceived anywhere, all of it is included within these two types.
The first is a contradiction in reality;
the second is a contradiction in conventional usage. // 72 //
To explain the statement regarding actual contradiction, he says: "without deficiency" (*avikala*).

When the manifestation of an entity that is to be removed by its causes occurs while the collection of those causes is complete, and there is a cessation upon the full accomplishment of another entity, then contradiction is perceived. // 73 //
How is there an absence of contradiction?
It is twofold; for [it is said]:
"Indeed."
Since contradiction is of only two kinds and no other, therefore there is no contradiction between the state of being a speaker and omniscience. // 72 //
What, then, is this twofold contradiction? To this he says: "Of that whose causes are unimpaired.
That which has its causes—meaning all its causes—unimpaired (complete) is described as such.
That which is absent due to a deficiency of causes cannot be understood as being in contradiction with anything;
for that reason, [the subject] has its causes unimpaired.
But surely, even for one whose causes are complete, their cessation cannot be brought about by anyone;
so how can there be an understanding of contradiction?
In that case, even for one whose causal factors are complete, there may be an absence [of an effect] due to the deficiency of some other cause; by this, the understanding of contradiction is reached.
And this being so, whatever is contradictory to something must produce some effect upon it.

For it is thus: having become the producer of a cold touch, the contradictory [cause] is that which brings about the cessation of the cold touch by obstructing its capacity to produce another cold touch;
therefore, the contradictory cause is precisely the producer of the cessation. And this is the contradiction of non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna-virodha*).
Therefore, one must avoid the possibility of two contradictory things coexisting even in a single moment.
Furthermore, since contradiction does not exist between things situated at a distance, the relationship of the sublated and the sublator exists only between those that are in close proximity.
Consequently, if something is the sublator of another, it can at most cause that other to cease in the third moment.
In the first moment, as it comes into contact, it becomes capable of bringing about a state of incapacity;
in the second, it produces an opposing incapacity;
but in the third, once that incapacity has ceased, it occupies its location.

In that regard, light, which has the nature of motion, gradually occupies space according to the analogy of waves on water; when it produces a moment of light in a region previously devoid of darkness, it produces a darkness near the light that is incapable [of persisting].
Consequently, that darkness which has light in its vicinity becomes incapable.

When [the light] is incapable [of reaching the location], darkness is removed by light through this sequence: once the [light] has ceased in that place, light arises there; in this manner, darkness is to be dispelled by light.
Likewise, cold touch is to be removed by hot touch.
However, when light is produced in that very same location where darkness was, [darkness is removed].
Then, from the very moment that the moment producing light arises in a region of darkness,
from that same moment the darkness becomes incapable of generating further darkness,
like cold and hot touch.
Or, it is like existence and non-existence, because their characteristics are defined by mutual exclusion.
Just as in the case of the sensations of cold and heat, when coldness—which has its causes fully present—is not yet fully realized as heat, there is the cessation of that coldness;
and in the world, these two are perceived as being in opposition. // 74 //

Those whose characteristics exist through mutual exclusion are "those characterized by mutual exclusion"; the state of being such is "the nature of being characterized by mutual exclusion," and [it is] by means of that [nature] that there is contradiction.
Just as existence is established by the exclusion of non-existence, and non-existence is established by the exclusion of existence. // 75 //

Once it has arisen, its very nature as a producer of an incapable state constitutes its status as a remover. Therefore, in the third moment after the moment in which it acts as a producer, the opposing factor has ceased, provided it ceases quickly.
Furthermore, the contradiction lies between two continuums (*santāna*) due to their relationship as producer and produced,
not between two moments (*kṣaṇa*).
And although there is no such thing as a "continuum" that exists as a real entity,
Nevertheless, the possessors of the continuum (*santānin*) are real entities;
therefore, this ultimate truth is not a contradiction between two moments,
but rather between many moments.

Since cold moments, even though they have arisen while the moments of fire exist, possess the nature of cessation, and since the contradiction between the two continua— based on the relationship between that which is to be averted and that which averts— is thus established, there is no contradiction among all atoms despite their lack of coexistence in a single location,
because they do not avert one another's continua.
Furthermore, illumination, which possesses the property of movement, dispels opposing entities as it traverses a particular direction.

Consequently, the light of a lamp situated in one part of a room does not dispel the darkness even in its immediate vicinity; for it lacks the capacity to produce a subsequent moment of illumination in a direction already occupied by darkness.
By demonstrating that contradiction— which is produced by the causal capacity of a cause and culminates in the continuum—
is merely a matter of the non-existence of the cold tactile continuum proceeding in succession [due to] the existence of another, the hot continuum, you have accomplished your purpose.
As for those who say that contradiction is not real (*vāstava*), [their view is refuted].

They should be addressed as follows: Just as when an effect has been produced, there exists no dual relation called "the state of producer and produced," yet the occurrence of the effect is preceded by its cause;
therefore, this [relation] is indeed real.

Similarly, when a thing has ceased to exist, there is no such thing as "enmity" (virodha) directed toward it. Rather, the cause of the fire is the incapacity of the cold sensation to produce its own subsequent moment.
Therefore, even contradiction (*virodha*) is indeed real. // 73 //
He states the illustration: "Cold," etc.
Cold and hot—these two are the cold touches; it is like those two.
For the contradiction between the touches of cold and heat is to be applied here as before. // 74 //
To demonstrate a second contradiction as well, he says "paraspara... and so forth.
"Parasparaparihāra" means mutual exclusion or abandonment;

that by which their characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*)—that is, their nature (*rūpa*)—is established is "parasparaparihārasthitalakṣaṇa," and the state of being such is "parasparaparihārasthitalakṣaṇatā. [The argument proceeds] by means of that.
And that twofold contradiction is not possible between the states of being a speaker and being omniscient.
Furthermore, neither of these two types of contradiction is possible between the speaker and the omniscient one.
For in this context, when one thing is being delimited, that which is excluded from it must be understood as existing in a form that stands by excluding what is not being delimited.
And when blue is being delimited, its deviation from that nature (tādrūpyapracyuti) is also delimited; for if that were not delimited, it would follow that blue itself could not be delimited.
Therefore, the existence and non-existence of a thing exist as forms established through mutual exclusion.
However, whatever form is other than blue is deviant from the absence of blue;
for when yellow or other colors are perceived, there is a certainty of the absence of the visible blue due to its non-perception.
And just as blue excludes its own nature, [so too does it exclude others].
In the same way, yellow and so forth are also non-deviating from absence.
Thus, there is a direct contradiction between existence and non-existence,
whereas between two entities, there is contradiction because they are non-deviating from each other's absence.
And of what is there the determination of non-existence elsewhere?
It is of that object which has a determinate form, not of that which has an indeterminate form.
It is like momentariness and so forth.
For momentariness is the very essence of the nature of all things such as blue and the rest;
therefore, it does not have a fixed form, because nothing is perceived apart from momentariness.
If that is so, then non-existence (abhāva) also does not have a determinate form.
How can it be said to have an indeterminate form,
given that non-existence is a conceptualized form distinguished from the nature of a real entity?
Therefore, a form that is either perceived or imagined as determinate is necessarily understood to be non-existent elsewhere, not one that is indeterminate.
In this same way, even [entities] such as the "permanence-ghost" (*nityatva-piśāca*) should be regarded as imagined with a determinate aspect.
Furthermore, this constitutes a contradiction with the principle of identity.
For when two things exist by way of mutual exclusion, there is an absence of identity between them;
for this very reason, this is called a "definitional" (lākṣaṇika) contradiction.
"Lakṣaṇa" means essential nature (rūpa).
This is because it has the purpose of [defining] entities (*vastu*).
For by means of this [negation], the nature of being an entity is distinguished and established through opposition.
Therefore, that which is negated while the visible form is being perceived—
Having accepted that very thing as perceptible (*dṛśya*), it is then negated.

For instance, when even a non-existent entity (*abhāva*) or even a *piśāca* is intended to be negated in a particular location, it must be negated by way of its being perceptible; thus, having accepted its perceptibility, its negation occurs precisely through the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*).
And this being so, when a form is being delimited, the absence of that [other form] within it is seen as excluded;
and that form which possesses the aspect of being characterized by that absence is also seen as excluded.

Therefore, just like the two [opposites] such as light and darkness, even those things that possess cessation—namely, all those whose natures exist through mutual exclusion—are negated by this [reasoning].
Furthermore, even if this contradiction exists, coexistence might still occur;
therefore, contradiction consists in having distinct functions.
By one contradiction, the identity of the sensations of cold and heat is precluded;
by another, their coexistence and their having different objects are precluded.
The contradiction of mutual exclusion applies to all things, whether real or unreal;
the contradiction of non-coexistence, however, applies only to certain real entities.
Therefore, their functions are distinct.
And since their objects are distinct, there is no mutual inclusion between these two. // 75 //
Moreover, this twofold contradiction does not obtain between the state of being a speaker and omniscience;
nor is there a comprehension of non-existence through the non-perception of something that is not contradictory [to its existence].
78. Because the causal relationship between passion and the like, and speech and the like, is established.
And when another thing that is not a cause is absent, there is no absence [of the effect] merely because of the absence of a statement.
Even when the complete cause exists, the cessation of the perfection of omniscience is not admitted.
Furthermore, omniscience is not established by the exclusion of speakerhood, nor is speakerhood established by the exclusion of omniscience. // 76 //

If it is argued that, in the absence of contradiction, the state of being a speaker who speaks as if there were no contradiction is perceived as the non-perversion of omniscience, he replies: "And not...
Where there is no statement [of contradiction], even if the two things are not perceived, a certainty of their non-existence is not possible.
When non-omniscience is the property to be proven, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of the reason "being a speaker" is likewise doubtful. // 77 //

Even though [the opponent] has stated [the reason] by way of possessing passion and so forth, [the author] says "of passion and so forth" for the purpose of expressing doubt regarding the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
That "the statement of passion and so forth is the reason" is unestablished (*asiddha*). // 78 //
Granted that the causal relationship between passion and the act of speaking is unestablished, one might ask: what follows from that? He replies:
For it is not the case that the absence of omniscience can be inferred from the presence of the state of being a speaker, since its cause—omniscience—is not deficient.
For omniscience is invisible; and the non-existence of that which is unseen cannot be determined. Therefore, no contradiction can be established by means of this.
Furthermore, omniscience does not reside in the exclusion of speakerhood;
for if it did, even wood and the like would be subject to the consequence of being omniscient, since they too are excluded from speakerhood.
Nor is there speakerhood apart from omniscience, for that would entail the absurd consequence that even pieces of wood and the like are speakers.
Therefore, because there is no contradiction, the affirmation of speakerhood does not constitute a negation of omniscience. // 76 //
It might be argued: if there were indeed no contradiction between them, as in the case of a jar and a cloth, then their coexistence might be observed;
however, since their coexistence is not observed, the cognition of contradiction arises.
Anticipating the objection, "Is the understanding of non-existence [attained] through contradiction?", he says: "And not from the prescription of what is non-contradictory.
Even in the case of non-perception, this is not a prescription of something contradictory.
Even though there is a non-perception of their coexistence, nevertheless there is no contradiction between them;

for contradiction does not arise from mere non-perception together, but rather from the determination of a relationship between the two perceived things as that which is to be excluded and that which excludes.
Therefore, even in the case of non-perception, there is no affirmation of the opposite of the affirmation of speakerhood;
hence, from this [non-perception], there is no comprehension of the absence of anything else. // 77 //
Likewise, there is no inference of the presence of passion and so forth from the fact of being a speaker;
for if speech and the like were the effect of passion and so forth,
then one could infer passion and so forth from speech and the like.
The cessation of passion and so forth would entail the cessation of speech and so forth, yet this is not an effect.
Why? Because the causal relationship between passion and the like, on one hand, and speech and the like, on the other, is unestablished.
The effect does not [arise] from the cause;
therefore, there is no transition from this. // 78 //
Let it be that there is no effect such as passion; however, speech is a concomitant [of passion].
Therefore, regarding passion and so forth...
Thus, speech and the like are inconclusive (anaikāntika) due to a doubtful negative concomitance (sandigdhavyatireka).
81. When two forms are established as contradictory, it is a contradiction (*viruddha*).
Of which two?
Of the presence [of the reason] in the similar class (sapakṣa) and its absence in the dissimilar class (asapakṣa).
For example, "being produced" and "occurring immediately after an effort" are fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa) that are contradictory when "permanence" is the property to be proven.
Regarding the phrase "of another thing":
another thing refers to passion and so forth.
If that [other thing], which is not the cause, ceases, how could there be a cessation of speech and the like? // 79 //
For instance, since there is no contradiction whatsoever between being a speaker and being omniscient,
nor is there a causal relationship between passion and the like and speech;
therefore, the cessation of speech through the cessation of non-omniscience, or through the cessation of passion and the like, remains doubtful.
Therefore, that which has a doubtful negative concomitance is called an inconclusive [reason]. // 80 //
If the establishment of the reversal of both forms [of the reason] occurs, then it would be a contradictory fallacy of the reason (*viruddha-hetvābhāsa*). // 81 //
When two forms [of a reason] are perceived in a contrary manner, it is called a contradictory fallacious reason (*viruddha-hetvābhāsa*). // 82 //
The words "positive and negative concomitance" (anvaya-vyatirekau) are to be understood as the ellipsis.
Thus, the general definition of the contradictory (viruddha) has been stated.
To explain it specifically, he says: "the state of being produced," and so forth.

Anticipating the objection, "When the concomitant has ceased, does the statement also cease?", he says: "The cessation of another thing, such as non-action, does not entail the cessation of something else, such as speech, merely by virtue of observing their concomitance.
Therefore, it could be that one possesses the capacity for speech while still being devoid of passion and the like. (79)
The word *iti* has the sense of "therefore.

Therefore, because there is a reversal of non-omniscience—that is, from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) consisting of omniscience—and because there is a reversal of possessing passion and so forth—that is, from [the counter-example] consisting of being free from passion and so forth—the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of speech and the like is doubtful.
Consequently, speech and the like are inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). // 80 //

Having thus explained the faults of the reason (*hetudoṣa*) regarding doubt as to the non-establishment of each individual form (*rūpa*) and so forth, [the author], wishing to state the faults of the reason regarding doubt as to the non-establishment of each pair of forms, says: "Of each pair.
When there is the establishment of the opposite of two forms, [the reason] is contradictory (*viruddha*). // 81 //
And since there are three forms, he says "of which two" in order to specify the distinction between them. // 82 //
He demonstrates this through specific forms: [the presence] in the similar class (sapakṣa) and the absence in the dissimilar class (asapakṣa).
This is to be connected with the phrase "for the sake of establishing the non-deviation" (avyabhicārasiddhau).
"Being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) is an essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*);
whereas "being immediately subsequent to volitional effort" (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*) is an effect-reason (*kāryahetu*).

For by the term "immediately subsequent to volitional effort," both the birth [of the sound] immediately following volitional effort and the cognition [of it] immediately following volitional effort are called "immediately subsequent to volitional effort."
Birth is the intrinsic nature of that which is being born;
knowledge is the effect of the object of knowledge.
Here, however, knowledge is understood as occurring immediately after an effort.
Therefore, this is a reason based on effect (*kāryahetu*).
Since these two [reasons] are absent from the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and present in the dissimilar class (*asapakṣa*), there is a proof by contraposition (*viparyayasiddhi*).
85. And these two are "contradictory" (viruddha) because they prove the opposite of what is to be proven (sādhyaviparyaya). 86. But is it not also desired as a third [type], such as:
"The eyes and other [faculties] are for the sake of another, because they are composite, like beds, seats, and so forth"? 87. [This is indeed intended.]
If permanence were to be proven by means of being produced or by being dependent on effort, then it would be a contradictory fallacy of reason (*viruddha-hetvābhāsa*). // 83 //
If it is asked, "How is the non-establishment of the contrary [reason] shown here?", he says:
"Of these two.
When permanence is the property to be proven (*sādhya*), the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) is space (*ākāśa*) and so forth.
In that case, both "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and "occurring immediately after an effort" (*prayatnāntarīyakatva*) are impossible [in the subject].
The counter-example (*vipakṣa*), however, is impermanent things such as a pot;
in that [counter-example], both of these properties are indeed present.
And thus, the establishment of the opposite of those two follows. // 84 //

Since the establishment of the opposite of both forms [of the reason] occurs, there is consequently the establishment of the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyaviparyayasiddhi*). And because it proves the opposite of the probandum, it is a contradictory fallacious reason (*viruddha hetvābhāsa*). // 85 //
That by which the destruction of what is desired (*iṣṭa*) is brought about is called "the destroyer of the desired" (*iṣṭavighātakṛt*);
for this is stated by the authors of the treatises to be the third type of contradictory reason (*viruddha*). // 86 //
The statement of the illustration begins with "aytha" (thus).
Its meaning has indeed already been explained. // 87 //
These two reasons are fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa) when "permanence" is the property to be proven. // 83 //
Why, then, are these two contradictory?
To this he says: "Of these two.

For, in the case of the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), which is eternal, the non-existence of both "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and "following immediately after effort" (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*) is indeed certain.
Since existence is ascertained only in the dissimilar class (vipakṣa) which is impermanent, there is the establishment of the contrapositive (viparyaya). // 84 //
But why are these two also contradictory even when their pervasion is established?
To this he says: "And these two establish the impermanence that is the opposite of the probandum, which is permanence;
therefore, they are contradictory because they prove the opposite of the probandum. (85)

If it were a contradictory reason (*viruddha-hetu*) because it proves the opposite of the probandum (*sādhya*), then it has been stated that in inference for others (*parārthānumāna*), the probandum must be explicitly stated, not left unstated.
And that which is intended but not explicitly stated is also [included];

therefore, showing that others besides these two constitute the "subverter of what is intended" (*iṣṭavighātakṛt*), he says: "By the particle *nanu*, even a third contradictory [reason] is stated; two [of these] establish the opposite of what was stated."

This third [type] is the "subverter of what is intended" (iṣṭavighātakṛt), because it thwarts the intended [proposition] by proving its opposite, even though that intended [proposition] was not explicitly stated in words. // 86 //
He illustrates this with the words "as follows" (*yathā*).
"The eye and so forth" is the subject (*dharmin*).

"For the sake of another" (*parārtha*) means having another as their purpose (*prayojana*); that which is the motivator (*prayojaka*), the object to be refined (*saṃskārya*), and the one to be benefited—those things which possess such [a purpose] are "for the sake of another. This is the thesis (*sādhya*).

The reason is "because they are composites" (saṅghātatvāt), meaning because they consist of accumulated forms. For the eyes and so forth are indeed of the nature of an accumulation of atoms; therefore, they are called composite forms.
That which has bedding and seating as its beginning is "bedding, seating, and so forth" (*śayanāsanādi*).
This very thing is the "member" (*aṅga*), because it is a member for the enjoyment of a person.
This is the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) for demonstrating pervasion (*vyāpti*); for in this case:
88. It is contradictory because it proves the opposite of the intended non-composite state of being for the sake of another.
Why is this not mentioned here?
Because it is included within these very two.
For it does not differ from these two [fallacies] by virtue of proving the opposite of what is to be proven (sādhyaviparyaya).
If it is asked, "And how is it contradictory, noble one? he says: "Because that is desired by others. This [treatise] is for the sake of others (*parārtha*) because it is intended for others.
The state of that [mind] is "being for the sake of another" (pārārthya).
"Being for the sake of another by one who is not withdrawn" is "asaṃhṛtapārārthya.
The analysis of the compound is: "that [state] is desired and it is asaṃhṛtapārārthya."
Its opposite has as its object the non-withdrawal of being for the sake of another;
the meaning is that it is the proof of that [opposite].

Therefore, because it proves the opposite of the "non-withdrawal of being for the sake of another" which is desired by [the proponent], this [reason] must be regarded as indeed contradictory (viruddha). // 88 //
The meaning is that it is accepted by the author of the treatise even though it possesses contradictory characteristics. // 89 //
And as for the two types of contradiction that were mentioned, they are not named separately because they are included within those very [two]. // 90 //
He says "for not" (*na hi*) in order to demonstrate precisely this inclusion:

it has been stated that the reason characterized by being produced (*kṛtakatva*) and following immediately upon effort (*prayatnāntarīyakatva*) is "contradictory" (*viruddha*) because it proves the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyaviparyayasādhana*) when proving permanence as the probandum.
This [other reason] is likewise contradictory for the same reason, namely, that it proves the opposite of the probandum. // 91 //

Being for the sake of another (pārārthya) is pervaded by being composite (saṃhatatva). For instance, things such as beds and seats, which are of a composite nature, are said to be "for the sake of another" because they serve as benefactors for the experiencing person (puruṣa). // 87 //
How does this [reason] bring about the frustration of what is desired?
To this he says: "Because it proves the opposite of that 'unrestricted other-directedness' (pārārthya) which was intended.
"Unrestricted other-directedness" means other-directedness with respect to an unrestricted object.

For that Sāṅkhya proponent, what is intended is "non-subsumed purposefulness for another" (asaṃhṛtapārārthya); thus, it is his "intended non-subsumed purposefulness for another. Its opposite is called "subsumed purposefulness for another" (saṃhṛtapārārthya).
Because it establishes that [opposite], it is a contradictory reason (viruddha).

When the Sāṅkhya, asserting that "the self exists," is questioned by the Buddhist as to why this is so, he states this as the proof for the self's existence in the Sāṅkhya system. Therefore, what remains to be proven is that the eyes and other sense organs serve as auxiliaries to an uncomposite self.
But this reason is pervaded by the opposite [of what it seeks to prove];
for that which is beneficial to something is its producer,
and that which is being produced must exist either simultaneously or sequentially, being thus withdrawn [from non-existence].
Therefore, it is established that the eyes and other sense organs exist for the sake of another, as they are withdrawn when that other’s purpose has been served. // 88 //
Moreover, this contradiction was stated by the teacher Diṅnāga; why was it not mentioned by you, who are the author of the Vārttika? // 89 //
The other says: because these two are included within the very two [types of fallacies] that establish the opposite of the probandum. // 90 //
But surely, does that which is the opposite of what has been stated not establish [the contrary]?
How then is it included within the two—namely, the establishment of the stated [thesis] and its opposite?
To this he says: "For it is not so."
The word "hi" is used in the sense of "because.
Because this [reason], which brings about the destruction of what is desired, does not differ from those two reasons in its being a means of proving the opposite of the thesis;
just as those two prove the opposite of the thesis.
"So too is this [case].
Whether one establishes the opposite of what was stated or not, what is the use of establishing the opposite? Therefore, these two are included within those very [categories]. // 91 //
For there is no difference whatsoever between what is desired and what is stated in terms of being the probandum (sādhya).
93. When there is non-establishment of one of two forms and doubt regarding the other, it is inconclusive (anaikāntika).
For example: "Someone is free from passion, or is omniscient, because he is a speaker.
Here, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is unestablished, and the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is doubtful.
95. Because of the remoteness of the omniscient being and the one free from passion, it is doubtful whether speech and so forth exist or do not exist in them.

If it is asked: "How can this [fallacy] be similar to those two, given that it is the establishment of the opposite of the very probandum (sādhya) previously stated by the word, and in that case, there is no establishment of the opposite of the intended object?"

Regarding this, he says: "No, indeed. Whatever was intended and whatever was stated—that when both are to be proven, there is no distinction whatsoever between them—this has already been explained. // 92 //

When either the positive concomitance (anvaya) or the negative concomitance (vyatireka) is unestablished, or when there is doubt regarding one of them, the reason is inconclusive (anaikāntika). // 93 //
The statement of the example begins with "yathā" (just as). Its meaning has already been stated. "Atre" means in this formal argument (*prayoga*).
There is no negative concomitance (vyatireka), while the positive concomitance (anvaya) is doubtful;
for when omniscience is the property to be proven (sādhya), the non-omniscient constitutes the counter-example (vipakṣa).
And speech is excluded from those who are not omniscient. // 94 //
He says "sarvajña" (omniscient) for the purpose of stating the doubt regarding the lineage:
since omniscience and freedom from passion are not objects of the senses, it remains precisely doubtful whether there is any statement concerning these two anywhere or not.
For instance, regarding the person mentioned as an example: is he a speaker who is omniscient, or is he a speaker who is not omniscient?
In this regard, there is no certainty. // 95 //

But has it not already been stated that this is the very point to be proven (*sādhya*); how then can there be no difference [between the two] on the grounds that both establish the opposite of what is to be proven?
To this he says: "For not... (*na hi*).
Since there is no distinction or difference between what is desired (*iṣṭa*) and what is stated (*ukta*) in terms of being the probandum (*sādhya*),
the conclusion is that these two are included within those very [categories].
For that which is sought to be known by the opponent is what constitutes the subject matter of the context (*prakaraṇāpanna*).

And that which is relevant to the context is intended as the probandum (sādhya) when it is made the object of the desire to prove it— whether it has been explicitly stated or not; for the probandum is not merely whatever has been stated.
Therefore, there is no distinction. // 92 //
The contradictory [reason] has been stated when both aspects are established as being the opposite; however,
between those two, it is [also contradictory] when one of them is unestablished.
And when there is doubt regarding the other [term], it is inconclusive (anaikāntika). // 93 //
"What is he like? To this he says: "Just as...
One thing to be proven is that he is one from whom passion has departed (*vītarāga*);
the second is that he is omniscient (*sarvajña*).
"Because of being a speaker" is the reason (*hetu*). Here, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is unestablished (*asiddha*),
because being a speaker is observed even in one's own self, which is both possessed of passion and not omniscient— thus serving as a counter-example (*vipakṣa*).
Therefore, the negative concomitance (vyatireka) is unestablished, and the positive concomitance (anvaya) is doubtful. // 94 //
Why?
He says: "Because of remoteness" (*viprakarṣāt*)—that is, because they are beyond the senses (*atīndriyatvāt*).

Since speech and so forth are cognizable by means of what is beyond the senses, the existence or non-existence of [these qualities] in those two who are beyond the senses—the omniscient and the dispassionate—is doubtful.
And consequently, it is not known whether one is omniscient because of being a speaker or not; thus, [the reason] is inconclusive (anaikāntika). // 95 //
96. When there is doubt regarding these very two forms, it is inconclusive (anaikāntika).
For example: "The living body possesses a self, because it possesses breath and so forth."
For there exists no third category, distinct from those possessing a self and those lacking a self, in which this [set of] vital breaths and so forth could reside.
If both the positive concomitance (anvaya) and the negative concomitance (vyatireka) are themselves doubtful, then that too is a fallacious reason (anaikāntika-hetvābhāsa). // 96 //
To provide an illustration, he says "just as" (yathā).
That which has breath (*prāṇa*) as its first member is "breath-and-the-rest" (*prāṇādi*).
By the word "breath," there is the inclusion of opening and closing the eyes, expansion and contraction, and so forth.
"Endowed with a self" means being the locus for the enjoyment of a self;
"the living body" means [that very same thing].
By this, the corpse is excluded. // 97 //
And therein, for the purpose of stating the doubt regarding the negative concomitance (vyatireka), he says: "For not...
Indeed, there are two categories: that which possesses a self (sātmaka) and that which is devoid of a self (nirātmaka).
There is nothing else included therein;
for if the possession of breath and so forth were an inherent property of an entity, it would be excluded from both that which possesses a self and that which is devoid of a self. (98)

Now, in order to state the inconclusive [reason] when there is doubt regarding both [the presence and absence of the probans], he says: "Because of doubt regarding these very two—positive and negative concomitance—it is a cause of uncertainty. (96)
The example is as follows:
"sātmakam" (possessing a self) is the probandum (*sādhya*), meaning that which exists together with a self;
"the body" (*śarīra*) is the subject (*dharmin*).
The inclusion of the term "living" (jīvat) is a qualification of the subject (dharmin).
For when dead, one does not desire the self.
"Prāṇādi" refers to that which has breath (śvāsa) and so forth as its beginning, [including] such biological functions (prāṇidharma) as the opening and closing of the eyes.
That which possesses [the vital breaths] is the living body endowed with breath and so forth; its state is "thatness" (tattva), and from that—this is the reason. // 97 //
This uncommon reason for doubt must be established;
furthermore, the property of the subject (pakṣadharma) functions as a cause for doubt due to two reasons:
namely, the two forms that constitute the objects of doubt.
Because all things are subsumed within those two,
and because there is no certainty that those two pervasive aspects exist even in a single instance;
for there is no doubt regarding those two aspects by which every object is not subsumed.
For if another alternative were possible, the property of the subject (pakṣadharma) would be unable to show the subject as inseparable from one of two properties;
therefore, it would not be a cause of doubt.
A cause of doubt is that which shows the existence of two properties as being non-exclusive [of each other].
However, one who is unable to demonstrate even an indeterminate state regarding two [alternatives] is a cause for non-comprehension;
whereas, by demonstrating a determinate state, one would be either a valid reason or a contradictory reason. Therefore, that by which all things are subsumed—
The cause of doubt regarding these two would exist if there were no certainty of their presence even in one of them; however,

if there is certainty of their presence, then the certainty of their restricted existence in one place would be the cause, whether it be perceived as a reason (*hetu*) or as a manifest object (*udbhūta*).
But when there is no certainty regarding the existence of non-fixed entities, it is a common inconclusive reason (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*);

it would either have a doubtful exclusion from the dissimilar instances (*sandigdhavipakṣavyāvṛttika*), a doubtful positive concomitance (*saṃdigdhānvaya*), or an unestablished negative concomitance (*asiddhavyatireka*).
However, because its occurrence in even one [of the two classes] is not certain, it becomes an uncommon inconclusive reason (*asādhāraṇānaikāntika*).
Therefore, he shows two reasons for the inconclusiveness of the uncommon inconclusive reason: "Because all things are included by way of both occurrence and exclusion with respect to the self. (99)
Nor, moreover, is there a certainty regarding the occurrence of these two in one and the same place.
Because [the subject] is not established as being either endowed with a self or devoid of a self, the means of valid cognition and so forth are unestablished.
Let it rest for now as to whether it exists elsewhere; if it is asked how there can be no third category, he says: "of the self."
"Functioning and exclusion" refers to functioning and exclusion;
functioning is existence,
and exclusion is non-existence.
The exclusion of the self’s modes and the exclusion of the self’s own modes:
by these two, indeed, there is the inclusion of all things.
For instance—that in which the self’s mode exists is possessed of a self (sātmaka).
In that regard, everything else is infinite and devoid of self;
therefore, how could a third category arise?
For thus, the exclusion of the possession of breath and so forth from both the "possessing-self" and the "devoid-of-self" is unestablished. // 99 //
If it is argued: "Even though its exclusion from those two is unestablished, nevertheless, let there be only positive concomitance (anvaya) with them," the author replies: "Nor even...
It is impossible to determine whether the possession of breath and so forth exists in that which possesses a self or in that which lacks a self. // 100 //
And if it is asked why that is so, he says: "By way of having a self.
That is, in the case of an object determined as having a self.

Or, when a thing has been ascertained as being devoid of self (nirātmaka), the possession of breath and so forth is not observed; therefore, how can there be certainty regarding its [continued] existence? // 101 //
To explain this, he says: "Not indeed.
That which exists together with a self is *sātmaka* (possessing a self);
that from which the self has departed is *nirātmaka* (selfless).
Since there is no third category other than those two, what kind [of category] could it be?
It would have to be one wherein this property of an entity, such as "living being" (prāṇa), might reside.
Therefore, because it arises from that [third category], it is a cause of doubt. // 98 //
Why is there no other category?
To this he says: the function of the self is its existence (*sadbhāva*), while exclusion is its non-existence (*abhāva*).
Because of the inclusion— that is, the embracing— of all things by those two;
for that in which there is a self is *sātman* (possessing a self),
while anything else is *nirātmaka* (selfless).
Therefore, the reason for the doubt is that there is no other head [than the one previously mentioned]. // 99 //

Having established the inclusion of all things within these two categories, he states the second point: "Nor is there a determination of existence for [the vital breath, etc. residing in either one of these two—either that which possesses a self or that which lacks a self;
nor does it exist apart from both heaps, because it is a property of real entities."
Therefore, only this much is known: that [the cognition] occurs in relation to these two alone;
the meaning is that there is no certainty regarding its occurrence in a specific instance. // 100 //

To this he says: When a thing is established, certain, and characterized by a specific attribute—either as possessing a self (*sātmaka*) or as being without a self (*anātmaka*)—the reason (*hetu*), such as "possessing breath" (*prāṇādi*), is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because its existence is not restricted to one of the two modes that pervade all things;
for it remains uncertain.
Thus, two reasons have been stated for the inconclusiveness of a unique property (*asādhāraṇadharma*). // 101 //

Therefore, the sense of smell and so forth, as connected to a living body, is not distinct from those two [categories], because it is unestablished by virtue of being excluded from everything both with a self and without a self.
It does not follow there.
104. Because [the reason] is unestablished even with respect to a single self.
Nor can there be a certainty regarding the absence of its positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) with both that which possesses a self and that which lacks a self.
In the conclusion, the property of the subject (pakṣadharma) is indicated.
The analysis of the compound is: "connected with a living body. That which possesses this [connection] is "that which is connected with a living body" (jīvaśarīrasambandhī).
The phrase "pakṣadharma" (property of the subject) is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. By this concluding statement, the absence of negative concomitance (vyatireka) is demonstrated. // 102 //
By this conclusion, the absence of positive concomitance (anvaya) has been demonstrated. // 103 //
And thus, the existence of both positive concomitance (anvaya) and negative concomitance (vyatireka) is unestablished. // 104 //

If it is objected that there must indeed be a certainty of their absence in that case, he replies: "Nor even... Just as the existence of positive and negative concomitance is not certain when [the subject] possesses a nature [of being absent].
In the same way, non-existence is also indeterminate;
this should be stated in exactly the same manner regarding that which is selfless as well. // 105 //
And every property that exists as a characteristic of the subject (pakṣadharma) is either common (sādhāraṇa) or uncommon (asādhāraṇa), and thus becomes inconclusive (anaikāntika).
Therefore, under the guise of a conclusion, he demonstrates its status as a property of the subject with the words "therefore" and so forth.
The meaning is that it is a property of the subject belonging to a living body.
Since there is no certainty of their exclusion even from one of those two, it is therefore not distinct from them.

For regarding the properties of real entities (*vastudharma*), if the existence of one of two modes that pervade all things is ascertained as being restricted to one [locus], it would necessarily exclude the other mode.

It is for this very reason that he says: "Because it is unestablished by virtue of being excluded from everything—both from that which possesses a self (*sātmaka*) and from that which lacks a self (*anātmaka*)."
The vital breath and so forth are indeed excluded from some things, such as a jar;
therefore, it can be determined only to this extent: from how many things—whether possessing a self or lacking a self—is it excluded? However, its exclusion from *all* things cannot be determined.
Therefore, there is no distinction from anything whatsoever. // 102 //
If this is so, let there be a certain positive concomitance (*anvaya*) between those two;

to this he says: "In that case, the vital breath and so forth, which possess positive concomitance, do not concomitantly follow an object that is either with self (*sātmaka*) or without self (*anātmaka*). (103)
Why? He says: "Even in a single self.
This is because [the reason] is unestablished (asiddhi) in a single self, whether that self possesses a nature (sātman) or lacks a nature (anātman).
By virtue of being a property of a real entity (vastudharmatā), it is determined that breath and so forth reside in either one of those two or in both together.
But since it does not exist as either possessing a self or being devoid of a self, how can there be certainty regarding positive concomitance (anvaya)? // 104 //
But surely, for the opponent, there exists nothing that possesses a self (sātmaka);

therefore, for this reason, there is neither positive concomitance (anvaya) nor negative concomitance (vyatireka) in that which possesses a self. Thus, there is a certainty regarding the absence of both anvaya and vyatireka in the case of the sātmaka, but not their presence.
106 Because the ascertainment of the absence of one thing is inseparable from the ascertainment of the presence of the other.

107. Because positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) consist in their mutual exclusion, the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) precisely because there is doubt regarding both positive and negative concomitance.
If it is asked, "Even in the absence of the ascertainment of existence, why should there not be the ascertainment of non-existence? he says in response: "The positive concomitance" (*anvaya*).
It is said that those two exist in the form of mutual exclusion.
If it is asked, "And what follows from that? he says: "One" (*ekā*).

If those two exist in the form of mutual absence, then wherever there is the certainty of the absence of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), there the certainty of the existence of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) necessarily follows; likewise, where there is the certainty of the absence of negative concomitance, the certainty of the existence of positive concomitance necessarily follows.
Thus, where there is the certainty that the presence of the property of possessing breath and so forth is absent, there is the certainty of its non-existence;
and where there is the certainty that its absence is not the case, there is the certainty of its existence.
For, in this way, when either the positive concomitance (anvaya) or the negative concomitance (vyatireka) is present, there is necessarily the certainty of the other's absence.
The certainty of the absence [of breath and so forth] in the other case—the one with a self—would necessarily follow;
therefore, there is likewise no certainty regarding the absence of breath and so forth in both that which possesses a self and that which lacks a self. // 106 //

If it is asked, "Even in the absence of a certainty regarding existence, why should there not be a certainty regarding non-existence?"—to that [it is replied]: "Because of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*)," etc.
For positive concomitance and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) exist in the form of mutual absence.

For instance, where there is an absence of positive concomitance (anvaya), there is the presence of negative concomitance (vyatireka); or where there is an absence of negative concomitance, there is the presence of positive concomitance.
Anticipating the doubt, "Is this not a case of uncertainty? he says: "Nor even... (nāpi).

Nor is there a determination of the absence of the concomitance and non-concomitance of that [reason], such as vital breath and so forth, from an entity possessing a self (*sātmaka*), nor from one devoid of a self (*nirātmaka*).
Furthermore, the ablative case in the words *sātmakāt* and *anātmakāt* should be understood as being used in relation to the term "non-concomitance" (*vyatireka*). // 105 //
How is there no certainty regarding the absence of both positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)?
To this he says: "Of one...

That certainty of the absence of either the positive concomitance or the negative concomitance is invariably concomitant with the certainty of the presence of the other, the second; that is, it is inseparable from the certainty of its presence.

The state of being that is "reality" (tattva); therefore, because the ascertainment of the absence of one is invariably concomitant with the ascertainment of the presence of the other, there is no ascertainment of the absence of both in a single location. // 106 //
But why is the ascertainment of the absence of one thing invariably concomitant with the ascertainment of the presence of the other?
To this he says: "Because positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) consist in the mutual exclusion of one another.
The exclusion of one from the other is its non-existence (*abhāva*).
The state of those two which possess that very nature is their "essence" (tattva);
for that reason,
positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) consist of presence and absence (bhāva-abhāva).

Existence and non-existence are of the nature of mutual exclusion. That which is determined through the exclusion of one thing is established by way of the avoidance of that very thing. And existence is determined through the exclusion of its own-nature (svabhāva).
Therefore, existence is established through the exclusion of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvavyavacchedena*). For non-existence is formless (*nīrūpa*), as it is presented by conceptual construction;
yet, having excluded that formlessness, it possesses form (*rūpa*) endowed with aspects (*sākāra*).
Therefore, because there is no certainty regarding either the probandum or its opposite.

109. Thus, when there is non-establishment or doubt regarding each one of these three characteristics, or regarding any two of them, as the case may be, there are the three fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*): the unestablished (*asiddha*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), and the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Therefore, because there is doubt regarding both positive and negative concomitance, this [reason] is indeed inconclusive (anaikāntika). // 107 //
If it is asked: "Even when there is doubt regarding positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), why should there necessarily be inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatva)?
To this he replies with the words beginning "sādhya" and so forth:
because there is no certainty regarding the possession of breath and so on in either the probandum (sādhya) or its opposite (sādhyavipakṣa).
Therefore, it is inconclusive. // 108 //
"Thus" means in the manner described. "Of the three forms" refers to the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*).
Positive concomitance (anvaya) and negative concomitance (vyatireka);
and [the fallacies arise] when either one or both of these two forms are unestablished or doubtful.
In some cases, the form of one [thing] is not distinguished;
and such being the case, there is a negative concomitance (vyatireka) in the absence of positive concomitance (anvaya).

The absence of negative concomitance (vyatireka) is positive concomitance (anvaya). Therefore, when the absence of positive concomitance is ascertained, negative concomitance becomes ascertained; and when the absence of negative concomitance is ascertained, positive concomitance becomes ascertained.

Therefore, even if that which possesses a self (*sātmaka*) is a non-entity and that which lacks a self (*nirātmaka*) is an entity, there can still be no certainty regarding the absence of the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of breath and so forth with respect to those two;
for it is contradictory for a single entity to simultaneously exist and not exist within another entity, and thus it is impossible to ascertain their absence.
Furthermore, the existence and non-existence of things— whether possessing a self or being selfless— are not determined by the requirements of the opposing argument,
but rather by the requirements of valid cognition;
thus, both remain doubtful.
Consequently, there arises a doubt regarding the existence or non-existence of the possession of breath and other such signs in those two.

Precisely because there is no certainty regarding existence nor certainty regarding non-existence in some cases with respect to positive and negative concomitance, for that very reason there is doubt concerning positive and negative concomitance.
If, however, there were a certain determination of the absence of even one of the two— positive concomitance (anvaya) or negative concomitance (vyatireka)— in any instance whatsoever,
that itself would constitute the certain determination of the presence of the second; thus, there would be no doubt regarding anvaya and vyatireka at all.
And since there is no certainty regarding existence or non-existence anywhere, for that very reason there is doubt concerning positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
And because of this doubt, [the reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). // 107 //
Why is it inconclusive? He says: "sādhyeti" (regarding the probandum).
This refers to the probandum and its opposite, the contradictory.
Therefore, because the positive and negative concomitances are doubtful, there is a lack of certainty;
for when there is doubt regarding the presence or absence [of the reason] in the similar and dissimilar instances, neither the probandum nor its opposite is established.
Furthermore, no category other than those possessing a self and those lacking a self is possible.

Consequently, since the subject—the living body—possesses breath and so forth, there arises a doubt regarding the existence or non-existence of the self; thus, breath and the like are inconclusive (anaikāntika). // 108 //
Having set forth the defects of the reason (*hetu*) in the case of the non-establishment or doubt regarding the three forms (*rūpa*), he concludes by saying:
"The contradictory-varying (*viruddhavyabhicārin*) has also been stated as a cause of doubt;
why is it not mentioned here?"
111 Because [it] is impossible in the domain of inference.
112. For there is no possibility of a contradiction between the effect (*kārya*) and the essential nature (*svabhāva*), as defined above, and non-apprehension (*anupalambha*).
There may be either certainty or doubt regarding two forms in some cases;
"as appropriate" means according to the application.

The three fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) are the unestablished (*asiddha*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), and the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*); such is the analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound. (109)
Non-deviation from the contradictory is "contradictory non-deviation" (*viruddhāvyabhicāra*).
That which possesses this [quality] is "possessing contradictory non-deviation" (*viruddhāvyabhicārī*).
Alternatively, it is called "possessing contradictory non-deviation" because it is both contradictory and has the nature of not deviating.
And that [reason] has been stated by the author of the treatise to be inconclusive;
the meaning is that it has not been pointed out here [by the opponent] himself. // 110 //
If it is asked why that is so, he says: "Because of inference.
For it is thus: its occurrence is impossible in that which functions by the power of real entities (vastu). // 111 //
If it is asked, "How is there no possibility [of this]? he says: "For not...
Indeed, the definition of an effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) is simply the existence of the effect when the cause exists.

And the definition of an essential nature (*svabhāva*) is precisely the state of being a reason that is invariably concomitant with that [nature] alone; this is according to the sequence just mentioned.

Among these, when one form is unestablished (*asiddha*) or doubtful (*sandigdha*), or when two or both are unestablished or doubtful, then they are the fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*): the unestablished, the contradictory (*viruddha*), and the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

"According to the application" (*yathāyogam*) means that whichever fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) is applicable when there is either non-establishment (*asiddhi*) or doubt (*sandeha*) regarding a particular [reason], it is established as such on account of that non-establishment or doubt; thus, "according to the application" refers to whatever is connected with whatever [circumstance].
[Objection: But surely the Teacher has stated that even the "non-erroneous contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārī*) is a cause of doubt?
That which does not deviate from what is established by another reason (*hetvantara*) is called *viruddhāvyabhicārī* (the contradictory non-deviant).

Alternatively, it is called *viruddhāvyabhicārī* because it is both "contradictory" (*viruddha*), insofar as it proves a property opposite to that established by another proof, and "non-deviant" (*avyabhicārī*), insofar as it does not deviate from its own probandum. // 110 //
True, it was stated by the Teacher, but it was not stated by me.
Why? To this he says: "by inference," and so forth.
The object of inference is the three-fold character established by valid cognition;
for that from which the occurrence of inference arises is the object of inference.
Since inference is possible based on the three characteristics established by valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*),
therefore that alone is the object of inference.
When that [triple-characterized mark] is employed, there is no possibility of a non-erroneous contradictory reason (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*).

For when the three-fold nature [of the reason] established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is under discussion, only that which possesses a form established by valid cognition can possibly be a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*).
However, the "non-erroneous contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*) possesses no form established by valid cognition;
therefore, its occurrence is impossible.
Therefore, because it is impossible, it was not mentioned. // 111 //
Why is there no possibility? He says: "For not," because there is no possibility of contradiction.

Regarding the effect (*kārya*) and the essential nature (*svabhāva*), which have been described by their respective definitions: since neither of these deviates from the other, it has been stated that in investigations of the meaning of scripture, the "non-deviating contradiction" (*viruddhāvyabhicārī*) is a defect of the proof (*sādhana*), occurring when one relies on an inference based on scripture that functions through the power of perceiving non-existent things.
The definition of a logical reason (*hetu*) is as follows:
non-perception is the definition of non-apprehension; it is the non-perception of that which has reached the conditions for perceptibility.
Furthermore, a contradictory reason (*viruddha*) cannot occur among those [reasons] characterized by the aforementioned definitions.

For instance, when a tree is established by means of a *śiṃśapā*, there is no possibility of a second [reason] with the aforementioned characteristics that would establish it as a different kind of tree. // 112 //

If it is argued that [the cause] is impossible within these three [categories] possessing the aforementioned characteristics, and that it must therefore exist elsewhere, he says in response: "And not... (na ca).
Among these three types of reasons, there is no other non-deviant reason that is infinite [in its scope], wherein the occurrence of a contradictory non-deviant reason would be possible. // 113 //
If it is asked why [the three types of objects] are impossible [to be determined by inference], he says:
"Therefore" (*tasmāt*).
That in which there is no determination by means of a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that is too restricted is that which functions through the power of seeing an unreal object (*avastu*).

"Relying on inference based on scripture" means that its basis (*āśraya*) is scripture (*āgama*); thus, it is "inference based on scripture. That [inference] in which the locus (*dharmin*), the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), and so forth are established by way of scripture is "inference based on scripture."
Regarding the phrase "in the investigations of their meaning":
the reality (*tattva*) of an effect is its arising from a cause;
and the reality of an essential nature (*svabhāva*) is its being pervaded by the probandum (*sādhya*).
How could that which is an effect and that which is an essential nature exist while abandoning its own cause and its pervasive essential nature, such that it would be contradictory?
And regarding "non-apprehension" as defined above:
the defining characteristic of non-apprehension is the non-apprehension of what is perceptible (*dṛśyānupalambhatva*).
Since this too does not deviate from the absence of the object, there is no possibility of its being contradictory. // 112 //
It might be argued: "Could there be something other than these?
To this he says: "And there is nothing other than these three that is non-deviant; for this very reason, the status of being a logical reason (hetu) belongs only to these. (113)
Where, then, was this fallacy of the reason stated by the teacher Diṅnāga?
He says: "Therefore," etc.

Since this is not possible in inference that proceeds by the force of real entities (*vastubalapravṛtta-anumāna*), therefore the "non-deviant contradiction" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*) is stated with reference to inference based on scripture (*āgamāśrayānumāna*).
For that inference whose three-fold character of the logical mark (*liṅga*) is established by scripture (*āgama*), its basis is scripture.
[Objection: But is not even the three-fold character established by scripture established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?
[Response: To this he says: "it proceeds by the power of perceiving non-existent things."
The perception of a non-entity is mere conceptual construction;
its power is its efficacy.
From that, the three-fold character of inference—which is established by scripture and functions as mere conceptual construction arising from what is not a valid means of knowledge—is determined.
But not from a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). [Objection:
In that case, where is this threefold character established by scripture (*āgama*) intended to apply?
[Response: He says: "tadartha" (for that purpose).
The meaning of that scripture which is beyond the senses and not made an object of perception or inference [is established],
because it is possible for authors of treatises to erroneously attribute a contrary nature to objects due to their own delusion.
For its occurrence is not possible when there is no perception of a self or of effects within things that abide according to their actual state.
117. An example of this is as follows: that which, while situated in all places, is simultaneously related to its own correlates is omnipresent (*sarvagata*), just like space (*ākāśa*).
And the universal (*sāmānya*), while situated in all places, is simultaneously related to its own correlates.

Regarding the investigations into the meaning of the scriptures, it has been stated that the "non-erroneous contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārī*) is a fault of the proof (*sādhana*). This is easy to understand. // 114 //
If it is argued: "If this person is indeed unfit, then how could inference based on scripture (āgamāśrayānumāna) be possible for him as well?
he replies: "The Teacher," and so forth.
Moreover, even though certain matters have not been established by all the authors of treatises, some are stated with a reversal of their true nature;
consequently, there arises the "non-erroneous contradictory" (viruddhāvyabhicārī) [reason]. // 115 //

If it is argued: "If its existence is accepted only through inference based on scripture (*āgama-pratibaddhānumāna*), then why is its operation through the force of real entities (*vastu-bala*) not also accepted?
To this, he says: "Not indeed" (*na hi*).
Those whose mode of existence is exactly as the thing itself exists are "those for whom the thing exists as it is situated" (*yathāvasthitavastusthitayaḥ*).
*Sthiti* means "establishment" (*vyavasthā*).
The analysis of the compound is: "the self (*ātman*), the effect (*kārya*), and non-perception (*anupalambha*)."
"Self" (ātman) is what is called "intrinsic nature" (svabhāva).

Just as there is a formal establishment of things based on their actual existence, so too are those [reasons] established as intrinsic nature, effect, and non-perception; how could there be any possibility of a "non-deviant contradictory" (viruddhāvyabhicārin) among them? // 116 //
"In that regard, 'an illustration' means the presentation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) based on scripture (*āgama*).
This refers to the possibility of an inference based on scripture when investigations concerning something situated in all locations have been undertaken."
"The teacher has stated that the 'non-erroneous contradictory' (viruddhāvyabhicārin) is based upon that. // 114 //

But why is there the possibility of inference even when it relies upon scripture? To this he says: "of the authors of treatises" (*śāstrakārāṇām*), that is, of those who compose treatises (*śāstrakṛtām*).
The "introduction" (*upasaṃhāra*) or presentation of the nature of that which is contrary—that is, opposed to the actual state of things—with respect to objects;
because of the possibility of such [an introduction], there is the possibility of a non-deviating contradictory reason (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*).
[This occurs] "through error" (*bhrāntyā*).
By way of inversion;
for authors of treatises, being under the influence of inversion, superimpose an intrinsic nature upon that which does not exist. // 115 //
If even the authors of the treatises were mistaken, what confidence can there be in other persons as well?
To this he says: "Not indeed."
The status of being a cause is not established through conceptual construction regarding causes, but rather through the actual state of things;
therefore, its occurrence is impossible in those cases where the nature and effects of things, as they actually exist, are not perceived.

That which is established as a real entity in the ultimate sense (*paramārthasadvastu*); those whose determination (*vyavasthā*)—the state of things as they truly are (*yathāvasthitavastusthiti*)—does not transcend that [reality] are "those for whom the state of things is established according to reality" (*yathāvasthitavastusthitayaḥ*).
For they abide exactly as the thing exists, and not through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*).
Therefore, there is no room for error regarding them, by which the occurrence of a "non-deviant contradictory" (viruddhāvyabhicārin) reason might be possible. // 116 //
The nature of being present in that location is necessarily connected solely with the very nature of its relation to that [object].

That which is connected with its own related things is "all-pervading" (*sarvagata*). "Abiding in all places" means abiding in every location. Those very things are "its own relations" because they are related to itself.
Whatever entity is simultaneously connected with its own related things situated in all locations is observed to be omnipresent;
for example, space.
Indeed, space is simultaneously connected with its own related things situated in all locations, and it is accepted as being omnipresent.
By this statement, the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is shown:
even a universal (*sāmānya*) is simultaneously connected with all its own correlates situated in every location;
for the particular individuals that are the correlates of the universal exist in all [places].
And by those [individuals], the universal is simultaneously connected.
By this, the property of the subject (pakṣadharma) has been stated. // 117 //

In order to demonstrate that the formal argument possesses the characteristic of being based on an essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*), he says: "tatsambandhi... [and so forth]. "Of that which is related" means of that which is connected to it.

That which has the habit of following after the mere essential nature of those things related to it is "that which follows after the mere essential nature of the related things" (*tatsambandhisvabhāvamātrānubandhinī*).

The countries belonging to them are "those countries" (taddeśāḥ). One who is present in those countries is "present in those countries" (taddeśasannihitaḥ). That which has a nature present in those countries is "that which has a nature present in those countries" (taddeśasannihitasvabhāvaḥ).
Its state is the nature of being present in that location;
the remainder [of the definition] is "presence in the location related [to it]. (118)

In this regard, the example of the "non-erroneous contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*) is as follows: "That which... and so forth. By restating that a universal (*sāmānya*) is related simultaneously with all its own relata situated in every location—that is, by restating its being related to those situated in all locations—its omnipresence (*sarvagatatva*) is being affirmed.
Therefore, it is stated that being simultaneously connected [with all things] is necessarily concomitant with omnipresence; it is pervaded by that.

Here, the Great Sage Kaṇāda has described the universal (*sāmānya*) as inactive, perceptible, and unitary, and as being simultaneously connected with all its own relata through inherence (*samavāya*).

In this regard, Pailuka, a disciple of Kaṇāda, presented the following means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish that the universal (*sāmānya*) resides both in individual entities (*vyakti*) and in locations devoid of individuals:
"Just as space" (*yathā ākāśam*). This is an example (*dṛṣṭānta*) intended to demonstrate pervasion (*vyāpti*).
For even space, being simultaneously connected with trees and other objects situated in all locations that are in conjunction with it, is omnipresent;
and it is indeed connected with its own correlates situated in all locations. This demonstrates the presence of the reason (hetu) in the subject (pakṣadharmatva). // 117 //
In order to apply the reason of essential identity (*svabhāvahetu*) to this, he says: "related to that" (*tatsambandhī*).
The nature of the universal (*sāmānya*) is related to those substances (*dravya*) situated in all locations; that very [nature] is merely its related essence (*tatsambandhisvabhāvamātra*).
It is "concomitant with that" (*tadanubandhinī*) because it follows after that.
"What is that? he asks, and replies: "The state of having its own nature present in that location. "That location" (*tad-deśa*) refers to the location belonging to those related things.
That which has a nature (*svabhāva*) present (*sannihita*) in that location is "that which has its nature present in that location" (*tad-deśa-sannihita-svabhāva*).

119. For it is not the case that whatever is not present in a certain place pervades that place by its own nature; this is an application of the reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). 120. The second formulation is as follows: whatever meets the conditions for perception and is not perceived does not exist there. For example, a jar that is not being found in a certain location.
Furthermore, a universal that meets the conditions for perception is not perceived in the intervals between individual instances.
This non-perception and the essential nature [of the universal] produce doubt regarding a single locus because they establish mutually contradictory properties.
If it is asked why it is that the related entities are pervaded by way of being omnipresent, he says: "That which.
For how can that which does not exist in a certain place possibly pervade that location?
[The phrase] "that location" refers to this.
That place belongs to it, thus it is "of that place. The remainder [of the meaning] is that in whatever place it does not exist, it is unable to pervade what is connected to that place.
Regarding the formulation of the essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*): this is easy to understand. // 119 //
Now, some followers of Kaṇāda have asserted that generality (*sāmānya*) is omnipresent, while other followers of Kaṇāda have denied its existence;
for [according to them], it is the very nature of those things with which it is related.
By that restriction, [the universal] becomes present in their location;
therefore, because it is connected to them, the presence of the universal in that location follows as a necessary consequence. // 118 //

But surely, the owner is related to the cows, yet he does not have the nature of being present in the region where the cows are; so how can he possess that same location simply by virtue of being related to them?
Thus he says: "For not...

That which does not exist in a certain place—that place belongs to it; thus, "that place" (taddeśa) refers to that which does not pervade it by way of its own nature (*ātmanā*), that is, its essential form (*svarūpeṇa*).
Here, the relationship between the universal and its possessors is characterized as inherence (*samavāya*).
And that [inherence] occurs only between two things occupying the same location.
Therefore, when [a substance] is inherent in something, it places itself within the location of its substratum while embracing that [substratum] with its own form;
for the very act of placing one's own form in that location is what constitutes embracing it.
From that [inherence], there is its inherence [in the substance].
Therefore, that which is inherent therein pervades that substance and, by means of its own nature, becomes present in that location.
This is the meaning: the pervasion of an object situated in a particular place is pervaded by the existence [of the pervader] in that same place.

In the absence of existence in that location, there would be no pervasion of it; consequently, the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), which is characterized by pervasion, would not exist. Yet, such pervasion does exist.
Therefore, "being present in that location" is this essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*). // 119 //
Showing the application of the *paiṭhara* [method], he says: "In the second case as well.
This means that which has attained the status of being a characteristic (*lakṣaṇatā*) or an object (*viṣayatā*) of perception is "visible" (*dṛśya*).
By this, having referred to the non-perception of the visible, the status of being subject to the conventional usage of non-existence—namely, "that is not there"—is established.

Thus, by means of the non-perception of the pervaded object (*vyāpyadṛśyānupalabdhi*), the absence of the pervader—the status of being conventionally treated as non-existent—is demonstrated. "That is not so" (*tadayathā*) refers to the example of a non-existent jar in a certain place. The three-featured logical reason (*trirūpī hetuḥ*) has been explained.
Since the meaning is not understood by that much alone, there is no such thing as a "separate example" (dṛṣṭānta) as a member of a proof (sādhanāvayava).
Therefore, its definition is not stated separately because its purpose is already established.
For [the opponent] has accepted that [the self] is merely omnipresent and dependent upon [the body].
To demonstrate that method, he says: "the second," which is easy to understand. Regarding the phrase "that which is perceived":
Here, the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of non-apprehension is stated:
the intervals between manifestations (*vyakti*) are the "intervals between manifestations" (*vyaktyantarālāni*);
in these, a universal (*sāmānya*) that has reached the conditions for apprehension (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*) is not apprehended.
By this, the property of the subject (pakṣadharma) has been stated;
and by the proponent, the all-pervasiveness of that which resides solely in its substratum has been asserted. // 119 //
By means of non-apprehension through immediate statement (*avyavahitokty-anupalabdhi*), the universal's state of being omnipresent only within its own substratum is established;

whereas previously, by means of the reason of essential nature (*svabhāva-hetu*), its omnipresence everywhere was established. Thus, because these two establish mutually contradictory meanings, [the question arises: is it the case that the non-apprehension of the universal in the intervals between individuals establishes only its omnipresence within its own substratum, [namely] in those things related to it that abide in all locations?
Or, because it is invariably concomitant [with all individuals], there arises a doubt regarding the universal (sāmānya) itself as being "all-pervading" (sarvasarvagata);
thus, by this much, inference for the sake of others (parārthānumāna) has been shown through its essential characteristics. // 120 //
If it is asked, "Why has the definition of an example (*dṛṣṭānta*) not been stated?", he replies to that: "It is threefold" (*trirūpa*).
By those very three characteristics of the reason (*hetu*) which were previously stated, the establishment of the probandum (*sādhyārtha*) occurs.
Therefore, what is called an "example" (dṛṣṭānta) is not a separate member of the proof;
consequently, its definition was not stated separately.
To demonstrate the property of being a characteristic of the subject (pakṣadharmatva), he says: "and it is not perceived."
The space between individuals, another individual, and space devoid of individuals are all visible;
yet, even though it is visible, the universal "cowness" is not perceived in any particular individual, nor in other individuals such as horses, nor in space devoid of individuals.
Therefore, it is understood that it does not exist in those [other individuals or in empty space].
