This non-apprehension and the previously mentioned intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) are two properties contradictory to the opponent's position; because they are established [as reasons], they produce doubt regarding a single subject (*dharmin*).
For a single entity cannot possess mutually contradictory intrinsic natures.
Furthermore, in this case, one [reason] establishes existence in other individual instances, while the other establishes existence in space, which is devoid of individuals.
Furthermore, non-existence is established by another non-perception;
yet it is not logical for one and the same thing to possess both existence and non-existence in the same place, because those two are contradictory.

Thus, regarding the universal established by scripture, these two reasons—its being omnipresent and its not being omnipresent—are a pair of "non-erroneous contradictories" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*) within the class of probanda.

Since it is accepted that a single universal is simultaneously related to those situated in all locations and is also visible, it follows from its being related to everything that it is omnipresent; yet, because it is visible and is not perceived in the intervening spaces, it is not omnipresent.

Therefore, since the author of the treatise himself did not perceive the pervasion by contradictory properties, he stated two properties pervaded by contradictories and thereby provided an opportunity for the "non-deviating contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*);
yet, this [fallacy] has no application to a real entity (*vastu*).
Thus have the fallacious reasons been explained.

Now, since they are members of a proof (*sādhanāvayava*), reasons (*hetu*) have been stated as such; and in connection with that, the nature of the reason and the non-reason has been described without distinction as "existence only in the similar class (*sapakṣa*)" and "exclusion from the dissimilar class (*asapakṣa*) in its entirety."

Furthermore, specifically regarding the effect (*kārya*) and the essential nature (*svabhāva*), whose characteristics have been stated, it has been declared that their arising and their necessary connection (*tanmātrānubandha*) must be demonstrated.
And demonstrating that: "Wherever there is smoke, there is fire;
where fire is absent, there is never smoke."
As in the case of the kitchen and other [places]:

"Where there is producedness, there is impermanence," because the meaning has already been conveyed; for the meaning of the example is understood through the very meaning of the reason (*hetu*). // 121 //

If one asks "How so?", he says: "Of the reason" (*hetor iti*). This alone is the definition of a reason regarding its mere formal application (*prayoga*): namely, existence only in the similar class (*sapakṣa*), and likewise, exclusion from the entire dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*).

Furthermore, regarding the specific definition of the reason (*hetu*): it has been stated that for the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*), its production (*janma*) must be demonstrated; for the essential-nature reason (*svabhāvahetu*), its necessary concomitance with that alone (*tanmātrānubandha*) must be explained.
The remainder of the sense is that one should demonstrate both the general definition (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) and the specific definition (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*).
For the effect-reason (kāryahetu), its own moment— both its specific characteristic (viśeṣalakṣaṇa) and its general characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa)— is suitable.
And by "showing" in this way, the meaning is "by stating through its specific [features]."

For instance: since the existence [of the reason] in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) was demonstrated here, examples (*dṛṣṭānta*) ought to have been stated as part of the proof (*sādhanāvayava*); and by extension, the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) should also have been mentioned. Why then were they not stated? To this he says: "The reason (*hetu*) has been stated as possessing three characteristics (*trirūpa*)."
What, then, is the purpose of the examples?
It might be argued: "Does the comprehension of the meaning not occur by that much alone?
To this he says: "And by that much," etc.
The cognition of the probandum arises by means of the reason precisely as it has been defined;
therefore, that [reason] alone is the indicator, and consequently, its verbal expression alone is the indicator.

The example (dṛṣṭānta) is not indeed a constituent part (avayava) of the proof (sādhana). Since it is not a constituent part, its definition is not stated separately from the definition of the reason (hetu).
If it is asked, "How then is the pervasion (vyāpti) of the reason ascertained,
if the reason is without an example?"— it is not said that the reason is indeed without an example.
Moreover, there is no such thing as an example separate from the reason;
the example is indeed included within the reason.
For this very reason it was said: "Its definition is not stated separately."
But it was not stated thus: "its definition is not being stated.
If that is so, should the definition of that which possesses the cause (*hetu*) also be stated?
He says: because its meaning is already understood (*gatārthatvāt*).
"Artha" means purpose or the subject matter; that whose [purpose or subject matter] is such is "tathā.
The state of being that is "tattva"; from that [reason].
For the definition of an example (dṛṣṭānta) is stated so that there may be a clear understanding of the example;
and since the example is already established by the very definition of the reason (hetu),
therefore the purpose of the definition of the example is simply the comprehension of the example itself.
That has been traversed, meaning it is accomplished; or, the subject matter called the "example" has been traversed, meaning it is known. // 121 //
How is the meaning already established?
To this he says: "The form of the reason has been stated without distinction," that is, in a general sense.
The meaning is that this characteristic is called "non-apprehension of the nature" (svabhāvānupalambha), which is a common [type of] evidence (sādhāraṇa).
What, then, is it?
It is the impossibility of being produced (kṛtakatva) in the absence of impermanence (anityatva).
This should be illustrated by the example of the jar and space;
for otherwise, the presence and absence of the reason in the similar and dissimilar instances could not be demonstrated in the manner described.
The necessity of being its effect is the defining characteristic of the "effect" (kārya) logical mark.

Furthermore, in the case of a reason that is an essential nature (*svabhāva-liṅga*), it must necessarily be stated by way of its own essential nature, such as "like a kitchen. Otherwise, it would be impossible to state its presence in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*).
In the same way, even when stating an exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), one must necessarily state the positive referent, such as "water";
otherwise, the exclusion itself would not have been stated.
By this, it is shown how the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) and the specific characteristic (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*) of the essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*) ought to be expressed.
In this context, if it were not stated as "just as a jar," then it would be impossible to express its presence in the similar class (*sapakṣa*).
If it were not stated as "just as space," then it would also be impossible to express its exclusion [from the dissimilar class].
Even the concomitance with that alone cannot be demonstrated in that same way;
for instance, if it were pointed out that "wherever there is the state of being produced, there necessarily is non-eternality, as in the case of a jar," [the following would apply].
In that case, it is said to be merely a connection with that alone:
existence only in the similar class (sapakṣa) and exclusion from all dissimilar classes (vipakṣa); these two forms are stated here without distinction.
Furthermore, even though the universal has been mentioned, it cannot be known;
therefore, that very [universal] must be stated as residing in its particulars.
Consequently, once again, the two possessors of the particular—namely, birth and its corresponding subtle element—must be shown and stated by means of their specific characteristics.
It has been stated that the birth of the effect must be known;
for when the birth of the effect is known, its presence only in the similar class (sapakṣa) and its exclusion from every dissimilar class (vipakṣa) become known.
The necessary concomitance (*anubandha*) of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) with that alone has been stated as what is to be shown.
"That" refers to the means of proof (*sādhana*);
"that alone" (*tanmātra*) means the means of proof alone.
Its "concomitance" (anubandha) is its following after;
that is, the existence of the probandum when there is the mere existence of the means of proof.
For it is precisely this state of existing only when that [means] exists which constitutes the identity (tādātmya) of the probandum with it.

When the nature of the probans (*sādhana*) is known, then for the reason based on essential identity (*svabhāvahetu*), its presence only in the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and its exclusion from the entire dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*) become known.
Thus, the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) must be understood as consisting of these specific features, and not otherwise.
Then the specific characteristic was stated. [The opponent asks: "What follows from this, even if it is so?
To this he says: "And that... (tacceti).
The connection is as follows: by one who wishes to show that general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), it must be shown precisely by means of showing the specific characteristic (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*).
"Where there is smoke, there is fire"—thus is the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) demonstrated.
And pervasion (vyāpti) is ascertained through the means of valid cognition that establishes the relationship of cause and effect.

Therefore, just as [the presence of fire] is shown by the example "in the kitchen," the negative concomitance (vyatireka)— that smoke does not exist at all in the absence of fire— is thereby demonstrated.
And that [absence] should be shown as it is in the other case;
for the cessation of fire is necessarily concomitant with the cessation of smoke,
and that [concomitance] should be shown as existing in the kitchen and elsewhere.
Pervasion [is established]. And when this meaning has been demonstrated, the example follows, because its nature consists of nothing more than that.

If, while demonstrating the presence in similar instances (*sapakṣatva*), one does not state "just as in a kitchen" or "just as in a jar," then the existence [of the reason] in similar instances would not have been stated at all.
And if, while demonstrating its absence in dissimilar instances (*vipakṣāsattva*), one does not state "just as in water" or "just as in space," [the same would follow].
In that case, exclusion itself would not have been stated.
Having thus stated the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), its impossibility was mentioned.
Immediately after stating the impossibility by means of the specific characteristic (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*), he says: "being its effect," and so forth.
Its effect is *tatkārya*;
the state of being that is *tatkāryatā*; the necessity of that is *tatkāryatāniyama*.
The rule that "when the cause exists, the effect must also exist" is precisely what constitutes the necessity of being its effect (*tatkāryatāniyama*).

Pervasion by way of essential nature (*svarūpeṇa vyāpti*) is simply pervasion by way of intrinsic identity (*svabhāvena vyāpti*); the remainder [of the definition] is "the necessary connection with that alone" (*tanmātrānubandha*).
Neither of these two can be stated without providing an example.
When, according to the aforementioned reasoning, a reason is stated with respect to some subject in terms of both its general and specific characteristics,
then the example has already been stated as well.
If it is asked why that is so, he says: "To this extent," and so forth;
[it means] wherever there is the state of being produced (*kṛtakatva*), there [is impermanence].

"Permanence" thus demonstrates the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*). "In the absence of impermanence, producedness does not exist" demonstrates the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). Furthermore, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes this pervasion must be shown in the example based on similarity (*sādharmyadṛṣṭānta*).
Furthermore, for a reason whose pervasion is well-established, its necessary absence in the absence of the probandum must be demonstrated;
therefore, it must necessarily be shown both in the case of a jar and in the case of space.

Why is this so? He says: "Because it is not otherwise. For, in the case where the presence and absence of [the reason] in the similar and dissimilar instances (sapakṣa and vipakṣa) are restricted in the manner described—that is, its existence only in the similar instances (sapakṣa)—[it constitutes a valid reason].
The restriction that the absence of the counter-positive (*vipakṣa*) is precisely as previously described cannot be demonstrated;
for it is only when the specific characteristic has been shown that existence and non-existence in the manner previously described are demonstrated.
And it is not possible to demonstrate the specific characteristic otherwise. Of that probandum, smoke is the effect;
its existence is "being-an-effect-of-that" (tatkāryatā).
That very restriction is what constitutes its being an effect, such that smoke is restricted to fire;
this restriction of being an effect cannot be demonstrated otherwise than as having the nature of a specific characteristic (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*).

Furthermore, for a reason based on essential identity (*svabhāva-liṅga*), the pervasion by the probandum which is an essential identity cannot be demonstrated [otherwise] than as having the nature of a specific characteristic.

Since both the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) and identity (*tādātmya*) must be known in the kitchen and in the pot respectively, therefore, one who demonstrates the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for establishing pervasion (*vyāpti*) should show an example based on similarity (*sādharmyadṛṣṭānta*). However, an example based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmyadṛṣṭānta*) is for the purpose of understanding the absence of the effect when the cause is absent, once that [causal] nature is well-established;
for that very reason, it need not necessarily be a real entity.
In the absence of a cause, there is an absence of the effect, whether the [subject] be a real entity or a non-entity;
therefore, this constitutes the dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) regarding both entities and non-entities.
By this very [principle], the faults of the example (*dṛṣṭānta-doṣa*) are also refuted.
124. For example: "Sound is eternal because it is incorporeal, like action, like an atom, or like a pot.
These are fallacious examples (dṛṣṭāntābhāsa), being deficient in the property to be proven (sādhya), the proving property (sādhana), or both.
For its nature is as follows:
that in which the concomitance of the reason with the probandum is observed is the example based on similarity (sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta).
And where the absence of the reason is pointed out in the case of the absence of the probandum, that is the example by dissimilarity (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta). // 122 //

Since a demonstration of the general and specific characteristics of a reason is called a "faultless example" (*nirduṣṭadṛṣṭānta*), it follows that where such a demonstration of those two characteristics is not possible, it is said to be a "pseudo-example" (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*). // 123 //

He states the examples, beginning with "as follows": [the fallacies] are those deficient in the property to be proven (*sādhya*), the proving property (*sādhana*), or both. For example: "Sound is eternal..."
"Because of being formless, like karma"—this lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma-vikala*).
"Like an atom"—this lacks the proving property (*sādhanadharma-vikala*). "Like a jar"—this lacks both. // 124 //
An example (dṛṣṭānta) is required.
Therefore, without an example, it is impossible to demonstrate the positive concomitance (anvaya) or negative concomitance (vyatireka) of a reason (hetu).

Consequently, the example based on similarity (sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta) is that which demonstrates the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that establishes the pervasion (vyāpti) of the reason, precisely by explaining the nature of that reason.

It is also shown that a dissimilar example (*vaidharmyadṛṣṭānta*) is to be employed by demonstrating the absence of the reason (*hetu*) in the absence of the probandum (*sādhya*) for one whose pervasion (*vyāpti*) is already established.
And it is only when this meaning has been demonstrated that there is an example.

He says that the example is demonstrated when this meaning is demonstrated—that is, the demonstration of some means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes pervasion, and the demonstration of its exclusion.
The nature (*tattva*) of that which has this much alone as its form is "thatness" (*tattvam*); [the word] "therefore" (*tasmāt*) refers to that.
For such is indeed the form of the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
Namely, the function of the similar instance (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) is to demonstrate the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes pervasion (*vyāpti*);

and the function of the dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*)—which possesses a well-known pervasion—is to demonstrate the cessation of the probans (*sādhana*) upon the cessation of the probandum (*sādhya*).
Since this is already explained by the very statement of the reason (*hetu*), what is the use of a separate definition of the instance? // 122 //

By this very demonstration of the nature of an example through the explanation of the form of the reason, the faults of examples (*dṛṣṭāntadoṣa*) and pseudo-examples (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*) are thereby stated.

For it is as follows: by implication, it is said that an example which, even when adduced for the sake of establishing what has been previously stated, is not capable of accomplishing its own function, is a "fault of the example. He provides examples of pseudo-examples: "For instance, sound is eternal."
When the permanence of sound is to be proven, "because it is formless" is the reason;
by way of similarity, [it is like] action, or like an atom.
"Like a jar"— these examples have been set forth;
and these are defects of the example, as well as [defects] of the probandum and the probans.
125. Likewise, there are cases where the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) and so forth are doubtful.

For example: "This person possesses lust and other passions because he speaks, like a man on the street"; or, "This person is subject to death because he possesses lust and other passions, like a man on the street."
"This person is not omniscient because he possesses passion and other defects, like a man in the street.
(126) Likewise, there is the non-concomitant (*ananvaya*) and that in which the concomitance is not demonstrated (*apradarśitānvaya*).
For example: "The speaker possesses passion and so forth, like a person who is desired [to be such]" and "Sound is impermanent because it is produced, like a jar.
The analysis of the compound is: "that in which the property to be proven (sādhyadharma) is doubtful."
Those for whom the property to be proven (sādhyadharma) is the first [member] are described as such.
He states the examples: "one who possesses passion and so forth.
This is an instance where the property to be proven is doubtful.
"Subject to death" is a property whose proof is doubtful;
"one who is not omniscient" is [another such case].
This is the case where both properties are doubtful. // 125 //
"Ananvaya" means where there is no positive concomitance at all; "apradarśitānvaya" means where the positive concomitance has not been demonstrated.
Where the positive concomitance (*anvaya*), though existing, is not demonstrated—
[the author] states an example with the words "for instance" (*yathā*).
In that case, there is no positive concomitance.
Therefore, in that case, there exists neither a relationship of pervader and pervaded nor a relationship of cause and effect between speech and passion and so forth.
As for the term "impermanent," although a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) exists here, it has not been demonstrated. (126)
And "both" refers to those [examples] which are deficient in both [aspects]:
1) action is deficient in the probandum (*sādhya*) because it is not constant;
2) the atom (*paramāṇu*) is deficient in the probans (*sādhana*).
Because atoms possess corporeality (*mūrtatva*). Corporeality is the dimension of a substance that is not omnipresent;
and atoms are both non-omnipresent and of the nature of substances.
The Vaiśeṣikas, however, maintain that [atoms] are eternal;
therefore, [the reason] is not devoid of the property to be proven (sādhyavikala). But the jar is devoid of both.
Because of its impermanence and because of its corporeality, [the pot is non-eternal]. // 124 //
Likewise, that in which the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is doubtful is "one whose property to be proven is doubtful" (*sandigdhasādhyadharma*).
Those for whom this is the first [characteristic] are described as such:
those whose property to be proven is doubtful.
One whose probans-property is doubtful, or one who is fearful of doubt;
for example: "he possesses passion and so forth."
The property to be proven (*sādhya*) is "possessing passion and so forth.
"Because of speech" is the logical reason (*hetu*).
In the example, "like a man on the street," the possession of passion and so forth is itself doubtful.

"One whose nature is death" (maraṇadharman) means one for whom death is a property; the state of being such is "the nature of being subject to death" (maraṇadharmatva), which is the probandum (sādhya).
"This person" is the subject (dharmin).
The reason (*hetu*) is "because of possessing passion and so forth.
Both of these—non-omniscience and the possession of passion and so forth—are doubtful (*sandigdha*) in the example of the man in the street. // 125 //

Likewise, "without positive concomitance" (ananvaya) refers to that example in which only the non-existence of both the probandum and the probans is observed, but the reason is not seen to be pervaded by the probandum. Such an example is one lacking positive concomitance.
And that example in which the positive concomitance (*anvaya*), though present, has not been demonstrated by the speaker is one where the positive concomitance is not shown (*apradarśitānvaya*).
He illustrates the lack of positive concomitance (*ananvaya*) with the words "for example" (*yathā*).
Regarding the phrase "he who speaks":

having restated the property of being a speaker (*vaktṛtva*), the possession of passion and so forth (*rāgādimattva*) is predicated. Consequently, there is a necessary concomitance (*pratiniyama*) between being a speaker and possessing passion and so forth.
127. Likewise, there is the inverted positive concomitance (*viparītānvaya*): "Whatever is impermanent is produced."

Regarding the term "contrary" (*viparīta*): the analysis of the compound is "that example in which the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is reversed. He states the illustration: "whatever is impermanent... and so forth.

In this case, to state that "whatever is produced is impermanent" regarding the category of motion (iryāpatha), while asserting that "whatever is impermanent is produced," is a contradictory statement. 127.
By this, pervasion (*vyāpti*) has been stated:
"as in the case of a person desired [by both parties].
By the inclusion of the word "desired," both the opponent (*prativādin*) and the proponent (*vādin*) are encompassed.
Therefore, while the mere existence of the properties of being a speaker and possessing passion and so forth is established in the person [who is the subject],
their pervasion [by omniscience] is not established.
Consequently, the example lacks positive concomitance (ananvaya).
"Sound is impermanent. Here, impermanence is the probandum (sādhya);
"because it is produced" is the reason (hetu).
In the example "like a pot," the positive concomitance (anvaya) is not demonstrated;
for although here sound is similar to a pot by virtue of being produced,
it cannot nevertheless be understood as being similar [to it] by virtue of impermanence as well.
Because it would lead to an over-extension [of the principle].

However, if the nature of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) is understood as being impermanent (*anityasvabhāva*), then in that case, the cognition of impermanence would arise from the state of being produced.

Therefore, having stated that "whatever is produced is impermanent"—thereby establishing that the property of being produced (kṛtakatva) is necessarily concomitant with impermanence (anityatva)—one must employ an example as the object for understanding the meaning of the positive concomitance (anvaya) sentence in order to prove that necessity.
And that [example] must be one in which the positive concomitance has already been demonstrated.
However, by this [proponent], an example was presented without even stating the positive concomitance sentence.
And such [an example] is useful only by way of mere similarity (*sādharmya*);

yet, since the probandum (*sādhya*) is not established from similarity alone, the example is intended for the purpose of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), and that purpose has not been fulfilled by this one.
Furthermore, the purpose of similarity has been introduced but is useless; thus, due to a defect in the speaker, this constitutes a defect of the example.
For in this case, the speaker must be established as the other party to be refuted;
therefore, even if the subject matter itself is not faulty, it is nonetheless considered faulty because the speaker has presented it in a faulty manner. // 126 //
Likewise, that example in which the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is reversed is described as such.
He illustrates this very point: "Whatever is impermanent, that is produced.
In the example, it must be shown that the state of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) is invariably concomitant with impermanence (*anityatva*).
In this way, there would be the comprehension of impermanence from the state of being produced.
However, here it is shown that impermanence is necessarily concomitant with the state of being produced,
whereas the state of being produced is not necessarily concomitant with impermanence.
Therefore, since the kind of "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) shown here as being non-necessary for impermanence does not exist [in the subject], there is no cognition of impermanence [from it].
For instance, by restating impermanence with the words "that which is impermanent," producedness is then predicated [of it] with the words "it is produced."
Therefore, impermanence is necessarily stated [as the reason] for being produced,
but being produced is not [necessarily stated] for impermanence.

Consequently, just as from impermanence— which is not restricted [to that specific effect]— there is no cognition of "being immediately subsequent to effort," [so too there is no such cognition from the other].
In the same way, the cognition of impermanence would not arise from the state of being produced (*kṛtakatva*),
because the state of being produced is not invariably concomitant with impermanence.
Even though, according to the actual nature of things, the state of being produced is necessarily concomitant with impermanence, [it would still fail to produce the cognition].
Nevertheless, an indefinite [reason] has been shown as a fallacy;
thus, even though it is not defective in itself, it is seen as such due to the fault of the speaker.
Therefore, even a case of inverted concomitance (viparītānvaya) is considered a fallacy because of the error of the [speaker].
It does not [apply] to the object itself; furthermore, in the case of inference for the sake of others (parārthānumāna), the fault of the speaker is also taken into consideration. // 127 //
128. Faults of the example by way of similarity (*sādharmya*).
129. Also by way of dissimilarity (vaidharmya): "like an atom," "like karma," and "like space"—these are [examples] where the probandum and so forth lack negative concomitance (avyatirekin).

130. Likewise, there are those where the exclusion of the probandum (sādhyavyatireka) and so forth are doubtful, such as: "Kapila and others are not omniscient or are non-authoritative, because they do not possess a teaching that is a superior means of valid cognition (pramāṇātiśaya) serving as a mark for the existence of omniscience and authoritativeness.
All these are fallacious examples based on similarity (sādharmya-dṛṣṭāntābhāsa). 128.
The fallacies of the example based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*) are now stated.
Those things for which the "probandum" (*sādhya*) and so forth are the beginning are called "those having the probandum as their beginning" (*sādhyādi*);
the non-exclusion (*avyatireka*) of these is "non-exclusion of the probandum and so forth."
And those [entities] where they exist are non-different from the probandum and so forth;
whereas there [in the case of atoms], as with atoms themselves, it is non-different from the probandum.
Because atoms are eternal, they are non-different from the probandum and so forth.
"Like action" (*karmavat*) is an example where there is no exclusion from the probans (*sādhanāvyatirekī*); because actions lack material form (*amūrtatva*), they are not excluded from the probans.
"Like space" (*ākāśavat*) is an example where there is no exclusion from either [the probandum or the probans] (*ubhayāvyatirekī*).
And space is non-different from both. // 129 //
Regarding the term *sandigdha*: the analysis of the compound is "that in which the absence (*vyatireka*) of the probandum (*sādhya*) is doubtful.
Alternatively, the analysis is "those for which the absence of the probandum is doubtful is the first [member]."
He states the examples with the words "yathā" (for example).
Two types of propositions (*pratijñā*) have been introduced.
Nine fallacies of the corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta-doṣa*) based on similarity (*sādharmya*) have been explained. // 128 //
He says "also by way of dissimilarity" (*vaidharmyeṇāpi*) in order to state the faults of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

When the eternality of sound is to be proven and the reason (*hetu*) is its formlessness (*amūrtatva*), the example of atoms (*paramāṇu*)—which is dissimilar to it—is not distinct from the probandum (*sādhyāvyatirekī*), because atoms are eternal. [The example of] action (*karman*) is not distinct from the means of proof (*sādhanāvyatirekī*), because action is formless.
Space is non-distinct from both [the probandum and the probans], because it is eternal and because it is unconditioned.
Those things of which the "probandum" (sādhya) is the first are the "probandum and so forth" (sādhyādi), namely: the probandum, the probans, and both.

The non-deviation of those [reasons] is the absence of exclusion [from the locus of the probandum]. Those which possess this are the "non-deviating" reasons, such as the probandum itself; these are what have been cited as examples. // 129 //
To provide another example, he says: "In the same way.
The absence of the probandum is the "absence of the probandum" (*sādhyavyatireka*).
That in which the absence of the probandum is doubtful is "that in which the absence of the probandum is doubtful" (*sandigdhasādhyavyatireka*).
Those things of which that is the first are so described.
He says "as follows" (yathā) in order to provide an example where the exclusion of the probandum (*sādhyavyatireka*) is doubtful:
"they are not omniscient" is one probandum.
The second [member] is: "those who have not attained [the goal] are those whose defects are not exhausted.
Here, "Kapila and others" is the subject (*dharmin*);
"the state of not possessing omniscience," and so forth, is the reason (*hetu*).

And their reliability (*āptatā*) consists in a preeminent means of valid cognition (*pramāṇātiśaya*) which serves as a mark (*liṅga*). That teaching in which such a preeminent means of valid cognition—characterized by being a mark and a specific excellence of valid cognition that is not found elsewhere, and which serves as the mark for their omniscience and reliability—is present is described as such;
they are those who possess such a teaching, and the state of being so is "thatness" (*tattva*).
Therefore, what is intended here by "preeminent means of valid cognition" is the instruction on the science of astrology (*jyotirjñāna*).
"If, however, [it is] 'Āditi'":
here is the example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*): whoever is omniscient or authoritative has taught such things as the science of astrology;
for example, Ṛṣabha, Vardhamāna, and others.
In that case, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) regarding the two properties to be proven—non-omniscience and non-authoritativeness—is doubtful.

An example of a doubtful negative concomitance of the probans (*sandigdhasādhanavyatireka*) is as follows: "No person intended by [the opponent] has speech that must be accepted by a Brahmin learned in the three Vedas (*trayīvid*), because he possesses passion and other such defects.
Herein is the statement of the dissimilar instance (*vaidharmyodāharaṇa*).
Omniscience (*sarvajñatva*) and freedom from passion (*vītarāgatva*), as well as omniscience and freedom from passion—

those [teachers] in whom the teaching of an extraordinary means of valid cognition (*pramāṇātiśayaśāsana*), which serves as the mark (*liṅga*) for those two, is not found, are "those in whom the teaching of an extraordinary means of valid cognition serving as the mark for omniscience and freedom from passion is not found" (*avidyamānasarvajñatvavītarāgatvaliṅgabhūtapramāṇātiśayaśāsanāḥ*);
the state of being such is their "nature" (*tattvam*).

Therefore, because his teaching possesses a preeminent means of valid cognition (*pramāṇātiśaya*) that serves as the mark (*liṅga*) for the non-existence of [others'] omniscience and freedom from passion (*vītarāgatva*), he is "examined"—this is the connection with what follows. "Knowledge of the luminaries" (*jyotirjñāna*) refers to the examination of the constellations (*nakṣatra*); this is the reason (*hetu*).
And that omniscience, which serves as the mark of freedom from passion, was taught by Ṛṣabha, Vardhamāna, and others;
therefore, it is possible to determine that they were omniscient or free from passion.
In this context, the dissimilar instance (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta) of Ṛṣabha, Mahāvīra, and so forth has been stated.
And regarding those [reasons], there is no certainty of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of non-omniscience and non-detachment from passion. // 130 //
"Sandigdha" and so forth; its meaning has already been explained. The example is "yathā" (as follows).
For if Kapila and others were omniscient or authoritative, why did they not teach [knowledge of] astrology and so forth?
Yet they did not teach them.
Therefore, [the Buddha] is neither omniscient nor authoritative with respect to this means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Here is the example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*): whoever is omniscient or authoritative has taught such things as astrology, which serve as the marks of omniscience and authoritativeness.
For example, the teacher of the Digambaras, such as Ṛṣabha and Vardhamāna, is both omniscient and authoritative (*āpta*).
In this case, the negative example (*vaidharmyodāharaṇa*)—namely, the exclusion (*vyatireka*) or absence of non-omniscience and lack of authority in the case of Ṛṣabha and others—is doubtful.
This is because [they] might still teach knowledge of the stars (*jyotirjñāna*).
And [the person] might be non-omniscient or unreliable;
what contradiction is there in this? This knowledge is merely instrumental and fallible; it cannot lead to the inference of omniscience. // 130 //
That in which the exclusion of the probans (*sādhanavyatireka*) is doubtful is so described;
he illustrates it with the words "for example" (*yathā*).
The *Ṛg*, *Sāman*, and *Yajus* [Vedas] are three; that is, the *trayī*.
"One who knows that [Veda] is a *trayīvit* (knower of the three Vedas). By this, it is established that the speech of one whose words are not to be accepted is intended."
Kapila and others are the subject (*dharmin*).
"Because of the existence of passion and so forth" is the reason (*hetu*).

Regarding this means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyodāharaṇa*) is as follows: that in which the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) is shown to be pervaded by the absence of the probans (*sādhanābhāva*) is the example by way of dissimilarity.

Those whose words are to be accepted are "those of acceptable speech. Without first stating the exclusion of the probandum—that they do not possess passion and so forth—the absence of the probans is established.
For example: those whose words are acceptable do not possess passion and so forth, just as Gautama and others, the authors of the Dharmaśāstras.
The exclusion of the probans-property—namely, the possession of passion and so forth—from Gautama and others is doubtful.
132. An example of doubtful exclusion from both [the subject and the similar class] is as follows: "Kapila and others are not free from passion, because they possess the grasping of possessions.
Here, the example by way of dissimilarity (vaidharmya) is: "In one who is free from passion, there is no grasping of possessions."
Regarding the phrase "as in the case of Ṛṣabha and others":

in the case of Ṛṣabha and others, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) between the property to be proven (*sādhya*)—the state of not being a hero—and the proving property (*sādhana*)—the possession or non-possession of a wife—is doubtful.
[This applies to] the *Ṛgveda*, the *Yajurveda*,...
The Sāmaveda—these are the three Vedas;
they alone are designated by the term *trayī*.
One who knows the *trayī* is called a *trayīvit*.
"One whose words are to be accepted" (grāhyavacanaḥ) means one whose speech is to be accepted; the remainder of the sense is "one whose words are authoritative.
By this, the following is stated: there is no word of a person favored by that Brahmin who knows the Three Vedas (trayīvit) that is not eternally authoritative.
Regarding this:
the meaning of that has already been explained.
For those whose words are to be accepted are not possessed of passion and the like.
Regarding the phrase "namely" (*tadyathā*):
Gautama, those treatises on Dharma (*dharmaśāstra*) composed by sages such as Vyāsa are indeed authoritative statements for those who know the three Vedas (*trayīvid*).
For from them, there is no certainty regarding the absence of passion and other defects. (131)
The compound *sandigdha-ubhayavyatireka* means that in which the exclusion (*vyatireka*) of both [the probans and the probandum] is doubtful.
An example is as follows:
*praigraha* = the appropriation of a substance.
*Āgraha* is attachment following acceptance;
*parigraha* and *āgraha* together constitute *parigrahāgraha*.
The meaning is "union with those two."
Those whose beginning is thus [stated] are so described; Manu and others are the authors of the *dharmaśāstras*, which are the *smṛtis*.

For the authors of the *dharmaśāstras* are those whose words are to be accepted by a Brahmin learned in the three Vedas (*trayīvit*), and they are free from passion (*vītarāga*). Here, "those who possess dharma" (*dharmī*) refers to Gautama and others as the locus of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka-viṣaya*).
Thus, the exclusion of the probans—namely, the possession of passion and so forth—from Gautama and others is doubtful.
Although they are authorities on what is to be accepted as they are knowers of the Three Vedas, there remains the doubt: are they still possessed of passion, or are they free from passion? // 131 //
That in which the exclusion (vyatireka) of both [reason and probandum] is doubtful is described as such.
He provides an example of this with the words "tathā" (thus) and "avītarāgāḥ" (those who have not abandoned passion).
The state of possessing passion and so forth is the probandum (*sādhya*). "Akapila and others" is the subject (*dharmin*).
"Acceptance" (*parigraha*) is the first [reason], meaning the taking possession of what is being obtained.
The greed and envy that follow after acceptance is "clinging" (*āgraha*) and "possessiveness" (*parigraha*).

Because of their connection with these two, Kapila and others accept what is being obtained and do not relinquish what has been accepted; thus they are understood to possess passion and other such defilements.
In this proof, the example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) must show that where there is an absence of possessiveness, there is an absence of the probandum.
Regarding the phrase "one who is free from passion":
by restating the absence of the probandum—that for such a person there is neither grasping nor non-grasping—the absence of the probans is established;
"like Ṛṣabha and others" serves as the illustrative example.

From this example of the bull (*ṛṣabha*) and others, the exclusion of the probans—namely, the state of not being free from passion and the connection with grasping or not grasping the thesis—is doubtful.
For there is no negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) regarding the bull and so forth, as in: "This person is not free from passion, because he is a speaker."
The example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyeṇodāharaṇam*): "Where there is no state of being free from passion, one is not a speaker;
for example, a piece of stone.

Although both [properties] are absent from the piece of stone, nevertheless, because the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not established through the pervasion that "everyone who is free from passion is not a speaker," there is a lack of negative concomitance (*avyatireka*).

134. An example where the exclusion [of the reason] from the dissimilar instance is not shown: "Sound is impermanent, because it is produced, like space"—this is by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).
For Ṛṣabha and the others do not accept even the slightest bit of food;
therefore, there is no grasping on their part.
And in the absence of grasping, there is an absence of attachment.
And by that, they are those free from passion (*vītarāga*);
"one not free from passion" means one who possesses passion and so forth.
Furthermore, "appropriation" (*parigraha*) is the act of taking [something] as one's own through the mind.
And grasping is craving;
and since all of these belong to the mental continuum of a sentient being, they do not fall within the range of the sense faculties.
Therefore, it is impossible to determine that there is an exclusion [of the term] from bulls and the like. // 132 //
"Non-exclusion" (*avyatireka*) means that exclusion (*vyatireka*) does not exist in this; such is the analysis of the compound.
"Just as" (*yathā*)... [is used].
The meaning of that has already been explained.
Regarding the term "vaidharmya":
this is an example by way of dissimilarity (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta).

Although a piece of stone, being insentient, possesses neither passion nor the capacity for speech, nevertheless, the pervasion that "everyone who is free from passion is not a speaker" is unestablished.
Since there is no necessary connection between possessing passion and being a speaker, the cessation of speech does not follow from the exclusion of possessing passion.
Therefore, there is no exclusion from the thing itself. // 133 //

"Unshown" means that although a negative concomitance (vyatireka) exists, it is not stated; furthermore, the connection between grasping and non-grasping is doubtful, as is the state of being free from passion (vītarāgatva).
Even if it is true that in their own system they are taught to be free from passion and without possessions, there remains doubt nonetheless. // 132 //
He speaks in order to cite three other [examples] as well: "avyatireka" means that in which there is no *vyatireka* (negative concomitance); thus it is "avyatireka.
Regarding the phrase "one who is not free from passion":
the state of possessing passion and so forth is the property to be proven (*sādhya*).
"Because of being a speaker" is the reason (*hetu*).
Thus, he states the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*): "where there is no state of not being free from passion.
This is a restatement of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*).
In that case, since even the state of being curved does not exist, this is a formulation of the absence of the probans (*sādhanābhāvavidhi*).
By means of that absence of the probans, the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) is stated to be pervaded.
The example is, for instance, a piece of stone.
How is this non-exclusion [established], given that both [properties] are absent from the piece of stone? What follows from this?

Even though both—possessing passion and being free from passion—are excluded from the piece of stone, nevertheless, because that exclusion which is by way of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not established, this is a case of non-exclusion.
What, then, is pervasion (vyāpti)?
To this he says: "Everyone is free from passion.
This is a restatement of the absence of the probandum (sādhyābhāva).
"Not [is] the speaker" is the formulation of the absence of the probans (*sādhana*);
by this, the absence of the probandum (*sādhya*) is shown to be necessarily concomitant with the absence of the probans.
Such is pervasion (*vyāpti*).
By that [reason], the negative concomitance (vyatireka) is not established.
And for this matter, the example is one that is well-known;
it is defective because it does not perform what has been accepted. // 133 //
135. An inverted negative concomitance (*viparītavyatireka*) is as follows: "Whatever is uncreated is eternal. He provides an example: "Sound is impermanent.
By someone [arguing] on the basis of a dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*): "Sound is impermanent because it is created..."
When it is stated, "like space," although the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) exists there, it remains unstated.
For instance, if it were said that whatever things are eternal are all unproduced, [the negative concomitance would still not be explicitly expressed].
In that case, the negative concomitance (vyatireka) is demonstrated, and not merely by means of an example alone. // 134 //
That in which the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not demonstrated is described as such.
"Sound is impermanent":
here, impermanence is the property to be proven (*sādhya*).
"Because it is produced" is the reason (*hetu*);
"like space" is the example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyeṇa dṛṣṭāntaḥ*).
In this inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*), the meaning must be understood from another.
Even if it is pure in itself, if it is declared impure by another, then it is not tenable as it has been so revealed;
nor is it tenable as it is not revealed in that way. And yet, it is a reason that has been revealed.
Therefore, even due to a fault of the speaker, the reason (*hetu*) or the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) might be defective in an inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*).
Furthermore, the realization of the probandum (*sādhyapratipatti*) does not arise from similarity or dissimilarity; rather, it arises from a reason that is invariably concomitant with the probandum.
Therefore, the reason, which is restricted to the probandum, must be stated either by a statement of positive concomitance (anvaya) or by a statement of negative concomitance (vyatireka);
otherwise, the indicator would not have been stated.
That which has been stated in such a manner must be demonstrated as established by means of an example (dṛṣṭānta).

Therefore, an example is that which demonstrates the meaning of the statement regarding positive concomitance (anvaya) and negative concomitance (vyatireka). And here, a statement of negative concomitance has not been employed.

Therefore, in this case, a dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) has been presented as a proof merely by way of dissimilarity; yet it is not a proof in that manner. Since it is a proof by virtue of being the domain of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), and it has not been presented as such, this is a "failure to demonstrate negative concomitance," which is flawed due to the fault of the speaker. // 134 //
That in which the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is inverted is called such [an example of dissimilarity].
He illustrates it with: "For example, that which is unproduced," and so forth.
Here, the reason must be shown as being necessarily restricted to the probandum (*sādhya*) by means of both positive and negative concomitance.

And when the reason must be shown as being necessarily concomitant with the probandum, then in the statement of negative concomitance (vyatireka), the absence of the probandum must be shown as being necessarily concomitant with the absence of the probans;
for in this way, the reason would be shown as being necessarily concomitant with the probandum.

If, however, the absence of the probandum is not stated as being necessarily concomitant with the absence of the probans, then the absence of the probandum might be suspected even when the probans is present;
and in that case, the probans would not be understood as being necessarily concomitant with the probandum.

Therefore, the absence of the probandum must be stated as being necessarily concomitant with the absence of the probandum. And in the case of an inverted negative concomitance, it is said that the absence of the probandum is necessarily concomitant with the absence of the probandum, not that the absence of the probandum is necessarily concomitant with the absence of the probans.
For instance: "that which is uncreated" is the restatement of the absence of the probans;
"it is eternal" is the affirmation of the absence of the probandum.
Therefore, this is the meaning: [the subject] is indeed uncreated and eternal.

And this being so, it has been stated that "uncreatedness" is necessarily present in the absence of the property to be proven (nityatva), but not that "eternality" is necessarily present in the absence of the probans (akṛtakatva).
Therefore, it is not restricted to the probandum;

for by means of these fallacious examples, it is impossible to demonstrate with certainty either the general characteristic of the reason— namely, its presence only in similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and its absolute absence in all dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*)— or its specific characteristic.
Therefore, their refutation should be understood as resulting from that very implication.
137. Refutations are arguments such as "deficiency" (nyūnatā) and so forth.
The analysis of the compound is: "that in which the negative concomitance (vyatireka) is reversed. He states an example with the word "yathā" (as follows):
in this case, while what ought to be stated is "whatever is eternal is unproduced," the opposite of that has been stated. // 135 //
And because those fallacious examples cannot demonstrate either the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) or the specific characteristic (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*) of the reason,
they are therefore called "fallacious examples" (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*).
This is because it is impossible to show both types of characteristics of the reason.
Therefore, their exclusion should be understood through presumptive testimony (arthāpatti).
By this much, right knowledge has been explained along with its essential characteristics. // 136 //
Now, he speaks in order to authorize the statement of its auxiliaries:
"Those which have deficiency (*nyūnatā*) as their first [member] are 'deficiency and so forth' (*nyūnatādi*);
the statement of these is 'the statement of deficiency and so forth' (*nyūnatādyukti*)."
And each of these is a refutation. // 137 //

By the use of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) here, the faults of the unestablished (*asiddha*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), and the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) are included. That by which [faults] are expressed is called "expression" (*ukti*), meaning speech; that speech by which faults are removed is the "refutation" (*dūṣaṇa*).
He states the sentence of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of the reason: "And thus, even a reversed negative concomitance is defective due to the fault of the speaker. (135)
Having cited the defects of examples, he says "For not by these... in order to demonstrate that they are the basis for invalidity.
For examples must be stated in order to demonstrate the necessary concomitance with the probandum (*sādhya*).

And by means of these [defective examples], it is impossible to definitively demonstrate that general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of the reason, which consists in its existence only in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and its absolute non-existence in all dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*).
But surely, the general characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) must be understood as being restricted to specific instances (viśeṣa), and not by itself?
To this he says: "Or [it is] the specific characteristic (viśeṣalakṣaṇa)."
If it were possible to demonstrate the specific characteristic (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*), then there would indeed be a comprehension of the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
However, it is impossible for these [means] to demonstrate the specific characteristic itself.

Therefore, their refutation should be understood through implication (*arthāpatti*) by virtue of their functional capacity (*sāmarthya*). They are employed for the sake of cognizing a means of proof that is restricted to the probandum;
those that are incapable of this are defective.
Incapacity [is established] because of the failure to perform its own function. // 136 //
By this much, endurance has been explained.
He says "dūṣaṇa" in order to state the refutation: what is to be understood as a refutation (*dūṣaṇā*)? It is the non-statement of deficiencies (*nyūnatā*) and so forth.
It is said that *ukti* means "that by which one speaks," namely, speech; it is the utterance of deficiencies and so forth. // 137 //

138. The pointing out of those previously mentioned defects of the proof, such as deficiency (*nyūnatā*) and so forth, constitutes refutation (*dūṣaṇa*), because it obstructs the establishment of the opponent's intended thesis.
139. Fallacious refutations, however, are *jātis*.
140. *Jātyuttaras* are the pointing out of non-existent faults.
If it is asked why that is so, he says there: "by that" (*tena*).
For by that statement, the establishment of the point intended to be proven by the proponent (*pūrvapakṣin*) is obstructed.
Therefore, that is a refutation;
these, then, are the non-manifest refutations. // 138 //
The fallacies of refutation (dūṣaṇābhāsa) are to be understood as being precisely of the same kinds [as the fallacies of proof]. // 139 //
And what, then, are those types? He says: "It has not come into being" (*abhūta*).
That which has not become is "unbecome" (*abhūta*).

Unreal faults are *abhūtadoṣāḥ*; the bringing forth of those is *abhūtadoṣodbhāvanāni*. Those statements by which defects in a proof are brought forth even though they do not exist should be understood as *jātayaḥ* (futile rejoinders). If it is asked: "At the occasion of defining right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), how is there a presentation of refutations (*dūṣaṇa*) and their fallacies (*tadābhāsa*)?"
It is said: in the investigation of those refutations as well as the fallacious refutations, correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) is also investigated along with its auxiliaries.
Thus, since these are indeed the refutations here, their rebuttal must be formulated;
or else, when these are fallacious refutations, [their nature must be determined].
When it is stated that the absence of doubt regarding these [factors] is to be understood, then right knowledge itself is established in every respect;
therefore, the aforementioned undesirable consequence does not apply. // 140 //

In order to explain *dūṣaṇa* (refutation), he says: those [faults] previously mentioned—namely, deficiency (*nyūnatā*) and so forth, as well as the unestablished (*asiddha*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), and the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*)—the statement that brings these to light is *dūṣaṇa*.
Now, one might object: "But deficiency and the others do not prove the opposite [of the thesis]."

How, then, is there refutation? To this he says: by that statement of deficiency and so forth, there is an obstruction to the establishment—that is, the ascertainment—of that very object which is desired by the opponents.

Refutation is not necessarily due to the establishment of the opposite, as in the case of a contradictory [reason]; rather, because it obstructs the opponent's intended certainty, there arises an absence of certainty, which is itself a "reversal of certainty. Thus, the establishment of the opposite certainly exists. // 138 //
The refutations have been stated.
"Fallacious refutations" (dūṣaṇābhāsāḥ):
they are called fallacious refutations because they appear to be like refutations. What are they? They are the "futile rejoinders" (jātayaḥ).

The word *jāti* signifies similarity. *Jātyuttaras* (futile rejoinders) are those that resemble a valid reply (*uttara*). Because a [genuine] reply has not been actually employed, those things resembling a reply are called *jātyuttaras*. // 139 //

To demonstrate that very subsequent similarity (uttarasādṛśya) by virtue of its being employed in the subsequent position, he says: "abhūta... etc. "Abhūtasya" means of a non-existent or unreal fault. "Udbhāvanāni" refers to those things by which [the fault] is brought to light; that is, the statements (vacanāni).
These are "futile rejoinders" (jātyuttara). They are called futile rejoinders because they are responses based on a "jāti," meaning a similarity. // 140 //
Through this very exposition today, I have obtained the vast, unconquerable, and meritorious state of those who know the right path— a state that is eternally immortal.
May the entire lineage of Prāṇi indeed attain the exhaustion of worldly existence through the path appropriate for them and by the instruction of the king.
This commentary, titled *Vistara*, has been composed by Vinītadeva for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of his disciples upon the *Nyāyabindu*.
The third chapter of the *Nyāyabinduvistaraṭīkā*, titled *Śiṣyahitā*, is completed.
One thousand and thirty verses have been stated here in this detailed commentary (*vistaraṭīkā*) on the treatise, summarized in total.
Thus ends the *Nyāyabindu-vistara-ṭīkā*, titled *Śiṣyahitā* (Beneficial for Disciples), the work of the master Vinītadeva.
Whatever stainless merit has been acquired by me through this commentary on a few words and topics of the *Nyāyabindu*, may it be like a ray of the moon. *Dharmottara-ṭīkā*.
Having attained that ageless state which is preeminent in wisdom and virtue,
I shall therefore be solely occupied with benefiting the world.
The third chapter of the Nyāyabinduṭīkā composed by Ācārya Dharmottara is completed.
And the treatise *Nyāyabindu* is completed.
Of those phenomena that arise from causes, the Tathāgata has declared their cause, as well as their cessation; such is the teaching of the Great Śramaṇa.
